(p-2) Surat al-Isra' (The Night Journey): 111 verses, Meccan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed, that We might show him of Our signs. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿And We gave Moses the Scripture and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel: "Do not take other than Me as a guardian."﴾ ﴿O descendants of those whom We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾ ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Scripture: "You will surely cause corruption on earth twice, and you will surely become arrogant with great arrogance."﴾ [al-Isra': 4] ﴿So when the promise of the first of them came, We sent against you servants of Ours of great might, and they went through the houses, and it was a promise fulfilled.﴾ [al-Isra': 5] ﴿Then We gave you the return of victory over them and supported you with wealth and sons and made you more numerous in manpower.﴾ [al-Isra': 6] ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves; and if you do evil, it is for them. So when the promise of the Hereafter came, to sadden your faces and to enter the masjid as they entered it the first time, and to destroy what they had conquered with complete destruction.﴾ [al-Isra': 7] ﴿Perhaps your Lord will have mercy upon you; but if you return, We will return. And We have made Hell a prison for the disbelievers.﴾ [al-Isra': 8] ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright and gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a great reward.﴾ [al-Isra': 9] ﴿And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter, We have prepared for them a painful punishment.﴾ [al-Isra': 10] ﴿And man supplicates for evil as he supplicates for good, and man is ever hasty.﴾ [al-Isra': 11] ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs, and We erased the sign of the night and made the sign of the day illuminating, that you may seek bounty from your Lord and that you may know the number of years and the reckoning. And all things We have detailed with full detail.﴾ [al-Isra': 12] ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird [of fate] to his neck, and We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record he will find spread open.﴾ [al-Isra': 13] ﴿"Read your record. Your soul is sufficient as a reckoner against you this Day."﴾ [al-Isra': 14] ﴿Whoever is guided is only guided for [the benefit of] himself, and whoever goes astray only goes astray against it. And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And We would never punish until We sent a messenger.﴾ [al-Isra': 15] ﴿And when We intend to destroy a city, We command its affluent ones, and they defiantly transgress therein, and the word is justified against it, and We destroy it with complete destruction.﴾ [al-Isra': 16] ﴿And how many generations We have destroyed after Noah! And sufficient is your Lord as Knower and Seer of the sins of His servants.﴾ [al-Isra': 17] ﴿Whoever desires the immediate [life] – We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We intend. Then We have made for him Hell; he will burn therein, reproached and banished.﴾ [al-Isra': 18] ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it its due striving while he is a believer – those are whose striving will be appreciated.﴾ [al-Isra': 19] ﴿To each – these and those – We extend from the gift of your Lord, and the gift of your Lord has never been restricted.﴾ [al-Isra': 20] ﴿Look how We have favored some of them over others; and the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in favor.﴾ [al-Isra': 21] ﴿Do not set up with Allah another deity, lest you sit reproached and forsaken.﴾ [al-Isra': 22]

(p-3) Jasa yajusu jawsan wa jawasanan: he roamed about in a raid; this is what al-Layth said. Abu 'Ubayda said: jasu means they searched to see whether anyone remained who had not been killed. Al-Farra' said: it means they killed. Hassan said:

Among us is the one who met the sword of Muhammad, so the enemies roamed among him, the breadth of the armies.

Qutrub said: it means they dismounted (or stopped). The poet said:

So we roamed their homes by force, and the sons of their masters were bound.

It was also said: it means they trampled, and from it:

To you we traversed the night with the mounts.

Abu Zayd said: al-jawsu, al-hawsu, al-'awsu and al-hawsu are going around at night. Al-jawsu and al-hawsu mean seeking a thing with thorough investigation. Hazartu al-shay': I prevented the thing, I forbade it.

﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed, that We might show him of Our signs. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿And We gave Moses the Scripture and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel: "Do not take other than Me as a guardian."﴾ ﴿O descendants of those whom We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾

The occasion of revelation of ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) told the Quraysh about the Night Journey, and they denied it, so Allah revealed this to confirm him. This surah is Meccan. The author of al-Ghunyan said it is Meccan by consensus. It was also said: except for two verses, ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you﴾ [al-Isra': 73] and ﴿And indeed, they almost drove you out﴾ [al-Isra': 76]. It was also said: except for four, these two, and His saying: ﴿And [mention] when We told you that your Lord has encompassed the people﴾ [al-Isra': 60], and His saying ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sincere entrance﴾ [al-Isra': 80].

(p-4) Muqatil added His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it﴾ [al-Isra': 107], to the end of the verse. Qatada said: except for eight verses, which were revealed in Medina, and they are from His saying ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you﴾ [al-Isra': 73] to the end of them.

The connection of the beginning of this surah with the end of what precedes it: when Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to patience and forbade him to grieve over them, and that his chest should be constricted by their plotting; and among their plotting was attributing to him lying, sorcery, poetry and other things with which they accused him, Allah, exalted is He, followed that by mentioning his nobility, his virtue, His special regard for him, and the loftiness of his station with Him. The discussion of "Glory be to Him" has already been covered in al-Baqarah. Al-Zamakhshari claimed that it is a proper name for glorification, like 'Uthman is a name for a man. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is not declined because it has two extra letters at its end, and it is definite by being a proper name, and its being in construct does not make it more definite. End of quote. They mean, Allah knows best, that when it is not in construct, as in his saying:

Glory be to the one of 'Alqama al-Fakhir.

As for when it is in construct, if we suppose it is a proper name, its indefiniteness would be intended, then it is put in construct, and at that point its definiteness comes from the construct, not from being a proper name.

"Asra" means "sara" (to travel by night), and the hamza in it is not for causation. It takes the preposition bi (with), and taking bi does not necessarily require sharing in the action; rather the meaning is: He caused him to travel by night, because travel (sura) indicates movement, like walking and running, and that is impossible for Allah, exalted is He. So it is like His saying: ﴿would have taken away their hearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20], meaning, would have taken away their hearing. Thus "asra" and "sara" by this reasoning are like "saqa" and "asqa," since they have the same meaning; for this reason the commentators said: its meaning is he traveled with His servant. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it appears that "asra" is transitive by the hamza to an omitted object, its estimate being "asra al-mala'ika bi-'abdihi" (He caused the angels to travel with His servant), because it would be objectionable to attribute "asra," which has the meaning of "sara," to Allah, exalted is He, since it is a verb that conveys movement, like walking, running, bringing forth and moving; so it is not good to attribute any of these to Him. We find an alternative, and when the Shari'a states something of this kind, such as His saying in the hadith: "I came to him walking, and I came to him running," it is interpreted in a way that frees it from attributing events [to Allah] (p-5). "Asra" in this verse comes out eloquent as we have mentioned, and there is no need for a forced figurative usage with such a word, since it is more binding for movement than "ataytuhu" (I came to him) and "ata Allahu bunyanahum" (Allah came upon their building). End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya only needed this claim because he believed that if "asra" means "sara," it would follow from the bi being transitive that the agent shares in the action with the object. This is a view held by al-Mubarrad. So when you say: "qumtu bi-Zaydin" (I stood with Zayd), it would entail that you stood and Zayd stood with him. But that is not the case; the bi of transitivity was confused with the bi of circumstance. The bi of circumstance requires sharing, since the meaning is "I stood while being in the company of Zayd." The bi of transitivity is synonymous with the hamza, so "qumtu bi-Zaydin," with bi being for transitivity, is like your saying "aqamtu Zaydan" (I made Zayd stand), and making him stand does not require that you stand.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible that "asra" means "sara" by omitting a modifier, like His saying exalted: ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], meaning that the estimate would be "asrat mala'ikatuhu bi-'abdihi" (His angels traveled with His servant), so the modifier is omitted and the modified is put in its place. This is based on the belief that sharing is required and bi is transitive. Also, the sources in the Qur'an of "fa-asri" with an initial hamza that is cut or connected indicate that both have the same meaning. Do you not see that His saying: ﴿So travel with your family﴾ [Hud: 81] and ﴿that travel with My servants﴾ [Ta-Ha: 77] are read both with cutting and connecting the hamza? With the cut hamza, it is unlikely to estimate an omitted object, since it is not stated explicitly anywhere, so one would derive the omitted from the stated. The apparent meaning is that this Night Journey was with his person, and for this reason Quraysh denied it and mocked him. When he related it to Umm Hani, she said: "Do not tell the people of it, for they will deny you." If it had been a dream, it would not have been deemed objectionable. This is the view of the majority of scholars, and it is what should be held. The hadith of the Night Journey is narrated in the collections of the Companions in every region of Islam, and it is said that twenty of the Companions narrated it. It was said: what was narrated from 'Aisha and Mu'awiya that it was a dream, perhaps it is not authentic from them; and even if it were authentic, there would be no proof in it, because they did not witness it, since 'Aisha was young and Mu'awiya was then a disbeliever; and because they did not attribute that to the Messenger (ﷺ) nor narrate it from him. According to al-Hasan, it was a dream that he saw. His saying ﴿His servant﴾ refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). Abu al-Qasim Sulayman al-Ansari said: when Muhammad (ﷺ) reached the high ranks and lofty stations in the ascensions, Allah revealed to him: "O Muhammad, shall I honor you?" He said: "O my Lord, by my attribution to You in servanthood." So He revealed concerning him ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾, the verse. End of quote. Also from him they said: "the servant of Allah and His Messenger," and also: "I am only a servant." This is an idafa (construct) of honor and distinction. The poet said:

Do not call me except "O servant of Her" (?), for it is the most noble of my names.

The scholars said: if the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a name more noble than this, he would have named himself by it at that time.

"Laylan" (by night) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf). It is known that in the language, travel by night (sura) can only be by night, but it was mentioned for emphasis. It was said: it means in the middle of the night, so it was not an early departure (idlal) nor a late departure (idilal). Al-Zamakhshari said: by his saying "laylan" in indefinite form he intended to minimize the duration of the Night Journey, and that he was taken by night for part of the night from Makkah to Syria, a distance of forty nights. That is because indefiniteness here indicates the meaning of partiality, and this is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah and Hudhayfa "min al-layl," meaning part of the night, like His saying: ﴿And from the night, perform tahajjud with it﴾ [al-Isra': 79], as a command to stand in prayer during part of the night. End of quote. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿from al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ is the Masjid itself which surrounds the Ka'bah, and this is the view of Anas. It was also said: it is from al-Hijr; it was said: from between Zamzam and the Maqam; it was said: from the valley of Abu Talib; it was said: from the house of Umm Hani; it was said: from the roof of his house, peace be upon him. According to these three views, the Masjid al-Haram is used to refer to Makkah. Qatada and Muqatil said: one year before the Hijrah. 'Aisha said: a year and a half, in Rajab. It was also said: on the seventeenth of Rabi' al-Awwal, when the Messenger, peace be upon him, was fifty-one years, nine months and twenty-eight days old. According to Ibn Shihab, it was seven years after the beginning of the prophethood. According to al-Harbi, it was the night of the twenty-seventh of Rabi' al-Akhir, one year before the Hijrah (p-6). What is certain is that it was after the splitting of the document (in the boycott) and before the Pledge of 'Aqabah. Shurayk ibn Abi Namir reported in the Sahih that it was before he received revelation, and there is no disagreement among the scholars of hadith that this was an error by Shurayk. Al-Zamakhshari related from Anas and al-Hasan that it was before the mission.

Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Qasim al-Ru'aini said in his History: He was taken by night (asra) from Mecca to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) and was ascended (uruja) to the heaven eighteen months before his prophetic mission (mab'ath). It is narrated that he was sleeping in the house of Umm Hani after the night prayer (salat al-'isha'), then he was taken by night and returned in the same night, and he recounted the story to Umm Hani and said: "The prophets were displayed before me, and I led them in prayer." He got up to go out to the mosque, but Umm Hani caught hold of his garment. He said: "What is the matter with you?" She said: "I fear that your people will deny you if you tell them." He said: "Even if they deny me." So he went out, and Abu Jahl sat with him, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ informed him of the hadith of the Isra'. Abu Jahl said: "O assembly of the Banu Ka'b ibn Lu'ayy, come here!" So he told them, and some clapped their hands, and some placed their hand on their head in amazement and denial. Some people who had believed in him apostatized, and men went to Abu Bakr and said: "If he said that, then he has spoken the truth." They said: "Do you believe him concerning that?" He said: "Indeed, I believe him concerning what is even more remote than that." Therefore he was named al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. And some of them traveled to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, and they asked him to describe it, so Bayt al-Maqdis was made manifest to him, and he began to look at it and describe it to them. They said: "As for the description, he has hit the mark." Then they said: "Tell us about our caravan." So he informed them of the number of its camels and their conditions, and he said: "It will arrive on such-and-such a day at sunrise, led by a grey-spotted camel." They set out running that day toward the pass (al-Thaniyya). One of them said: "By Allah, this is the sun, it has risen." Another said: "And by Allah, this is the caravan that has come, led by a grey-spotted camel, just as Muhammad said." Yet they did not believe, and they said: "This is nothing but evident magic." He had been ascended to the heaven on that night, and the ascent was from Bayt al-Maqdis. He also informed the Quraysh of what he saw of the wonders in the heavens, and that he met the prophets, and reached the Bayt al-Ma'mur and the Sidrat al-Muntaha. This is according to the view of those who say that this night is the night of the Mi'raj (ascension), and it is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and a group. Some scholars went to the view that the night of the Mi'raj is other than the night of the Isra'.

(Al-Masjid al-Aqsa) is the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis, and it was named al-Aqsa because at that time it was the furthest of the excellent houses of Allah from the Ka'ba. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that by al-Aqsa is meant the distant, without any comparison between it and others, and the purpose is to show the wonder of the Isra' to such a distance in one night. End of quote. The word (ila, "to") requires that the Isra' ended with him at the limit of that mosque, and it does not indicate, in terms of its linguistic meaning, his entering it.

(Whose surroundings We have blessed) is a descriptive praise (sifat madh) added to remove an incidental restriction. Its blessing is by what it was specifically given of religious good, such as prophethood, the laws, and the messengers who were in that region and its surroundings and its districts, and worldly good, such as the abundance of trees and rivers and the goodness of the land. In a hadith: "Indeed He, may He be exalted, blessed what lies between 'Arish and the Euphrates, and singled out Palestine for sanctification."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (li-nurayahu, "that We might show him") with nun, which is an iltifat (shift) from the third-person pronoun to the first-person pronoun. The reading of al-Hasan is (liyurayahu, "that He might show him") with ya', so the iltifat occurs in (ayatina, "Our signs"). This is a sight of the eye (ru'ya 'ayn). The signs which he was shown are the wonders that he informed the people of: his isra' from Mecca, his ascent to the heaven, and his description of the prophets one by one, as established in the Sahih. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that it means that He showed Muhammad to the people as a sign, i.e., the Prophet ﷺ would be a sign in that God does this deed with a human, and in this case the seeing is seeing of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb).

Al-Zamakhshari said: (Indeed He is the All-Hearing) of the sayings of Muhammad (the All-Seeing) of his deeds, the Knower of their refinement and purity, so He honors him and brings him near according to that. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is a threat from Allah to the disbelievers for their denial of Muhammad ﷺ concerning the matter of the Isra'; this is a subtle and eloquent allusion to that, i.e., He is the All-Hearing of what you say, the All-Seeing of your deeds. End of quote.

When He mentioned the honoring of the Messenger ﷺ with the Isra' and His showing him the signs, He mentioned the honoring of Musa by giving him the Torah. (Wa-atayna, "and We gave") is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the preceding sentence about the glorification of Allah and His freedom from imperfection, and conjoining sentences does not necessarily require sharing in the report or otherwise. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The conjunction of His saying "and We gave" with what is in His saying "took His servant by night" is by way of an implied predicate: as if he said: "We took Our servant by night, and We showed him Our signs, and We gave." Al-'Ukbari said: "And We gave" is conjoined to "took by night." End of quote. This is far-fetched. The Book here is the Torah, and the apparent reference of the pronoun in (wa-ja'alnahu, "and We made it") is to the Book, though it may refer to Musa. It is permissible that (an, "that") is explanatory (tafsiriyya) with no prohibition, or that it is verbal-masdar (masdariyya) indicating cause, i.e., "so that they would not take," with a negation; it is not permissible that (an) is extra (za'ida), and that (la tattakhidhu, "do not take") is an object of an omitted saying, contrary to the one who permits that, since this is not among the places of the extra (an).

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, 'Isa, Abu Raja' and Abu 'Amr from the Seven read (yattakhidhu, "they take") with ya' in the third person, and the rest of the Seven read with ta' of address (tatta-khidhu). The wakil (protector) is fa'il from tawakkul, i.e., one relied upon. Al-Zamakhshari said: a lord to whom you commit your affairs. Ibn Jarir said: a guardian for you other than Me. Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said: It is said of the Lord: wakil, for His sufficiency and His administration of the affairs of His servants, not in the sense of raising the station of the one who entrusts and lowering the matter of the protector. End of quote. (Dhurriyyata, "offspring") is in the accusative either by address, i.e., "O offspring," or as a substitute for (wakilan), or as the second object of (yattakhidhu), in the sense of the plural, i.e., they should not take protectors, the offspring, or by an implied "I mean." A group read (dhurriyyatu) in the nominative, and it was explained as a substitute for the pronoun in (yattakhidhu) on the reading of the one who reads with the ya' of the third person. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is not permissible in the reading with ta' because you do not substitute from a pronoun of the addressee: if you said, "I struck you, Zayd," as a substitute, it would not be permissible. End of quote. What he mentioned as an absolute statement that one does not substitute from a pronoun of the addressee requires detail: if it is partitive substitution (badal ba'd min kull) or substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal), it is permissible without disagreement; if it is substitution of a thing from a thing, and they are of one referent, and it gives emphasis, it is permissible without disagreement, as in: "I passed by you, your young and your old." If it does not give emphasis, the view of the majority of the Basrans is prohibition, while the view of al-Akhfash and the Kufans is permissibility, and this is the correct view, because this occurs in the speech of the Arabs. We have argued for the correctness of this in the commentary on the Kitab al-Tashil. He mentioned those whom We carried with Nuh as a reminder of the blessing by which He saved them from drowning. Zayd ibn Thabit, Aban ibn 'Uthman, Zayd ibn 'Ali, and Mujahid in one narration read dhirriyyata with kasra on the dhal. Mujahid also read with fatha. From Zayd ibn Thabit: dharriyyata with fatha on the dhal, lightened ra', and shaddah on the ya', on the pattern fa'iliyya like matiyya.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in (innahu, "indeed he") is to Nuh. Salman al-Farisi said: He used to praise Allah for his food. Ibrahim said: His thanks was that when he ate he would say: "In the name of Allah," and when he finished he would say: "Praise be to Allah." Qatada said: When he put on a garment he would say: "In the name of Allah," and when he took it off he would say: "Praise be to Allah." It was said: the pronoun in (innahu) refers to Musa. End of quote. He drew attention to gratitude, because it entails monotheism, since the blessings for which gratitude is due are from Him, may He be exalted. So it is as if it were said: Be monotheists, grateful for the blessings of Allah, following the example of Nuh, of whose offspring you are the descendants of those who were carried with him.

To you we traversed the night with the mounts.

Abu Zayd said: al-jawsu, al-hawsu, al-'awsu and al-hawsu are going around at night. Al-jawsu and al-hawsu mean seeking a thing with thorough investigation. Hazartu al-shay': I prevented the thing, I forbade it.

﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed, that We might show him of Our signs. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿And We gave Moses the Scripture and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel: "Do not take other than Me as a guardian."﴾ ﴿O descendants of those whom We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾

The occasion of revelation of ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) told the Quraysh about the Night Journey, and they denied it, so Allah revealed this to confirm him. This surah is Meccan. The author of al-Ghunyan said it is Meccan by consensus. It was also said: except for two verses, ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you﴾ [al-Isra': 73] and ﴿And indeed, they almost drove you out﴾ [al-Isra': 76]. It was also said: except for four, these two, and His saying: ﴿And [mention] when We told you that your Lord has encompassed the people﴾ [al-Isra': 60], and His saying ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sincere entrance﴾ [al-Isra': 80].

(p-4) Muqatil added His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it﴾ [al-Isra': 107], to the end of the verse. Qatada said: except for eight verses, which were revealed in Medina, and they are from His saying ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you﴾ [al-Isra': 73] to the end of them.

The connection of the beginning of this surah with the end of what precedes it: when Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to patience and forbade him to grieve over them, and that his chest should be constricted by their plotting; and among their plotting was attributing to him lying, sorcery, poetry and other things with which they accused him, Allah, exalted is He, followed that by mentioning his nobility, his virtue, His special regard for him, and the loftiness of his station with Him. The discussion of "Glory be to Him" has already been covered in al-Baqarah. Al-Zamakhshari claimed that it is a proper name for glorification, like 'Uthman is a name for a man. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is not declined because it has two extra letters at its end, and it is definite by being a proper name, and its being in construct does not make it more definite. End of quote. They mean, Allah knows best, that when it is not in construct, as in his saying:

Glory be to the one of 'Alqama al-Fakhir.

As for when it is in construct, if we suppose it is a proper name, its indefiniteness would be intended, then it is put in construct, and at that point its definiteness comes from the construct, not from being a proper name.

"Asra" means "sara" (to travel by night), and the hamza in it is not for causation. It takes the preposition bi (with), and taking bi does not necessarily require sharing in the action; rather the meaning is: He caused him to travel by night, because travel (sura) indicates movement, like walking and running, and that is impossible for Allah, exalted is He. So it is like His saying: ﴿would have taken away their hearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20], meaning, would have taken away their hearing. Thus "asra" and "sara" by this reasoning are like "saqa" and "asqa," since they have the same meaning; for this reason the commentators said: its meaning is he traveled with His servant. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it appears that "asra" is transitive by the hamza to an omitted object, its estimate being "asra al-mala'ika bi-'abdihi" (He caused the angels to travel with His servant), because it would be objectionable to attribute "asra," which has the meaning of "sara," to Allah, exalted is He, since it is a verb that conveys movement, like walking, running, bringing forth and moving; so it is not good to attribute any of these to Him. We find an alternative, and when the Shari'a states something of this kind, such as His saying in the hadith: "I came to him walking, and I came to him running," it is interpreted in a way that frees it from attributing events [to Allah] (p-5). "Asra" in this verse comes out eloquent as we have mentioned, and there is no need for a forced figurative usage with such a word, since it is more binding for movement than "ataytuhu" (I came to him) and "ata Allahu bunyanahum" (Allah came upon their building). End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya only needed this claim because he believed that if "asra" means "sara," it would follow from the bi being transitive that the agent shares in the action with the object. This is a view held by al-Mubarrad. So when you say: "qumtu bi-Zaydin" (I stood with Zayd), it would entail that you stood and Zayd stood with him. But that is not the case; the bi of transitivity was confused with the bi of circumstance. The bi of circumstance requires sharing, since the meaning is "I stood while being in the company of Zayd." The bi of transitivity is synonymous with the hamza, so "qumtu bi-Zaydin," with bi being for transitivity, is like your saying "aqamtu Zaydan" (I made Zayd stand), and making him stand does not require that you stand.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible that "asra" means "sara" by omitting a modifier, like His saying exalted: ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], meaning that the estimate would be "asrat mala'ikatuhu bi-'abdihi" (His angels traveled with His servant), so the modifier is omitted and the modified is put in its place. This is based on the belief that sharing is required and bi is transitive. Also, the sources in the Qur'an of "fa-asri" with an initial hamza that is cut or connected indicate that both have the same meaning. Do you not see that His saying: ﴿So travel with your family﴾ [Hud: 81] and ﴿that travel with My servants﴾ [Ta-Ha: 77] are read both with cutting and connecting the hamza? With the cut hamza, it is unlikely to estimate an omitted object, since it is not stated explicitly anywhere, so one would derive the omitted from the stated. The apparent meaning is that this Night Journey was with his person, and for this reason Quraysh denied it and mocked him. When he related it to Umm Hani, she said: "Do not tell the people of it, for they will deny you." If it had been a dream, it would not have been deemed objectionable. This is the view of the majority of scholars, and it is what should be held. The hadith of the Night Journey is narrated in the collections of the Companions in every region of Islam, and it is said that twenty of the Companions narrated it. It was said: what was narrated from 'Aisha and Mu'awiya that it was a dream, perhaps it is not authentic from them; and even if it were authentic, there would be no proof in it, because they did not witness it, since 'Aisha was young and Mu'awiya was then a disbeliever; and because they did not attribute that to the Messenger (ﷺ) nor narrate it from him. According to al-Hasan, it was a dream that he saw. His saying ﴿His servant﴾ refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). Abu al-Qasim Sulayman al-Ansari said: when Muhammad (ﷺ) reached the high ranks and lofty stations in the ascensions, Allah revealed to him: "O Muhammad, shall I honor you?" He said: "O my Lord, by my attribution to You in servanthood." So He revealed concerning him ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾, the verse. End of quote. Also from him they said: "the servant of Allah and His Messenger," and also: "I am only a servant." This is an idafa (construct) of honor and distinction. The poet said:

Do not call me except "O servant of Her" (?), for it is the most noble of my names.

The scholars said: if the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a name more noble than this, he would have named himself by it at that time.

"Laylan" (by night) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf). It is known that in the language, travel by night (sura) can only be by night, but it was mentioned for emphasis. It was said: it means in the middle of the night, so it was not an early departure (idlal) nor a late departure (idilal). Al-Zamakhshari said: by his saying "laylan" in indefinite form he intended to minimize the duration of the Night Journey, and that he was taken by night for part of the night from Makkah to Syria, a distance of forty nights. That is because indefiniteness here indicates the meaning of partiality, and this is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah and Hudhayfa "min al-layl," meaning part of the night, like His saying: ﴿And from the night, perform tahajjud with it﴾ [al-Isra': 79], as a command to stand in prayer during part of the night. End of quote. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿from al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ is the Masjid itself which surrounds the Ka'bah, and this is the view of Anas. It was also said: it is from al-Hijr; it was said: from between Zamzam and the Maqam; it was said: from the valley of Abu Talib; it was said: from the house of Umm Hani; it was said: from the roof of his house, peace be upon him. According to these three views, the Masjid al-Haram is used to refer to Makkah. Qatada and Muqatil said: one year before the Hijrah. 'Aisha said: a year and a half, in Rajab. It was also said: on the seventeenth of Rabi' al-Awwal, when the Messenger, peace be upon him, was fifty-one years, nine months and twenty-eight days old. According to Ibn Shihab, it was seven years after the beginning of the prophethood. According to al-Harbi, it was the night of the twenty-seventh of Rabi' al-Akhir, one year before the Hijrah (p-6). What is certain is that it was after the splitting of the document (in the boycott) and before the Pledge of 'Aqabah. Shurayk ibn Abi Namir reported in the Sahih that it was before he received revelation, and there is no disagreement among the scholars of hadith that this was an error by Shurayk. Al-Zamakhshari related from Anas and al-Hasan that it was before the mission.

Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Qasim al-Ru'aini said in his History: He was taken by night (asra) from Mecca to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) and was ascended (uruja) to the heaven eighteen months before his prophetic mission (mab'ath). It is narrated that he was sleeping in the house of Umm Hani after the night prayer (salat al-'isha'), then he was taken by night and returned in the same night, and he recounted the story to Umm Hani and said: "The prophets were displayed before me, and I led them in prayer." He got up to go out to the mosque, but Umm Hani caught hold of his garment. He said: "What is the matter with you?" She said: "I fear that your people will deny you if you tell them." He said: "Even if they deny me." So he went out, and Abu Jahl sat with him, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ informed him of the hadith of the Isra'. Abu Jahl said: "O assembly of the Banu Ka'b ibn Lu'ayy, come here!" So he told them, and some clapped their hands, and some placed their hand on their head in amazement and denial. Some people who had believed in him apostatized, and men went to Abu Bakr and said: "If he said that, then he has spoken the truth." They said: "Do you believe him concerning that?" He said: "Indeed, I believe him concerning what is even more remote than that." Therefore he was named al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. And some of them traveled to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, and they asked him to describe it, so Bayt al-Maqdis was made manifest to him, and he began to look at it and describe it to them. They said: "As for the description, he has hit the mark." Then they said: "Tell us about our caravan." So he informed them of the number of its camels and their conditions, and he said: "It will arrive on such-and-such a day at sunrise, led by a grey-spotted camel." They set out running that day toward the pass (al-Thaniyya). One of them said: "By Allah, this is the sun, it has risen." Another said: "And by Allah, this is the caravan that has come, led by a grey-spotted camel, just as Muhammad said." Yet they did not believe, and they said: "This is nothing but evident magic." He had been ascended to the heaven on that night, and the ascent was from Bayt al-Maqdis. He also informed the Quraysh of what he saw of the wonders in the heavens, and that he met the prophets, and reached the Bayt al-Ma'mur and the Sidrat al-Muntaha. This is according to the view of those who say that this night is the night of the Mi'raj (ascension), and it is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and a group. Some scholars went to the view that the night of the Mi'raj is other than the night of the Isra'.

(Al-Masjid al-Aqsa) is the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis, and it was named al-Aqsa because at that time it was the furthest of the excellent houses of Allah from the Ka'ba. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that by al-Aqsa is meant the distant, without any comparison between it and others, and the purpose is to show the wonder of the Isra' to such a distance in one night. End of quote. The word (ila, "to") requires that the Isra' ended with him at the limit of that mosque, and it does not indicate, in terms of its linguistic meaning, his entering it.

(Whose surroundings We have blessed) is a descriptive praise (sifat madh) added to remove an incidental restriction. Its blessing is by what it was specifically given of religious good, such as prophethood, the laws, and the messengers who were in that region and its surroundings and its districts, and worldly good, such as the abundance of trees and rivers and the goodness of the land. In a hadith: "Indeed He, may He be exalted, blessed what lies between 'Arish and the Euphrates, and singled out Palestine for sanctification."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (li-nurayahu, "that We might show him") with nun, which is an iltifat (shift) from the third-person pronoun to the first-person pronoun. The reading of al-Hasan is (liyurayahu, "that He might show him") with ya', so the iltifat occurs in (ayatina, "Our signs"). This is a sight of the eye (ru'ya 'ayn). The signs which he was shown are the wonders that he informed the people of: his isra' from Mecca, his ascent to the heaven, and his description of the prophets one by one, as established in the Sahih. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that it means that He showed Muhammad to the people as a sign, i.e., the Prophet ﷺ would be a sign in that God does this deed with a human, and in this case the seeing is seeing of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb).

Al-Zamakhshari said: (Indeed He is the All-Hearing) of the sayings of Muhammad (the All-Seeing) of his deeds, the Knower of their refinement and purity, so He honors him and brings him near according to that. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is a threat from Allah to the disbelievers for their denial of Muhammad ﷺ concerning the matter of the Isra'; this is a subtle and eloquent allusion to that, i.e., He is the All-Hearing of what you say, the All-Seeing of your deeds. End of quote.

When He mentioned the honoring of the Messenger ﷺ with the Isra' and His showing him the signs, He mentioned the honoring of Musa by giving him the Torah. (Wa-atayna, "and We gave") is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the preceding sentence about the glorification of Allah and His freedom from imperfection, and conjoining sentences does not necessarily require sharing in the report or otherwise. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The conjunction of His saying "and We gave" with what is in His saying "took His servant by night" is by way of an implied predicate: as if he said: "We took Our servant by night, and We showed him Our signs, and We gave." Al-'Ukbari said: "And We gave" is conjoined to "took by night." End of quote. This is far-fetched. The Book here is the Torah, and the apparent reference of the pronoun in (wa-ja'alnahu, "and We made it") is to the Book, though it may refer to Musa. It is permissible that (an, "that") is explanatory (tafsiriyya) with no prohibition, or that it is verbal-masdar (masdariyya) indicating cause, i.e., "so that they would not take," with a negation; it is not permissible that (an) is extra (za'ida), and that (la tattakhidhu, "do not take") is an object of an omitted saying, contrary to the one who permits that, since this is not among the places of the extra (an).

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, 'Isa, Abu Raja' and Abu 'Amr from the Seven read (yattakhidhu, "they take") with ya' in the third person, and the rest of the Seven read with ta' of address (tatta-khidhu). The wakil (protector) is fa'il from tawakkul, i.e., one relied upon. Al-Zamakhshari said: a lord to whom you commit your affairs. Ibn Jarir said: a guardian for you other than Me. Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said: It is said of the Lord: wakil, for His sufficiency and His administration of the affairs of His servants, not in the sense of raising the station of the one who entrusts and lowering the matter of the protector. End of quote. (Dhurriyyata, "offspring") is in the accusative either by address, i.e., "O offspring," or as a substitute for (wakilan), or as the second object of (yattakhidhu), in the sense of the plural, i.e., they should not take protectors, the offspring, or by an implied "I mean." A group read (dhurriyyatu) in the nominative, and it was explained as a substitute for the pronoun in (yattakhidhu) on the reading of the one who reads with the ya' of the third person. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is not permissible in the reading with ta' because you do not substitute from a pronoun of the addressee: if you said, "I struck you, Zayd," as a substitute, it would not be permissible. End of quote. What he mentioned as an absolute statement that one does not substitute from a pronoun of the addressee requires detail: if it is partitive substitution (badal ba'd min kull) or substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal), it is permissible without disagreement; if it is substitution of a thing from a thing, and they are of one referent, and it gives emphasis, it is permissible without disagreement, as in: "I passed by you, your young and your old." If it does not give emphasis, the view of the majority of the Basrans is prohibition, while the view of al-Akhfash and the Kufans is permissibility, and this is the correct view, because this occurs in the speech of the Arabs. We have argued for the correctness of this in the commentary on the Kitab al-Tashil. He mentioned those whom We carried with Nuh as a reminder of the blessing by which He saved them from drowning. Zayd ibn Thabit, Aban ibn 'Uthman, Zayd ibn 'Ali, and Mujahid in one narration read dhirriyyata with kasra on the dhal. Mujahid also read with fatha. From Zayd ibn Thabit: dharriyyata with fatha on the dhal, lightened ra', and shaddah on the ya', on the pattern fa'iliyya like matiyya.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in (innahu, "indeed he") is to Nuh. Salman al-Farisi said: He used to praise Allah for his food. Ibrahim said: His thanks was that when he ate he would say: "In the name of Allah," and when he finished he would say: "Praise be to Allah." Qatada said: When he put on a garment he would say: "In the name of Allah," and when he took it off he would say: "Praise be to Allah." It was said: the pronoun in (innahu) refers to Musa. End of quote. He drew attention to gratitude, because it entails monotheism, since the blessings for which gratitude is due are from Him, may He be exalted. So it is as if it were said: Be monotheists, grateful for the blessings of Allah, following the example of Nuh, of whose offspring you are the descendants of those who were carried with him.

(p-2) Surat al-Isra' (The Night Journey): 111 verses, Meccan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed, that We might show him of Our signs. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿And We gave Moses the Scripture and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel: "Do not take other than Me as a guardian."﴾ ﴿O descendants of those whom We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾ ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Scripture: "You will surely cause corruption on earth twice, and you will surely become arrogant with great arrogance."﴾ [al-Isra': 4] ﴿So when the promise of the first of them came, We sent against you servants of Ours of great might, and they went through the houses, and it was a promise fulfilled.﴾ [al-Isra': 5] ﴿Then We gave you the return of victory over them and supported you with wealth and sons and made you more numerous in manpower.﴾ [al-Isra': 6] ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves; and if you do evil, it is for them. So when the promise of the Hereafter came, to sadden your faces and to enter the masjid as they entered it the first time, and to destroy what they had conquered with complete destruction.﴾ [al-Isra': 7] ﴿Perhaps your Lord will have mercy upon you; but if you return, We will return. And We have made Hell a prison for the disbelievers.﴾ [al-Isra': 8] ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright and gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a great reward.﴾ [al-Isra': 9] ﴿And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter, We have prepared for them a painful punishment.﴾ [al-Isra': 10] ﴿And man supplicates for evil as he supplicates for good, and man is ever hasty.﴾ [al-Isra': 11] ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs, and We erased the sign of the night and made the sign of the day illuminating, that you may seek bounty from your Lord and that you may know the number of years and the reckoning. And all things We have detailed with full detail.﴾ [al-Isra': 12] ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird [of fate] to his neck, and We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record he will find spread open.﴾ [al-Isra': 13] ﴿"Read your record. Your soul is sufficient as a reckoner against you this Day."﴾ [al-Isra': 14] ﴿Whoever is guided is only guided for [the benefit of] himself, and whoever goes astray only goes astray against it. And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And We would never punish until We sent a messenger.﴾ [al-Isra': 15] ﴿And when We intend to destroy a city, We command its affluent ones, and they defiantly transgress therein, and the word is justified against it, and We destroy it with complete destruction.﴾ [al-Isra': 16] ﴿And how many generations We have destroyed after Noah! And sufficient is your Lord as Knower and Seer of the sins of His servants.﴾ [al-Isra': 17] ﴿Whoever desires the immediate [life] – We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We intend. Then We have made for him Hell; he will burn therein, reproached and banished.﴾ [al-Isra': 18] ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it its due striving while he is a believer – those are whose striving will be appreciated.﴾ [al-Isra': 19] ﴿To each – these and those – We extend from the gift of your Lord, and the gift of your Lord has never been restricted.﴾ [al-Isra': 20] ﴿Look how We have favored some of them over others; and the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in favor.﴾ [al-Isra': 21] ﴿Do not set up with Allah another deity, lest you sit reproached and forsaken.﴾ [al-Isra': 22]

(p-3) Jasa yajusu jawsan wa jawasanan: he roamed about in a raid; this is what al-Layth said. Abu 'Ubayda said: jasu means they searched to see whether anyone remained who had not been killed. Al-Farra' said: it means they killed. Hassan said:

Among us is the one who met the sword of Muhammad, so the enemies roamed among him, the breadth of the armies.

Qutrub said: it means they dismounted (or stopped). The poet said:

So we roamed their homes by force, and the sons of their masters were bound.

It was also said: it means they trampled, and from it:

To you we traversed the night with the mounts.

Abu Zayd said: al-jawsu, al-hawsu, al-'awsu and al-hawsu are going around at night. Al-jawsu and al-hawsu mean seeking a thing with thorough investigation. Hazartu al-shay': I prevented the thing, I forbade it.

﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed, that We might show him of Our signs. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿And We gave Moses the Scripture and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel: "Do not take other than Me as a guardian."﴾ ﴿O descendants of those whom We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾

The occasion of revelation of ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) told the Quraysh about the Night Journey, and they denied it, so Allah revealed this to confirm him. This surah is Meccan. The author of al-Ghunyan said it is Meccan by consensus. It was also said: except for two verses, ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you﴾ [al-Isra': 73] and ﴿And indeed, they almost drove you out﴾ [al-Isra': 76]. It was also said: except for four, these two, and His saying: ﴿And [mention] when We told you that your Lord has encompassed the people﴾ [al-Isra': 60], and His saying ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sincere entrance﴾ [al-Isra': 80].

(p-4) Muqatil added His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it﴾ [al-Isra': 107], to the end of the verse. Qatada said: except for eight verses, which were revealed in Medina, and they are from His saying ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you﴾ [al-Isra': 73] to the end of them.

The discussion of "Glory be to Him" has already been covered in al-Baqarah. Al-Zamakhshari claimed that it is a proper name for glorification, like 'Uthman is a name for a man. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is not declined because it has two extra letters at its end, and it is definite by being a proper name, and its being in construct does not make it more definite. End of quote. They mean, Allah knows best, that when it is not in construct, as in his saying:

Glory be to the one of 'Alqama al-Fakhir.

As for when it is in construct, if we suppose it is a proper name, its indefiniteness would be intended, then it is put in construct, and at that point its definiteness comes from the construct, not from being a proper name.
