It was also said: *nafir* is a verbal noun, meaning "more in going forth to raids," as in the words of the poet:

*So honour Qahtan for its father, and Himyar: honour a people of nafir (going forth).*

It is also narrated as "honour the Himyarites, honour nafiran." The one compared to is elided. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "more than what you were," and others estimated it as "more than the enemies."

﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves﴾: that is, if you obey God, the reward of obedience is for yourselves; ﴿and if you do evil﴾ by disobeying Him, the punishment of evil is for yourselves. Good and evil do not extend to others. The answer to *wa-in asa'tum* is His words *fa-laha* ("then to it"), with an elided, understood subject, and *laha* is its predicate, the sense being: "so the evil is for it." Al-Karmani said: "fa-laha" came with a *lam* for symmetry. End of quotation, meaning that he matched His words "for yourselves" with His words "fa-laha." Al-Tabari said: the *lam* means *ila* ("to"), that is, "to it returns the evil." It was also said: the *lam* means *ala* ("upon"), that is, "upon it," as in the words of the poet:

*So he fell prostrate on his hands and on his mouth.*

﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter came﴾: that is, the last occurrence of your corruption and your haughtiness. The answer to *idha* is elided, indicated by the answer to the first *idha*, the sense being: "We sent them against you," and their corruption in that was by killing Yahya ibn Zakariya, peace be upon them both. The reason for his killing, as related from Ibn Abbas and others, is that a king wanted to marry a woman whom it was not lawful for him to marry. Yahya ibn Zakariya forbade him. That woman had a need every day from the king which he would fulfil, so her mother urged her to ask him for the slaughter of Yahya ibn Zakariya, because he had prevented his marriage to her daughter. She asked him for that, and he refused her; she pressed him, so he called for a basin and slaughtered him. A drop fell to the ground, and it kept boiling until God sent Bukhtansar against them, and it was cast into his heart that he should kill on account of that blood among them until it became calm, so he killed seventy thousand of them over it. Al-Suhayli said: it is not sound that the one sent in the last occurrence was Bukhtansar, because the killing of Yahya was after the raising of Isa, and Bukhtansar was a long time before Isa. It was also said: the one sent against them was Alexander, and between Alexander and Isa there were about three hundred years. But if by the second occurrence is meant the time when they killed Ashya', then Bukhtansar was then alive, and he is the one who killed them, ruined Bayt al-Maqdis, pursued them to Egypt, and expelled them from it. It is related from Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that the one who invaded them last was a king named Khardus, and that a commander of his undertook their killing on account of the blood of Yahya ibn Zakariya, and the blood became calm. It was also said: a king of the kings of the Children of Israel killed him, called Lahib. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: Yahya had been given beauty and handsomeness, and the wife of the king sought to seduce him, but he refused. She said to her daughter: "Ask your father for the head of Yahya," and he gave her what she asked.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read *liyasū'ū* (لِيَسُوءُوا) with the *lām kay* (the lām of purpose), a *yā'* of the third person, and a plural pronoun referring to "those sent forth" (al-mab'uthīn). Ibn 'Āmir, Ḥamzah and Abū Bakr read *liyasū'a* (لِيَسُوءَ) with a *yā'* and an open *hamzah*, in the singular. The hidden subject then refers either to God the Exalted, or to the promise, or to the raising up (al-ba'th), which is indicated by the omitted apodosis (jumlat al-jazā' al-maḥdhūfah).

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Zayd ibn ʿAlī and al-Kisā'ī read *linasū'a* (لِنَسُوءَ) with the *nūn* of majesty (al-nūn allatī lil-ʿaẓamah), and in it there is a pronoun referring to God. Ubayy read *linasū'unna* (لِنَسُوءُنَّ) with the *lām al-amr* (the imperative lām), the *nūn* of majesty, and a light *nūn al-tawkīd* (emphatic nūn) at the end. It is also reported from ʿAlī that he read *lanasū'unna wa-liyasū'unna* (لَنَسُوءُنَّ وَلَيَسُوءُنَّ) with the *nūn* and the *yā'* and a heavy *nūn al-tawkīd*, and this is the *lām al-qasam* (the lām of oath). The *lām al-amr* entered upon the first person in Ubayy's reading, as in His saying: ﴿And let us bear your sins﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt 29:12]. The response of *idhā* (إذا, "when") is the imperative clause, with a *fā'* understood before it.

In the Muṣḥaf of Ubayy it is *liyusī'* (لِيُسِيءَ) with a *yā'* that is *ḍammah*-vowelled and without a *wāw*. In the Muṣḥaf of Anas it is *liyasū'a wujūhakum* (لِيَسُوءَ وُجُوهَكم), in the singular. The apparent meaning is that "faces" is intended literally, because the effects of inner emotional states appear on the face: in joy there appears brightness and radiance, and in sorrow there appear gloom and dust. It is also possible that the face is used to express the whole person, since they harmed them through killing, plunder and captivity, so that the harm reached all the persons, or that it reached their masters and elders by way of "faces." From this is their saying in address: "O face of the Arabs" (yā wajh al-ʿarab).

The *lām* in *wa-liyadkhulū* (وَلِيَدْخُلُوا) is the *lām kay*, coordinated with the *lām kay* that precedes it. Whoever reads with the *lām al-amr* or the *lām al-qasam* may take *wa-liyadkhulū* and what follows it as an imperative, and it may also be a *lām kay*, meaning: "and We sent them forth in order that they might enter." The *masjid* is the Masjid of Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis). The meaning of *kamā dakhalūhu awwala marrah* (كَمَا دَخَلُوهُ أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ) is: by the sword, by force, by conquest and by humiliation. This weakens the view of those who held that in the first of the two occasions there was no killing, no fighting and no plunder. The discussion of "the first time" has already been given in the commentary on Sūrat al-Tawbah.

*Wa-liyutabbirū* (وَلِيُتَبِّرُوا) means: they destroy or ruin. Quṭrub said: they demolish. The poet said:

*So people are nothing but two workers: one who ruins what he builds, and another who raises.*

The apparent reading is that *mā* (ما) is the object of *yutabbirū*, meaning: they destroy what they have overcome of the lands. It is also possible that *mā* is temporal, meaning: for the duration of their domination. *ʿAsā rabbukum an yarḥamakum* (عَسى رَبُّكم أَنْ يَرْحَمَكم), "perhaps your Lord will have mercy on you," after the second occasion, if you repent and refrain from sins. This deferral is not for the return of a state; it is rather from the category of God's mercy toward the obedient among them. Obedience would have meant following ʿĪsā and Muḥammad (ﷺ), but they did not do so.

*Wa-in ʿudtum* (وَإِنْ عُدْتُمْ), "and if you return," to disobedience a third time, We return to punishment. They did return, and God brought down retribution upon them again by setting over them the Kisrās (Persian kings) and imposing tribute upon them. It is reported from al-Ḥasan: "They returned, so God sent Muḥammad (ﷺ), and they now give the jizyah (poll tax) from a position of submission, and they are humbled." It is reported from Qatādah: "The final outcome of that was that God sent against them this tribe of the Arabs, and they are under torment from them until the Day of Resurrection." End of quotation. The meaning of *ʿudnā* (عُدْنا) is: back in this world, to punishment.

God the Exalted said: ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed that He would surely send against them, until the Day of Resurrection, those who would inflict upon them the worst of torment﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:167]. Then He mentioned what He has prepared for them in the Hereafter, which is that He makes Jahannam for them a *ḥaṣīr* (حَصِيرًا). *Ḥaṣīr* means a prison. Labīd said:

*And his station overpowered the men, as though they were jinn standing at the gate of the ḥaṣīr.*

al-Ḥasan said: it means a bed or carpet. He also said: it is derived from *ḥaṣr* (confinement). What appears to be the case is that it confines them and encloses them from all their sides. So *ḥaṣīr* means "possessing confinement," for if it were an intensive form (of the type *faʿīl*), the *tā'* would be attached, because it applies to a feminine noun, as you say *raḥīmah* and *ʿalīmah*. But it is of the sense of the relative adjective (nisbah), like His saying: ﴿the sky will be split by it﴾ [al-Muzzammil 73:18], meaning: possessing splitting.

[p. 8] *Qada'* (قَضى) takes its object directly, as in His words: ﴿So when Moses had fulfilled the term﴾ [Al-Qasas: 29]. Here, since it is used with the sense of *al-iha'* (revelation, inspiration) or *al-infadh* (execution, decree), it takes *ila* (to). The meaning is: "We revealed to, or decreed to, the Children of Israel in the decree that is binding and final." It is related from Ibn Abbas that its meaning is "We informed them." It is also related from him that it means "We decreed against them," and also "We wrote [it down]."

The *lam* in ﴿they will surely cause corruption﴾ (*latufsidunna*) is the answer to an oath. It may be taken as having an elided oath, so that the object of *qada'* is also elided. The sense would be: "We decreed to the Children of Israel their corruption on earth and their haughtiness," and then He swore to the occurrence of this and that it would certainly happen. Thus the object of "qadayna" is elided, and the accusative of the elided oath is retained. It is also possible that "qadayna" is treated as an oath, and "latufsidunna" is its answer, like the saying of people: *qada'u Allahi la-aqumanna* ("the decree of God, I will surely stand").

Abu al-Aliya and Ibn Jubayr read *fi al-kutubi* in the plural. The majority read it in the singular, so it may mean the genus, but the apparent meaning is the Torah.

Ibn Abbas, Nasr ibn Ali and Jabir ibn Zayd read *latufsadunna* (with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a *fatha* on the *sin*), in the passive, meaning "others will cause you to be corrupt." It was said: this is from misguidance; it was also said: this is from domination. Isa read *latafsudunna* (with a *fatha* on the *ta'* and a *damma* on the *sin*), meaning: "you will become corrupt through your own doing, by committing sins, twice."

[p. 9] The first of the two was the killing of Zakariya, peace be upon him. This was said by al-Suddi, on the authority of his teachers, and by Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas. The reason is that when their king, Siddiqa, died, they competed for the kingdom and killed one another, and they would not listen to Zakariya. God said to him: "Stand among your people and convey what I reveal to you by your tongue." When he finished what God had revealed to him, they attacked him to kill him, so he fled. A tree split open for him and he entered into it. Satan came upon him and took a fringe of his garment and showed it to them. They placed the saw in the middle of the tree and sawed it through its middle. It was also said: the reason for the killing of Zakariya was that they accused him concerning Maryam. It was said: when Maryam became pregnant they said: "He has neglected the daughter of our master until she committed fornication," so they sawed him with the saw in the tree. It was also said: [the one killed was] Ashya' (Isaiah), as related by Ibn Ishaq, and that Zakariya died a natural death and was not killed; that the one who entered the tree and was cut in two with the saw in its middle was Ashya', who lived before Zakariya. Armiya (Jeremiah) was imprisoned when he warned them of God's wrath and of the Hereafter, before Yahya ibn Zakariya; and they intended to kill Isa son of Maryam. God informed the Children of Israel in the Torah that there would come from them disobedience and disbelief towards the blessings of God, the Most High, in the messengers, in the books and otherwise, and that He would send against them a nation that would overcome them, kill them and humiliate them, and then He would show mercy to them after that, grant them victory again, and return them to their former state of ascendancy. Then sins, ingratitude for blessings, injustice, killing and disbelief in God would occur among some of them, so God would send against them another nation that would ruin their homes, kill them and expel them with a severe expulsion. Events after that confirmed this entire matter. It was said: between the last of the first and the second there were two hundred and ten years of a sustained, firm kingdom; it was also said: seventy years. Al-Kalbi said: "they will be disobedient in the holy land, and they will be haughty," that is, they will transgress and become arrogant.

Zayd ibn Ali read *'uliyyan kabiran* in both places, with a *kasra* on the *lam* and a shaddah on the *ya'*. The reading of the majority is *'uluwwan*. The sound form of the *fu'ul* pattern in the verbal noun is more common, as in His words: ﴿and they will have become arrogant with great arrogance﴾ [Al-Furqan: 21], unlike the plural, where the *i'lal* (grammatical alteration of weak letters) is the regular form. The unaltered form is an anomaly, as in *nahuwa* and *nuhuwwun*, contrary to al-Farra' who took it as a regular pattern.

﴿So when the promise of the first came﴾: that is, the appointed time of the first. This is because the "promise" had already preceded that, and what was promised is the punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is "the promise of punishment of the first of them." It was also said: "promise" means "threat," and it was said: means "appointment," in the sense of the time. The pronoun in *ula-humā* refers to the two occurrences.

The majority read *'ibadan* ("servants"). Al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Ali read *'abidan* ("slaves"). Ibn Abbas said: "He invaded them." Qatada said: Jalut, from the people of the Jazira. Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Ishaq said: Sanjarib and his armies invaded them, the king of Babylon. It was also said: Bukhtansar. It is related that he had earlier entered with an army of Persians, being obscure, working in the king's kitchen, and he learned, from the oppression of the Children of Israel, what the Persians did not know, since he used to mix with them. When the army withdrew, he mentioned that to the Great King. After some time the king made him commander of an army and sent him, and he ruined Bayt al-Maqdis, killed them and expelled them. Then he returned and found that the king had died, so he took over his position, and his condition continued until he ruled the earth after that. It was also said: they were the Amalekites, who were unbelievers. It was also said: those sent were a believing people whom God sent and commanded to raid the Children of Israel. The word *al-ba'th* here means sending and empowering. Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is "We left them free between them and what they did, and did not prevent them." This is because God attributed the sending of the unbelievers to Himself, as in His words: ﴿Thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others, because of what they earn﴾ [Al-An'am: 129], and like the words of the one who supplicates: "Sow discord among their word." He attributed the trampling, which is wandering through the homes with corruption, to them. Thus the destruction of the mosque and the burning of the Torah are part of the trampling attributed to them. End of quotation. In his words "We left them free between them and what they did" there is a trace of Mu'tazilite subtlety.

Ibn Atiyya said: "We sent" may mean that God sent a messenger to the king of that nation commanding him to raid the Children of Israel, so the sending is by command. It may also mean that the word "sending" is used for what was cast into the king's soul, that is, he raided them. End of quotation.

﴿having men of great might﴾: that is, of fighting and of severe war, because of their strength, their courage, their great number and their equipment. The majority read [p. 10] ﴿fa-jasu﴾ with a *jim*. Abu al-Sammal and Talha read *fa-hasu* with an unpointed *ha'*. It was also read *fa-tajawwasu* on the pattern of *takassaru*, with a *jim*. Al-Hasan read ﴿khilala al-diyar﴾ as a singular, which may be pluralized as *khalal*, like *jabal* and *jibal*. It may also be that *khilal* is singular, like *khalal*, meaning the middle of the homes and what lies between them. The majority hold that in this first sending he ruined Bayt al-Maqdis, and killing, exile and capture occurred among them. It is related from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid that when they were invaded, the invaders roamed through the homes, and there was no killing or fighting among the Children of Israel, and the armies withdrew from them. The pronoun in *wa-kana* refers to the promise of the first. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The promise of punishment was a promise that must be carried out." End of quotation. It was also said: it refers to the armies.

﴿Then We returned to you the turn against them﴾: this is information from God to the Children of Israel in the Torah. He used *radadna* in place of *narudd*, since at the time of informing them the matter had not yet occurred, but because God's promise was in the utmost certainty that it would happen, He expressed its future by the past. *Al-karrah* means dominion and victory over those who had been sent against them, until they repented and returned from corruption. They possessed Bayt al-Maqdis before the turn, before Bukhtansar, and [God] let the Children of Israel keep their captives and their wealth, and the kingdom returned to them. It is mentioned as the cause of this that a king invaded the people of Babylon, and Bukhtansar had killed forty thousand of the Children of Israel who recited the Torah and left the remainder with them in Babylon in humiliation. When that king invaded them and overcame Babylon, he married a woman from the Children of Israel. She asked him to return the Children of Israel to Bayt al-Maqdis, and he did so. After a time, prophets arose among them, and they returned to the best of what they had been. It was also said: *al-karrah* refers to the strengthening of Talut until he fought Jalut, and to David's victory over the killing of Jalut. Qatada said: they were more wicked in the time of David, peace be upon him.

﴿nafiran﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*, the noun clarifying an ambiguity). It was said: *al-nafir* and *al-nafir* are the same, and its origin is from "going forth with a man from his clan and household," as Abu Muslim said. Al-Zajjaj said: it may be the plural of *nafr*, like *kalb* and *kalib*, *abd* and *abid*, and they are those who gather to go against the enemies. It was also said: *nafir* is a verbal noun, meaning "more in going forth to raids," as in the words of the poet:

*So honour Qahtan for its father, and Himyar: honour a people of nafir (going forth).*

It is also narrated as "honour the Himyarites, honour nafiran." The one compared to is elided. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "more than what you were," and others estimated it as "more than the enemies."

﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves﴾: that is, if you obey God, the reward of obedience is for yourselves; ﴿and if you do evil﴾ by disobeying Him, the punishment of evil is for yourselves. Good and evil do not extend to others. Al-Tabari said: the *lam* means *ila* ("to"), that is, "to it returns the evil." It was also said: the *lam* means *ala* ("upon"), that is, "upon it," as in the words of the poet:

*So he fell prostrate on his hands and on his mouth.*

She asked him for that, and he refused her; she pressed him, so he called for a basin and slaughtered him. *Wa-in ʿudtum* (وَإِنْ عُدْتُمْ), "and if you return," to disobedience a third time, We return to punishment. They did return, and God brought down retribution upon them again by setting over them the Kisrās (Persian kings) and imposing tribute upon them. It is reported from al-Ḥasan: "They returned, so God sent Muḥammad (ﷺ), and they now give the jizyah (poll tax) from a position of submission, and they are humbled." It is reported from Qatādah: "The final outcome of that was that God sent against them this tribe of the Arabs, and they are under torment from them until the Day of Resurrection." End of quotation. The meaning of *ʿudnā* (عُدْنا) is: back in this world, to punishment.

God the Exalted said: ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed that He would surely send against them, until the Day of Resurrection, those who would inflict upon them the worst of torment﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:167]. Then He mentioned what He has prepared for them in the Hereafter, which is that He makes Jahannam for them a *ḥaṣīr* (حَصِيرًا). *Ḥaṣīr* means a prison. Labīd said:

*And his station overpowered the men, as though they were jinn standing at the gate of the ḥaṣīr.*

al-Ḥasan said: it means a bed or carpet. He also said: it is derived from *ḥaṣr* (confinement). What appears to be the case is that it confines them and encloses them from all their sides. So *ḥaṣīr* means "possessing confinement," for if it were an intensive form (of the type *faʿīl*), the *tā'* would be attached, because it applies to a feminine noun, as you say *raḥīmah* and *ʿalīmah*. But it is of the sense of the relative adjective (nisbah), like His saying: ﴿the sky will be split by it﴾ [al-Muzzammil 73:18], meaning: possessing splitting.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verse 9–15 (part 1 of 2):

(p-12) ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright, and gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a great reward. And [it gives warning] that those who do not believe in the Hereafter, We have prepared for them a painful punishment. And man prays for evil as he prays for good, and man has always been hasty.﴾ ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs. Then We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day as a means of sight, that you might seek bounty from your Lord and that you might know the number of years and the reckoning. And every matter We have detailed with full detail.﴾ ﴿And every person's omen We have fastened to his neck, and We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record he will find spread open. [It will be said], "Read your record. Sufficient is yourself against you this Day as a reckoner."﴾ ﴿Whoever is guided is only guided for [the benefit of] himself, and whoever goes astray only goes astray to its detriment. And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And We would never punish until We send a messenger.﴾

(p-13) When the Exalted mentioned those whom He singled out for the Night Journey, who is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and those to whom He gave the Torah, who is Musa (peace be upon him), and that it was a guidance for the Children of Israel, and mentioned what He decreed upon them therein of domination over them because of their sins, this was a deterrent for whoever understands against the disobedience of Allah. So He mentioned what Allah honored His Messenger with, the Qur'an, which abrogates the ruling of the Torah and of every divine book, and that it guides to the path or the state that is most upright. Al-Dahhak, al-Kalbi and al-Farra' said: "that which is most upright" refers to the testimony of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness). Muqatil said: it refers to the commands and prohibitions. The word "aqwam" here is the elative (af'al al-tafdil) according to the view of al-Zajjaj, when it is understood as "the most upright of states." Others estimated it as "more upright than what is other than it" or "more upright than every state." What appears in terms of meaning is that "aqwam" here is not intended as a comparative, since there is no sharing between the path to which the Qur'an guides and another path, such that this one is preferred over it. Rather the meaning is: "that which is qayyimah," i.e., upright, as He said: ﴿And that is the upright religion﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5] and ﴿therein are correct books﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 3], meaning: upright in its path, standing with what is needed of the matter of religion. Al-Zamakhshari said: "that which is most upright" refers to the state that is the most upright of states and the most firm, or to the creed, or to the path; wherever you estimate it, you will not find with the affirmation the eloquence that you find with the omission, because of the grandeur in the ambiguity of the described thing which is lost when it is made explicit. End.

﴿And gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds﴾ is a restriction on complete faith, since action is the perfection of faith. He pointed to the complete state so that the believer may adorn himself with it. The believer who falls short in his deeds still has a share in righteous deeds through his faith, and the great reward is Paradise. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how did He mention the righteous believers and the disbelievers, and not mention the sinners? I say: at that time people were either a pious believer or a polytheist, and the people of an intermediate position (al-manzilah bayn al-manzilatayn) only arose after that. End. This is obstinacy; rather, among some believers during the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) there occurred lapses and failings, some of which are mentioned in the Qur'an and some in the authentic, established Hadith.

﴿And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ is conjoined to His saying: ﴿that they will have a great reward﴾. They were given good tidings of their success with Paradise, and of the existence of a painful punishment for their enemies, the disbelievers, since in the believers' knowledge of this and their being given good tidings of it there is joy for them; so these are two good tidings, and in it is a warning for the disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that it means "and it informs that those who do not believe [...]." End. Then it would not be included under the good tidings. In His saying: ﴿And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ is evidence that whoever believes in the Hereafter will not have a painful punishment prescribed for him, and that doing righteous deeds is not a condition of his salvation from punishment.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿wa-yubashshiru﴾ with a shadda, the present tense of bashsha·ra (form II). ʿAbdullah, Talhah, Ibn Thabit and the two brothers (al-Akhawan) read ﴿wa-yabshuru﴾, the present tense of bashara (form I, unshadda). The meaning of ﴿a'tadna﴾ is "we prepared and made ready." This verse came after the mention of the states of the Jews, and they are included among those who do not believe in the Hereafter, because most of them do not hold to reward and punishment of a physical nature; and some of them said: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80], so they did not believe in the Hereafter with the true reality of belief in it.

﴿And man prays for evil﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: it was revealed as a reproach for what people do of supplicating against their wealth and children in times of anger and irritation. Its connection to what precedes it is that some of those who do not believe in the Hereafter used to pray against themselves for the hastening of what they were promised of evil in the Hereafter, like the saying of al-Nadr: ﴿So rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], etc. ﴿wa-yadʿu﴾ is written without a waw according to what is heard. ﴿al-insan﴾ here is not one specific individual; the meaning is that it is in man's nature that when he is irritated and angry he prays against himself, his family and his wealth for evil to befall him, just as he prays for good to befall him. Then the Exalted mentioned that this is from his lack of steadfastness and his scant patience. It is related from Salman al-Farisi and Ibn ʿAbbas: it refers to Adam, when the spirit was blown into his head he sneezed and saw; when the spirit walked in his body before reaching his legs, he was impressed with himself and set off walking hastily, but could not manage; or the meaning is "one with a hereditary haste from your father." End. This view is far from the wording of the verse. Another group said: this verse is a rebuke of Quraysh who said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], etc. The better course would have been for them to say: "Guide us to it and have mercy upon us." Another group said: it is a rebuke of people that when evil and harm befall them they supplicate and insist in supplication and hasten relief, like the supplication they should have made in a state of good. End. The preposition "bi" in "bi-al-sharr" and "bi-al-khayr" according to this view means "in," and what is called upon is neither evil nor good; the meaning according to this is that his states in evil and good should be equal in supplication, humility to Allah, desire and remembrance. This meaning is confirmed by His saying: ﴿his supplication﴾, since it is a comparative infinitive that requires its existence; in this view, ﴿his supplication﴾ in the state of evil is compared to a intended supplication which ought to have occurred in the state of good.

It is said: the meaning of ﴿And man prays﴾ is seeking what is forbidden, just as he prays seeking what is permissible.

﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾ When the Exalted mentioned the Qur'an and that it guides to the upright path, He mentioned what He bestowed upon them, which benefit is not complete except by it, and what indicates His oneness from the wonders of the higher world. Also, when He mentioned man's haste and his moving from state to state, He mentioned that this whole world is likewise in constant movement and does not remain in one state: light after darkness and the reverse, and increase of light and decrease. The apparent meaning is that "the night and the day" is the first object of "ja'ala" in the sense of "sayyara" (made), and ﴿two signs﴾ is the second object, and they are in themselves two signs, since they are indications for reflection and lesson; the idafah in "sign of the night" and "sign of the day" is for specification, like the idafah of a number to the counted thing: i.e., "We effaced the sign which is the night, and made the sign which is the day a means of sight." It is said: it is by omitting a modifier, which some estimated as "We made the two luminaries of night and day two signs," and some estimated as "We made the two possessors of night and day two signs," meaning the two companions of night and day; on both estimates the sun and moon are intended. It appears that ﴿two signs﴾ is the first object, and "the night and the day" are adverbial expressions in the position of the second object, i.e., "We made in the night and the day two signs." Al-Karmani said: "ja'ala" here is not in the sense of "sayyara," since that requires a prior state from which a thing is transferred to another state, nor in the sense of "sammaa" or "hakama"; the sign therein is the advance and retreat of each of them from where it is not known, the decrease of one by the increase of the other, and the light of day and darkness of night. ﴿Then We effaced the sign of the night﴾: if we say the night and day are the two made signs, then effacing the sign of the night is an expression for the blackness within it, rather it was created black at the outset; and the "fa" does not require sequence, as one says: "I built my house, then I began with the foundation." If we say the two signs are the sun and moon, it is said: the effacing of the moon is that He did not give it light; it is said: its effacing is its rising small, then growing, then decreasing until it is concealed; it is said: its effacing is its diminishing from what it was created with of brightness, and that He made the light of the sun seventy parts and the light of the moon likewise, then He effaced from the light of the moon until it became one part, and made what was effaced from it an increase in the light of the sun. This is related from ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas.

Ibn ʿIsa said: We made them such that visible things are not seen therein, just as what is effaced from a book is not seen. He said: this is an extremely fine eloquence. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Then We effaced the sign of the night﴾ means: We made the night effaced of light, obliterated, dark, such that nothing can be distinguished in it, just as nothing can be distinguished in an effaced tablet; and We made the day "seeing," i.e., things are seen and made clear in it. Or: ﴿Then We effaced the sign of the night﴾ which is the moon, in that We did not create for it a ray like the ray of the sun, so that things are seen by it with clear sight; and We made the sun possessed of a ray in whose light everything is seen. End. The attribution of seeing to ﴿the sign of the day﴾ is by way of metaphor, as you say: "a night standing and sleeping," i.e., one stands in it and sleeps in it. The meaning is: it is seen by it.

It is said: the meaning of ﴿mubsirah﴾ is "luminous." It is said: it is of the pattern af'ala, and the intended is other than the one to whom the af'ala is attributed, like His saying: "ajbana al-rajulu" when his family are cowards, and "adʿafa" when his beasts are weak; so "the sign was made seeing" when its people are seeing. Qatadah and ʿAli ibn al-Husayn read ﴿mabsarah﴾ with fatha on the mim and the sad; it is a verbal noun placed in the position of a noun, and such usage is frequent in descriptions of places, as in their saying: "a land abounding in lions (masbaʿah)" and "a place abounding in mud (madabbah)." He gave as the reason for the effacing and the seeing the seeking of bounty and knowledge of the number of years and the reckoning. The reason with "seeking" follows what follows the sign of the day, and the reason with knowledge is delayed after the sign of the night. In His saying: ﴿And of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Qasas: 73] the beginning is with the reason for the earlier, then the reason for the later with the later cause; these are two methods whose discussion has already preceded.

The meaning of ﴿li-tabtaghu﴾ is "that you may reach the clarification of your works and your dealings in your livelihoods." ﴿wa-al-hisab﴾ is for the months, days and hours; knowledge of that in the law comes only from the sign of the night, not from the sign of the day. ﴿wa-kulla shay'in﴾ refers to what you need in your religion and your worldly life; ﴿fassalnahu﴾: We made it clear with a clarification free of ambiguity. The apparent reading is that ﴿wa-kulla shay'in﴾ is in the accusative by way of "ishtighal" (verbal preoccupation), and that was preferable to the nominative because of the prior verbal sentence in ﴿wa-ja'alna al-layla wa-al-nahar﴾; and whoever went to the view that ﴿wa-kulla shay'in﴾ is conjoined to "wa-al-hisab" and "al-ta'ir" is further off.

Ibn Abbas said: "[It means] what has been decreed for him and against him." God addressed the Arabs in this verse in terms they understood, since it was their custom to take omens (tayammun) and to regard birds as bearers of luck or misfortune (tashaʾum), whether a bird flew from right to left (sanihah) or from left to right (barihah). This practice became so widespread that they applied it to gazelles and wild animals as well, and all of it was called tatayyur (augury). They believed that this omen determined the good and evil a person encountered. God therefore informed them, in the most concise wording and the most eloquent indication, that everything good and evil a person meets has already been decreed, and that his portion (ḥazz), his deeds, and his earnings are fastened to his neck. He expressed the portion and the deed by "the bird," since the two are inseparable. This was the view of Mujahid and Qatada, in accordance with the belief of the Arabs regarding tatayyur, and with their saying about affairs, "[it is] by the auspicious bird" and "by the luckiest bird." From the same usage comes the phrase "the bird flew for us" in the context of lots and arrows (al-muḥāṣṣah wa-al-sahm), and from it the saying about Uthman ibn Maz'un, "Uthman ibn Maz'un flew for us from among the newcomers," meaning: that was our portion.

It is related from Ibn Abbas that ṭāʾirahu (his bird) means his deed. It is related from al-Suddi that it means his book, to which it flies. It is related from Abu Ubayda that among the Arabs al-ṭāʾir means the portion, which is what they call al-bakht (fortune). It is related from al-Hasan: "O son of Adam, a scroll has been spread out for you; when you are resurrected, it will be hung around your neck." The neck is singled out because it is the place of adornment and of disgrace: if the deed is good, it adorns him, as a necklace or jewelry adorns; if it is evil, it disgraces him, as a shackle on the neck.

Mujahid, al-Hasan and Abu Raja read ṭayrahu (with the vowel on the yāʾ and without alif). It is also read fī ʿunqihi with the nūn sukūn (ʿunqihi). The majority reading, including Ibn Jaʿfar, is ﴿wa-nukhriju﴾ with nūn, the imperfect of akhraja (we bring forth), with kitāban in the accusative. It is also related from Abu Jaʿfar that yukhraju with yāʾ, in the passive voice (mabniyyan lil-mafʿūl), with kitāban, meaning: the bird is brought forth as a book. Also from him: kitābun in the nominative, as the substitute for the subject of the passive (nāʾib al-fāʿil). Al-Hasan, Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid read yakhruju with a fatḥah on the yāʾ and a ḍammah on the rāʾ, meaning: his bird comes forth as a book. Al-Hasan alone read kitābun as the subject of yakhruju. A group read yukhriju with a ḍammah on the yāʾ and a kasrah on the rāʾ, meaning: God brings it forth. The majority read yalqāhu with a fatḥah on the yāʾ and sukūn on the lām. Ibn Amir, Abu Jaʿfar, al-Jahdari, and al-Hasan (according to one report) read yulaqqāhu with a ḍammah on the yāʾ, a fatḥah on the lām and a shaddah on the qāf.

﴿Manshūran﴾ means not folded, so that he can read it. Both yalqāhu and manshūran are attributes (ṣifatān) of kitāban. It is also permissible for manshūran to be a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from the object of yalqāhu. ﴿Iqraʾ kitābaka﴾ ("Read your book") is governed by a verb of saying that is omitted, meaning: it will be said to him, "Read your book." Qatada said: On that day whoever was not a reader in this world will read.

Al-Zamakhshari and others said: bi-nafsika is the subject (fāʿil) of kafā ("suffices"). The end of his statement. This is the view of the majority, and the bāʾ is superfluous (zāʾidah) in the sense of permissibility, not obligation. This is shown by the fact that when it is omitted, that noun takes the nominative after kafā. The poet said:

"Old age and Islam suffice a man as a deterrent."

Another said:

"His guidance informs me about the absent [inner state] of a man; guidance suffices as an informant about what a man has hidden."

It has also been said that the subject of kafā is a pronoun referring to the act of sufficing, meaning: it suffices, namely the sufficing, by yourself. It has also been said that kafā is a verb-noun meaning ikhtafi ("be content"), with a hidden subject referring to the addressee; on these two views the bāʾ is not superfluous. If we follow the view of the majority that bi-nafsika is the subject of kafā, then the expected form would be to add the feminine marker (tāʾ al-taʾnīth) because the subject is feminine, so the construction would be kafat bi-nafsika, as it is attached when min is added to a feminine subject, as in His saying (p-16) ﴿mā āmanat qablahum min qaryatin ahlaknāhā﴾ ("No town which We destroyed believed before them") [al-Anbiyaʾ: 6], and His saying "wa-mā tatīhim min āyatin" (no sign comes to them), which we do not know from this form. The feminization of kafā when the subject is feminine and governed by bāʾ is not attested; the apparent meaning is that by nafsika means your very self, i.e., "sufficient is you." Muqatil said: he means by his own self his limbs, which will bear witness against him if he denies. Abu Ubayda said: that is, how sufficient is what you knew of what you did. Al-yawma is an accusative governed by kafā, and ʿalayka is attached to ḥasīban. The meaning of ḥasīban is "judging against you by your deeds." This was said by al-Hasan, who said: O son of Adam, God has been just to you and made you the reckoner of your own self. Al-Kalbi said: "muḥāsiban" (one who reckons), meaning faʿīl in the sense of mufāʿil, like jalīs (companion) and khalīṭ (associate). It has also been said: ḥāsiban, like ḍarīb al-qidāḥ (the one who strikes the arrows) and ṣarīm in the sense of ṣārim; meaning it is an intensive form (binā' mubālaghah), like raḥīm and ḥafīẓ. He mentioned ḥasīban because it stands in the position of shahīd (witness), qāḍī (judge) and amīr (ruler), since generally such matters are undertaken by a man; it is as if it were said: "sufficient is yourself as a man who reckons."

Al-Anbari said: He said ḥasīban although nafs is feminine because by nafs he means the person, or because the word nafs has no mark of feminity, so it was likened to samāʾ and arḍ, as God says: ﴿al-samāʾu munfaṭirun bihi﴾ ("the sky will be split by it") [al-Muzzammil: 18]. The poet said:

"Nor a land that has sprouted as its herbage sprouts."

﴿Man ihtadā﴾ (whoever is guided), the verse. One group said: the indication of guidance refers to Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Asad, and the indication of misguidance refers to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. It was also said that it was revealed about this al-Walid, who said: "O people of Mecca, disbelieve in Muhammad, and his sin shall be upon me." The explanation of ﴿wa-lā taziru wāziratun wizra ukhrā﴾ ("no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another") [al-Anʿam: 164] has already been given at the end of Surat al-Anʿam.

﴿Wa-mā kunnā muʿadhdhibīna ḥattā nabʿatha rasūlan﴾ ("We would never punish until We send a messenger") sets the limit (ghayyā) for the negation of punishment by the sending of a messenger (peace be upon him). The meaning: until He sends a messenger and he is denied and does not believe in what he brought from God. The negation of punishment is more general, whether it be in this world by destruction or by other torments, or in the Hereafter by the Fire; the verse includes both. The inclusiveness is indicated by His saying about destruction in this world after this verse, ﴿wa-idhā aradnā﴾ ("when We intend") [al-Isrāʾ: 16], and about the Hereafter, ﴿fa-ḥaqqa ʿalayhā al-qawlu fa-dammarnāhā tadmīran﴾ ("the word is due against them, and We destroy them with complete destruction") [al-Isrāʾ: 16]. There are many verses that explicitly state destruction in this world by various kinds of punishment when the messengers were denied. And His saying about the punishment of the Hereafter: ﴿kullamā ulqiya fīhā fawjun sa'alahum khazanatuhā alam yaʾtikum nadhīrun﴾ ("Whenever a group is cast into it, its keepers ask them, 'Did no warner come to you?'") [al-Mulk: 8], ﴿qālū balā qad jāʾanā nadhīrun﴾ ("They say, 'Yes, a warner did come to us'") [al-Mulk: 9]. Kullamā indicates the generality of the times of casting, so it encompasses those cast. And His saying: ﴿wa-in min ummatin illā khalā fīhā nadhīrun﴾ ("There was no community but a warner passed among them") [Fāṭir: 24]. The majority held that this applies to the affairs of this world, meaning that God does not destroy a community with punishment except after a messenger has been sent to them and a warning given.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: the proof is binding upon them before the sending of a messenger, because with them are the proofs of reason by which God is known, and they neglected reflection while being able to do it, and their deserving of punishment is due to their neglect of reflection on what was with them; their adherence to that neglect is what makes the laws that can only be known by revelation, and acting upon them is not valid except after faith. I say: the sending of the Messenger (ﷺ) is part of the admonition to reflection and of awakening from the sleep of heedlessness, lest they say, "We were heedless" (cf. al-Aʿrāf: 172). "Had You not sent to us a messenger to remind us to reflect upon the proofs of reason." The end of his statement. Muqatil said: the meaning is: We would not have destroyed them utterly in this world, according to what divine wisdom required, until We sent a messenger, to establish the proof against them and to cut off their excuse, as We did with ʿĀd, Thamūd, the overturned cities (al-Mu'tafikāt), and others.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "that which is most upright" refers to the state that is the most upright of states and the most firm, or to the creed, or to the path; wherever you estimate it, you will not find with the affirmation the eloquence that you find with the omission, because of the grandeur in the ambiguity of the described thing which is lost when it is made explicit. End.

﴿And gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds﴾ is a restriction on complete faith, since action is the perfection of faith. He pointed to the complete state so that the believer may adorn himself with it. The believer who falls short in his deeds still has a share in righteous deeds through his faith, and the great reward is Paradise. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how did He mention the righteous believers and the disbelievers, and not mention the sinners? I say: at that time people were either a pious believer or a polytheist, and the people of an intermediate position (al-manzilah bayn al-manzilatayn) only arose after that. End. This is obstinacy; rather, among some believers during the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) there occurred lapses and failings, some of which are mentioned in the Qur'an and some in the authentic, established Hadith.

﴿And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ is conjoined to His saying: ﴿that they will have a great reward﴾. They were given good tidings of their success with Paradise, and of the existence of a painful punishment for their enemies, the disbelievers, since in the believers' knowledge of this and their being given good tidings of it there is joy for them; so these are two good tidings, and in it is a warning for the disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that it means "and it informs that those who do not believe [...]." End. Then it would not be included under the good tidings. In His saying: ﴿And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ is evidence that whoever believes in the Hereafter will not have a painful punishment prescribed for him, and that doing righteous deeds is not a condition of his salvation from punishment.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿wa-yubashshiru﴾ with a shadda, the present tense of bashsha·ra (form II). ʿAbdullah, Talhah, Ibn Thabit and the two brothers (al-Akhawan) read ﴿wa-yabshuru﴾, the present tense of bashara (form I, unshadda). The meaning of ﴿a'tadna﴾ is "we prepared and made ready." This verse came after the mention of the states of the Jews, and they are included among those who do not believe in the Hereafter, because most of them do not hold to reward and punishment of a physical nature; and some of them said: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80], so they did not believe in the Hereafter with the true reality of belief in it.

﴿And man prays for evil﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: it was revealed as a reproach for what people do of supplicating against their wealth and children in times of anger and irritation. Its connection to what precedes it is that some of those who do not believe in the Hereafter used to pray against themselves for the hastening of what they were promised of evil in the Hereafter, like the saying of al-Nadr: ﴿So rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], etc. ﴿wa-yadʿu﴾ is written without a waw according to what is heard. ﴿al-insan﴾ here is not one specific individual; the meaning is that it is in man's nature that when he is irritated and angry he prays against himself, his family and his wealth for evil to befall him, just as he prays for good to befall him. Then the Exalted mentioned that this is from his lack of steadfastness and his scant patience. It is related from Salman al-Farisi and Ibn ʿAbbas: it refers to Adam, when the spirit was blown into his head he sneezed and saw; when the spirit walked in his body before reaching his legs, he was impressed with himself and set off walking hastily, but could not manage; or the meaning is "one with a hereditary haste from your father." End. This view is far from the wording of the verse. Another group said: this verse is a rebuke of Quraysh who said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], etc. The better course would have been for them to say: "Guide us to it and have mercy upon us." Another group said: it is a rebuke of people that when evil and harm befall them they supplicate and insist in supplication and hasten relief, like the supplication they should have made in a state of good. End. The preposition "bi" in "bi-al-sharr" and "bi-al-khayr" according to this view means "in," and what is called upon is neither evil nor good; the meaning according to this is that his states in evil and good should be equal in supplication, humility to Allah, desire and remembrance. This meaning is confirmed by His saying: ﴿his supplication﴾, since it is a comparative infinitive that requires its existence; in this view, ﴿his supplication﴾ in the state of evil is compared to a intended supplication which ought to have occurred in the state of good.

It is said: the meaning of ﴿And man prays﴾ is seeking what is forbidden, just as he prays seeking what is permissible.

﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾ When the Exalted mentioned the Qur'an and that it guides to the upright path, He mentioned what He bestowed upon them, which benefit is not complete except by it, and what indicates His oneness from the wonders of the higher world. Also, when He mentioned man's haste and his moving from state to state, He mentioned that this whole world is likewise in constant movement and does not remain in one state: light after darkness and the reverse, and increase of light and decrease. The apparent meaning is that "the night and the day" is the first object of "ja'ala" in the sense of "sayyara" (made), and ﴿two signs﴾ is the second object, and they are in themselves two signs, since they are indications for reflection and lesson; the idafah in "sign of the night" and "sign of the day" is for specification, like the idafah of a number to the counted thing: i.e., "We effaced the sign which is the night, and made the sign which is the day a means of sight." It is said: it is by omitting a modifier, which some estimated as "We made the two luminaries of night and day two signs," and some estimated as "We made the two possessors of night and day two signs," meaning the two companions of night and day; on both estimates the sun and moon are intended. It appears that ﴿two signs﴾ is the first object, and "the night and the day" are adverbial expressions in the position of the second object, i.e., "We made in the night and the day two signs." Al-Karmani said: "ja'ala" here is not in the sense of "sayyara," since that requires a prior state from which a thing is transferred to another state, nor in the sense of "sammaa" or "hakama"; the sign therein is the advance and retreat of each of them from where it is not known, the decrease of one by the increase of the other, and the light of day and darkness of night. ﴿Then We effaced the sign of the night﴾: if we say the night and day are the two made signs, then effacing the sign of the night is an expression for the blackness within it, rather it was created black at the outset; and the "fa" does not require sequence, as one says: "I built my house, then I began with the foundation." If we say the two signs are the sun and moon, it is said: the effacing of the moon is that He did not give it light; it is said: its effacing is its rising small, then growing, then decreasing until it is concealed; it is said: its effacing is its diminishing from what it was created with of brightness, and that He made the light of the sun seventy parts and the light of the moon likewise, then He effaced from the light of the moon until it became one part, and made what was effaced from it an increase in the light of the sun. This is related from ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas.

Ibn ʿIsa said: We made them such that visible things are not seen therein, just as what is effaced from a book is not seen. He said: this is an extremely fine eloquence. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Then We effaced the sign of the night﴾ means: We made the night effaced of light, obliterated, dark, such that nothing can be distinguished in it, just as nothing can be distinguished in an effaced tablet; and We made the day "seeing," i.e., things are seen and made clear in it. Or: ﴿Then We effaced the sign of the night﴾ which is the moon, in that We did not create for it a ray like the ray of the sun, so that things are seen by it with clear sight; and We made the sun possessed of a ray in whose light everything is seen. End. The attribution of seeing to ﴿the sign of the day﴾ is by way of metaphor, as you say: "a night standing and sleeping," i.e., one stands in it and sleeps in it. The meaning is: it is seen by it.

It is said: the meaning of ﴿mubsirah﴾ is "luminous." It is said: it is of the pattern af'ala, and the intended is other than the one to whom the af'ala is attributed, like His saying: "ajbana al-rajulu" when his family are cowards, and "adʿafa" when his beasts are weak; so "the sign was made seeing" when its people are seeing. Qatadah and ʿAli ibn al-Husayn read ﴿mabsarah﴾ with fatha on the mim and the sad; it is a verbal noun placed in the position of a noun, and such usage is frequent in descriptions of places, as in their saying: "a land abounding in lions (masbaʿah)" and "a place abounding in mud (madabbah)." He gave as the reason for the effacing and the seeing the seeking of bounty and knowledge of the number of years and the reckoning. The reason with "seeking" follows what follows the sign of the day, and the reason with knowledge is delayed after the sign of the night. In His saying: ﴿And of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Qasas: 73] the beginning is with the reason for the earlier, then the reason for the later with the later cause; these are two methods whose discussion has already preceded.

The meaning of ﴿li-tabtaghu﴾ is "that you may reach the clarification of your works and your dealings in your livelihoods." ﴿wa-al-hisab﴾ is for the months, days and hours; knowledge of that in the law comes only from the sign of the night, not from the sign of the day. ﴿wa-kulla shay'in﴾ refers to what you need in your religion and your worldly life; ﴿fassalnahu﴾: We made it clear with a clarification free of ambiguity. The apparent reading is that ﴿wa-kulla shay'in﴾ is in the accusative by way of "ishtighal" (verbal preoccupation), and that was preferable to the nominative because of the prior verbal sentence in ﴿wa-ja'alna al-layla wa-al-nahar﴾; and whoever went to the view that ﴿wa-kulla shay'in﴾ is conjoined to "wa-al-hisab" and "al-ta'ir" is further off.

Ibn Abbas said: "[It means] what has been decreed for him and against him." God addressed the Arabs in this verse in terms they understood, since it was their custom to take omens (tayammun) and to regard birds as bearers of luck or misfortune (tashaʾum), whether a bird flew from right to left (sanihah) or from left to right (barihah). This practice became so widespread that they applied it to gazelles and wild animals as well, and all of it was called tatayyur (augury). They believed that this omen determined the good and evil a person encountered. God therefore informed them, in the most concise wording and the most eloquent indication, that everything good and evil a person meets has already been decreed, and that his portion (ḥazz), his deeds, and his earnings are fastened to his neck. He expressed the portion and the deed by "the bird," since the two are inseparable. This was the view of Mujahid and Qatada, in accordance with the belief of the Arabs regarding tatayyur, and with their saying about affairs, "[it is] by the auspicious bird" and "by the luckiest bird." From the same usage comes the phrase "the bird flew for us" in the context of lots and arrows (al-muḥāṣṣah wa-al-sahm), and from it the saying about Uthman ibn Maz'un, "Uthman ibn Maz'un flew for us from among the newcomers," meaning: that was our portion.

It is related from Ibn Abbas that ṭāʾirahu (his bird) means his deed. It is related from al-Suddi that it means his book, to which it flies. It is related from Abu Ubayda that among the Arabs al-ṭāʾir means the portion, which is what they call al-bakht (fortune). It is related from al-Hasan: "O son of Adam, a scroll has been spread out for you; when you are resurrected, it will be hung around your neck." The neck is singled out because it is the place of adornment and of disgrace: if the deed is good, it adorns him, as a necklace or jewelry adorns; if it is evil, it disgraces him, as a shackle on the neck.

Mujahid, al-Hasan and Abu Raja read ṭayrahu (with the vowel on the yāʾ and without alif). It is also read fī ʿunqihi with the nūn sukūn (ʿunqihi). The majority reading, including Ibn Jaʿfar, is ﴿wa-nukhriju﴾ with nūn, the imperfect of akhraja (we bring forth), with kitāban in the accusative. It is also related from Abu Jaʿfar that yukhraju with yāʾ, in the passive voice (mabniyyan lil-mafʿūl), with kitāban, meaning: the bird is brought forth as a book. Also from him: kitābun in the nominative, as the substitute for the subject of the passive (nāʾib al-fāʿil). Al-Hasan, Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid read yakhruju with a fatḥah on the yāʾ and a ḍammah on the rāʾ, meaning: his bird comes forth as a book. Al-Hasan alone read kitābun as the subject of yakhruju. A group read yukhriju with a ḍammah on the yāʾ and a kasrah on the rāʾ, meaning: God brings it forth. The majority read yalqāhu with a fatḥah on the yāʾ and sukūn on the lām. Ibn Amir, Abu Jaʿfar, al-Jahdari, and al-Hasan (according to one report) read yulaqqāhu with a ḍammah on the yāʾ, a fatḥah on the lām and a shaddah on the qāf.

﴿Manshūran﴾ means not folded, so that he can read it. Both yalqāhu and manshūran are attributes (ṣifatān) of kitāban. It is also permissible for manshūran to be a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from the object of yalqāhu. ﴿Iqraʾ kitābaka﴾ ("Read your book") is governed by a verb of saying that is omitted, meaning: it will be said to him, "Read your book." Qatada said: On that day whoever was not a reader in this world will read.

Al-Zamakhshari and others said: bi-nafsika is the subject (fāʿil) of kafā ("suffices"). The end of his statement. This is the view of the majority, and the bāʾ is superfluous (zāʾidah) in the sense of permissibility, not obligation. This is shown by the fact that when it is omitted, that noun takes the nominative after kafā. The poet said:

"Old age and Islam suffice a man as a deterrent."

Another said:

"His guidance informs me about the absent [inner state] of a man; guidance suffices as an informant about what a man has hidden."

It has also been said that the subject of kafā is a pronoun referring to the act of sufficing, meaning: it suffices, namely the sufficing, by yourself. It has also been said that kafā is a verb-noun meaning ikhtafi ("be content"), with a hidden subject referring to the addressee; on these two views the bāʾ is not superfluous. If we follow the view of the majority that bi-nafsika is the subject of kafā, then the expected form would be to add the feminine marker (tāʾ al-taʾnīth) because the subject is feminine, so the construction would be kafat bi-nafsika, as it is attached when min is added to a feminine subject, as in His saying (p-16) ﴿mā āmanat qablahum min qaryatin ahlaknāhā﴾ ("No town which We destroyed believed before them") [al-Anbiyaʾ: 6], and His saying "wa-mā tatīhim min āyatin" (no sign comes to them), which we do not know from this form. The feminization of kafā when the subject is feminine and governed by bāʾ is not attested; the apparent meaning is that by nafsika means your very self, i.e., "sufficient is you." Muqatil said: he means by his own self his limbs, which will bear witness against him if he denies. Abu Ubayda said: that is, how sufficient is what you knew of what you did. Al-yawma is an accusative governed by kafā, and ʿalayka is attached to ḥasīban. The meaning of ḥasīban is "judging against you by your deeds." This was said by al-Hasan, who said: O son of Adam, God has been just to you and made you the reckoner of your own self. Al-Kalbi said: "muḥāsiban" (one who reckons), meaning faʿīl in the sense of mufāʿil, like jalīs (companion) and khalīṭ (associate). It has also been said: ḥāsiban, like ḍarīb al-qidāḥ (the one who strikes the arrows) and ṣarīm in the sense of ṣārim; meaning it is an intensive form (binā' mubālaghah), like raḥīm and ḥafīẓ. He mentioned ḥasīban because it stands in the position of shahīd (witness), qāḍī (judge) and amīr (ruler), since generally such matters are undertaken by a man; it is as if it were said: "sufficient is yourself as a man who reckons."

Al-Anbari said: He said ḥasīban although nafs is feminine because by nafs he means the person, or because the word nafs has no mark of feminity, so it was likened to samāʾ and arḍ, as God says: ﴿al-samāʾu munfaṭirun bihi﴾ ("the sky will be split by it") [al-Muzzammil: 18]. The poet said:

"Nor a land that has sprouted as its herbage sprouts."

﴿Man ihtadā﴾ (whoever is guided), the verse. One group said: the indication of guidance refers to Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Asad, and the indication of misguidance refers to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. It was also said that it was revealed about this al-Walid, who said: "O people of Mecca, disbelieve in Muhammad, and his sin shall be upon me." The explanation of ﴿wa-lā taziru wāziratun wizra ukhrā﴾ ("no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another") [al-Anʿam: 164] has already been given at the end of Surat al-Anʿam.

﴿Wa-mā kunnā muʿadhdhibīna ḥattā nabʿatha rasūlan﴾ ("We would never punish until We send a messenger") sets the limit (ghayyā) for the negation of punishment by the sending of a messenger (peace be upon him). The meaning: until He sends a messenger and he is denied and does not believe in what he brought from God. The negation of punishment is more general, whether it be in this world by destruction or by other torments, or in the Hereafter by the Fire; the verse includes both. The inclusiveness is indicated by His saying about destruction in this world after this verse, ﴿wa-idhā aradnā﴾ ("when We intend") [al-Isrāʾ: 16], and about the Hereafter, ﴿fa-ḥaqqa ʿalayhā al-qawlu fa-dammarnāhā tadmīran﴾ ("the word is due against them, and We destroy them with complete destruction") [al-Isrāʾ: 16]. There are many verses that explicitly state destruction in this world by various kinds of punishment when the messengers were denied. And His saying about the punishment of the Hereafter: ﴿kullamā ulqiya fīhā fawjun sa'alahum khazanatuhā alam yaʾtikum nadhīrun﴾ ("Whenever a group is cast into it, its keepers ask them, 'Did no warner come to you?'") [al-Mulk: 8], ﴿qālū balā qad jāʾanā nadhīrun﴾ ("They say, 'Yes, a warner did come to us'") [al-Mulk: 9]. Kullamā indicates the generality of the times of casting, so it encompasses those cast. And His saying: ﴿wa-in min ummatin illā khalā fīhā nadhīrun﴾ ("There was no community but a warner passed among them") [Fāṭir: 24]. The majority held that this applies to the affairs of this world, meaning that God does not destroy a community with punishment except after a messenger has been sent to them and a warning given.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: the proof is binding upon them before the sending of a messenger, because with them are the proofs of reason by which God is known, and they neglected reflection while being able to do it, and their deserving of punishment is due to their neglect of reflection on what was with them; their adherence to that neglect is what makes the laws that can only be known by revelation, and acting upon them is not valid except after faith. I say: the sending of the Messenger (ﷺ) is part of the admonition to reflection and of awakening from the sleep of heedlessness, lest they say, "We were heedless" (cf. al-Aʿrāf: 172). "Had You not sent to us a messenger to remind us to reflect upon the proofs of reason." The end of his statement. Muqatil said: the meaning is: We would not have destroyed them utterly in this world, according to what divine wisdom required, until We sent a messenger, to establish the proof against them and to cut off their excuse, as We did with ʿĀd, Thamūd, the overturned cities (al-Mu'tafikāt), and others.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verse 9–15 (part 1 of 2):

(p-12) ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright, and gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a great reward. And [it gives warning] that those who do not believe in the Hereafter, We have prepared for them a painful punishment. And man prays for evil as he prays for good, and man has always been hasty.﴾ ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs. Then We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day as a means of sight, that you might seek bounty from your Lord and that you might know the number of years and the reckoning. And every matter We have detailed with full detail.﴾ ﴿And every person's omen We have fastened to his neck, and We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record he will find spread open. [It will be said], "Read your record. Sufficient is yourself against you this Day as a reckoner."﴾ ﴿Whoever is guided is only guided for [the benefit of] himself, and whoever goes astray only goes astray to its detriment. And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And We would never punish until We send a messenger.﴾

(p-13) When the Exalted mentioned those whom He singled out for the Night Journey, who is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and those to whom He gave the Torah, who is Musa (peace be upon him), and that it was a guidance for the Children of Israel, and mentioned what He decreed upon them therein of domination over them because of their sins, this was a deterrent for whoever understands against the disobedience of Allah. So He mentioned what Allah honored His Messenger with, the Qur'an, which abrogates the ruling of the Torah and of every divine book, and that it guides to the path or the state that is most upright. Al-Dahhak, al-Kalbi and al-Farra' said: "that which is most upright" refers to the testimony of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness). Muqatil said: it refers to the commands and prohibitions. The word "aqwam" here is the elative (af'al al-tafdil) according to the view of al-Zajjaj, when it is understood as "the most upright of states." Others estimated it as "more upright than what is other than it" or "more upright than every state." What appears in terms of meaning is that "aqwam" here is not intended as a comparative, since there is no sharing between the path to which the Qur'an guides and another path, such that this one is preferred over it. Rather the meaning is: "that which is qayyimah," i.e., upright, as He said: ﴿And that is the upright religion﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5] and ﴿therein are correct books﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 3], meaning: upright in its path, standing with what is needed of the matter of religion. Al-Zamakhshari said: "that which is most upright" refers to the state that is the most upright of states and the most firm, or to the creed, or to the path; wherever you estimate it, you will not find with the affirmation the eloquence that you find with the omission, because of the grandeur in the ambiguity of the described thing which is lost when it is made explicit. End.

He pointed to the complete state so that the believer may adorn himself with it. The believer who falls short in his deeds still has a share in righteous deeds through his faith, and the great reward is Paradise. I say: at that time people were either a pious believer or a polytheist, and the people of an intermediate position (al-manzilah bayn al-manzilatayn) only arose after that. End. This is obstinacy; rather, among some believers during the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) there occurred lapses and failings, some of which are mentioned in the Qur'an and some in the authentic, established Hadith.

﴿And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ is conjoined to His saying: ﴿that they will have a great reward﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that it means "and it informs that those who do not believe [...]." End. Then it would not be included under the good tidings. In His saying: ﴿And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ is evidence that whoever believes in the Hereafter will not have a painful punishment prescribed for him, and that doing righteous deeds is not a condition of his salvation from punishment.
