So He mentioned what Allah honored His Messenger with, the Qur'an, which abrogates the ruling of the Torah and of every divine book, and that it guides to the path or the state that is most upright. Al-Dahhak, al-Kalbi and al-Farra' said: "that which is most upright" refers to the testimony of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness). Muqatil said: it refers to the commands and prohibitions. The word "aqwam" here is the elative (af'al al-tafdil) according to the view of al-Zajjaj, when it is understood as "the most upright of states." Others estimated it as "more upright than what is other than it" or "more upright than every state." What appears in terms of meaning is that "aqwam" here is not intended as a comparative, since there is no sharing between the path to which the Qur'an guides and another path, such that this one is preferred over it. Rather the meaning is: "that which is qayyimah," i.e., upright, as He said: ﴿And that is the upright religion﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5] and ﴿therein are correct books﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 3], meaning: upright in its path, standing with what is needed of the matter of religion. Al-Zamakhshari said: "that which is most upright" refers to the state that is the most upright of states and the most firm, or to the creed, or to the path; wherever you estimate it, you will not find with the affirmation the eloquence that you find with the omission, because of the grandeur in the ambiguity of the described thing which is lost when it is made explicit. End.

﴿And gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds﴾ is a restriction on complete faith, since action is the perfection of faith. He pointed to the complete state so that the believer may adorn himself with it. The believer who falls short in his deeds still has a share in righteous deeds through his faith, and the great reward is Paradise. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how did He mention the righteous believers and the disbelievers, and not mention the sinners? I say: at that time people were either a pious believer or a polytheist, and the people of an intermediate position (al-manzilah bayn al-manzilatayn) only arose after that. End. This is obstinacy; rather, among some believers during the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) there occurred lapses and failings, some of which are mentioned in the Qur'an and some in the authentic, established Hadith.

﴿And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ is conjoined to His saying: ﴿that they will have a great reward﴾. They were given good tidings of their success with Paradise, and of the existence of a painful punishment for their enemies, the disbelievers, since in the believers' knowledge of this and their being given good tidings of it there is joy for them; so these are two good tidings, and in it is a warning for the disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that it means "and it informs that those who do not believe [...]." End. Then it would not be included under the good tidings. In His saying: ﴿And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ is evidence that whoever believes in the Hereafter will not have a painful punishment prescribed for him, and that doing righteous deeds is not a condition of his salvation from punishment.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿wa-yubashshiru﴾ with a shadda, the present tense of bashsha·ra (form II). ʿAbdullah, Talhah, Ibn Thabit and the two brothers (al-Akhawan) read ﴿wa-yabshuru﴾, the present tense of bashara (form I, unshadda). The meaning of ﴿a'tadna﴾ is "we prepared and made ready." This verse came after the mention of the states of the Jews, and they are included among those who do not believe in the Hereafter, because most of them do not hold to reward and punishment of a physical nature; and some of them said: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80], so they did not believe in the Hereafter with the true reality of belief in it.

﴿And man prays for evil﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: it was revealed as a reproach for what people do of supplicating against their wealth and children in times of anger and irritation. Its connection to what precedes it is that some of those who do not believe in the Hereafter used to pray against themselves for the hastening of what they were promised of evil in the Hereafter, like the saying of al-Nadr: ﴿So rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], etc. ﴿wa-yadʿu﴾ is written without a waw according to what is heard. ﴿al-insan﴾ here is not one specific individual; the meaning is that it is in man's nature that when he is irritated and angry he prays against himself, his family and his wealth for evil to befall him, just as he prays for good to befall him. Then the Exalted mentioned that this is from his lack of steadfastness and his scant patience. It is related from Salman al-Farisi and Ibn ʿAbbas: it refers to Adam, when the spirit was blown into his head he sneezed and saw; when the spirit walked in his body before reaching his legs, he was impressed with himself and set off walking hastily, but could not manage; or the meaning is "one with a hereditary haste from your father." End. This view is far from the wording of the verse. Another group said: this verse is a rebuke of Quraysh who said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], etc. The better course would have been for them to say: "Guide us to it and have mercy upon us." Another group said: it is a rebuke of people that when evil and harm befall them they supplicate and insist in supplication and hasten relief, like the supplication they should have made in a state of good. End. The preposition "bi" in "bi-al-sharr" and "bi-al-khayr" according to this view means "in," and what is called upon is neither evil nor good; the meaning according to this is that his states in evil and good should be equal in supplication, humility to Allah, desire and remembrance. This meaning is confirmed by His saying: ﴿his supplication﴾, since it is a comparative infinitive that requires its existence; in this view, ﴿his supplication﴾ in the state of evil is compared to a intended supplication which ought to have occurred in the state of good.

It is said: the meaning of ﴿And man prays﴾ is seeking what is forbidden, just as he prays seeking what is permissible.

﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾ When the Exalted mentioned the Qur'an and that it guides to the upright path, He mentioned what He bestowed upon them, which benefit is not complete except by it, and what indicates His oneness from the wonders of the higher world. Also, when He mentioned man's haste and his moving from state to state, He mentioned that this whole world is likewise in constant movement and does not remain in one state: light after darkness and the reverse, and increase of light and decrease. The apparent meaning is that "the night and the day" is the first object of "ja'ala" in the sense of "sayyara" (made), and ﴿two signs﴾ is the second object, and they are in themselves two signs, since they are indications for reflection and lesson; the idafah in "sign of the night" and "sign of the day" is for specification, like the idafah of a number to the counted thing: i.e., "We effaced the sign which is the night, and made the sign which is the day a means of sight." It is said: it is by omitting a modifier, which some estimated as "We made the two luminaries of night and day two signs," and some estimated as "We made the two possessors of night and day two signs," meaning the two companions of night and day; on both estimates the sun and moon are intended. It appears that ﴿two signs﴾ is the first object, and "the night and the day" are adverbial expressions in the position of the second object, i.e., "We made in the night and the day two signs." Al-Karmani said: "ja'ala" here is not in the sense of "sayyara," since that requires a prior state from which a thing is transferred to another state, nor in the sense of "sammaa" or "hakama"; the sign therein is the advance and retreat of each of them from where it is not known, the decrease of one by the increase of the other, and the light of day and darkness of night. ﴿Then We effaced the sign of the night﴾: if we say the night and day are the two made signs, then effacing the sign of the night is an expression for the blackness within it, rather it was created black at the outset; and the "fa" does not require sequence, as one says: "I built my house, then I began with the foundation." If we say the two signs are the sun and moon, it is said: the effacing of the moon is that He did not give it light; it is said: its effacing is its rising small, then growing, then decreasing until it is concealed; it is said: its effacing is its diminishing from what it was created with of brightness, and that He made the light of the sun seventy parts and the light of the moon likewise, then He effaced from the light of the moon until it became one part, and made what was effaced from it an increase in the light of the sun. This is related from ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas.

Ibn ʿIsa said: We made them such that visible things are not seen therein, just as what is effaced from a book is not seen. He said: this is an extremely fine eloquence. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Then We effaced the sign of the night﴾ means: We made the night effaced of light, obliterated, dark, such that nothing can be distinguished in it, just as nothing can be distinguished in an effaced tablet; and We made the day "seeing," i.e., things are seen and made clear in it. Or: ﴿Then We effaced the sign of the night﴾ which is the moon, in that We did not create for it a ray like the ray of the sun, so that things are seen by it with clear sight; and We made the sun possessed of a ray in whose light everything is seen. End. The attribution of seeing to ﴿the sign of the day﴾ is by way of metaphor, as you say: "a night standing and sleeping," i.e., one stands in it and sleeps in it. The meaning is: it is seen by it.

It is said: the meaning of ﴿mubsirah﴾ is "luminous." It is said: it is of the pattern af'ala, and the intended is other than the one to whom the af'ala is attributed, like His saying: "ajbana al-rajulu" when his family are cowards, and "adʿafa" when his beasts are weak; so "the sign was made seeing" when its people are seeing. Qatadah and ʿAli ibn al-Husayn read ﴿mabsarah﴾ with fatha on the mim and the sad; it is a verbal noun placed in the position of a noun, and such usage is frequent in descriptions of places, as in their saying: "a land abounding in lions (masbaʿah)" and "a place abounding in mud (madabbah)." He gave as the reason for the effacing and the seeing the seeking of bounty and knowledge of the number of years and the reckoning. The reason with "seeking" follows what follows the sign of the day, and the reason with knowledge is delayed after the sign of the night. In His saying: ﴿And of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Qasas: 73] the beginning is with the reason for the earlier, then the reason for the later with the later cause; these are two methods whose discussion has already preceded.

The meaning of ﴿li-tabtaghu﴾ is "that you may reach the clarification of your works and your dealings in your livelihoods." ﴿wa-al-hisab﴾ is for the months, days and hours; knowledge of that in the law comes only from the sign of the night, not from the sign of the day. ﴿wa-kulla shay'in﴾ refers to what you need in your religion and your worldly life; ﴿fassalnahu﴾: We made it clear with a clarification free of ambiguity. The apparent reading is that ﴿wa-kulla shay'in﴾ is in the accusative by way of "ishtighal" (verbal preoccupation), and that was preferable to the nominative because of the prior verbal sentence in ﴿wa-ja'alna al-layla wa-al-nahar﴾; and whoever went to the view that ﴿wa-kulla shay'in﴾ is conjoined to "wa-al-hisab" and "al-ta'ir" is further off.

Ibn Abbas said: "[It means] what has been decreed for him and against him." God addressed the Arabs in this verse in terms they understood, since it was their custom to take omens (tayammun) and to regard birds as bearers of luck or misfortune (tashaʾum), whether a bird flew from right to left (sanihah) or from left to right (barihah). This practice became so widespread that they applied it to gazelles and wild animals as well, and all of it was called tatayyur (augury). They believed that this omen determined the good and evil a person encountered. God therefore informed them, in the most concise wording and the most eloquent indication, that everything good and evil a person meets has already been decreed, and that his portion (ḥazz), his deeds, and his earnings are fastened to his neck. He expressed the portion and the deed by "the bird," since the two are inseparable. This was the view of Mujahid and Qatada, in accordance with the belief of the Arabs regarding tatayyur, and with their saying about affairs, "[it is] by the auspicious bird" and "by the luckiest bird." From the same usage comes the phrase "the bird flew for us" in the context of lots and arrows (al-muḥāṣṣah wa-al-sahm), and from it the saying about Uthman ibn Maz'un, "Uthman ibn Maz'un flew for us from among the newcomers," meaning: that was our portion.

It is related from Ibn Abbas that ṭāʾirahu (his bird) means his deed. It is related from al-Suddi that it means his book, to which it flies. It is related from Abu Ubayda that among the Arabs al-ṭāʾir means the portion, which is what they call al-bakht (fortune). It is related from al-Hasan: "O son of Adam, a scroll has been spread out for you; when you are resurrected, it will be hung around your neck." The neck is singled out because it is the place of adornment and of disgrace: if the deed is good, it adorns him, as a necklace or jewelry adorns; if it is evil, it disgraces him, as a shackle on the neck.

Mujahid, al-Hasan and Abu Raja read ṭayrahu (with the vowel on the yāʾ and without alif). It is also read fī ʿunqihi with the nūn sukūn (ʿunqihi). The majority reading, including Ibn Jaʿfar, is ﴿wa-nukhriju﴾ with nūn, the imperfect of akhraja (we bring forth), with kitāban in the accusative. It is also related from Abu Jaʿfar that yukhraju with yāʾ, in the passive voice (mabniyyan lil-mafʿūl), with kitāban, meaning: the bird is brought forth as a book. Also from him: kitābun in the nominative, as the substitute for the subject of the passive (nāʾib al-fāʿil). Al-Hasan, Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid read yakhruju with a fatḥah on the yāʾ and a ḍammah on the rāʾ, meaning: his bird comes forth as a book. Al-Hasan alone read kitābun as the subject of yakhruju. A group read yukhriju with a ḍammah on the yāʾ and a kasrah on the rāʾ, meaning: God brings it forth. The majority read yalqāhu with a fatḥah on the yāʾ and sukūn on the lām. Ibn Amir, Abu Jaʿfar, al-Jahdari, and al-Hasan (according to one report) read yulaqqāhu with a ḍammah on the yāʾ, a fatḥah on the lām and a shaddah on the qāf.

﴿Manshūran﴾ means not folded, so that he can read it. Both yalqāhu and manshūran are attributes (ṣifatān) of kitāban. It is also permissible for manshūran to be a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from the object of yalqāhu. ﴿Iqraʾ kitābaka﴾ ("Read your book") is governed by a verb of saying that is omitted, meaning: it will be said to him, "Read your book." Qatada said: On that day whoever was not a reader in this world will read.

Al-Zamakhshari and others said: bi-nafsika is the subject (fāʿil) of kafā ("suffices"). The end of his statement. This is the view of the majority, and the bāʾ is superfluous (zāʾidah) in the sense of permissibility, not obligation. This is shown by the fact that when it is omitted, that noun takes the nominative after kafā. The poet said:

"Old age and Islam suffice a man as a deterrent."

Another said:

"His guidance informs me about the absent [inner state] of a man; guidance suffices as an informant about what a man has hidden."

It has also been said that the subject of kafā is a pronoun referring to the act of sufficing, meaning: it suffices, namely the sufficing, by yourself. It has also been said that kafā is a verb-noun meaning ikhtafi ("be content"), with a hidden subject referring to the addressee; on these two views the bāʾ is not superfluous. If we follow the view of the majority that bi-nafsika is the subject of kafā, then the expected form would be to add the feminine marker (tāʾ al-taʾnīth) because the subject is feminine, so the construction would be kafat bi-nafsika, as it is attached when min is added to a feminine subject, as in His saying (p-16) ﴿mā āmanat qablahum min qaryatin ahlaknāhā﴾ ("No town which We destroyed believed before them") [al-Anbiyaʾ: 6], and His saying "wa-mā tatīhim min āyatin" (no sign comes to them), which we do not know from this form. The feminization of kafā when the subject is feminine and governed by bāʾ is not attested; the apparent meaning is that by nafsika means your very self, i.e., "sufficient is you." Muqatil said: he means by his own self his limbs, which will bear witness against him if he denies. Abu Ubayda said: that is, how sufficient is what you knew of what you did. Al-yawma is an accusative governed by kafā, and ʿalayka is attached to ḥasīban. The meaning of ḥasīban is "judging against you by your deeds." This was said by al-Hasan, who said: O son of Adam, God has been just to you and made you the reckoner of your own self. Al-Kalbi said: "muḥāsiban" (one who reckons), meaning faʿīl in the sense of mufāʿil, like jalīs (companion) and khalīṭ (associate). It has also been said: ḥāsiban, like ḍarīb al-qidāḥ (the one who strikes the arrows) and ṣarīm in the sense of ṣārim; meaning it is an intensive form (binā' mubālaghah), like raḥīm and ḥafīẓ. He mentioned ḥasīban because it stands in the position of shahīd (witness), qāḍī (judge) and amīr (ruler), since generally such matters are undertaken by a man; it is as if it were said: "sufficient is yourself as a man who reckons."

Al-Anbari said: He said ḥasīban although nafs is feminine because by nafs he means the person, or because the word nafs has no mark of feminity, so it was likened to samāʾ and arḍ, as God says: ﴿al-samāʾu munfaṭirun bihi﴾ ("the sky will be split by it") [al-Muzzammil: 18]. The poet said:

"Nor a land that has sprouted as its herbage sprouts."

﴿Man ihtadā﴾ (whoever is guided), the verse. One group said: the indication of guidance refers to Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Asad, and the indication of misguidance refers to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. It was also said that it was revealed about this al-Walid, who said: "O people of Mecca, disbelieve in Muhammad, and his sin shall be upon me." The explanation of ﴿wa-lā taziru wāziratun wizra ukhrā﴾ ("no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another") [al-Anʿam: 164] has already been given at the end of Surat al-Anʿam.

﴿Wa-mā kunnā muʿadhdhibīna ḥattā nabʿatha rasūlan﴾ ("We would never punish until We send a messenger") sets the limit (ghayyā) for the negation of punishment by the sending of a messenger (peace be upon him). The meaning: until He sends a messenger and he is denied and does not believe in what he brought from God. The negation of punishment is more general, whether it be in this world by destruction or by other torments, or in the Hereafter by the Fire; the verse includes both. The inclusiveness is indicated by His saying about destruction in this world after this verse, ﴿wa-idhā aradnā﴾ ("when We intend") [al-Isrāʾ: 16], and about the Hereafter, ﴿fa-ḥaqqa ʿalayhā al-qawlu fa-dammarnāhā tadmīran﴾ ("the word is due against them, and We destroy them with complete destruction") [al-Isrāʾ: 16]. There are many verses that explicitly state destruction in this world by various kinds of punishment when the messengers were denied. And His saying about the punishment of the Hereafter: ﴿kullamā ulqiya fīhā fawjun sa'alahum khazanatuhā alam yaʾtikum nadhīrun﴾ ("Whenever a group is cast into it, its keepers ask them, 'Did no warner come to you?'") [al-Mulk: 8], ﴿qālū balā qad jāʾanā nadhīrun﴾ ("They say, 'Yes, a warner did come to us'") [al-Mulk: 9]. Kullamā indicates the generality of the times of casting, so it encompasses those cast. And His saying: ﴿wa-in min ummatin illā khalā fīhā nadhīrun﴾ ("There was no community but a warner passed among them") [Fāṭir: 24]. The majority held that this applies to the affairs of this world, meaning that God does not destroy a community with punishment except after a messenger has been sent to them and a warning given.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: the proof is binding upon them before the sending of a messenger, because with them are the proofs of reason by which God is known, and they neglected reflection while being able to do it, and their deserving of punishment is due to their neglect of reflection on what was with them; their adherence to that neglect is what makes the laws that can only be known by revelation, and acting upon them is not valid except after faith. I say: the sending of the Messenger (ﷺ) is part of the admonition to reflection and of awakening from the sleep of heedlessness, lest they say, "We were heedless" (cf. al-Aʿrāf: 172). "Had You not sent to us a messenger to remind us to reflect upon the proofs of reason." The end of his statement. Muqatil said: the meaning is: We would not have destroyed them utterly in this world, according to what divine wisdom required, until We sent a messenger, to establish the proof against them and to cut off their excuse, as We did with ʿĀd, Thamūd, the overturned cities (al-Mu'tafikāt), and others.

(p-17) When He, exalted is He, mentioned that He does not punish anyone until He sends a messenger to them, He then explained the cause of their destruction, which is opposing the command of the Messenger (ﷺ) and persisting in corruption. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿And when We intend﴾ means at the time of destroying a people, when only a little of the time of their destruction remains." The end of his quotation. So "aradna" (We intended) is interpreted to mean "the time of their destruction drew near," and this is according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist school). The majority of readers recited "amarna" (We commanded). In this reading there are two opinions:

The first, which is the apparent meaning, is that it derives from "amr" (command), the opposite of "nahy" (prohibition). Scholars differed about its object. Most, including Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr, held that the sense is: "We commanded them to obey, but they disobeyed and transgressed." Al-Zamakhshari held that the sense is: "We commanded them to transgress, so they transgressed." He rejected those who said "We commanded them to obey," saying: "That is, We commanded them to transgress, so they did it. The command is metaphorical, because the literal sense of commanding them to transgress would be for Him to say to them: 'Transgress!' and this does not happen. (p-18) So it remains that it is metaphorical. The basis of the metaphor is that He poured blessings upon them abundantly, and they made them a means to sins and the pursuit of desires. So they are as though commanded to that, because bestowing blessing on them caused it. He only granted them these so that they would give thanks, do good with them, and be able to achieve benevolence and righteousness, just as He created them healthy and strong and made them able to do good and evil, and asked them to prefer obedience over disobedience. But they preferred transgression, and when they transgressed, the word became due against them, which is the word of punishment, and He destroyed them. If you say: 'Why not assume its meaning is: We commanded them to obey, so they transgressed?' I say: Because omitting what has no indication is not permissible, so how can one omit what the evidence stands against its opposite? The commanded object was omitted only because 'fasaqu' (they transgressed) indicates it, and this is a well-known usage. One says: 'I commanded him and he stood,' and 'I commanded him and he read,' and nothing is understood from it except that the commanded thing was standing or reading. If you try to supply something else, you have demanded of your listener knowledge of the unseen. This does not apply to their saying: 'I commanded him and he disobeyed me,' or 'he did not comply with my command,' because that contradicts the command and opposes it, and what opposes a command cannot be commanded. So it would be impossible for it to be intended at all so that it could be made to indicate the commanded thing. Therefore the commanded thing in this statement is neither indicated nor intended, because whoever speaks in this way does not intend for his command an object of command. He is as though saying: 'There was a command from me, but there was no obedience from him,' just as one who says: 'So-and-so gives, withholds, commands and forbids' does not intend a specific object. If you say: 'Could not the established knowledge that God does not command indecency, but commands justice and goodness, be evidence that the intended meaning is: We commanded them to goodness (p-19) ﴿so they transgressed﴾?' I say: That is not valid, because His saying ﴿so they transgressed﴾ contradicts it. It is as though you had displayed something while claiming to conceal its opposite. So directing the command to a metaphorical sense is the correct view." Ibn Abbas's view and that of the majority are the correct one. The verb "amara" (command) resembles "shaa" (He willed) in that its object is frequently omitted when indicated by what follows. You say: "If He had willed, He would have been kind to you," and "If He had willed, He would have harmed you," meaning: if He had willed kindness, and if He had willed harm. If you tried to conceal the opposite of what you stated, and said: "The state of the one to whom you attributed will indicates he is among the people of kindness or of harm, so leave the apparent words spoken and conceal what the state of the one who wills indicates," that would not be sound. End of quotation.

As for his metaphor, namely that "amarna mutrafiha" (We commanded its affluent ones) means "we poured blessings upon them abundantly," this is very far-fetched. As for his statement, "and He made them able to do good and evil," to the end, this is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. His statement "because omitting what has no indication is not permissible" is a reason that does not hold in the matter we are dealing with, since there is indeed something that indicates its omission. As for his statement "how can one omit what the evidence stands against its opposite," up to "knowledge of the unseen," we say: omission of a thing sometimes occurs due to an agreeing indication, such as the example he gave with "I commanded him and he stood" and "I commanded him and he read." Sometimes it occurs due to an indication of its opposite, its contrary, or its contradictory. Among this is His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever rests in the night and the day﴾ [al-An'am: 13]. They said: its meaning is "whatever rests and whatever moves." And His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81]. They said: "the heat and the cold." And the poet's words:

"I do not know, when I set out for a land, desiring good, which of the two will prevail over me:
Is it the good that I seek, or the evil that seeks me?"

Its sense: "I desire good and avoid evil." You say: "I commanded him and he did not do well," meaning not "I commanded him to not do well, and he did not do well," but rather "I commanded him to do well and he did not do well." This verse is of this kind: omission of the contradictory is inferred from the affirmation of its contradictory, and the contradictory's indication of the contradictory is like the analogue's indication of its analogue. Similarly, "I commanded him and he harmed me" does not mean "I commanded him to harm, and he harmed me." It is understood only as "I commanded him to do good, and he harmed me." As for his statement "it is not the case that this is said as 'I commanded him and he disobeyed me.'" We say: rather it is the case, and his statement "because that" means "because disobedience" opposes it, and this is a correct statement. As for his statement: "the commanded thing was neither indicated nor intended," this is not sound. Rather it is indicated and intended, not by the indication of the agreeing, but by the indication of the contradictory, as we have explained. As for his statement: "because whoever speaks this way does not intend for his command an object of command," this too is not sound. As for his answer to the objection, "because His saying ﴿so they transgressed﴾ contradicts it, as though you displayed something while claiming to conceal its opposite": we say, yes, he claims to conceal its opposite, and the contradictory indicates that. As for his statement: "the similarity of 'amara' to 'shaa' in that its object is frequently omitted": I say it is not similar to it, because the object of "amara" is not frequently omitted when indicated by what follows it. Rather, something like "shaa" is hardly used with its object omitted when indicated by what follows it, and its most common usage is with the object stated, since there is no indication of its omission. Almighty God says: ﴿Say: Indeed God does not command indecency﴾ [al-A'raf: 28]; ﴿To God belongs the command that you worship none but Him﴾ [Yusuf: 40]; ﴿Do their minds command them to this?﴾ [al-Tur: 32]; ﴿Say: My Lord has commanded justice﴾ [al-A'raf: 29]; ﴿Shall we prostrate to what you command us?﴾ [al-Furqan: 60]; that is, to it, and He does not command you to take the angels. The poet said:

"I commanded you to good, so do what you were commanded."

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "One may say that just as His saying 'I commanded him and he disobeyed me' shows that the commanded thing is other than transgression, because transgression is an expression for doing the opposite of what is commanded, so its being transgression contradicts its being commanded, just as its being disobedience contradicts its being commanded. Therefore this expression must indicate that the commanded thing is not transgression." This statement is most evident, and I do not know why the author of al-Kashshaf persisted in his view despite its evident error. Thus it is established that the truth is what they mentioned, namely that the meaning is: "We commanded them to righteous deeds, which are faith and obedience, but the people opposed that out of obstinacy and committed transgression." End of quotation.

The second opinion: that the meaning of "amarna" is "we multiplied," i.e., "We multiplied its affluent ones" (p-20). It is said: "Allah amara the people," meaning He multiplied them. Abu Hatim related this from Abu Zayd. Al-Wahidi said: "The Arabs say: 'amara the people' when they increased, and 'amarahum Allah' when He multiplied them." End of quotation. Abu Ali al-Farisi said: "The best interpretation of 'amarna' is that it means 'we multiplied.'" Abu Ubayda cited as evidence for the soundness of this usage what came in the hadith: "The best property is a straight-lined date-palm rich in fruit, and a mare that is multiplied in offspring" (khayr al-mal sikkatun ma'bura wa muhratun ma'mura), meaning abundant in offspring. It is said: "Allah amara the mare," meaning He multiplied her offspring. Whoever denies that "amara Allah al-qawm" means "He multiplied them" is not to be heeded, since this is established in the language. It belongs to the category of verbs that are intransitive and transitive with different vowels: one says "amara al-qawm" (the people increased) and "amarahum Allah" (God multiplied them). It is of the category of reflexive verbs: "amarahum Allah fa-amiru" (God multiplied them so they were multiplied), like your saying "shatara Allah 'aynahu fa-shutirat" (God split his eye so it was split) and "jada'a anfahu wa thalama sinnahu fa-thulimat" (he cut off his nose and broke his tooth so it was broken).

Al-Hasan, Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Ikrima recited "amirna" with a kasra on the mim, and al-Nahhas and the author of al-Lawami' related it from Ibn Abbas. Al-Farra' rejected this reading and said it is not to be heeded, since it is transmitted as a dialect like the fatha on the mim, and its meaning is "we multiplied." Abu Hatim related from Abu Zayd: "One says: 'amara Allah malahu' and 'amirahu,' meaning He multiplied his property, with kasra and fatha on the mim."

Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Raja', Isa ibn Umar, Sallam, Abdullah ibn Abi Yazid and al-Kalbi recited "amarna" with a long alif (ʾāmarnā). This is also transmitted from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, Abu al-Aliya, Ibn Hurmuz, Asim, Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr and Nafi', and it is the choice of Ya'qub. Its meaning is "we multiplied." It is said: "Allah amara the people and amarahum," so it is transitive by the hamza. Ibn Abbas, Abu Uthman al-Nahdi, al-Suddi, Zayd ibn Ali and Abu al-Aliya recited "ammarna" with a doubled mim (shadda), and this is related from Ali, al-Hasan, al-Baqir, Asim and Abu Amr. "Amara" is made transitive by doubling, and the meaning is also "we multiplied." "Ammarna" with doubling may also mean "we made them rulers and appointed them amirs (commanders)." The intransitive of this is "ummira fulan" when he became an amir, i.e., took charge of the affair. Abu Ali al-Farisi said: "There is no basis for taking 'amarna' to derive from 'imara' (rule), because their leadership would only be one after another, while destruction occurs during the period of one of them." What Abu Ali said does not necessarily follow, because we do not grant that the amir is the king. Rather, he is one who commands and is obeyed, and the Arabs call amir whoever is obeyed, even if he is not a king. And even if we grant that the king is meant, what he said does not follow, because when a town is ruled by an affluent person who then transgresses, and then another who transgresses, and so on, corruption multiplies and disbelief follows in succession, and destruction comes upon them through the last of their kings. I saw in a dream that I read, and it was recited in my presence: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We make its affluent ones amirs (ammarna mutrafiha)﴾ with doubling of the mim. So I said in the dream: "How eloquent this reading is!" The word that became due against them is the threat of God which their messenger had stated. It has also been said that the "word" is: "I will certainly fill (Hell)" [al-Sajda: 13], and "these are in the Fire and I do not care."

The destruction (al-tadmir) is annihilation (al-ihlak) together with the erasure of traces and the demolition of buildings. (Kam) is in the accusative position as the object of ahlakna, meaning: We destroyed many generations (al-qurun). Min al-qurun is an explanation (bayan) of kam and a specification (tamyiz) for it, just as a number is specified by its kind. The generations are 'Ad, Thamud and others. By destruction here he means destruction by punishment, and in this there is a threat and warning to the polytheists of Makkah. He said ﴿after Nuh﴾ and did not say "after Adam," because Nuh was the first prophet whose people went to the utmost extent in denying him, and his people were the first upon whom the greatest punishment fell, which is total annihilation by the flood. The discussion of the lifespan of a qarn (generation) has already been mentioned. The first min is for clarification (tabyin), and the second min is for the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah). Both are connected to ahlakna because their meanings differ.

Al-Hawfi said: ﴿min ba'di Nuh﴾ — the second min is a substitute (badal) for the first. End of quote. This is not good. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this ba' — meaning in (wa-kafa bi-rabbika) — usually comes in praise or dispraise. End of quote. (bi-dhunubi 'ibadihi) is a reminder that sins are the causes of destruction, and (khabiran basiran) is a reminder that He knows them and therefore punishes for them. (Bi-dhunub) may be connected to khabiran or to basiran. Al-Hawfi said: it is connected to kafa. End of quote. This is a mistake.

(Al-'ajilah) is the worldly life (al-dunya). Its meaning of desiring it is preferring it over the Hereafter, and there must be an omitted element indicated by the contrast in His words: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it its due striving, while being a believer﴾. So the estimate is: whoever was desiring the worldly life and striving for it its striving while being a disbeliever. It was also said: what is meant by ﴿whoever desires the worldly life﴾ is one who performs the deeds of the Hereafter for worldly ends, like the hypocrite, the show-off, the emigrant for worldly gain, and the fighter for spoils or fame. As he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever's emigration was for a worldly thing he would obtain, or a woman he would marry, his emigration is to what he emigrated for." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever seeks the worldly life by the deeds of the Hereafter, he will have no share in the Hereafter."

It was also said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, who used to fight alongside the Muslims for spoils, not for reward. (Min) is a conditional particle, and its response is ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will﴾, so the hastened portion is restricted by His will, meaning: what He wills to hasten. ﴿For whom We will﴾ is a substitute (badal) for (lahu), a substitute of part for whole (badal ba'd min kull), because the pronoun in (lahu) refers to the conditional man, which has the sense of plurality. But the pronouns here came according to the wording and not according to the meaning. So the hastened portion is restricted by His will, and so whoever desires the worldly life does not necessarily obtain what he desires. Do you not see that many people choose the worldly life, yet they obtain from it only what Allah has apportioned to them, and many of them wish for a little trifle and it is not obtained for them, and it gathers for them the misery of this world and the misery of the Hereafter.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (ma nasha'u) with the nun, and it is narrated from Nafi' ma yasha'u with the ya'. It was said: the pronoun in yasha' refers to Allah, and it is an instance of iltifat (a shift of grammatical person), so the reading with nun and with ya' are the same. It was also said: it may refer to the one to whom the pronoun in (lahu) refers, but this is not general; rather, he will only have what he wills in individual cases for which Allah wills it. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿for whom We will﴾ is to be estimated along with an omitted genitive construction indicated by what precedes it, meaning: for whom We will its hastening for him, that is, the hastening of what We will. Abu Ishaq al-Fazari said: the meaning is: for whom We will its ruin. What he said is not indicated by any word in the verse.

* *

(Ja'alna) means "made" (sayyarna). The first object is (jahannam) and the second is (lahu), because from them a subject and predicate are formed, so we say: Jahannam is for the disbelievers, just as these say the Fire is for them and those say Paradise is for them. (Yaslaha) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from jahannam. Abu al-Baqa' said: or from the pronoun in (lahu). The author of al-Ghuniyan said: the second object of (ja'alna) is omitted, its estimate being "a destination" (masiran) or "a recompense" (jaza'an). End of quote. (Madhmuman) indicates humiliation. (Madhhuran) indicates distance and expulsion from the mercy of Allah.

﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter﴾, meaning the reward of the Hereafter, by preferring it over the worldly life and fixing his intention upon it, (and strives) in what he is charged with of deeds and words, (its striving) meaning the striving prepared for salvation therein. (And he is a believer) is the greatest condition for salvation, so neither intention nor striving benefits except with its existence. In reality, faith is the source of the desire for the Hereafter, the striving for salvation therein, and the attainment of reward. It is reported from some earlier scholars: whoever does not have three things with him, his deed will not benefit him: firm faith, sincere intention, and correct action. And he recited this verse. ﴿Those﴾ refers to whoever possesses these qualities, and it took account of the meaning of man, so it came in the plural form. Allah the Exalted thanks them for their obedience, and He is the One thanked for what He has given of intellect, sending down books, clarifying proofs, and He is truly the one deserving thanks. The meaning of His thanking the obedient one is praising him and rewarding him for his obedience.

(Kullan) is in the accusative by (numiddu). Imdad is continuing to supply something. The meaning: each of the two groups (numiddu) — so al-Zamakhshari estimated it. They parsed (ha'ula'i) as a substitute (badal) for (kullan). It cannot be a substitute for kull on the estimate "each one," because then it would be a substitute of a part for a whole. So the estimate should be "all of the two groups," so that it becomes a substitute of whole for whole by way of detail. The apparent meaning is that this supplying is in provision in this world, and this is the interpretation of al-Hasan and Qatadah, meaning: Allah provides in this world both those who desire the worldly life, the disbelievers, and those who desire the Hereafter, the believers, and He supplies all with provision. Disparity only occurs in the Hereafter. This interpretation is supported by ﴿And the gift of your Lord was not restricted﴾, meaning: His provision is not narrowed for believer or disbeliever.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning of ﴿from the gift of your Lord﴾ is: from acts of obedience for one who desires the Hereafter, and from acts of disobedience for one who desires the worldly life. So the gift is an expression for what Allah has apportioned to the servant of good or evil, and the word "gift" is used for supplying with disobedience. The apparent meaning is that (unzur) is visual, because disparity in this world is observable. (Kayfa) is in the accusative position after the omission of the preposition, because "look" (nazara) takes it. So unzur here is suspended (mu'allaqah). Since looking leads to and is a cause of knowledge, it is permissible to suspend it. It is also possible that (unzur) is from the looking of thought, so there is no discussion about suspending it, since it is a verb of the heart. The preference here is an expression for the acts of obedience that lead to Paradise, and the ones preferred over are the disbelievers, as if it were said: look at the preference of one group over another. And on the first interpretation, it is as if it were said regarding the preference of one person over another among the believers and the disbelievers. The one preferred over in His words ﴿greater in degrees and greater in preference﴾ is omitted, its estimate being: of the degrees of this world and of the preference of this world.

It is reported that some of the nobles and those below them gathered at the door of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. Permission was granted to Bilal and Suhayb, and this was difficult for Abu Sufyan. Suhayl ibn 'Amr said: "We were only brought low from our side: they were called and we were called" — meaning to Islam — "they hastened and we delayed. This is the door of 'Umar, so how is there disparity in the Hereafter? If you envy them over the door of 'Umar, then what Allah has prepared for them in Paradise is greater." And it was read ﴿akthar﴾ with the thaa' (ath-thalatha). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: His words ﴿greater in degrees﴾ are not in the wording of any particular thing, but it is in the meaning, and ﴿greater in degrees﴾ must be from anything that is added, either by existence or by supposition. Some scholars held that these degrees and the preference are only among believers. Al-Tabari transmitted a hadith in this regard, its text: "Indeed the lowest of the people of Paradise in rank is like a star seen in the easts and wests of the earth, and Allah has been pleased with all of them, so none envies another."

The address in (la taj'al) is to the listener other than the Messenger. Al-Tabari and others said: the address is to Muhammad ﷺ, and what is meant is all creation. (Fa-taq'uda): al-Zamakhshari said: from the saying of them: "He sharpened the knife until it sat (qa'adat) as if it were a spear," meaning it became. He means: then you will become one who gathers upon himself blame and what follows it of ruin, of humiliation and abandonment, and inability to be helped by the one you made a partner with Him. End of quote. What he went to of using (fa-taq'uda) in the sense of "fa-tasir" is not permitted according to our companions (the Basran grammarians). (Qa'ada) in the sense of "sara" is restricted to the idiom. Al-Farra' held that making qa'ada to mean sara is regular, and he took as an example the verse of the rajaz poet:

Neither the henna nor the two necklaces nor the outer garment satisfies the girl,
Without the riders meeting, and the penis sitting (yaq'ud) with saliva on it.

Al-Kisa'i related: "qa'ada does not ask for a need except that he fulfills it," meaning sara. Al-Zamakhshari took in the verse the view of al-Farra'. Sitting here is an expression for remaining, meaning: he remains among people ﴿blamed, forsaken﴾, as you say of one who asks about the condition of a person: he is sitting in the worst condition, meaning he remains and abides, whether standing or sitting. Sitting may be meant literally, because it is characteristic of the blamed, forsaken one to sit bewildered and reflecting, and the predominant state, which is sitting, was used as the expression. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿fa-taq'uda﴾ is "then you will be incapable," as the Arabs say: "What has made you sit back (aq'adaka) from noble deeds?" The blame here is from Allah the Exalted, and from people of intellect, in that a person makes a log or a stone better than himself, singles it out for honor, attributes divinity to it, and associates it with Allah who created him, provided for him, and bestowed blessings upon him. Abandonment in this case is by Allah withdrawing His support, and He does not guarantee him victory. The forsaken one is one whom the one he loves to help does not help. ﴿Blamed, forsaken﴾ is in the accusative as circumstantial clauses (hal). According to al-Farra' and al-Zamakhshari, they are predicates of (taq'uda).

(Kullan), used for two masculine things, is dual in meaning by agreement, singular in wording according to the Basrans, on the pattern fa'l like ma'y, whose final radical is an alif transformed from waw according to most. Dual in wording according to the Kufans, and al-Suhayli followed them. So its alif is for the dual and is not a root letter, and its final radical is an omitted lam according to al-Suhayli, and there is no explicit statement from the Kufans regarding it. It is possible that it was originally formed on two letters according to the principle of their school. It is never separated from an attribution (idafah), and if it is attributed to an explicit noun, its alif remains in all the well-known dialects, while the Kinanah tribe treats it like the well-known dual; or if it is attributed to a pronoun, the well-known practice is to turn its alif into a ya' in the accusative and genitive, and the thing to which the dual is attributed is a dual or what has its meaning. Separation occurred in poetry with an attribution to an explicit noun. The Kufans preserved kilay and kilak (as forms of the dual) as stood. It is used as an appositive for emphasis, as a subject, in the accusative, and in the genitive. Its reference is treated like the singular, which is eloquent, and sometimes it is obligatory; and its reference is treated like the dual, which is rare, and sometimes it is obligatory.

(p-17) When He, exalted is He, mentioned that He does not punish anyone until He sends a messenger to them, He then explained the cause of their destruction, which is opposing the command of the Messenger (ﷺ) and persisting in corruption. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿And when We intend﴾ means at the time of destroying a people, when only a little of the time of their destruction remains." The end of his quotation. So "aradna" (We intended) is interpreted to mean "the time of their destruction drew near," and this is according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist school). The majority of readers recited "amarna" (We commanded). In this reading there are two opinions:

The first, which is the apparent meaning, is that it derives from "amr" (command), the opposite of "nahy" (prohibition). Scholars differed about its object. Most, including Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr, held that the sense is: "We commanded them to obey, but they disobeyed and transgressed." Al-Zamakhshari held that the sense is: "We commanded them to transgress, so they transgressed." He rejected those who said "We commanded them to obey," saying: "That is, We commanded them to transgress, so they did it. The command is metaphorical, because the literal sense of commanding them to transgress would be for Him to say to them: 'Transgress!' and this does not happen. (p-18) So it remains that it is metaphorical. The basis of the metaphor is that He poured blessings upon them abundantly, and they made them a means to sins and the pursuit of desires. So they are as though commanded to that, because bestowing blessing on them caused it. He only granted them these so that they would give thanks, do good with them, and be able to achieve benevolence and righteousness, just as He created them healthy and strong and made them able to do good and evil, and asked them to prefer obedience over disobedience. But they preferred transgression, and when they transgressed, the word became due against them, which is the word of punishment, and He destroyed them. If you say: 'Why not assume its meaning is: We commanded them to obey, so they transgressed?' I say: Because omitting what has no indication is not permissible, so how can one omit what the evidence stands against its opposite? The commanded object was omitted only because 'fasaqu' (they transgressed) indicates it, and this is a well-known usage. One says: 'I commanded him and he stood,' and 'I commanded him and he read,' and nothing is understood from it except that the commanded thing was standing or reading. If you try to supply something else, you have demanded of your listener knowledge of the unseen. This does not apply to their saying: 'I commanded him and he disobeyed me,' or 'he did not comply with my command,' because that contradicts the command and opposes it, and what opposes a command cannot be commanded. So it would be impossible for it to be intended at all so that it could be made to indicate the commanded thing. Therefore the commanded thing in this statement is neither indicated nor intended, because whoever speaks in this way does not intend for his command an object of command. He is as though saying: 'There was a command from me, but there was no obedience from him,' just as one who says: 'So-and-so gives, withholds, commands and forbids' does not intend a specific object. If you say: 'Could not the established knowledge that God does not command indecency, but commands justice and goodness, be evidence that the intended meaning is: We commanded them to goodness (p-19) ﴿so they transgressed﴾?' I say: That is not valid, because His saying ﴿so they transgressed﴾ contradicts it. It is as though you had displayed something while claiming to conceal its opposite. So directing the command to a metaphorical sense is the correct view." Ibn Abbas's view and that of the majority are the correct one. The verb "amara" (command) resembles "shaa" (He willed) in that its object is frequently omitted when indicated by what follows. You say: "If He had willed, He would have been kind to you," and "If He had willed, He would have harmed you," meaning: if He had willed kindness, and if He had willed harm. If you tried to conceal the opposite of what you stated, and said: "The state of the one to whom you attributed will indicates he is among the people of kindness or of harm, so leave the apparent words spoken and conceal what the state of the one who wills indicates," that would not be sound. End of quotation.

As for his metaphor, namely that "amarna mutrafiha" (We commanded its affluent ones) means "we poured blessings upon them abundantly," this is very far-fetched. As for his statement, "and He made them able to do good and evil," to the end, this is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. His statement "because omitting what has no indication is not permissible" is a reason that does not hold in the matter we are dealing with, since there is indeed something that indicates its omission. As for his statement "how can one omit what the evidence stands against its opposite," up to "knowledge of the unseen," we say: omission of a thing sometimes occurs due to an agreeing indication, such as the example he gave with "I commanded him and he stood" and "I commanded him and he read." Sometimes it occurs due to an indication of its opposite, its contrary, or its contradictory. Among this is His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever rests in the night and the day﴾ [al-An'am: 13]. They said: its meaning is "whatever rests and whatever moves." And His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81]. They said: "the heat and the cold." And the poet's words:

"I do not know, when I set out for a land, desiring good, which of the two will prevail over me:
Is it the good that I seek, or the evil that seeks me?"

Its sense: "I desire good and avoid evil." You say: "I commanded him and he did not do well," meaning not "I commanded him to not do well, and he did not do well," but rather "I commanded him to do well and he did not do well." This verse is of this kind: omission of the contradictory is inferred from the affirmation of its contradictory, and the contradictory's indication of the contradictory is like the analogue's indication of its analogue. Similarly, "I commanded him and he harmed me" does not mean "I commanded him to harm, and he harmed me." It is understood only as "I commanded him to do good, and he harmed me." As for his statement "it is not the case that this is said as 'I commanded him and he disobeyed me.'" We say: rather it is the case, and his statement "because that" means "because disobedience" opposes it, and this is a correct statement. As for his statement: "the commanded thing was neither indicated nor intended," this is not sound. Rather it is indicated and intended, not by the indication of the agreeing, but by the indication of the contradictory, as we have explained. As for his statement: "because whoever speaks this way does not intend for his command an object of command," this too is not sound. As for his answer to the objection, "because His saying ﴿so they transgressed﴾ contradicts it, as though you displayed something while claiming to conceal its opposite": we say, yes, he claims to conceal its opposite, and the contradictory indicates that. As for his statement: "the similarity of 'amara' to 'shaa' in that its object is frequently omitted": I say it is not similar to it, because the object of "amara" is not frequently omitted when indicated by what follows it. Rather, something like "shaa" is hardly used with its object omitted when indicated by what follows it, and its most common usage is with the object stated, since there is no indication of its omission. Almighty God says: ﴿Say: Indeed God does not command indecency﴾ [al-A'raf: 28]; ﴿To God belongs the command that you worship none but Him﴾ [Yusuf: 40]; ﴿Do their minds command them to this?﴾ [al-Tur: 32]; ﴿Say: My Lord has commanded justice﴾ [al-A'raf: 29]; ﴿Shall we prostrate to what you command us?﴾ [al-Furqan: 60]; that is, to it, and He does not command you to take the angels. The poet said:

"I commanded you to good, so do what you were commanded."

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "One may say that just as His saying 'I commanded him and he disobeyed me' shows that the commanded thing is other than transgression, because transgression is an expression for doing the opposite of what is commanded, so its being transgression contradicts its being commanded, just as its being disobedience contradicts its being commanded. Therefore this expression must indicate that the commanded thing is not transgression." This statement is most evident, and I do not know why the author of al-Kashshaf persisted in his view despite its evident error. Thus it is established that the truth is what they mentioned, namely that the meaning is: "We commanded them to righteous deeds, which are faith and obedience, but the people opposed that out of obstinacy and committed transgression." End of quotation.

The second opinion: that the meaning of "amarna" is "we multiplied," i.e., "We multiplied its affluent ones" (p-20). It is said: "Allah amara the people," meaning He multiplied them. Abu Hatim related this from Abu Zayd. Al-Wahidi said: "The Arabs say: 'amara the people' when they increased, and 'amarahum Allah' when He multiplied them." End of quotation. Abu Ali al-Farisi said: "The best interpretation of 'amarna' is that it means 'we multiplied.'" Abu Ubayda cited as evidence for the soundness of this usage what came in the hadith: "The best property is a straight-lined date-palm rich in fruit, and a mare that is multiplied in offspring" (khayr al-mal sikkatun ma'bura wa muhratun ma'mura), meaning abundant in offspring. It is said: "Allah amara the mare," meaning He multiplied her offspring. Whoever denies that "amara Allah al-qawm" means "He multiplied them" is not to be heeded, since this is established in the language. It belongs to the category of verbs that are intransitive and transitive with different vowels: one says "amara al-qawm" (the people increased) and "amarahum Allah" (God multiplied them). It is of the category of reflexive verbs: "amarahum Allah fa-amiru" (God multiplied them so they were multiplied), like your saying "shatara Allah 'aynahu fa-shutirat" (God split his eye so it was split) and "jada'a anfahu wa thalama sinnahu fa-thulimat" (he cut off his nose and broke his tooth so it was broken).

Al-Hasan, Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Ikrima recited "amirna" with a kasra on the mim, and al-Nahhas and the author of al-Lawami' related it from Ibn Abbas. Al-Farra' rejected this reading and said it is not to be heeded, since it is transmitted as a dialect like the fatha on the mim, and its meaning is "we multiplied." Abu Hatim related from Abu Zayd: "One says: 'amara Allah malahu' and 'amirahu,' meaning He multiplied his property, with kasra and fatha on the mim."

Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Raja', Isa ibn Umar, Sallam, Abdullah ibn Abi Yazid and al-Kalbi recited "amarna" with a long alif (ʾāmarnā). This is also transmitted from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, Abu al-Aliya, Ibn Hurmuz, Asim, Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr and Nafi', and it is the choice of Ya'qub. Its meaning is "we multiplied." It is said: "Allah amara the people and amarahum," so it is transitive by the hamza. Ibn Abbas, Abu Uthman al-Nahdi, al-Suddi, Zayd ibn Ali and Abu al-Aliya recited "ammarna" with a doubled mim (shadda), and this is related from Ali, al-Hasan, al-Baqir, Asim and Abu Amr. "Amara" is made transitive by doubling, and the meaning is also "we multiplied." "Ammarna" with doubling may also mean "we made them rulers and appointed them amirs (commanders)." The intransitive of this is "ummira fulan" when he became an amir, i.e., took charge of the affair. Abu Ali al-Farisi said: "There is no basis for taking 'amarna' to derive from 'imara' (rule), because their leadership would only be one after another, while destruction occurs during the period of one of them." What Abu Ali said does not necessarily follow, because we do not grant that the amir is the king. Rather, he is one who commands and is obeyed, and the Arabs call amir whoever is obeyed, even if he is not a king. And even if we grant that the king is meant, what he said does not follow, because when a town is ruled by an affluent person who then transgresses, and then another who transgresses, and so on, corruption multiplies and disbelief follows in succession, and destruction comes upon them through the last of their kings. I saw in a dream that I read, and it was recited in my presence: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We make its affluent ones amirs (ammarna mutrafiha)﴾ with doubling of the mim. So I said in the dream: "How eloquent this reading is!" The word that became due against them is the threat of God which their messenger had stated. It has also been said that the "word" is: "I will certainly fill (Hell)" [al-Sajda: 13], and "these are in the Fire and I do not care."

The destruction (al-tadmir) is annihilation (al-ihlak) together with the erasure of traces and the demolition of buildings. (Kam) is in the accusative position as the object of ahlakna, meaning: We destroyed many generations (al-qurun). Min al-qurun is an explanation (bayan) of kam and a specification (tamyiz) for it, just as a number is specified by its kind. The generations are 'Ad, Thamud and others. By destruction here he means destruction by punishment, and in this there is a threat and warning to the polytheists of Makkah. He said ﴿after Nuh﴾ and did not say "after Adam," because Nuh was the first prophet whose people went to the utmost extent in denying him, and his people were the first upon whom the greatest punishment fell, which is total annihilation by the flood. The discussion of the lifespan of a qarn (generation) has already been mentioned. The first min is for clarification (tabyin), and the second min is for the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah). Both are connected to ahlakna because their meanings differ.

Al-Hawfi said: ﴿min ba'di Nuh﴾ — the second min is a substitute (badal) for the first. End of quote. This is not good. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this ba' — meaning in (wa-kafa bi-rabbika) — usually comes in praise or dispraise. End of quote. (bi-dhunubi 'ibadihi) is a reminder that sins are the causes of destruction, and (khabiran basiran) is a reminder that He knows them and therefore punishes for them. (Bi-dhunub) may be connected to khabiran or to basiran. Al-Hawfi said: it is connected to kafa. End of quote. This is a mistake.

(Al-'ajilah) is the worldly life (al-dunya). Its meaning of desiring it is preferring it over the Hereafter, and there must be an omitted element indicated by the contrast in His words: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it its due striving, while being a believer﴾. So the estimate is: whoever was desiring the worldly life and striving for it its striving while being a disbeliever. It was also said: what is meant by ﴿whoever desires the worldly life﴾ is one who performs the deeds of the Hereafter for worldly ends, like the hypocrite, the show-off, the emigrant for worldly gain, and the fighter for spoils or fame. As he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever's emigration was for a worldly thing he would obtain, or a woman he would marry, his emigration is to what he emigrated for." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever seeks the worldly life by the deeds of the Hereafter, he will have no share in the Hereafter."

It was also said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, who used to fight alongside the Muslims for spoils, not for reward. (Min) is a conditional particle, and its response is ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will﴾, so the hastened portion is restricted by His will, meaning: what He wills to hasten. ﴿For whom We will﴾ is a substitute (badal) for (lahu), a substitute of part for whole (badal ba'd min kull), because the pronoun in (lahu) refers to the conditional man, which has the sense of plurality. But the pronouns here came according to the wording and not according to the meaning. So the hastened portion is restricted by His will, and so whoever desires the worldly life does not necessarily obtain what he desires. Do you not see that many people choose the worldly life, yet they obtain from it only what Allah has apportioned to them, and many of them wish for a little trifle and it is not obtained for them, and it gathers for them the misery of this world and the misery of the Hereafter.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (ma nasha'u) with the nun, and it is narrated from Nafi' ma yasha'u with the ya'. It was said: the pronoun in yasha' refers to Allah, and it is an instance of iltifat (a shift of grammatical person), so the reading with nun and with ya' are the same. It was also said: it may refer to the one to whom the pronoun in (lahu) refers, but this is not general; rather, he will only have what he wills in individual cases for which Allah wills it. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿for whom We will﴾ is to be estimated along with an omitted genitive construction indicated by what precedes it, meaning: for whom We will its hastening for him, that is, the hastening of what We will. Abu Ishaq al-Fazari said: the meaning is: for whom We will its ruin. What he said is not indicated by any word in the verse.

* *

(Ja'alna) means "made" (sayyarna). The first object is (jahannam) and the second is (lahu), because from them a subject and predicate are formed, so we say: Jahannam is for the disbelievers, just as these say the Fire is for them and those say Paradise is for them. (Yaslaha) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from jahannam. Abu al-Baqa' said: or from the pronoun in (lahu). The author of al-Ghuniyan said: the second object of (ja'alna) is omitted, its estimate being "a destination" (masiran) or "a recompense" (jaza'an). End of quote. (Madhmuman) indicates humiliation. (Madhhuran) indicates distance and expulsion from the mercy of Allah.

﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter﴾, meaning the reward of the Hereafter, by preferring it over the worldly life and fixing his intention upon it, (and strives) in what he is charged with of deeds and words, (its striving) meaning the striving prepared for salvation therein. (And he is a believer) is the greatest condition for salvation, so neither intention nor striving benefits except with its existence. In reality, faith is the source of the desire for the Hereafter, the striving for salvation therein, and the attainment of reward. It is reported from some earlier scholars: whoever does not have three things with him, his deed will not benefit him: firm faith, sincere intention, and correct action. And he recited this verse. ﴿Those﴾ refers to whoever possesses these qualities, and it took account of the meaning of man, so it came in the plural form. Allah the Exalted thanks them for their obedience, and He is the One thanked for what He has given of intellect, sending down books, clarifying proofs, and He is truly the one deserving thanks. The meaning of His thanking the obedient one is praising him and rewarding him for his obedience.

(Kullan) is in the accusative by (numiddu). Imdad is continuing to supply something. The meaning: each of the two groups (numiddu) — so al-Zamakhshari estimated it. They parsed (ha'ula'i) as a substitute (badal) for (kullan). It cannot be a substitute for kull on the estimate "each one," because then it would be a substitute of a part for a whole. So the estimate should be "all of the two groups," so that it becomes a substitute of whole for whole by way of detail. The apparent meaning is that this supplying is in provision in this world, and this is the interpretation of al-Hasan and Qatadah, meaning: Allah provides in this world both those who desire the worldly life, the disbelievers, and those who desire the Hereafter, the believers, and He supplies all with provision. Disparity only occurs in the Hereafter. This interpretation is supported by ﴿And the gift of your Lord was not restricted﴾, meaning: His provision is not narrowed for believer or disbeliever.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning of ﴿from the gift of your Lord﴾ is: from acts of obedience for one who desires the Hereafter, and from acts of disobedience for one who desires the worldly life. So the gift is an expression for what Allah has apportioned to the servant of good or evil, and the word "gift" is used for supplying with disobedience. The apparent meaning is that (unzur) is visual, because disparity in this world is observable. (Kayfa) is in the accusative position after the omission of the preposition, because "look" (nazara) takes it. So unzur here is suspended (mu'allaqah). Since looking leads to and is a cause of knowledge, it is permissible to suspend it. It is also possible that (unzur) is from the looking of thought, so there is no discussion about suspending it, since it is a verb of the heart. The preference here is an expression for the acts of obedience that lead to Paradise, and the ones preferred over are the disbelievers, as if it were said: look at the preference of one group over another. And on the first interpretation, it is as if it were said regarding the preference of one person over another among the believers and the disbelievers. The one preferred over in His words ﴿greater in degrees and greater in preference﴾ is omitted, its estimate being: of the degrees of this world and of the preference of this world.

It is reported that some of the nobles and those below them gathered at the door of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. Permission was granted to Bilal and Suhayb, and this was difficult for Abu Sufyan. Suhayl ibn 'Amr said: "We were only brought low from our side: they were called and we were called" — meaning to Islam — "they hastened and we delayed. This is the door of 'Umar, so how is there disparity in the Hereafter? If you envy them over the door of 'Umar, then what Allah has prepared for them in Paradise is greater." And it was read ﴿akthar﴾ with the thaa' (ath-thalatha). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: His words ﴿greater in degrees﴾ are not in the wording of any particular thing, but it is in the meaning, and ﴿greater in degrees﴾ must be from anything that is added, either by existence or by supposition. Some scholars held that these degrees and the preference are only among believers. Al-Tabari transmitted a hadith in this regard, its text: "Indeed the lowest of the people of Paradise in rank is like a star seen in the easts and wests of the earth, and Allah has been pleased with all of them, so none envies another."

The address in (la taj'al) is to the listener other than the Messenger. Al-Tabari and others said: the address is to Muhammad ﷺ, and what is meant is all creation. (Fa-taq'uda): al-Zamakhshari said: from the saying of them: "He sharpened the knife until it sat (qa'adat) as if it were a spear," meaning it became. He means: then you will become one who gathers upon himself blame and what follows it of ruin, of humiliation and abandonment, and inability to be helped by the one you made a partner with Him. End of quote. What he went to of using (fa-taq'uda) in the sense of "fa-tasir" is not permitted according to our companions (the Basran grammarians). (Qa'ada) in the sense of "sara" is restricted to the idiom. Al-Farra' held that making qa'ada to mean sara is regular, and he took as an example the verse of the rajaz poet:

Neither the henna nor the two necklaces nor the outer garment satisfies the girl,
Without the riders meeting, and the penis sitting (yaq'ud) with saliva on it.

Al-Kisa'i related: "qa'ada does not ask for a need except that he fulfills it," meaning sara. Al-Zamakhshari took in the verse the view of al-Farra'. Sitting here is an expression for remaining, meaning: he remains among people ﴿blamed, forsaken﴾, as you say of one who asks about the condition of a person: he is sitting in the worst condition, meaning he remains and abides, whether standing or sitting. Sitting may be meant literally, because it is characteristic of the blamed, forsaken one to sit bewildered and reflecting, and the predominant state, which is sitting, was used as the expression. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿fa-taq'uda﴾ is "then you will be incapable," as the Arabs say: "What has made you sit back (aq'adaka) from noble deeds?" The blame here is from Allah the Exalted, and from people of intellect, in that a person makes a log or a stone better than himself, singles it out for honor, attributes divinity to it, and associates it with Allah who created him, provided for him, and bestowed blessings upon him. Abandonment in this case is by Allah withdrawing His support, and He does not guarantee him victory. The forsaken one is one whom the one he loves to help does not help. ﴿Blamed, forsaken﴾ is in the accusative as circumstantial clauses (hal). According to al-Farra' and al-Zamakhshari, they are predicates of (taq'uda).

(Kullan), used for two masculine things, is dual in meaning by agreement, singular in wording according to the Basrans, on the pattern fa'l like ma'y, whose final radical is an alif transformed from waw according to most. Dual in wording according to the Kufans, and al-Suhayli followed them. So its alif is for the dual and is not a root letter, and its final radical is an omitted lam according to al-Suhayli, and there is no explicit statement from the Kufans regarding it. It is possible that it was originally formed on two letters according to the principle of their school. It is never separated from an attribution (idafah), and if it is attributed to an explicit noun, its alif remains in all the well-known dialects, while the Kinanah tribe treats it like the well-known dual; or if it is attributed to a pronoun, the well-known practice is to turn its alif into a ya' in the accusative and genitive, and the thing to which the dual is attributed is a dual or what has its meaning. Separation occurred in poetry with an attribution to an explicit noun. The Kufans preserved kilay and kilak (as forms of the dual) as stood. It is used as an appositive for emphasis, as a subject, in the accusative, and in the genitive. Its reference is treated like the singular, which is eloquent, and sometimes it is obligatory; and its reference is treated like the dual, which is rare, and sometimes it is obligatory.

(p-17) When He, exalted is He, mentioned that He does not punish anyone until He sends a messenger to them, He then explained the cause of their destruction, which is opposing the command of the Messenger (ﷺ) and persisting in corruption. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿And when We intend﴾ means at the time of destroying a people, when only a little of the time of their destruction remains." The end of his quotation. So "aradna" (We intended) is interpreted to mean "the time of their destruction drew near," and this is according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist school). The majority of readers recited "amarna" (We commanded). In this reading there are two opinions:

The first, which is the apparent meaning, is that it derives from "amr" (command), the opposite of "nahy" (prohibition). Scholars differed about its object. Most, including Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr, held that the sense is: "We commanded them to obey, but they disobeyed and transgressed." Al-Zamakhshari held that the sense is: "We commanded them to transgress, so they transgressed." He rejected those who said "We commanded them to obey," saying: "That is, We commanded them to transgress, so they did it. The command is metaphorical, because the literal sense of commanding them to transgress would be for Him to say to them: 'Transgress!' and this does not happen. (p-18) So it remains that it is metaphorical. The basis of the metaphor is that He poured blessings upon them abundantly, and they made them a means to sins and the pursuit of desires. So they are as though commanded to that, because bestowing blessing on them caused it. He only granted them these so that they would give thanks, do good with them, and be able to achieve benevolence and righteousness, just as He created them healthy and strong and made them able to do good and evil, and asked them to prefer obedience over disobedience. But they preferred transgression, and when they transgressed, the word became due against them, which is the word of punishment, and He destroyed them. If you say: 'Why not assume its meaning is: We commanded them to obey, so they transgressed?' I say: Because omitting what has no indication is not permissible, so how can one omit what the evidence stands against its opposite? The commanded object was omitted only because 'fasaqu' (they transgressed) indicates it, and this is a well-known usage. One says: 'I commanded him and he stood,' and 'I commanded him and he read,' and nothing is understood from it except that the commanded thing was standing or reading. If you try to supply something else, you have demanded of your listener knowledge of the unseen. This does not apply to their saying: 'I commanded him and he disobeyed me,' or 'he did not comply with my command,' because that contradicts the command and opposes it, and what opposes a command cannot be commanded. So it would be impossible for it to be intended at all so that it could be made to indicate the commanded thing. Therefore the commanded thing in this statement is neither indicated nor intended, because whoever speaks in this way does not intend for his command an object of command. He is as though saying: 'There was a command from me, but there was no obedience from him,' just as one who says: 'So-and-so gives, withholds, commands and forbids' does not intend a specific object. If you say: 'Could not the established knowledge that God does not command indecency, but commands justice and goodness, be evidence that the intended meaning is: We commanded them to goodness (p-19) ﴿so they transgressed﴾?' I say: That is not valid, because His saying ﴿so they transgressed﴾ contradicts it. It is as though you had displayed something while claiming to conceal its opposite. So directing the command to a metaphorical sense is the correct view." Ibn Abbas's view and that of the majority are the correct one. The verb "amara" (command) resembles "shaa" (He willed) in that its object is frequently omitted when indicated by what follows. You say: "If He had willed, He would have been kind to you," and "If He had willed, He would have harmed you," meaning: if He had willed kindness, and if He had willed harm. If you tried to conceal the opposite of what you stated, and said: "The state of the one to whom you attributed will indicates he is among the people of kindness or of harm, so leave the apparent words spoken and conceal what the state of the one who wills indicates," that would not be sound. End of quotation.

As for his metaphor, namely that "amarna mutrafiha" (We commanded its affluent ones) means "we poured blessings upon them abundantly," this is very far-fetched. As for his statement, "and He made them able to do good and evil," to the end, this is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. His statement "because omitting what has no indication is not permissible" is a reason that does not hold in the matter we are dealing with, since there is indeed something that indicates its omission.
