The meaning becomes: that one of the two parents reaches, or both of them reach ﴿عِنْدَكَ الْكِبَرَ﴾ (old age with you).

The answer to the condition is ﴿فَلَا تَقُلْ لَهُمَا أُفٍّ﴾ (then do not say to them, "Uff"). The meaning of the word *uff* has already been mentioned in the discussion of vocabulary and its dialects. Since He has forbidden addressing them with this word, which signals annoyance and exasperation with them, then forbidding what is worse, such as insulting or striking them, is a fortiori. The indication of *uff* does not signify the various kinds of harm by verbal indication (*dalāla lafẓiyya*), contrary to those who held that view.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "﴿أُفٍّ﴾ is a word of aversion. He, exalted is He, emphasised in His command concerning the parents, the use of gentle manners, lowering oneself, and tolerance, so that we do not say this word to them when we are annoyed, let alone anything more than it." Al-Qurtubi said: "Our scholars said: the word *uff* said to parents became the worst of things, because it rejects them in the manner of ingratitude for blessings, denies their upbringing, and rejects the command of God. *Uff* is a word transmitted for everything that is rejected. For this reason Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said: ﴿أُفٍّ لَكُمْ وَلِمَا تَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ﴾ (Uff to you and to what you worship besides God) [al-Anbiya': 67], meaning: rejection of you and of these idols with you." End of quotation.

The readings of *uff* vary. Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, 'Isa, Nafi' and Hafs read ﴿أُفٍّ﴾ with a kasra and shadda with tanwin. Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read it the same way without tanwin. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha and shadda without tanwin. Harun reported a reading with a damma and tanwin. Abu al-Sammal read *uffu* with a damma on the fa' and no tanwin. Zayd ibn 'Ali read *uffan* with a fatha, shadda and tanwin. Ibn 'Abbas read *uff* lightly. These are seven readings of the dialects that have been related for *uff*.

Mujahid said: "Its meaning is: if you see from them in old age the excrement and urine which they saw from you in childhood, do not be disgusted by them and say *uff*." End of quotation. But the verse is more general than that. When He forbade him to say to them what signifies "Am I annoyed by you?", He advanced to forbidding what is in its essence worse than *uff*, which is rebuking them. Although forbidding rebuking them is indicated by the forbidding of saying *uff*, because when the lesser is forbidden, the greater is forbidden a fortiori. The meaning is: do not reprimand them for what they do that does not please you. ﴿وَقُلْ لَهُمَا﴾ (and say to them), in place of *uff* and rebuking them, ﴿قَوْلًا كَرِيمًا﴾ (a generous word), that is, one combining excellence of goodness and beauty of expression.

Ibn al-Musayyab said: "It is the word of a servant who has done wrong to a harsh master." It was also said: ﴿قَوْلًا كَرِيمًا﴾ means "a beautiful word, as the excellence of good manners requires." 'Umar said: "That you say: O my father, O my mother." End of quotation. This is as Ibrahim addressed his father, "O my father" (*yā abati*), despite his disbelief. Do not call them by their names, because that is harshness and bad manners. There is no harm in it when it is not in the proper context, as 'A'isha said: "Abu Bakr gave me such-and-such (as a gift)."

When He, exalted is He, forbade him from a harmful word, and this did not necessarily entail a command to speak good words, He commanded him to say to them good, pleasing, and beautiful words, and that his speech should indicate their honour and veneration.

'Ata' said: "You speak with them on condition that you do not raise your gaze to them and do not fix your look on them, because that contradicts a generous word." Al-Zajjaj said: "a gentle, easy word with no harshness in it." Then God, exalted is He, commanded him to be extremely humble towards them by His words: ﴿وَاخْفِضْ لَهُمَا جَنَاحَ الذُّلِّ مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ﴾ (and lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy).

Al-Qaffal said, in explaining it, there are two views. The first: when a bird gathers its young to it for rearing, it lowers its wing for it, so lowering the wing is a metaphor for good management. It is as if it were said to the child: "Care for your parents by gathering them to yourself, as they did for you in your childhood." The second: when a bird wants to fly and rise, it spreads its wing, and when it wants to stop flying and rising, it lowers its wing, so lowering the wing becomes a metaphor for the act of humility in this respect. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is a metaphor, meaning: cut off from yourself the side of humility to them, and make yourself and your character gentle towards them. Humility is emphasised here, and it is not mentioned in His words ﴿وَاخْفِضْ جَنَاحَكَ لِمَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ (and lower your wing to those believers who follow you) [al-Shu'ara': 215], because of the greatness of the right (of the parents)." End of quotation. It is also because of the nobility of the one addressed, since it does not fit to attribute humility to him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the meaning of ﴿جَنَاحَ الذُّلِّ﴾ (the wing of humility)? I answer: there are two views. The first: that the meaning is 'lower your wing to them,' as He said: ﴿وَاخْفِضْ جَنَاحَكَ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ (and lower your wing to the believers) [al-Hijr: 88], and He attributed it to humility (*al-dhull*) or to *al-dhill* (abasement), as Hatim is attributed to generosity (*al-jūd*), meaning: lower to them your humble or humbled wing. The second: that He makes for their humility or abasement a lowered wing, as Labid made for the north wind a hand and for the cold a time, as an exaggeration in self-abasement and humility towards them." End of quotation. The meaning is that He made gentleness into humility and borrowed a wing for it, then reinforced this metaphor by commanding that it be lowered.

It is related that when Abu Tammam composed his line:

*"Do not give me the water of blame, for I am a lover who has found the water of my weeping sweet."*

a man came to him with a bowl and said, "Give me some of the water of blame." He said to him: "Not until you bring me a feather from the wing of humility."

The two wings of a person are his two sides. The meaning is: lower to them your side and do not raise it in the manner of an arrogant person towards them. One of the later scholars said well:

*"They clipped my wings, then wet them with dew, so I could not fly from their land."*

The majority read ﴿مِنَ الذُّلِّ﴾ [al-Isra': 111] with a damma on the dhal. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, al-Jahdari and Ibn Wathhab read it with a kasra on the dhal. This is a metaphor applied to people, because it is used of animals in the sense of the opposite of difficulty, just as *al-dhull* with a damma is the opposite of other people. It is evident that the *min* here is causal, meaning: what moves you to lower the wing is your mercy towards them, since they have become in need of you in old age, just as you were in need of them in childhood. Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ﴾ means "out of mercy," that is, out of gentleness towards them, so *min* is connected to *ikhfiḍ* (lower). It may also be a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from *janāḥ*. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*Min al-raḥma* here is explanatory of the genus, meaning: this lowering comes from the mercy that dwells in the soul, not that it is a mere performance. It is also possible that it indicates the starting point." End of quotation.

Then He, exalted is He, commanded him to pray to God that He show them His lasting mercy, since His mercy upon them does not last. Then He drew attention to the cause that makes kindness to them, goodness towards them, and seeking God's mercy for them necessary: their raising him when he was young. That state is one that increases his compassion and mercy towards them, since it reminds him of their kindness to him at a time when he could not do good for himself.

Qatada said: "God abrogated from this verse this phrase, meaning ﴿وَقُلْ رَبِّ ارْحَمْهُمَا﴾ (and say, 'My Lord, have mercy on them'), by His words: ﴿مَا كَانَ لِلنَّبِيِّ وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَنْ يَسْتَغْفِرُوا لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ (It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to seek forgiveness for the polytheists) [al-Tawba: 113]." It was also said that it is specific to the polytheists. It was also said: there is neither abrogation nor specification, because he may pray to God for his disbelieving parents for guidance and right direction, and may seek mercy for them after faith has been attained.

The apparent view is that the *kāf* in *kamā* is causal, meaning: "My Lord, have mercy on them because they raised me, and as a recompense for their kindness to me in my childhood and need." Al-Hawfi said: "The *kāf* is in the position of an accusative, an adjective for an omitted verbal noun, its sense being: mercy like my upbringing when I was young."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verse 23–31 (part 3 of 4):

Abu al-Baqa said: "(kama)" is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: mercy like their mercy (to me when I was young). Al-Zamakhshari and others related many hadiths and reports (athar) about being dutiful to one's parents, which can be found in their books. When Allah, exalted is He, forbade worshipping other than Him and commanded kindness to the two parents, especially in old age, and a person may display worship and kindness to his parents without true inner resolve, doing so out of showing off and seeking reputation, Allah, exalted is He, informed that He knows best what the hearts conceal, apart from intending the worship of Allah and kindness to parents. Then He said: ﴿If you are righteous﴾, that is, people of righteousness, and then some shortcoming in worship or dutifulness occurs from you, but you turn back to goodness, then indeed He is Forgiving of what has passed from your lapses. The apparent meaning is that this is general to everyone who has committed a wrong and then repented from it, and it includes one who wronged his parents and then repented of his wrong. Ibn Jubayr said: it refers to the case of a man who, out of rebellion (al-mubarazah) against his father, intends only good.

﴿And give the near relative his right, and the needy, and the wayfarer, and do not squander wastefully. Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils, and the devil has ever been ungrateful to his Lord.﴾ ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle word.﴾ ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched, lest you sit reproached and destitute. Indeed, your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it. Indeed, He is ever, of His servants, Aware and Seeing.﴾

When Allah commanded kindness to the two parents, He commanded maintaining ties of kinship. Al-Hasan said: it was revealed concerning the kin of the Messenger (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that it is addressed to the one addressed by His saying ﴿If one of them or both reach old age with you﴾, and here He includes what is required of maintaining ties of kinship, relieving need, and helping with wealth and support in every way when there is necessity (p-30). Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, al-Hasan and others said similarly. Ali ibn al-Husayn said concerning it: they are the kin of the Messenger (peace be upon him); He commanded giving them their rights from the public treasury (bayt al-mal). The apparent meaning is that "the right" here is general, and that "dhu al-qurba" is general to kinsfolk, so the determination of the right and the specification of kinsfolk is referred back to the Sunnah. From Abu Hanifa: if the relatives are unmarriageable kin (mahram), poor and unable to earn, and he is wealthy, their right is that he spend on them. According to al-Shafi'i: one spends on children and parents only, as established in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh).

Allah forbade wastefulness (al-tabdhir). The Jahiliyyah used to slaughter their camels and gamble for them (tayassara), and squander their wealth for boasting and reputation, and they would mention that in their poetry; so Allah forbade spending in other than the ways of righteousness and what brings one closer to Him. From Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas: wastefulness is spending wealth in what is not right. Mujahid said: even if one spent all his wealth in what is right, he would not be a squanderer. Al-Mawardi mentioned that it is extravagance that destroys wealth, and he argued from this verse for placing a restriction (hajr) on the wasteful; so it is obligatory upon the ruler to prevent him from it by restriction and by barring between him and his wealth, except for the amount of his family's maintenance. Abu Hanifa does not regard restriction for wastefulness, even though it is forbidden.

Al-Qurtubi said: he is restricted if he spends it on desires and there is fear that it will be exhausted; but if he spends and preserves the principal, he is not a squanderer. The "brotherhood" of the devils means that they are their companions in this world and in the Fire in the Hereafter. This brotherhood indicates that wastefulness is in disobedience to Allah, or that they obey them in what they command them of extravagance in this world. Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak read "ikhwan al-shaytan" in the singular, and it is likewise attested in the Mushaf of Anas. The disbelief of the devil towards his Lord is mentioned so that he may be warned against and not obeyed, since he does not call to anything good, as He said: ﴿He only calls his party that they may be among the companions of the Blaze﴾ [Fatir: 6].

﴿And if you turn away﴾. It is said: it was revealed concerning some people of Muzaynah who asked the Messenger to provide them with mounts, and he said: "I do not find anything to carry you upon." So they wept. It was also said: concerning Bilal, Suhayb, Salim and Khabbab, who asked him for what he did not have, so he turned away from them. It is related that after the revelation of this verse, whenever he did not have anything to give and was asked, he (peace be upon him) would say: "May Allah provide for us and for you from His bounty." So the "mercy" here is the awaited provision, and this is the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ikrimah. Ibn Zayd said: "mercy" means reward and recompense, and the verse was revealed concerning people who used to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and he would refuse to give them, because he knew they would spend the wealth in corruption; so he turned away from them, and sought reward in withholding from them, lest he assist them in their corruption; so Allah commanded him to say to them: ﴿a gentle word﴾, which includes supplication for them for opening (provision) and rectification. End of Ibn Atiyyah's words.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "And if you turn away from the near relative, the needy and the wayfarer out of shame at refusing, then say to them a gentle word, and do not leave them unanswered when they ask you. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked for something he did not have, he would turn away from the petitioner and remain silent out of modesty. It may also be that the meaning of ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾ is: even if you do not benefit them and raise their poverty due to lack of ability; and the turning away is not intended literally with the face, but as a metaphor for turning away from that, since whoever refuses to give turns away with his face." End of quotation. What appears is that when Allah commanded giving the near relative his right and those mentioned with him, and forbade him from wastefulness, He said: "And if there is no turning away from them on your part, then the pronoun refers to them." He gave as the reason for turning away the seeking of mercy, which is a metaphor for provision and ease; and seeking that arises from lacking what one could bestow on one who asks. It is as if the meaning is: "And if you turn away from them due to your hardship," so He placed the effect, which is seeking mercy, in place of the cause, which is hardship. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that ﴿seeking mercy from your Lord﴾ be a reason for the answer of the conditional, so it is connected to it and placed before it, meaning: "then say to them an easy, gentle word, promise them a good promise, out of mercy to them and to comfort their hearts, seeking mercy from your Lord," that is: seek the mercy of Allah which you hope for through your mercy towards them. End of quotation. What he permitted is not permissible, because what follows the response particle (fa’) does not operate on what precedes it; it is not allowed in your saying: "in yaqum fa-idrib Khalidan" to say "in yaqum Khalidan fa-idrib." This is explicitly stated. If you omit the fa’ in a case like "in yaqum yadrib Khalidan," the view of Sibawayh and al-Kisa'i is that it is permitted, so you say "in yaqum Khalidan nadrib." The view of al-Farra' is that it is prohibited. If the verb's object is in the nominative, as in "in taf'al yaf'al Zaydun," then it is not permissible to place Zayd before "yaf'alu" so as to be nominative by it. Sibawayh permitted that it be nominative by a verb which "yaf'alu" explains, as if you said: "in taf'al yaf'al Zaydun yaf'alu." Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' prohibited that.

Ibn Jubayr said: the pronoun in ("anhum") refers to the polytheists, and the meaning of ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾ is: because of their denial of you, seeking mercy, that is, victory for you over them, or guidance from Allah for them. According to this view, "maysur" is: placating them with the tongue; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. "Yassara" may be intransitive and transitive, so "maysur" is from the transitive; you say: "yassartu laka kadha" when you prepare it for him. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is said "yasara al-amr wa 'asara," like "sa'ada and nahasa," so it is a passive participle (maf'ul). End of quotation.

To the meaning of this verse the poet alluded in the poem called "al-Yatimah," in his saying:

"Let there be for the petitioner some relief from you; if there is none, let the refusal be made graceful."

And another said:

"If there is no silver one day that I may give to the petitioners, then I am gentle in disposition.
The petitioners shall not lack good from my character: either my giving, or the goodness of my refusal."

﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾, the verse. It is said: it was revealed concerning his (ﷺ) giving away his shirt when he had no other, and he remained naked. It is also said: he gave al-Aqra' ibn Habis one hundred camels, and Uyaynah the same, and al-Abbas ibn Mirdas fifty, then completed it to one hundred, and then this verse was revealed. This is a metaphor in which the perceptible is borrowed for the intelligible: stinginess is a quality present in a person that prevents him from disposing of his wealth, so the chain (ghull), which is the joining of the hand to the neck, is borrowed for it, so the hand is prevented from its action and from moving about as it wishes. He mentioned the hand because by it one takes and gives. Extending the hand is borrowed for the squandering of wealth, since gripping the hand holds what is in it, and extending it releases what is in it. In the metaphor he matched between the extending of the hand and its gripping in meaning, because making the hand chained is its gripping, and chaining is more emphatic in gripping. Abu Tammam matched between these two as well, saying concerning al-Mu'tasim:

"He became accustomed to extending the palm, so that if he folded it for gripping, his fingertips would not respond to it."

Al-Zamakhshari said: this is an illustration of the withholding of the miser and the giving of the spendthrift, and a command to moderation which lies between extravagance and niggardliness. End of quotation. The apparent meaning is that the address is intended for the community of the Messenger (ﷺ); otherwise he (ﷺ) did not store anything for the morrow, and likewise whoever trusted in Allah with true trust, like Abu Bakr when he gave away all his wealth in charity. Ibn Jurayj and others said: the meaning is: do not withhold from spending in what I have commanded you of right, and do not extend it in what I have forbidden you from. It was related from Qalun: "kulla al-bass" with the sad, and "fa-taq'uda" is the answer to both states according to the two conditions; so "malum" refers to His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand﴾. As the poet said:

"Indeed the miser is blameworthy wherever he is, but the generous, despite his faults, is ever enduring."

And "mahsur" refers to His saying ﴿nor extend it fully outstretched﴾, as if it was said: "then you will be blamed and left regretful." Then Allah, exalted is He, consoled him for what he used to suffer from poverty, by saying that this is not out of contempt for him from Him, nor out of stinginess towards him from Him; rather, because the expansion and restriction of provision are only by His will and desire, according to what He knows of the benefit for His servants in it. Or the meaning may be: restriction and expansion are from the will of Allah; as for you, it is incumbent upon you to be moderate. He concluded this with His saying "Khabiran," which is knowledge of hidden matters, and "Basiran," that is, of the interests of His servants, in that He expands for some people and restricts for others.

﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for them and for you. Indeed, their killing is ever a great sin.﴾

When Allah, exalted is He, explained that He is the one who undertakes the provision of the servants, saying ﴿Indeed your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts﴾, He followed it with the prohibition of killing children. The explanation of a parallel to this verse has already been mentioned, and the difference between ﴿for fear of poverty﴾ and ﴿out of poverty﴾ [al-An'am: 151], and between His saying "We provide for them" and "We provide for you." Al-A'mash and Ibn Thabit read "wa-la tuqattilu" with doubling. "Khashyah" was read with a kasra on the kha'. The majority read "khit'an" with a kasra on the kha' and sukun on the ta'; Ibn Kathir read it with a kasra and a fatha on the ta' with madd, and this is the reading of Talhah, Shibl, al-A'mash, Yahya, Khalid ibn Ilyas, Qatadah, al-Hasan and al-A'raj with a variant from them. Al-Nahhas said: I do not know a valid basis for this reading, and therefore Abu Hatim considered it an error. Al-Farisi said: it is a verbal noun from "khata'a yukhti'u," though we have not found "khata'a," but we have found "takhata'a," which is its reflexive form, and he pointed to it with the saying of the poet:

"I dodged the arrow, fearing it, and my day was delayed, so it did not hasten."

And the saying of another about a truffle:

"The hunter missed it (takhata'ahu) until I found it, and its snout was sunk in the stagnant water."

So these people who kill their children were sinning against the truth and justice.

Ibn Dhakwan read "khata'an" (خَطَأً) on the pattern of "naba'" (نَبَأٍ). Al-Hasan read "khata'an" (خَطاءً) with both letters vowelled with a fatha and with a long vowel (madd), taking it as an ism al-masdar (verbal noun) from akhta'a, like "ata'" (العَطاءُ) from a'ta, as Ibn Jinni said. Abu Hatim said: "This is an error that is not permissible, and this is not known in the language." He also reported from him (i.e. al-Hasan) "khata" (خَطى) on the pattern of "hawa" (هَوى), lightening the hamza so it became an alif and was dropped because of the meeting of the two alifs (of the long vowel and the lightened hamza).

Abu Raja' and al-Zuhri read it likewise, except that they both pronounced the kha' with a kasra, so it became like "riba" (رِبًا). Both come from khati'a in religion (خَطِئَ فِي الدِّينِ) and akhta'a in opinion (أخْطَأ فِي الرَّأْيِ), but each of the two may stand in place of the other.

Ibn 'Amir's reading is also transmitted as "khat'an" (خَطْأً) with a fatha and a short vowel, with the ta' sukun, and this is a third verbal noun from khati'a with a kasra (on the ع-form, khati'a).

(p-23) ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be good to your parents. Whether one or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them, "Uff," and do not repel them, but speak to them a noble word.﴾ ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy, and say, "My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small."﴾ ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls. If you are righteous, then indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back (to Him).﴾ ﴿And give the near relative his right, and the needy, and the wayfarer, and do not squander wastefully.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils, and Satan has ever been ungrateful to his Lord.﴾ ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle word.﴾ ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched, lest you sit down blamed and destitute.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it. Indeed, He is ever, regarding His servants, All-Aware and All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for them and for you. Indeed, killing them is ever a great sin.﴾ ﴿And do not approach adultery. Indeed, it is ever an abomination and an evil way.﴾ [Al-Isra: 32] ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right. And whoever is killed unjustly, We have given his heir authority, but let him not exceed bounds in killing. Indeed, he is ever supported.﴾ [Al-Isra: 33] ﴿And do not approach the property of an orphan except in the best manner, until he reaches maturity. And fulfill (every) covenant. Indeed, the covenant is ever questioned.﴾ [Al-Isra: 34] ﴿And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with an accurate balance. That is best and best in result.﴾ [Al-Isra: 35] ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart, about all of those one will be questioned.﴾ [Al-Isra: 36] ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly. Indeed, you will never tear through the earth, nor will you reach the mountains in height.﴾ [Al-Isra: 37] ﴿All of that - its evil is detestable in the sight of your Lord.﴾ [Al-Isra: 38] ﴿That is from what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom. And do not make with Allah another deity, lest you be thrown into Hell, blamed and banished.﴾ [Al-Isra: 39] ﴿Has your Lord then favored you with sons and taken for Himself daughters from the angels? Indeed, you are saying an enormous saying.﴾ [Al-Isra: 40] ﴿And We have certainly varied in this Qur'an that they may be reminded, but it increases them only in aversion.﴾ [Al-Isra: 41] ﴿Say, "If there were with Him other gods, as they say, they would have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne."﴾ [Al-Isra: 42] ﴿Exalted is He, and high above what they say, by a great elevation.﴾ [Al-Isra: 43] ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them exalt Him. And there is not a thing except that it exalts Him with His praise, but you do not understand their exaltation. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving.﴾ [Al-Isra: 44] ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier.﴾ [Al-Isra: 45] ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness. And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn back on their heels in aversion.﴾ [Al-Isra: 46] ﴿We are most knowing of what they listen to when they listen to you, and when they are in private conference, when the wrongdoers say, "You follow not but a man affected by magic."﴾ [Al-Isra: 47] ﴿Look how they strike for you comparisons, so they have strayed and cannot find a way.﴾ [Al-Isra: 48] ﴿And they say, "When we are bones and crumbled dust, will we indeed be resurrected in a new creation?"﴾ [Al-Isra: 49] ).

﴿Uff﴾ is an ism al-fi'l (a verb-noun, a word functioning as a verb) meaning "I am annoyed." Verb-nouns with the meaning of the present tense are rare, except for words such as uff and awwah, meaning "I am in pain." By analogy it should not be indeclinable (mabni), since it does not occupy a position of an indeclinable word. Al-Zanati in his book Al-Hulal mentions that uff has about forty dialectal forms, and we list them as we have seen them, vocalized: uffa, uffi, uffu, uff-a (doubled), uffin, uffun, uffan, uffin, uffun, uffan, uffin, uffun, uff, uff'a, uffa (with no imala), uffiyy (with full imala), uffiyy (with intermediate imala), uffiy, uffuw, uffahu, uffihi, uffuhu. This makes twenty-two, together with the initial hamza vocalized with a damma: ifa, ifi, ifu, iffa, iffi, iffan, ifin, ifun, ifan, iffiy (with imala), iffa. These are eleven, together with the initial hamza vocalized with a kasra: af, afun, aafun, aafin, aaffa. Ibn 'Atiyya mentions uffah with the silent ha' (ha' al-sakt), which completes the forty.

al-Nahr: rebuking with shouting and harshness. Al-Askari said: its root meaning is "to appear," from which come nahr and intihar (to rebuke), and anhara al-dam (he made the blood appear and flow), and intahara al-rajul (he displayed contempt for him by harsh and vile rebuke and expulsion). Ibn 'Atiyya said: intihar is displaying anger in voice and speech. al-Zamakhshari said: nahy (prohibiting), nahr (rebuking), and nahm (scolding) are siblings.

al-Tabdhir: extravagance. Abu 'Ubayda said it means extravagance in spending. Its root meaning is scattering, and from it the seed is called badhr (seed), because it is scattered in the field. The poet said:

*Ta'a'ib yastadi'u al-halyu fiha / ka-jamri al-nari budhdha bi-l-dhalam*
(Breasts in which the jewelry shines, like embers of fire scattered in the darkness.)

It is also narrated as *budedda*, meaning scattered.

al-Mahsur: al-Farra' said: the Arabs say, "a camel is mahsur" when its journey is cut off, and "the animal became hasir" when its journey was ended. It is said: hasir, a form meaning maf‘ul (passive), and its plural is hasra. The poet said:

*Bi-ha judhayfu al-hasra fa-amma 'izamuha / fa-bidun wa-amma jiladuha fa-saliab*
(In it are the carcasses of the exhausted; as for their bones, they are white, and as for their hides, they are hard.)

al-Qistas: with a damma or kasra on the qaf, and with the first sin or the sad. Mu'arrij al-Sadusi said: it is the balance in the language of the Romans. The statements of the commentators concerning it will come.

al-Maraḥ: extreme joy. It is said: marija yamrahu maraḥan. al-Tul: the opposite of short, and from it comes al-tul as opposed to al-'ard (width). al-Hijab: that which screens a thing from reaching it. al-Rufat: al-Farra' said: dust. It is said: that which is pounded thoroughly until it crumbles. It is said: rafata al-shay' (he broke it), yarfituhu, with kasra. Al-rufat are the crumbling fragments of any broken thing. The form fu'al is a pattern for this meaning, like hutam, futat, rudad, and diqaq.

(p-23) ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be good to your parents. Whether one or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them, "Uff," and do not repel them, but speak to them a noble word.﴾ ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy, and say, "My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small."﴾ ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls. If you are righteous, then indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back (to Him).﴾.

(p-25) The majority of readers recite (*wa-qada*) as a past-tense verb from qada'. Some of the offspring of Mu'adh ibn Jabal recite *wa-qada'u Rabbika*, with the verbal noun of *qada* in the nominative as a subject, and (*an la ta'budu*) as the predicate. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud and his companions, and Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Nakha'i, and Maymun ibn Mihran, it is read as *wa-wassa* (and commanded) from al-tawsiya. Some recited *wa-awsa* from al-iy'a'. That reading should be interpreted accordingly, because it is a reading that differs from the consonantal text of the codex, whereas the widely transmitted reading is *wa-qada*, which is well known from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, and others in the chains of the seven readers.

Here, *qada* is interpreted by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Qatada as "commanded." Ibn Mas'ud and his companions said it means "enjoined." It is also said: "obligated and required," and "judged." It is also said: "decided firmly." Ibn 'Atiyya said: I say, the meaning of *Wa-qada Rabbuka* is His command, *an la ta'budu illa iyyahu*. These words contain nothing but a command to restrict worship to Allah, and that is what is decreed, not worship itself, and what is decreed here is the command. End of quote. It seems he wanted to leave *qada* in its well-known sense of "decreed," so he made its object the command to worship rather than worship itself, because it is not correct to decree something in the sense of determining it without its occurring. What the commentators understood, other than this, is that the object of *qada* is *an la ta'budu* (that you not worship), whether *an* is explanatory or verbal. Abu al-Baqa' said: it may be in the accusative position, meaning: your Lord has obligated His worship, and *la* is extra. End of quote. This is an error, because *illa* enters upon the object of *ta'budu*, so it must be negated or prohibited, and the address in *la ta'budu* is general to all creation.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is also possible that *qada* is in its well-known usage in speech, and the pronoun in *ta'budu* refers to believers among people until the Day of Resurrection. End of quote.

al-Hawfi said: the *ba'* is connected to *qada*. It may also be connected to a deleted verb, its estimated form being *wa-awsa* (and He commanded), *bi-al-walidayn ihsanan* (good treatment to the parents). *Ihsanan* is a verbal noun, meaning: you should show goodness, *tuhsinu ihsanan*. Ibn 'Atiyya said: His statement *wa-bi-al-walidayni ihsanan* is conjoined to the first *an*, meaning: Allah commanded *an la ta'budu illa iyyahu* and that you be good *bi-al-walidayni ihsanan*. On this possibility we mentioned, *wa-bi-al-walidayni ihsanan* is cut off from the first, as if He informed them of Allah's decree and then commanded them to be good to their parents. al-Zamakhshari said: the *ba'* in *bi-al-walidayn* may not be connected to *ihsan*, because the verbal noun cannot have its complement precede it. al-Wahidi in al-Basit said: the *ba'* in His statement *bi-al-walidayn* is part of the complement of *ihsan*, and it has been placed before it, as you say: *bi-Zaydin fa-mrur* (pass by Zayd). End of quote.

*Ahsana* and *asa'a* are transitive with *ila* and with *ba'*. Allah says: ﴿And He has been good to me﴾ [Yusuf: 100]. The poet said:

*Asii'i bina aw ahsini la malumata*
(Mistreat us or be good to us, there is no blame.)

It seems *ahsana* was taken to include the meaning of *lataffa* (to be kind), so it was followed by *ba'*. If *ihsanan* is a verbal noun, it resolves to *an* and a verb, so it is not permitted to place its complement before it. If it means *ahsinu* (be good!), then it is a substitute for the verb's own word, like *darban Zaydan*, so it is permitted to place its object before it. What we choose is that *an* is an explanatory particle, *la ta'budu* is a prohibition, and *ihsanan* is a verbal noun with the meaning of a command, conjoined to the prohibition, as in:

*Yaqulna la tahlik asan wa-tajammal*
(They say, "Do not perish from grief, and be patient.")

The command to good treatment of parents is emphasized by its juxtaposition with *la ta'budu*, and by putting the parents first, which is an emphasis on them. The reason for linking good treatment of parents with the singling out of Allah in worship is that He, exalted is He, is the true originator, while the parents are an intermediary in bringing a person into being, and He, exalted is He, is the bestower of blessing by creating and providing, while they strive for his welfare.

al-Zamakhshari said: *Imma* is the conditional particle, to which *ma* was added for emphasis, and therefore the emphatic *nun* enters the verb. If it were used alone, that would not be correct. You do not say, *in tukrimanna Zaydan yukrimka*, but you say *imma tukrimannahu*. End of quote. What he mentioned is contrary to the position of Sibawayh, because his view is that it is permitted to combine *imma* with the emphatic *nun*, to bring *an* alone with the emphatic *nun*, and to bring *imma* alone without the emphatic *nun*. Sibawayh said regarding this issue: If you wish, you do not insert the *nun*, just as if you wish you do not bring what is meant with or without the *nun*. *Indan* is an adverbial complement governed by *yablughanna*. The meaning of *indiyya* here is that they are with him in his house and in his care, with no guardian for them other than him, because of their old age and weakness, and because they are a burden upon him. *Ahadu huma* is the subject of *yablughanna*, and *aw kilahuma* is conjoined to *ahadu huma*.

(p-26) and their being placed first is an emphasis on them over the statement *ihsanan*.

(p-24) ﴿And give the near relative his right, and the needy, and the wayfarer, and do not squander wastefully.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils, and Satan has ever been ungrateful to his Lord.﴾ ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle word.﴾ ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched, lest you sit down blamed and destitute.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it. Indeed, He is ever, regarding His servants, All-Aware and All-Seeing.﴾

Note: The rest of the text is in its original form and is included in the translation above.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on surah 17, verses 23–31 (part 2 of 4):

The majority of reciters read ﴿إِمَّا يَبْلُغَنَّ﴾ (*yablughanna*) with the heavy emphatic nun (*nun al-tawkid*, the emphatic nun that adds certainty to the verb), and the verb is attributed to *aḥaduhumā* (one of them). Ibn Dhakwan is reported to have read it with the light emphatic nun. The two brothers (Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i, or, in some transmissions, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim) read ﴿إِمَّا يَبْلُغَانِّ﴾ (*yablughānni*), with the dual alif and the heavy emphatic nun. This is also the reading of al-Sulami, Ibn Wathhab, Ṭalḥa, al-A'mash and al-Jahdari. Some have said that the alif is a sign of the dual and not a pronoun, following the dialect in which one says *akalūnī al-barāghīth* ("the fleas ate me"). On this view *aḥaduhumā* is the subject, and *aw kilāhumā* (or both of them) is coordinated with it. This is not permissible, because the condition for a subject of a verb carrying the dual sign is that the subject be a dual noun or be defined by coordination with *wa* (and). Compare *qāmā akhawāka* ("your two brothers stood up") or *qāmā Zaydun wa 'Amrun* ("Zayd and 'Amr stood up"). There is a disagreement over whether the last of these is permissible, and the correct view is that it is. But *aḥaduhumā* is neither a dual nor defined by *wa* with a singular.

Others have said that the alif is a pronoun referring to the two parents, that *aḥaduhumā* is a substitute (*badal*, a noun that replaces the pronoun it follows) for the pronoun, and that *kilāhumā* is coordinated with *aḥaduhumā*, so that what is coordinated with a substitute is itself a substitute.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say, 'If both of them reach old age,' with *kilāhumā* placed after the verb, then *kilāhumā* would be an emphasis (*tawkid*, a noun that reinforces the word before it) and not a substitute. Why then do you claim it is a substitute?" I say: "Because it is coordinated with something that cannot be an emphasis, so it falls under the same ruling and must be like it." You may ask: "What harm is there if you make it an emphasis while the item it is coordinated with is a substitute, and you coordinate the emphasis with the substitute?" I answer: "If the intention had been to emphasise the dual, one would have said *kilāhumā* alone. But since it was said ﴿أَحَدُهُمَا أَوْ كِلَاهُمَا﴾ (either of them or both of them), it is known that emphasis is not intended, so it is a substitute like the first."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "On this third reading, *yablughānni*, *aḥaduhumā* is a substitute for the pronoun in *yablughānni*, and it is a *badal muqassam*, a 'divided' substitute, like the verse of the poet:

*"I was like one with two legs: one healthy, and the other, which time has struck, is paralysed."*"

End of quotation. It follows from his words that *kilāhumā* is coordinated with *aḥaduhumā*, which is a substitute, and what is coordinated with a substitute is a substitute. The substitute is problematic here, because if *aḥaduhumā* is a substitute for the pronoun, it can only be a substitute of part for whole (*badal ba'ḍ min kull*). If you coordinate *kilāhumā* with it, it cannot be a substitute of part for whole, because *kilāhumā* is equivalent to the pronoun in terms of duality, so it cannot be a substitute of part for whole. Nor can it be a substitute of whole for whole (*badal kull min kull*), because what the pronoun conveys is duality, and that is also what *kilāhumā* conveys, so the substitute adds nothing beyond the item it replaces.

As for Ibn 'Atiyya's words "it is a divided substitute like the verse of the poet, 'I was like one with two legs,'" this is not a *badal al-taqsim* (divided substitute), because the condition for that is coordination with *wa*. Also, in a divided substitute the item substituted must not apply to one of its two divisions, whereas *kilāhumā* applies to the pronoun which is the item substituted, so it is not one of the divisions.

It is reported from Abu 'Ali that *kilāhumā* is an emphasis. This is not complete except by parsing *aḥaduhumā* as a substitute of part for whole, and supposing after it a verb that takes the pronoun as its subject, with *kilāhumā* as an emphasis of that pronoun. The sense would be *aw yablughā kilāhumā* (or both of them reach), but this involves omitting the item being emphasised. Sibawayh and al-Khalil permitted this. Al-Khalil said: "I passed by Zayd and his brother himself (*ṣāḥibāya anfusuhumā*) with a nominative or accusative." The nominative reads as "my two companions, themselves," and the accusative as "their eyes, themselves." However, what is reported from Abu 'Ali, Ibn Jinni and al-Akhfash before them is that it is not permissible to omit the item being emphasised and put the emphasis in its place.

What we choose is that *aḥaduhumā* is a substitute for the pronoun, and *kilāhumā* is in the nominative by a verb omitted in the sense "or both of them reach" (*aw yablugha kilāhumā*). Thus it is a coordination of clauses (*'aṭf al-jumal*) and not a coordination of single words (*'aṭf al-mufradāt*). The meaning becomes: that one of the two parents reaches, or both of them reach ﴿عِنْدَكَ الْكِبَرَ﴾ (old age with you).

The answer to the condition is ﴿فَلَا تَقُلْ لَهُمَا أُفٍّ﴾ (then do not say to them, "Uff"). The meaning of the word *uff* has already been mentioned in the discussion of vocabulary and its dialects. Since He has forbidden addressing them with this word, which signals annoyance and exasperation with them, then forbidding what is worse, such as insulting or striking them, is a fortiori. The indication of *uff* does not signify the various kinds of harm by verbal indication (*dalāla lafẓiyya*), contrary to those who held that view.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "﴿أُفٍّ﴾ is a word of aversion. He, exalted is He, emphasised in His command concerning the parents, the use of gentle manners, lowering oneself, and tolerance, so that we do not say this word to them when we are annoyed, let alone anything more than it." Al-Qurtubi said: "Our scholars said: the word *uff* said to parents became the worst of things, because it rejects them in the manner of ingratitude for blessings, denies their upbringing, and rejects the command of God. *Uff* is a word transmitted for everything that is rejected. For this reason Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said: ﴿أُفٍّ لَكُمْ وَلِمَا تَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ﴾ (Uff to you and to what you worship besides God) [al-Anbiya': 67], meaning: rejection of you and of these idols with you." End of quotation.

The readings of *uff* vary. Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, 'Isa, Nafi' and Hafs read ﴿أُفٍّ﴾ with a kasra and shadda with tanwin. Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read it the same way without tanwin. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha and shadda without tanwin. Harun reported a reading with a damma and tanwin. Abu al-Sammal read *uffu* with a damma on the fa' and no tanwin. Zayd ibn 'Ali read *uffan* with a fatha, shadda and tanwin. Ibn 'Abbas read *uff* lightly. These are seven readings of the dialects that have been related for *uff*.

Mujahid said: "Its meaning is: if you see from them in old age the excrement and urine which they saw from you in childhood, do not be disgusted by them and say *uff*." End of quotation. But the verse is more general than that. When He forbade him to say to them what signifies "Am I annoyed by you?", He advanced to forbidding what is in its essence worse than *uff*, which is rebuking them. Although forbidding rebuking them is indicated by the forbidding of saying *uff*, because when the lesser is forbidden, the greater is forbidden a fortiori. The meaning is: do not reprimand them for what they do that does not please you. ﴿وَقُلْ لَهُمَا﴾ (and say to them), in place of *uff* and rebuking them, ﴿قَوْلًا كَرِيمًا﴾ (a generous word), that is, one combining excellence of goodness and beauty of expression.

Ibn al-Musayyab said: "It is the word of a servant who has done wrong to a harsh master." It was also said: ﴿قَوْلًا كَرِيمًا﴾ means "a beautiful word, as the excellence of good manners requires." 'Umar said: "That you say: O my father, O my mother." End of quotation. This is as Ibrahim addressed his father, "O my father" (*yā abati*), despite his disbelief. Do not call them by their names, because that is harshness and bad manners. There is no harm in it when it is not in the proper context, as 'A'isha said: "Abu Bakr gave me such-and-such (as a gift)."

When He, exalted is He, forbade him from a harmful word, and this did not necessarily entail a command to speak good words, He commanded him to say to them good, pleasing, and beautiful words, and that his speech should indicate their honour and veneration.

'Ata' said: "You speak with them on condition that you do not raise your gaze to them and do not fix your look on them, because that contradicts a generous word." Al-Zajjaj said: "a gentle, easy word with no harshness in it." Then God, exalted is He, commanded him to be extremely humble towards them by His words: ﴿وَاخْفِضْ لَهُمَا جَنَاحَ الذُّلِّ مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ﴾ (and lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy).

Al-Qaffal said, in explaining it, there are two views. The first: when a bird gathers its young to it for rearing, it lowers its wing for it, so lowering the wing is a metaphor for good management. It is as if it were said to the child: "Care for your parents by gathering them to yourself, as they did for you in your childhood." The second: when a bird wants to fly and rise, it spreads its wing, and when it wants to stop flying and rising, it lowers its wing, so lowering the wing becomes a metaphor for the act of humility in this respect. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is a metaphor, meaning: cut off from yourself the side of humility to them, and make yourself and your character gentle towards them. Humility is emphasised here, and it is not mentioned in His words ﴿وَاخْفِضْ جَنَاحَكَ لِمَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ (and lower your wing to those believers who follow you) [al-Shu'ara': 215], because of the greatness of the right (of the parents)." End of quotation. It is also because of the nobility of the one addressed, since it does not fit to attribute humility to him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the meaning of ﴿جَنَاحَ الذُّلِّ﴾ (the wing of humility)? I answer: there are two views. The first: that the meaning is 'lower your wing to them,' as He said: ﴿وَاخْفِضْ جَنَاحَكَ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ (and lower your wing to the believers) [al-Hijr: 88], and He attributed it to humility (*al-dhull*) or to *al-dhill* (abasement), as Hatim is attributed to generosity (*al-jūd*), meaning: lower to them your humble or humbled wing. The second: that He makes for their humility or abasement a lowered wing, as Labid made for the north wind a hand and for the cold a time, as an exaggeration in self-abasement and humility towards them." End of quotation. The meaning is that He made gentleness into humility and borrowed a wing for it, then reinforced this metaphor by commanding that it be lowered.

It is related that when Abu Tammam composed his line:

*"Do not give me the water of blame, for I am a lover who has found the water of my weeping sweet."*

a man came to him with a bowl and said, "Give me some of the water of blame." He said to him: "Not until you bring me a feather from the wing of humility."

The two wings of a person are his two sides. The meaning is: lower to them your side and do not raise it in the manner of an arrogant person towards them. One of the later scholars said well:

*"They clipped my wings, then wet them with dew, so I could not fly from their land."*

The majority read ﴿مِنَ الذُّلِّ﴾ [al-Isra': 111] with a damma on the dhal. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, al-Jahdari and Ibn Wathhab read it with a kasra on the dhal. This is a metaphor applied to people, because it is used of animals in the sense of the opposite of difficulty, just as *al-dhull* with a damma is the opposite of other people. It is evident that the *min* here is causal, meaning: what moves you to lower the wing is your mercy towards them, since they have become in need of you in old age, just as you were in need of them in childhood. Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ﴾ means "out of mercy," that is, out of gentleness towards them, so *min* is connected to *ikhfiḍ* (lower). It may also be a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from *janāḥ*. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*Min al-raḥma* here is explanatory of the genus, meaning: this lowering comes from the mercy that dwells in the soul, not that it is a mere performance. It is also possible that it indicates the starting point." End of quotation.

Then He, exalted is He, commanded him to pray to God that He show them His lasting mercy, since His mercy upon them does not last. Then He drew attention to the cause that makes kindness to them, goodness towards them, and seeking God's mercy for them necessary: their raising him when he was young. That state is one that increases his compassion and mercy towards them, since it reminds him of their kindness to him at a time when he could not do good for himself.

Qatada said: "God abrogated from this verse this phrase, meaning ﴿وَقُلْ رَبِّ ارْحَمْهُمَا﴾ (and say, 'My Lord, have mercy on them'), by His words: ﴿مَا كَانَ لِلنَّبِيِّ وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَنْ يَسْتَغْفِرُوا لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ (It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to seek forgiveness for the polytheists) [al-Tawba: 113]." It was also said that it is specific to the polytheists. It was also said: there is neither abrogation nor specification, because he may pray to God for his disbelieving parents for guidance and right direction, and may seek mercy for them after faith has been attained.

The apparent view is that the *kāf* in *kamā* is causal, meaning: "My Lord, have mercy on them because they raised me, and as a recompense for their kindness to me in my childhood and need." Al-Hawfi said: "The *kāf* is in the position of an accusative, an adjective for an omitted verbal noun, its sense being: mercy like my upbringing when I was young."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verse 23–31 (part 3 of 4):

Abu al-Baqa said: "(kama)" is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: mercy like their mercy (to me when I was young). Al-Zamakhshari and others related many hadiths and reports (athar) about being dutiful to one's parents, which can be found in their books. When Allah, exalted is He, forbade worshipping other than Him and commanded kindness to the two parents, especially in old age, and a person may display worship and kindness to his parents without true inner resolve, doing so out of showing off and seeking reputation, Allah, exalted is He, informed that He knows best what the hearts conceal, apart from intending the worship of Allah and kindness to parents. Then He said: ﴿If you are righteous﴾, that is, people of righteousness, and then some shortcoming in worship or dutifulness occurs from you, but you turn back to goodness, then indeed He is Forgiving of what has passed from your lapses. The apparent meaning is that this is general to everyone who has committed a wrong and then repented from it, and it includes one who wronged his parents and then repented of his wrong. Ibn Jubayr said: it refers to the case of a man who, out of rebellion (al-mubarazah) against his father, intends only good.

﴿And give the near relative his right, and the needy, and the wayfarer, and do not squander wastefully. Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils, and the devil has ever been ungrateful to his Lord.﴾ ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle word.﴾ ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched, lest you sit reproached and destitute. Indeed, your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it. Indeed, He is ever, of His servants, Aware and Seeing.﴾

When Allah commanded kindness to the two parents, He commanded maintaining ties of kinship. Al-Hasan said: it was revealed concerning the kin of the Messenger (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that it is addressed to the one addressed by His saying ﴿If one of them or both reach old age with you﴾, and here He includes what is required of maintaining ties of kinship, relieving need, and helping with wealth and support in every way when there is necessity (p-30). Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, al-Hasan and others said similarly. Ali ibn al-Husayn said concerning it: they are the kin of the Messenger (peace be upon him); He commanded giving them their rights from the public treasury (bayt al-mal). The apparent meaning is that "the right" here is general, and that "dhu al-qurba" is general to kinsfolk, so the determination of the right and the specification of kinsfolk is referred back to the Sunnah. From Abu Hanifa: if the relatives are unmarriageable kin (mahram), poor and unable to earn, and he is wealthy, their right is that he spend on them. According to al-Shafi'i: one spends on children and parents only, as established in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh).

Allah forbade wastefulness (al-tabdhir). The Jahiliyyah used to slaughter their camels and gamble for them (tayassara), and squander their wealth for boasting and reputation, and they would mention that in their poetry; so Allah forbade spending in other than the ways of righteousness and what brings one closer to Him. From Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas: wastefulness is spending wealth in what is not right. Mujahid said: even if one spent all his wealth in what is right, he would not be a squanderer. Al-Mawardi mentioned that it is extravagance that destroys wealth, and he argued from this verse for placing a restriction (hajr) on the wasteful; so it is obligatory upon the ruler to prevent him from it by restriction and by barring between him and his wealth, except for the amount of his family's maintenance. Abu Hanifa does not regard restriction for wastefulness, even though it is forbidden.

Al-Qurtubi said: he is restricted if he spends it on desires and there is fear that it will be exhausted; but if he spends and preserves the principal, he is not a squanderer. The "brotherhood" of the devils means that they are their companions in this world and in the Fire in the Hereafter. This brotherhood indicates that wastefulness is in disobedience to Allah, or that they obey them in what they command them of extravagance in this world. Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak read "ikhwan al-shaytan" in the singular, and it is likewise attested in the Mushaf of Anas. The disbelief of the devil towards his Lord is mentioned so that he may be warned against and not obeyed, since he does not call to anything good, as He said: ﴿He only calls his party that they may be among the companions of the Blaze﴾ [Fatir: 6].

﴿And if you turn away﴾. It is said: it was revealed concerning some people of Muzaynah who asked the Messenger to provide them with mounts, and he said: "I do not find anything to carry you upon." So they wept. It was also said: concerning Bilal, Suhayb, Salim and Khabbab, who asked him for what he did not have, so he turned away from them. It is related that after the revelation of this verse, whenever he did not have anything to give and was asked, he (peace be upon him) would say: "May Allah provide for us and for you from His bounty." So the "mercy" here is the awaited provision, and this is the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ikrimah. Ibn Zayd said: "mercy" means reward and recompense, and the verse was revealed concerning people who used to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and he would refuse to give them, because he knew they would spend the wealth in corruption; so he turned away from them, and sought reward in withholding from them, lest he assist them in their corruption; so Allah commanded him to say to them: ﴿a gentle word﴾, which includes supplication for them for opening (provision) and rectification. End of Ibn Atiyyah's words.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "And if you turn away from the near relative, the needy and the wayfarer out of shame at refusing, then say to them a gentle word, and do not leave them unanswered when they ask you. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked for something he did not have, he would turn away from the petitioner and remain silent out of modesty. It may also be that the meaning of ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾ is: even if you do not benefit them and raise their poverty due to lack of ability; and the turning away is not intended literally with the face, but as a metaphor for turning away from that, since whoever refuses to give turns away with his face." End of quotation. What appears is that when Allah commanded giving the near relative his right and those mentioned with him, and forbade him from wastefulness, He said: "And if there is no turning away from them on your part, then the pronoun refers to them." He gave as the reason for turning away the seeking of mercy, which is a metaphor for provision and ease; and seeking that arises from lacking what one could bestow on one who asks. It is as if the meaning is: "And if you turn away from them due to your hardship," so He placed the effect, which is seeking mercy, in place of the cause, which is hardship. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that ﴿seeking mercy from your Lord﴾ be a reason for the answer of the conditional, so it is connected to it and placed before it, meaning: "then say to them an easy, gentle word, promise them a good promise, out of mercy to them and to comfort their hearts, seeking mercy from your Lord," that is: seek the mercy of Allah which you hope for through your mercy towards them. End of quotation. What he permitted is not permissible, because what follows the response particle (fa’) does not operate on what precedes it; it is not allowed in your saying: "in yaqum fa-idrib Khalidan" to say "in yaqum Khalidan fa-idrib." This is explicitly stated. If you omit the fa’ in a case like "in yaqum yadrib Khalidan," the view of Sibawayh and al-Kisa'i is that it is permitted, so you say "in yaqum Khalidan nadrib." The view of al-Farra' is that it is prohibited. If the verb's object is in the nominative, as in "in taf'al yaf'al Zaydun," then it is not permissible to place Zayd before "yaf'alu" so as to be nominative by it. Sibawayh permitted that it be nominative by a verb which "yaf'alu" explains, as if you said: "in taf'al yaf'al Zaydun yaf'alu." Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' prohibited that.

Ibn Jubayr said: the pronoun in ("anhum") refers to the polytheists, and the meaning of ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾ is: because of their denial of you, seeking mercy, that is, victory for you over them, or guidance from Allah for them. According to this view, "maysur" is: placating them with the tongue; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. "Yassara" may be intransitive and transitive, so "maysur" is from the transitive; you say: "yassartu laka kadha" when you prepare it for him. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is said "yasara al-amr wa 'asara," like "sa'ada and nahasa," so it is a passive participle (maf'ul). End of quotation.

To the meaning of this verse the poet alluded in the poem called "al-Yatimah," in his saying:

"Let there be for the petitioner some relief from you; if there is none, let the refusal be made graceful."

And another said:

"If there is no silver one day that I may give to the petitioners, then I am gentle in disposition.
The petitioners shall not lack good from my character: either my giving, or the goodness of my refusal."

﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾, the verse. It is said: it was revealed concerning his (ﷺ) giving away his shirt when he had no other, and he remained naked. It is also said: he gave al-Aqra' ibn Habis one hundred camels, and Uyaynah the same, and al-Abbas ibn Mirdas fifty, then completed it to one hundred, and then this verse was revealed. This is a metaphor in which the perceptible is borrowed for the intelligible: stinginess is a quality present in a person that prevents him from disposing of his wealth, so the chain (ghull), which is the joining of the hand to the neck, is borrowed for it, so the hand is prevented from its action and from moving about as it wishes. He mentioned the hand because by it one takes and gives. Extending the hand is borrowed for the squandering of wealth, since gripping the hand holds what is in it, and extending it releases what is in it. In the metaphor he matched between the extending of the hand and its gripping in meaning, because making the hand chained is its gripping, and chaining is more emphatic in gripping. Abu Tammam matched between these two as well, saying concerning al-Mu'tasim:

"He became accustomed to extending the palm, so that if he folded it for gripping, his fingertips would not respond to it."

Al-Zamakhshari said: this is an illustration of the withholding of the miser and the giving of the spendthrift, and a command to moderation which lies between extravagance and niggardliness. End of quotation. The apparent meaning is that the address is intended for the community of the Messenger (ﷺ); otherwise he (ﷺ) did not store anything for the morrow, and likewise whoever trusted in Allah with true trust, like Abu Bakr when he gave away all his wealth in charity. Ibn Jurayj and others said: the meaning is: do not withhold from spending in what I have commanded you of right, and do not extend it in what I have forbidden you from. It was related from Qalun: "kulla al-bass" with the sad, and "fa-taq'uda" is the answer to both states according to the two conditions; so "malum" refers to His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand﴾. As the poet said:

"Indeed the miser is blameworthy wherever he is, but the generous, despite his faults, is ever enduring."

And "mahsur" refers to His saying ﴿nor extend it fully outstretched﴾, as if it was said: "then you will be blamed and left regretful." Then Allah, exalted is He, consoled him for what he used to suffer from poverty, by saying that this is not out of contempt for him from Him, nor out of stinginess towards him from Him; rather, because the expansion and restriction of provision are only by His will and desire, according to what He knows of the benefit for His servants in it. Or the meaning may be: restriction and expansion are from the will of Allah; as for you, it is incumbent upon you to be moderate. He concluded this with His saying "Khabiran," which is knowledge of hidden matters, and "Basiran," that is, of the interests of His servants, in that He expands for some people and restricts for others.

﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for them and for you. Indeed, their killing is ever a great sin.﴾

When Allah, exalted is He, explained that He is the one who undertakes the provision of the servants, saying ﴿Indeed your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts﴾, He followed it with the prohibition of killing children. The explanation of a parallel to this verse has already been mentioned, and the difference between ﴿for fear of poverty﴾ and ﴿out of poverty﴾ [al-An'am: 151], and between His saying "We provide for them" and "We provide for you." Al-A'mash and Ibn Thabit read "wa-la tuqattilu" with doubling. "Khashyah" was read with a kasra on the kha'. The majority read "khit'an" with a kasra on the kha' and sukun on the ta'; Ibn Kathir read it with a kasra and a fatha on the ta' with madd, and this is the reading of Talhah, Shibl, al-A'mash, Yahya, Khalid ibn Ilyas, Qatadah, al-Hasan and al-A'raj with a variant from them. Al-Nahhas said: I do not know a valid basis for this reading, and therefore Abu Hatim considered it an error. Al-Farisi said: it is a verbal noun from "khata'a yukhti'u," though we have not found "khata'a," but we have found "takhata'a," which is its reflexive form, and he pointed to it with the saying of the poet:

"I dodged the arrow, fearing it, and my day was delayed, so it did not hasten."

And the saying of another about a truffle:

"The hunter missed it (takhata'ahu) until I found it, and its snout was sunk in the stagnant water."

So these people who kill their children were sinning against the truth and justice.

Ibn Dhakwan read "khata'an" (خَطَأً) on the pattern of "naba'" (نَبَأٍ). Al-Hasan read "khata'an" (خَطاءً) with both letters vowelled with a fatha and with a long vowel (madd), taking it as an ism al-masdar (verbal noun) from akhta'a, like "ata'" (العَطاءُ) from a'ta, as Ibn Jinni said. Abu Hatim said: "This is an error that is not permissible, and this is not known in the language." He also reported from him (i.e. al-Hasan) "khata" (خَطى) on the pattern of "hawa" (هَوى), lightening the hamza so it became an alif and was dropped because of the meeting of the two alifs (of the long vowel and the lightened hamza).

Abu Raja' and al-Zuhri read it likewise, except that they both pronounced the kha' with a kasra, so it became like "riba" (رِبًا). Both come from khati'a in religion (خَطِئَ فِي الدِّينِ) and akhta'a in opinion (أخْطَأ فِي الرَّأْيِ), but each of the two may stand in place of the other.

Ibn 'Amir's reading is also transmitted as "khat'an" (خَطْأً) with a fatha and a short vowel, with the ta' sukun, and this is a third verbal noun from khati'a with a kasra (on the ع-form, khati'a).

(p-23) ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be good to your parents. Whether one or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them, "Uff," and do not repel them, but speak to them a noble word.﴾ ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy, and say, "My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small."﴾ ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls. If you are righteous, then indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back (to Him).﴾ ﴿And give the near relative his right, and the needy, and the wayfarer, and do not squander wastefully.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils, and Satan has ever been ungrateful to his Lord.﴾ ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle word.﴾ ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched, lest you sit down blamed and destitute.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it. Indeed, He is ever, regarding His servants, All-Aware and All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for them and for you. Indeed, killing them is ever a great sin.﴾ ﴿And do not approach adultery. Indeed, it is ever an abomination and an evil way.﴾ [Al-Isra: 32] ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right. And whoever is killed unjustly, We have given his heir authority, but let him not exceed bounds in killing. Indeed, he is ever supported.﴾ [Al-Isra: 33] ﴿And do not approach the property of an orphan except in the best manner, until he reaches maturity. And fulfill (every) covenant. Indeed, the covenant is ever questioned.﴾ [Al-Isra: 34] ﴿And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with an accurate balance. That is best and best in result.﴾ [Al-Isra: 35] ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart, about all of those one will be questioned.﴾ [Al-Isra: 36] ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly. Indeed, you will never tear through the earth, nor will you reach the mountains in height.﴾ [Al-Isra: 37] ﴿All of that - its evil is detestable in the sight of your Lord.﴾ [Al-Isra: 38] ﴿That is from what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom. And do not make with Allah another deity, lest you be thrown into Hell, blamed and banished.﴾ [Al-Isra: 39] ﴿Has your Lord then favored you with sons and taken for Himself daughters from the angels? Indeed, you are saying an enormous saying.﴾ [Al-Isra: 40] ﴿And We have certainly varied in this Qur'an that they may be reminded, but it increases them only in aversion.﴾ [Al-Isra: 41] ﴿Say, "If there were with Him other gods, as they say, they would have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne."﴾ [Al-Isra: 42] ﴿Exalted is He, and high above what they say, by a great elevation.﴾ [Al-Isra: 43] ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them exalt Him. And there is not a thing except that it exalts Him with His praise, but you do not understand their exaltation. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving.﴾ [Al-Isra: 44] ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier.﴾ [Al-Isra: 45] ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness. And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn back on their heels in aversion.﴾ [Al-Isra: 46] ﴿We are most knowing of what they listen to when they listen to you, and when they are in private conference, when the wrongdoers say, "You follow not but a man affected by magic."﴾ [Al-Isra: 47] ﴿Look how they strike for you comparisons, so they have strayed and cannot find a way.﴾ [Al-Isra: 48] ﴿And they say, "When we are bones and crumbled dust, will we indeed be resurrected in a new creation?"﴾ [Al-Isra: 49] ).

﴿Uff﴾ is an ism al-fi'l (a verb-noun, a word functioning as a verb) meaning "I am annoyed." Verb-nouns with the meaning of the present tense are rare, except for words such as uff and awwah, meaning "I am in pain." By analogy it should not be indeclinable (mabni), since it does not occupy a position of an indeclinable word. Al-Zanati in his book Al-Hulal mentions that uff has about forty dialectal forms, and we list them as we have seen them, vocalized: uffa, uffi, uffu, uff-a (doubled), uffin, uffun, uffan, uffin, uffun, uffan, uffin, uffun, uff, uff'a, uffa (with no imala), uffiyy (with full imala), uffiyy (with intermediate imala), uffiy, uffuw, uffahu, uffihi, uffuhu. This makes twenty-two, together with the initial hamza vocalized with a damma: ifa, ifi, ifu, iffa, iffi, iffan, ifin, ifun, ifan, iffiy (with imala), iffa. These are eleven, together with the initial hamza vocalized with a kasra: af, afun, aafun, aafin, aaffa. Ibn 'Atiyya mentions uffah with the silent ha' (ha' al-sakt), which completes the forty.

al-Nahr: rebuking with shouting and harshness. Al-Askari said: its root meaning is "to appear," from which come nahr and intihar (to rebuke), and anhara al-dam (he made the blood appear and flow), and intahara al-rajul (he displayed contempt for him by harsh and vile rebuke and expulsion). Ibn 'Atiyya said: intihar is displaying anger in voice and speech. al-Zamakhshari said: nahy (prohibiting), nahr (rebuking), and nahm (scolding) are siblings.

al-Tabdhir: extravagance. Abu 'Ubayda said it means extravagance in spending. Its root meaning is scattering, and from it the seed is called badhr (seed), because it is scattered in the field. The poet said:

*Ta'a'ib yastadi'u al-halyu fiha / ka-jamri al-nari budhdha bi-l-dhalam*
(Breasts in which the jewelry shines, like embers of fire scattered in the darkness.)

It is also narrated as *budedda*, meaning scattered.

al-Mahsur: al-Farra' said: the Arabs say, "a camel is mahsur" when its journey is cut off, and "the animal became hasir" when its journey was ended. It is said: hasir, a form meaning maf‘ul (passive), and its plural is hasra. The poet said:

*Bi-ha judhayfu al-hasra fa-amma 'izamuha / fa-bidun wa-amma jiladuha fa-saliab*
(In it are the carcasses of the exhausted; as for their bones, they are white, and as for their hides, they are hard.)

al-Qistas: with a damma or kasra on the qaf, and with the first sin or the sad. Mu'arrij al-Sadusi said: it is the balance in the language of the Romans. The statements of the commentators concerning it will come.

al-Maraḥ: extreme joy. It is said: marija yamrahu maraḥan. al-Tul: the opposite of short, and from it comes al-tul as opposed to al-'ard (width). al-Hijab: that which screens a thing from reaching it. al-Rufat: al-Farra' said: dust. It is said: that which is pounded thoroughly until it crumbles. It is said: rafata al-shay' (he broke it), yarfituhu, with kasra. Al-rufat are the crumbling fragments of any broken thing. The form fu'al is a pattern for this meaning, like hutam, futat, rudad, and diqaq.

(p-23) ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be good to your parents. Whether one or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them, "Uff," and do not repel them, but speak to them a noble word.﴾ ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy, and say, "My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small."﴾ ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls. If you are righteous, then indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back (to Him).﴾.

(p-25) The majority of readers recite (*wa-qada*) as a past-tense verb from qada'. Some of the offspring of Mu'adh ibn Jabal recite *wa-qada'u Rabbika*, with the verbal noun of *qada* in the nominative as a subject, and (*an la ta'budu*) as the predicate. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud and his companions, and Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Nakha'i, and Maymun ibn Mihran, it is read as *wa-wassa* (and commanded) from al-tawsiya. Some recited *wa-awsa* from al-iy'a'. That reading should be interpreted accordingly, because it is a reading that differs from the consonantal text of the codex, whereas the widely transmitted reading is *wa-qada*, which is well known from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, and others in the chains of the seven readers.

Here, *qada* is interpreted by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Qatada as "commanded." Ibn Mas'ud and his companions said it means "enjoined." It is also said: "obligated and required," and "judged." It is also said: "decided firmly." Ibn 'Atiyya said: I say, the meaning of *Wa-qada Rabbuka* is His command, *an la ta'budu illa iyyahu*. These words contain nothing but a command to restrict worship to Allah, and that is what is decreed, not worship itself, and what is decreed here is the command. End of quote. It seems he wanted to leave *qada* in its well-known sense of "decreed," so he made its object the command to worship rather than worship itself, because it is not correct to decree something in the sense of determining it without its occurring. What the commentators understood, other than this, is that the object of *qada* is *an la ta'budu* (that you not worship), whether *an* is explanatory or verbal. Abu al-Baqa' said: it may be in the accusative position, meaning: your Lord has obligated His worship, and *la* is extra. End of quote. This is an error, because *illa* enters upon the object of *ta'budu*, so it must be negated or prohibited, and the address in *la ta'budu* is general to all creation.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is also possible that *qada* is in its well-known usage in speech, and the pronoun in *ta'budu* refers to believers among people until the Day of Resurrection. End of quote.

al-Hawfi said: the *ba'* is connected to *qada*. It may also be connected to a deleted verb, its estimated form being *wa-awsa* (and He commanded), *bi-al-walidayn ihsanan* (good treatment to the parents). *Ihsanan* is a verbal noun, meaning: you should show goodness, *tuhsinu ihsanan*. Ibn 'Atiyya said: His statement *wa-bi-al-walidayni ihsanan* is conjoined to the first *an*, meaning: Allah commanded *an la ta'budu illa iyyahu* and that you be good *bi-al-walidayni ihsanan*. On this possibility we mentioned, *wa-bi-al-walidayni ihsanan* is cut off from the first, as if He informed them of Allah's decree and then commanded them to be good to their parents. al-Zamakhshari said: the *ba'* in *bi-al-walidayn* may not be connected to *ihsan*, because the verbal noun cannot have its complement precede it. al-Wahidi in al-Basit said: the *ba'* in His statement *bi-al-walidayn* is part of the complement of *ihsan*, and it has been placed before it, as you say: *bi-Zaydin fa-mrur* (pass by Zayd). End of quote.

*Ahsana* and *asa'a* are transitive with *ila* and with *ba'*. Allah says: ﴿And He has been good to me﴾ [Yusuf: 100]. The poet said:

*Asii'i bina aw ahsini la malumata*
(Mistreat us or be good to us, there is no blame.)

It seems *ahsana* was taken to include the meaning of *lataffa* (to be kind), so it was followed by *ba'*. If *ihsanan* is a verbal noun, it resolves to *an* and a verb, so it is not permitted to place its complement before it. If it means *ahsinu* (be good!), then it is a substitute for the verb's own word, like *darban Zaydan*, so it is permitted to place its object before it. What we choose is that *an* is an explanatory particle, *la ta'budu* is a prohibition, and *ihsanan* is a verbal noun with the meaning of a command, conjoined to the prohibition, as in:

*Yaqulna la tahlik asan wa-tajammal*
(They say, "Do not perish from grief, and be patient.")

The command to good treatment of parents is emphasized by its juxtaposition with *la ta'budu*, and by putting the parents first, which is an emphasis on them. The reason for linking good treatment of parents with the singling out of Allah in worship is that He, exalted is He, is the true originator, while the parents are an intermediary in bringing a person into being, and He, exalted is He, is the bestower of blessing by creating and providing, while they strive for his welfare.

al-Zamakhshari said: *Imma* is the conditional particle, to which *ma* was added for emphasis, and therefore the emphatic *nun* enters the verb. If it were used alone, that would not be correct. You do not say, *in tukrimanna Zaydan yukrimka*, but you say *imma tukrimannahu*. End of quote.
