It is said to a person: why did you hear what it was not permissible for you to hear? Why did you look at what it was not permissible for you to look at? Why did you resolve upon what it was not permissible for you to resolve upon? End of quotation.

What he went to, that "anhu" is in the place of the nominative as agent, and by this he means that it is a non-named object, is not permissible. This is because the prepositional phrase and what takes the place of the agent, whether a direct object, a verbal noun or an adverbial, under their conditions, function as the agent. Just as the agent may not be fronted, so too what functions like it and takes its place. So when you say "ghadiba 'ala Zayd," it is not permissible to say "'ala Zayd ghadiba," unlike "ghadibtu 'ala Zayd," where "'ala Zayd ghadibtu" is permissible. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas has related the consensus of the grammarians that a prepositional phrase that takes the place of the agent may not be fronted before the verb. He mentioned this in his book al-Muqni'. So ﴿عَنْهُ مَسْئُولًا﴾ is not like ﴿المَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾, because in ﴿عَنْهُ مَسْئُولًا﴾ the prepositional phrase is fronted, while in ﴿المَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ it is delayed. Al-Zamakhshari's statement "wa lima nazarta ma lam yahill laka" omitted "ila," and this is not permissible except in poetic necessity, since "nazara" is transitive with "ila," so the construction should have been "wa lima nazarta ila ma lam yahill laka," as he said "al-nazar ilayhi," thus transitive with "ila."

(Maraḥan) is accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning "marihan" (exulting), as you say "ja'a Zayd rakdan," meaning "rakidan" (running). Or it is accusative by eliding a modifier, meaning "dha maraḥ" (possessed of exultation). Some allowed that it be an object of purpose: "wa la tamshi fi al-ard limaraḥ" (do not walk on the earth for exultation). This does not appear. It has preceded that maraḥ is joy and exhilaration in ease and happiness, and it seems it was implicitly given the meaning of arrogance (al-ikhtiyal), because the predominance of joy and happiness is accompanied by haughtiness and arrogance. For this reason it is given as the cause by His saying ﴿إنَّكَ لَنْ تَخْرِقَ الأرْضَ﴾.

A group, as transmitted by Ya'qub, read "maraḥan" with a kasra on the ra', and it is a state: do not walk arrogant and haughty. Mujahid said: "You will not tear the earth with your walking on your heels in pride and luxury, and you will not reach the mountains" with walking on the fronts of your feet in boasting. (Tulan) — the interpretation is that your power does not reach this extent, so that would be a means to arrogance. Al-Zajjaj said: "Do not walk on the earth" arrogant, boastful, and its counterpart is ﴿وعِبادُ الرَّحْمَنِ الَّذِينَ يَمْشُونَ عَلى الأرْضِ هَوْنًا﴾ [al-Furqan: 63] and ﴿اقْصِدْ في مَشْيِكَ﴾ [Luqman: 19], and ﴿ولا تَمْشِ في الأرْضِ مَرَحًا إنَّ اللَّهَ لا يُحِبُّ كُلَّ مُخْتالٍ فَخُورٍ﴾ [Luqman: 18].

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿لَنْ تَخْرِقَ الأرْضَ﴾ means you will not make a rent in it by your treading on it and the severity of your stamping, ﴿ولَنْ تَبْلُغَ الجِبالَ طُولًا﴾ by your stretching yourself, and this is a mockery of the arrogant.

Al-Jarrah al-A'rabi read "﴿لَنْ تَخْرِقَ﴾" with a damma on the ra'. Abu Hatim said: this dialect is not known. It was said: by this is indicated that man is confined between two inanimate things, weak in affecting them by tearing or reaching height, and whoever is in this position is not fit for arrogance.

The poet said:

"Do not walk above the earth except in humility, / for beneath it are people who are higher than you."

The better parsing of His saying ﴿طُولًا﴾ is as a specification (tamyiz), meaning your height will not reach the mountains. Al-Hawfi said: ﴿طُولًا﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial state, and the agent of the state is (tabluga), and it may be that the agent is (takhraqa), and ﴿طُولًا﴾ means "mutatawil" (stretching). End of quotation.

Abu al-Baqa said: ﴿طُولًا﴾ is a verbal noun in the place of a state from the subject or the object, and it may be a specification, an object of purpose, and a verbal noun from the meaning of (tabluga). End of quotation.

The two Haramis (Ibn Kathir and Nafi' — Meccan and Medinan), Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and al-A'raj read "sayyi'atan" in the accusative and feminine. The rest of the Seven, and al-Hasan and Masruq, read ﴿سَيِّئُهُ﴾ with a damma on the hamza, as a construct with the masculine third-person pronoun. 'Abd Allah read "sayyi'atuhu" in the plural as a construct with the pronoun, and also from him "sayyi'at" without it, and also from him "kana khabithuhu."

As for the first reading, the apparent meaning is that this refers to the verbal nouns of the two prohibitions preceding, namely following what one has no knowledge of, and walking on the earth exultantly. It was said: it refers to all the prohibitions mentioned earlier in this sura. "Sayyi'atan" is the predicate of kana and is feminine; then He said "makruhan," which is masculine. Al-Zamakhshari said: sayyi'a in the category of nouns is like dhanb (sin), and the noun has lost the rule of adjectives, so no account is taken of its feminine form, and there is no difference between one who reads "sayyi'atan" and one who reads "sayyi'an." Do you not see that you say "al-zina sayyi'a" just as you say "al-sariqa sayyi'a," so you do not distinguish in attributing it to masculine or feminine. End of quotation. And this is a good explanation.

It was said: "makruhan" was mentioned according to the wording of (kull). They permitted that "makruhan" be a second predicate of kana according to the view of one who permits multiple predicates of kana, and that it be an apposition to sayyi'a, though apposition with a derived noun is weak, and that it be a state from the pronoun concealed in the adverbial preceding it, the adverbial being in the place of a qualifier. It was said: it is also permissible that it be an attribute of sayyi'a: since its feminine is metaphorical, it may be described by a masculine. This was deemed weak, because the permissibility of this is only when the verb with a metaphorical feminine subject precedes; when it follows and is attributed to its pronoun, it is ugly. You say "abqala al-ardu iblalaha" (the earth sprouted its vegetation), which is eloquent, but "al-ardu abqala" is ugly.

As for one who reads "sayyi'uhu" with the masculine and the construct, then "sayyi'uhu" is the subject of kana and "makruhan" is the predicate. Since among the attributes mentioned there are both bad and good, He pointed to the whole with "dhalika," and He used the singular "sayyi'a," which is what is forbidden, so the judgment of disapproval applies to it from His saying "la taj'al" to the end of the prohibitions.

As for the reading of 'Abd Allah, it is parsed as a case in which the plural is predicated with a singular masculine, which is rare, like His saying:

"Fa inna al-hawadith awda biha"
(since misfortunes have destroyed them),

because "al-hidthan" is permissible in place of "al-hawadith." Similarly here, "kana ma yasu'u" (what displeases) stands in place of its bad deeds. That (dhalika) refers to all kinds of obligations from His saying ﴿لا تَجْعَلْ مَعَ اللَّهِ إلَهًا آخَرَ﴾ [al-Isra: 22] to His saying ﴿ولا تَمْشِ في الأرْضِ مَرَحًا﴾, and they are twenty-four types of obligations, some of them commands and some prohibitions, beginning with His saying ﴿لا تَجْعَلْ﴾ [al-Isra: 22]. He concluded the verses with His saying ﴿ولا تَجْعَلْ﴾ and said "mimma awha" (of what He revealed), because that is part of what was revealed to him, since other obligations were revealed to him. ﴿مِمّا أوْحى﴾ is a predicate of that. ﴿مِنَ الحِكْمَةِ﴾ may be attached to "awha," may be an apposition to "ma," or may be a state from the accusative pronoun elided that returns to "ma." These obligations are wisdom, because their sum returns to the command of monotheism, the various acts of obedience, turning away from the world and turning toward the Hereafter; reason indicates their soundness, and they are laws in all religions that do not admit abrogation (naskh).

From Ibn 'Abbas: these verses were on the tablets of Moses, peace be upon him, the first of which is ﴿لا تَجْعَلْ مَعَ اللَّهِ إلَهًا آخَرَ﴾ [al-Isra: 22]. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وكَتَبْنا لَهُ في الألْواحِ مِن كُلِّ شَيْءٍ مَوْعِظَةً وتَفْصِيلًا لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [al-A'raf: 145]. And Allah the Exalted repeated the prohibition of association; in the first prohibition...

﴿فَتَقْعُدَ مَذْمُومًا مَخْذُولًا﴾ [الإسراء: 22]. وفي الثاني: ﴿فَتُلْقى في جَهَنَّمَ مَلُومًا مَدْحُورًا﴾. والفرق بين «مذمومٍ» و«ملومٍ» أنّ كونه مذمومًا هو أن يُذكر أنّ الفعل الذي أقدم عليه قبيحٌ مُنكَرٌ، وكونه ملومًا هو أن يُقال له بعد الفعل والذمّ: لِمَ فعلتَ كذا؟ وما حملك عليه؟ وما استفدتَ منه إلّا إلحاقَ الضررِ بنفسك؟ فأوّلُ الأمر الذمُّ وآخرُه اللومُ. والفرق بين «مخذولٍ» و«مدحورٍ» أنّ المخذول هو المتروكُ إعانتُه ونصرُه والمفوَّضُ إلى (p-39) نفسِه، والمدحورُ المطرودُ المُبعَدُ على سبيل الإهانة له والاستخفاف به، فأوّلُ الأمر الخِذلان وآخرُه الطردُ مُهانًا. وكان وصفُ الذمّ والخِذلان يكون في الدنيا، ووصفُ اللوم والدُّحور يكون في الآخرة، ولذلك جاء ﴿فَتُلْقى في جَهَنَّمَ﴾. والخطابُ بالنهي في هذه الآيات للسامع غيرِ الرسول.

وقال الزمخشري: ولقد جعل الله ‑ عزّ وعلا ‑ فاتحتَها وخاتمتَها النهيَ عن الشرك؛ لأنّ التوحيدَ هو رأسُ كلِّ حكمةٍ وملاكُها، ومَن عَدِمه لم تنفعْه حِكَمُه وعلومُه وإن بذّ فيها الحكماءَ وحكّ بيافوخِه السماءَ، وما أغنتْ عن الفلاسفةِ أسفارُ الحِكَم وهم عن دين الله أضلُّ من النَّعَم.

﴿أفَأصْفاكم رَبُّكم بِالبَنِينَ واتَّخَذَ مِنَ المَلائِكَةِ إناثًا إنَّكم لَتَقُولُونَ قَوْلًا عَظِيمًا﴾ ﴿ولَقَدْ صَرَّفْنا في هَذا القُرْآنِ لِيَذَّكَّرُوا وما يَزِيدُهم إلّا نُفُورًا﴾ ﴿قُلْ لَوْ كانَ مَعَهُ آلِهَةٌ كَما يَقُولُونَ إذًا لابْتَغَوْا إلى ذِي العَرْشِ سَبِيلًا﴾ ﴿سُبْحانَهُ وتَعالى عَمّا يَقُولُونَ عُلُوًّا كَبِيرًا﴾ ﴿تُسَبِّحُ لَهُ السَّماواتُ السَّبْعُ والأرْضُ ومَن فِيهِنَّ وإنْ مِن شَيْءٍ إلّا يُسَبِّحُ بِحَمْدِهِ ولَكِنْ لا تَفْقَهُونَ تَسْبِيحَهم إنَّهُ كانَ حَلِيمًا غَفُورًا﴾.

لمّا نبّه تعالى على فساد مَن أثبت لله شريكًا ونظيرًا، أتبعه بفساد طريقة مَن أثبت لله ولدًا. والاستفهامُ معناه الإنكارُ والتوبيخ، والخطابُ لِمَن اعتقد أنّ الملائكةَ بناتُ الله. ومعنى ﴿أفَأصْفاكم﴾ آثركم وخصّكم، وهذا كما قال: ﴿ألَهُ البَناتُ ولَكُمُ البَنُونَ﴾ [الطور: 39]، ﴿ألَكُمُ الذَّكَرُ ولَهُ الأُنْثى﴾ [النجم: 21]. وهذا خلافُ الحكمةِ وما عليه معقولُكم وعادتُكم، فإنّ العبيدَ لا يُؤْثَرون بأجودِ الأشياء وأصفاها من الشَّوب، ويكون أرداها وأدونها للسادات. ومعنى ﴿عَظِيمًا﴾ مُبالغًا في المنكر والقبح، حيث أضفتم إليه الأولاد، ثم حيث فضّلتم عليه تعالى أنفسَكم فجعلتم له ما تكرهون، ثم نسبةُ الملائكةِ الذين هم من شريفِ ما خلق إلى الأنوثة.

ومعنى ﴿صَرَّفْنا﴾ نوّعنا من جهةٍ إلى جهةٍ ومن مثالٍ إلى مثالٍ، والتصريفُ لغةً: صرفُ الشيءِ من جهةٍ إلى جهةٍ، ثم صار كنايةً عن التبيين. وقرأ الجمهور ﴿صَرَّفْنا﴾ بتشديد الراء. فقال: لم نجعلْه نوعًا واحدًا، بل وعدًا ووعيدًا، ومحكَمًا ومتشابهًا، وأمرًا ونهيًا، وناسخًا ومنسوخًا (نَسْخ: رفعُ حكمٍ شرعيٍّ بدليلٍ متأخرٍ)، وأخبارًا وأمثالًا، مثلَ تصريفِ الرياحِ من صَبًا ودَبورٍ وجَنوبٍ وشَمالٍ. ومفعولُ ﴿صَرَّفْنا﴾ على هذا المعنى محذوفٌ، وهي هذه الأشياءُ، أي: صرّفنا الأمثالَ والعِبَرَ والحِكَمَ والأحكامَ والأعلامَ. وقيل: المعنى لم نُنزِلْه مرةً واحدةً بل نجومًا، ومعناه: أكثرنا صرفَ جبريلَ إليك، والمفعولُ محذوفٌ، أي: صرّفنا جبريلَ.

وقيل: (في) زائدةٌ، أي: صرّفنا هذا القرآنَ، كما قال: ﴿وأصْلِحْ لِي في ذُرِّيَّتِي﴾ [الأحقاف: 15]. وهذا ضعيفٌ؛ لأنّ «في» لا تُزاد. وقال الزمخشري: يجوز أن يريد بهذا القرآنِ إبطالَ إضافتِهم إلى الله البناتِ؛ لأنه مما صرّفه وكرّر ذكره، والمعنى: ولقد (p-40) صرّفنا القولَ في هذا المعنى، وأوقعنا التصريفَ فيه وجعلناه مكانًا للتكرير، ويجوز أن يشير بهذا (القرآنِ) إلى التنزيل، ويريد: ولقد صرّفناه، يعني هذا المعنى في مواضعَ من التنزيل، فترك الضميرَ لأنه معلومٌ. انتهى. فجعل التصريفَ خاصًّا بما دلّت عليه الآيةُ قبله، وجعل مفعولَ ﴿صَرَّفْنا﴾ إمّا القولَ في هذا المعنى أو المعنى، وهو الضميرُ الذي قدّره في صرّفناه، وغيرُه جعل التصريفَ عامًّا في أشياءَ فقدّر ما يشمل ما سيق له ما قبلَه وغيرَه.

وقرأ الحسنُ بتخفيف الراء. فقال صاحبُ اللوامح: هو بمعنى العامّة، يعني بالعامّة: قراءةَ الجمهور، قال: لأنّ فَعَلَ وفَعَّلَ ربما تعاقبا على معنًى واحدٍ. وقال ابن عطية: على معنى صرَفْنا فيه الناسَ إلى الهدى بالدعاء إلى الله.

وقرأ الجمهور ﴿لِيَذَّكَّرُوا﴾ أي: ليتذكّروا من التذكير، أُدغمت التاءُ في الذال. وقرأ الأخَوانِ وطلحةُ وابنُ وثّابٍ والأعمشُ «لِيَذْكُرُوا» بسكون الذال وضمّ الكاف من الذِّكْرِ أو الذُّكْرِ، أي: ليتّعظوا ويعتبروا وينظروا فيما يُحتجّ به عليهم ويطمئنّوا إليه. ﴿وما يَزِيدُهُمْ﴾ أي: التصريفُ ﴿إلّا نُفُورًا﴾ أي: بُعدًا وفرارًا عن الحق، كما قال: ﴿فَزادَتْهم رِجْسًا إلى رِجْسِهِمْ﴾ [التوبة: 125]، وقال: ﴿فَما لَهم عَنِ التَّذْكِرَةِ مُعْرِضِينَ﴾ [المدثر: 49] ﴿كَأنَّهم حُمُرٌ مُسْتَنْفِرَةٌ﴾ [المدثر: 50]. والنُّفورُ من أوصاف الدوابّ الشديدةِ الشِّماس. ولمّا ذكر تعالى نسبةَ الولد إليهم وردّ عليهم في ذلك، ذكر قولَهم إنه تعالى معه آلهةٌ وردّ عليهم.

وقرأ ابنُ كثيرٍ وحفصٌ ﴿كَما يَقُولُونَ﴾ بالياء من تحت، والجمهورُ بالتاء. ومعنى ﴿لابْتَغَوْا إلى ذِي العَرْشِ سَبِيلًا﴾: إلى مغالبته وإفسادِ ملكه؛ لأنهم شركاؤه كما يفعل الملوكُ بعضُهم مع بعضٍ، وقال هذا المعنى أو مثلَه ابنُ جُبيرٍ وأبو عليٍّ الفارسيُّ والنقّاشُ والمتكلِّمون، أبو منصورٍ وغيرُه، وعلى هذا تكون الآيةُ بيانًا للتمانُع، كما في قوله: ﴿لَوْ كانَ فِيهِما آلِهَةٌ إلّا اللَّهُ لَفَسَدَتا﴾ [الأنبياء: 22]، ويأتي تفسيرُها إن شاء الله تعالى.

وقال قتادةُ ما معناه: لابتغَوْا إلى التقرّبِ إلى ذي العرش والزُّلفى لديه، وكانوا يقولون: إنّ الأصنامَ تُقرِّبهم إلى الله، فإذا علموا أنها تحتاج إلى الله فقد بطل كونُها آلهةً، ويكون كقوله: ﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ يَبْتَغُونَ إلى رَبِّهِمُ الوَسِيلَةَ أيُّهم أقْرَبُ﴾ [الإسراء: 57]. والكافُ من (كما) في موضعِ نصبٍ.

وقال الحوفي: متعلقةٌ بما تعلّقت به (مَعَ)، وهو الاستقرارُ، و(مَعَهُ) خبرُ كان.

وقال أبو البقاء: كَوْنًا لقولِكم.

وقال الزمخشري: و(إذًا) دالّةٌ على أنّ ما بعدها، وهو (لابتغَوْا)، جوابٌ عن مقالةِ المشركين وجزاءٌ لـ(لو). انتهى. وعُطِف (وتعالى) على قوله: (سبحانَه)؛ لأنه اسمٌ قام مقامَ المصدرِ الذي هو في معنى الفعل، أي: براءةَ الله، وقُدِّر تنزَّهَ، و(تعالى) يتعلّق به على سبيل الإعمال، إذ يصحّ لـ(سبحانَ) أن يتعلّق به (عن) كما في قوله: ﴿سُبْحانَ رَبِّكَ رَبِّ العِزَّةِ عَمّا يَصِفُونَ﴾ [الصافات: 180]، والتعالي في حقّه تعالى هو بالمكانةِ لا بالمكانِ. وقرأ الأخَوانِ: «عمّا تقولون» بالتاء من فوق، وباقي السبعة بالياء. وانتصب (عُلُوًّا) على أنه مصدرٌ على غير الصدر، أي: تعاليًا، ووُصف بـ(كبيرًا) مبالغةً في معنى البراءةِ والبُعدِ عمّا وصفوه به؛ لأنّ المنافاةَ بين الواجبِ لذاتِه والممكنِ لذاتِه، وبين القديمِ والمحدَثِ، وبين الغنيِّ والمحتاجِ منافاةٌ لا تقبل الزيادةَ.

ونسبةُ التسبيح للسماوات والأرض ومَن فيهنّ من مَلَكٍ وإنسٍ وجنٍّ حملَه بعضُهم على النطقِ بالتسبيح حقيقةً، وأنّ ما لا حياةَ فيه ولا نُموَّ يُحدِث الله له نطقًا، وهذا هو ظاهرُ اللفظ، ولذلك جاء ﴿ولَكِنْ لا تَفْقَهُونَ تَسْبِيحَهُمْ﴾. وقال بعضُهم: ما كان من نامٍ حيوانٍ وغيرِه يُسبّح حقيقةً، وبه قال عكرمةُ، قال: الشجرةُ تُسبّح والأُسطوانةُ لا تُسبّح.

وسُئل الحسنُ عن الخِوان: أيُسبّح؟ فقال: قد كان يُسبّح مرةً، يشير إلى أنه حين كان شجرةً كان يسبّح، وحين صار خِوانًا مدهونًا صار جمادًا لا يسبّح. وقيل: التسبيحُ المنسوبُ لما لا يعقل مجازٌ، ومعناه: أنها تسبّح بلسانِ الحال، حيث يدلّ على الصانع وعلى قدرتِه وحكمتِه وكمالِه، فكأنها تنطق بذلك، وكأنها تُنزّه اللهَ عمّا لا يجوز عليه من الشركاء وغيرِها. ويكون قولُه: ﴿ولَكِنْ لا تَفْقَهُونَ تَسْبِيحَهُمْ﴾ (p-41) خطابًا للمشركين، وهم وإن كانوا معترفين بالخالق أنه الله، لكنهم لمّا جعلوا معه آلهةً لم ينظروا ولم يُقِرّوا؛ لأنّ نتيجةَ النظرِ الصحيحِ والإقرارِ الثابتِ خلافُ ما كانوا عليه، فإذا لم يفقهوا التسبيحَ ولم يستوضحوا الدلالةَ على الخالق، فيكون التسبيحُ المسنَدُ إلى السماوات والأرض ومَن فيهنّ على سبيل المجاز قدرًا مشتركًا بين الجميع، وإن كان يصدر التسبيحُ حقيقةً ممّن فيهنّ من مَلَكٍ وإنسٍ وجانٍّ، ولا يُحمل نسبتُه إلى السماوات والأرض على المجاز، ونسبتُه إلى الملائكة والثَّقَلَين على الحقيقة؛ لئلّا يكون جمعًا بين المجاز والحقيقة بلفظٍ واحدٍ.

وقال ابن عطية: ثم أعاد على السماوات والأرض ضميرَ مَن يعقل لمّا أسند إليها فعلَ العاقل، وهو التسبيح. انتهى. ويُعنى بالضمير في قوله: ﴿ومَن فِيهِنَّ﴾، وكأنه تُخيّل أنّ (هُنّ) لا يكون إلا لمن يعقل من المؤنثات، وليس كما تُخيّل، بل (هُنّ) يكون ضميرَ الجمعِ المؤنثِ مطلقًا. وقرأ النحويّان وحمزةُ وحفصٌ: ﴿تُسَبِّحُ﴾ بالتاء من فوق، وباقي السبعة بالياء، وفي بعض المصاحف «سَبَّحَتْ» له السماواتُ بلفظ الماضي وتاءِ التأنيث، وهي قراءةُ عبدِ الله والأعمشِ وطلحةَ بنِ مُصرِّفٍ.

﴿إنَّهُ كانَ حَلِيمًا﴾ حيث لا يعاجلكم بالعقوبة على سوءِ نظرِكم ﴿غَفُورًا﴾ إن رجعتم ووحّدتم الله تعالى.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verses 45–49 (part 1 of 2):

﴿When you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier.﴾ ﴿And We place over their hearts coverings, so that they do not understand it, and in their ears deafness. And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn their backs in aversion.﴾ ﴿We know best what they listen to when they listen to you, and when they are in private conversation, when the wrongdoers say, "You follow only a man under enchantment."﴾ ﴿Look how they strike for you comparisons, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way.﴾ ﴿And they say, "When we have become bones and dust, shall we really be resurrected in a new creation?"﴾.

It was revealed, "When you recite the Qur'an," concerning Abu Sufyan, al-Nadr, Abu Jahl, and Umm Jamil, the wife of Abu Lahab (p-٤٢). They used to harm the Messenger when he recited the Qur'an, so God veiled their sight when he recited, and they would pass by him and not see him. This was related by al-Kalbi. And from Ibn Abbas: "It was revealed concerning the wife of Abu Lahab. She entered the house of Abu Bakr with a stone in her hand while the Messenger ﷺ was with him. She said, 'Your companion has satirized me.' He said, 'He is not a poet.' She said, 'He said: ﴿a rope of palm fiber around her neck﴾ [al-Masad: 5], and what does he know of my neck?' The Prophet said to Abu Bakr, 'Ask her whether she can see anyone besides you, for an angel has continually been concealing me from her.' He asked her, and she said, 'Do you mock me? I see no one but you.' Then she left and did not see the Messenger ﷺ." It was also said: it was revealed concerning a group from the Banu Abd al-Dar who used to harm him at night when he prayed and recited aloud, so God came between them and his harm.

When the discussion of establishing the divinity (al-ilahiyyah) had preceded, it was followed by the establishment of prophethood and a mention of some of the conditions of the disbelievers in denying it and in denying the return (al-ma'ad). The meaning is: "When you begin to recite." The meaning is not "when you have finished reciting," but rather "when you are engaged in reciting the Qur'an." The Qur'an here does not refer to all of it, but to what the term applies to. For you say of someone who recites a portion of the Qur'an, "This one is reciting the Qur'an." The apparent meaning of "the Qur'an" here is what is recited of the Qur'an, whatever portion of it. It was also said that three specific verses of it are meant: in al-Nahl, ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts God has sealed﴾ [al-Nahl: 108] up to ﴿the heedless﴾ [al-Nahl: 108]; in al-Kahf, ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ [al-Kahf: 57] up to ﴿never ever﴾ [al-Kahf: 57]; and in al-Jathiyah, ﴿Have you seen one who takes his desire as his god﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23] up to ﴿will you not remember?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23]. It is related from Ka'b that the Messenger used to conceal himself with these verses. It is related from Ibn Sirin that a caller from the side of the house designated them for him. It is related from some of them that he kept them secret for a time, then was guided to recite them, and he went out, and the disbelievers could not see him while they were searching for him, their garments touching his garments. Al-Qurtubi said: To these verses may be added the beginning of Ya-Sin up to ﴿so they do not see﴾ [Ya-Sin: 9]. In the biography (al-Sirah) it is related that when the Messenger ﷺ lay down on his bed, he went out scattering dust over the heads of the disbelievers, and they did not see him, while he recited these verses from Ya-Sin; and he did not leave anyone among them without placing dust on his head.

The apparent meaning is: "We placed between your seeing and the sight of those who do not believe in the Hereafter" [a barrier], as is mentioned in the occasion of revelation.

Qatadah, al-Zajjaj, and a group said something to the effect that: "We placed between their understanding of what you recite and them a ﴿barrier﴾, so they do not acknowledge your prophethood or the resurrection." The meaning is close to that of the verse after it. The apparent sense is that ﴿concealed﴾ retains its form as a passive participle, meaning concealed from the eyes of the disbelievers, so they do not see it; or ﴿concealed﴾ means that the Messenger is concealed from their sight. The attribution of concealment to it (the barrier) is because it is concealed by it, as al-Mubarrad said. Its meaning may be interpreted as "possessing concealment," as in the pattern of "laban" and "tamr" (milk-possessor and date-possessor), i.e., "possessor of milk" and "possessor of dates." They also say: "a man marhub" meaning "one possessing softness" (ruṭbah), and one does not say "rattabtuhu"; "a place mahul" meaning "possessing terror" (hawl), and one does not say "hultu al-makan"; "a girl maghnuga," and one does not say "ghanijat al-jariyah." Al-Akhfash and a group said: ﴿mastur﴾ means "concealing (sakir)," and the active participle may come in the form of the passive, as they say "mash'um" and "maymun," meaning "shu'um" (ill-omened) and "yaman" (auspicious). It was also said: "mastur" is an attribute in the sense of intensification, as they say "shi'r sha'ir" (poetry that is poetic). It was refuted on the grounds that intensification occurs only with the active participle.

As for the first phrase, ﴿And We place over their hearts coverings, so that they do not understand it, and in their ears deafness﴾: its interpretation has already been given at the beginning of al-An'am.

﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an﴾: It was said: "The chiefs of Quraysh entered upon Abu Talib to visit him. The Messenger of God ﷺ entered and recited, and passed over the monotheism (tawhid). Then he said: 'O assembly of Quraysh, say: there is no god but God, by which you will rule the Arabs and the non-Arabs (al-ajam) will submit to you.' So they turned and fled, and this verse was revealed." The apparent meaning is that the verse describes the state of those who flee at the time of his recitation and his passing over the oneness of God. The meaning is: when the passages of monotheism came, the disbelievers fled, denying it, finding it repugnant, and rejecting and discarding their gods.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Wahada, yahidu, wahdan and wahdah, like wa'ada, ya'idu, wa'dan and 'idah; and ﴿wahdah﴾ is of the pattern of raja'a, its return being to its beginning; and do it with your utmost effort and capacity; in that it is a verbal noun (masdar) substituting for the state (hal), its origin being yahidu wahdahu, meaning 'alone.'" End of quotation. What he holds, that ﴿wahdah﴾ is a verbal noun substituting for the state, is contrary to the school of Sibawayh. For Sibawayh, ﴿wahdah﴾ is not a verbal noun but a noun placed in the position of a verbal noun which is placed in the position of the state; so ﴿wahdah﴾ for him is placed in the position of "iyhad," and "iyhad" is placed in the position of "muwahhid." Yunus held that ﴿wahdah﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarf). Others held that it is a verbal noun with no verb of its own; others that it is a verbal noun of "awhada" with the augment dropped; and others that it is a verbal noun of "wahd," as al-Zamakhshari held. The arguments for these views are mentioned in the books of grammar. When ﴿wahdah﴾ is mentioned after a subject and object, as in "I struck Zayd," Sibawayh's view is that it is a state of the subject, meaning "singling him out in striking"; al-Mubarrad's view is that it may be a state of the object. So on Sibawayh's view the sense is ﴿when you mention your Lord﴾ singling Him out in mention; and on Abu al-Abbas's view it may mean singling Him out in mention.

﴿Nufuran﴾ is a state, the plural of "nafir," like "qa'id" and "qu'ud," or a verbal noun of a non-original form, because the meaning of ﴿they turned﴾ is "they fled." The apparent sense is that the pronoun in ﴿they turned﴾ refers to the disbelievers already mentioned. One group said it refers to the devils, because they flee from the Qur'an, and this meaning is indicated even though they had not been mentioned. Abu al-Hawra' Aws ibn Abd Allah said: "Nothing drives Satan from the heart more than 'There is no god but God,'" then he recited ﴿And when you mention...﴾, the verse. Ali ibn al-Husayn said: it is the basmalah (the invocation "In the name of God").

﴿We know best what they listen to with it﴾: that is, with the mockery by which they listen, and the derision toward you and the idle talk. When he ﷺ recited, two men from the Banu Abd Allah would stand on his right and two on his left, clapping, whistling, and mixing poetry into his recitation to confuse him. "Bi-ma" is connected to "a'lam." Whatever carries the meaning of knowledge and ignorance, even if it transitively takes a direct object, when it is in the form of "af'al" in the exclamatory (ta'ajjub) and in the comparative (af'al al-tafdil), it takes the preposition "bi." You say: "How knowledgeable is Zayd of such-and-such" and "How ignorant he is of such-and-such," and "He is more knowledgeable of such-and-such" and "more ignorant of such-and-such." This is unlike other transitive verbs taking a direct object, which in the exclamatory and comparative "af'al" take "li" (for): "How striking Zayd is to Amr," and "Zayd is more striking to Amr than to Bakr." Al-Zamakhshari said it is in the position of a state, as you say: "they listen with mockery," meaning "mocking." ﴿When they listen﴾ is in the accusative governed by "a'lam," meaning: "I know best the time of their listening, with what they listen, and with what they confer secretly, when they are in private conversation." End of quotation.

Al-Hawfi said: "He did not say 'yastami'unahu' or 'yastami'unaka,' because the purpose is not only to report the listening; since it implies that the listening was in a manner of mockery, by saying 'a madman' or 'a bewitched man,' the listening was expressed with 'bi' and 'ila,' so that it is known that the listening intended is not the understanding of what is heard, apart from this purpose." ﴿When they listen to you, and when they are in private conversation﴾: so the first "idh" is connected to ﴿listen﴾ with "bi," and likewise ﴿and when they are in private conversation﴾, because the meaning is: "We know best what they listen with, to you and to your recitation and your speech; they listen only to find your slip and to track your flaw and to seek what they may use to criticize you," in their supposition. For this reason the transitivity with "bi" and "ila" is mentioned. End of quotation.

Abu al-Baqa' said: "They listen with it." It is said: the "ba'" means "lam," and "idh" is an adverb to the first "yastami'un," and "al-najwa" is a verbal noun; it may be the plural of "najiy," like "qatil" and "qatla"; and "idh" is a substitute for the first "idh." It was said: the estimate is: "Remember when you say." End of quotation.

Ibn Atiyyah said: "The pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ refers to what has the meaning of 'alladhi,' and the intended meaning is disdain and aversion, as if he said: 'We know best of the disdain and mockery with which they listen,' that is, it is constant with them. So God exposed their secret by this verse. The governing element of the first ﴿idh﴾ and of the conjoined ﴿yastami'un﴾ is the first ﴿yastami'un﴾." End of quotation.

They conferred privately. Al-Nadr said: "I do not understand what you are saying." Abu Sufyan said: "I see some of it as true." Abu Jahl said: "He is mad." Abu Lahab said: "He is a soothsayer." Huwaytib said: "He is a poet." Some said: "Fables of the ancients." Others said: "A human is teaching him." It is related that their private conference took place at the house of Utbah, who had invited the chiefs of Quraysh to a meal. The Prophet ﷺ entered upon them, recited the Qur'an to them, and invited them to God. They conferred, saying: "He is a magician, a madman."

The apparent meaning of ﴿mashuran﴾ is from "sihr" (magic), meaning that magic has deprived his intellect. Mujahid said: "Deceived (makhdu'an)," like ﴿How then are you deluded?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 89], meaning "you are deceived." Abu Ubaydah said: ﴿mashuran﴾ means that he has a "sahr," that is, a lung, so he cannot do without food and drink; thus he is like you and is not an angel. The Arabs say of a coward, "his sahr has swollen," and any human or other who eats or drinks is "mashur." He said:

"We see ourselves as having been appointed for some unseen matter, and we are nourished (nusharu) by food and drink."

That is, we are fed, sustained, and "nusharu" (nourished). Labid said:

"If you ask us what we are about, we are, indeed, sparrows of this nourished (musahhar) human kind."

Ibn Qutaybah said: "I do not know what led Abu Ubaydah to this strained interpretation, when the early scholars interpreted it in clear ways." And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn their backs in aversion.﴾ ﴿We know best what they listen to when they listen to you, and when they are in private conversation, when the wrongdoers say, "You follow only a man under enchantment."﴾ ﴿Look how they strike for you comparisons, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way.﴾ ﴿And they say, "When we have become bones and dust, shall we really be resurrected in a new creation?"﴾.

The apparent meaning is: "We placed between your seeing and the sight of those who do not believe in the Hereafter" [a barrier], as is mentioned in the occasion of revelation.

Its meaning may be interpreted as "possessing concealment," as in the pattern of "laban" and "tamr" (milk-possessor and date-possessor), i.e., "possessor of milk" and "possessor of dates." They also say: "a man marhub" meaning "one possessing softness" (ruṭbah), and one does not say "rattabtuhu"; "a place mahul" meaning "possessing terror" (hawl), and one does not say "hultu al-makan"; "a girl maghnuga," and one does not say "ghanijat al-jariyah." As for the first phrase, ﴿And We place over their hearts coverings, so that they do not understand it, and in their ears deafness﴾: its interpretation has already been given at the beginning of al-An'am.

One group said it refers to the devils, because they flee from the Qur'an, and this meaning is indicated even though they had not been mentioned. Abu al-Hawra' Aws ibn Abd Allah said: "Nothing drives Satan from the heart more than 'There is no god but God,'" then he recited ﴿And when you mention...﴾, the verse. Ali ibn al-Husayn said: it is the basmalah (the invocation "In the name of God").

For this reason the transitivity with "bi" and "ila" is mentioned. End of quotation.

Abu al-Baqa' said: "They listen with it." It is said: the "ba'" means "lam," and "idh" is an adverb to the first "yastami'un," and "al-najwa" is a verbal noun; it may be the plural of "najiy," like "qatil" and "qatla"; and "idh" is a substitute for the first "idh." Ibn Atiyyah said: "The pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ refers to what has the meaning of 'alladhi,' and the intended meaning is disdain and aversion, as if he said: 'We know best of the disdain and mockery with which they listen,' that is, it is constant with them. Then he said: 'O assembly of Quraysh, say: there is no god but God, by which you will rule the Arabs and the non-Arabs (al-ajam) will submit to you.' So they turned and fled, and this verse was revealed." The apparent meaning is that the verse describes the state of those who flee at the time of his recitation and his passing over the oneness of God. The meaning is: when the passages of monotheism came, the disbelievers fled, denying it, finding it repugnant, and rejecting and discarding their gods.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Wahada, yahidu, wahdan and wahdah, like wa'ada, ya'idu, wa'dan and 'idah; and ﴿wahdah﴾ is of the pattern of raja'a, its return being to its beginning; and do it with your utmost effort and capacity; in that it is a verbal noun (masdar) substituting for the state (hal), its origin being yahidu wahdahu, meaning 'alone.'" End of quotation. What he holds, that ﴿wahdah﴾ is a verbal noun substituting for the state, is contrary to the school of Sibawayh. For Sibawayh, ﴿wahdah﴾ is not a verbal noun but a noun placed in the position of a verbal noun which is placed in the position of the state; so ﴿wahdah﴾ for him is placed in the position of "iyhad," and "iyhad" is placed in the position of "muwahhid." Yunus held that ﴿wahdah﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarf). Others held that it is a verbal noun with no verb of its own; others that it is a verbal noun of "awhada" with the augment dropped; and others that it is a verbal noun of "wahd," as al-Zamakhshari held. The arguments for these views are mentioned in the books of grammar. When ﴿wahdah﴾ is mentioned after a subject and object, as in "I struck Zayd," Sibawayh's view is that it is a state of the subject, meaning "singling him out in striking"; al-Mubarrad's view is that it may be a state of the object. So on Sibawayh's view the sense is ﴿when you mention your Lord﴾ singling Him out in mention; and on Abu al-Abbas's view it may mean singling Him out in mention.

﴿Nufuran﴾ is a state, the plural of "nafir," like "qa'id" and "qu'ud," or a verbal noun of a non-original form, because the meaning of ﴿they turned﴾ is "they fled." The apparent sense is that the pronoun in ﴿they turned﴾ refers to the disbelievers already mentioned. One group said it refers to the devils, because they flee from the Qur'an, and this meaning is indicated even though they had not been mentioned. Abu al-Hawra' Aws ibn Abd Allah said: "Nothing drives Satan from the heart more than 'There is no god but God,'" then he recited ﴿And when you mention...﴾, the verse. Ali ibn al-Husayn said: it is the basmalah (the invocation "In the name of God").

﴿We know best what they listen to with it﴾: that is, with the mockery by which they listen, and the derision toward you and the idle talk. When he ﷺ recited, two men from the Banu Abd Allah would stand on his right and two on his left, clapping, whistling, and mixing poetry into his recitation to confuse him. "Bi-ma" is connected to "a'lam." Whatever carries the meaning of knowledge and ignorance, even if it transitively takes a direct object, when it is in the form of "af'al" in the exclamatory (ta'ajjub) and in the comparative (af'al al-tafdil), it takes the preposition "bi." You say: "How knowledgeable is Zayd of such-and-such" and "How ignorant he is of such-and-such," and "He is more knowledgeable of such-and-such" and "more ignorant of such-and-such." This is unlike other transitive verbs taking a direct object, which in the exclamatory and comparative "af'al" take "li" (for): "How striking Zayd is to Amr," and "Zayd is more striking to Amr than to Bakr." Al-Zamakhshari said it is in the position of a state, as you say: "they listen with mockery," meaning "mocking." ﴿When they listen﴾ is in the accusative governed by "a'lam," meaning: "I know best the time of their listening, with what they listen, and with what they confer secretly, when they are in private conversation." End of quotation.

Al-Hawfi said: "He did not say 'yastami'unahu' or 'yastami'unaka,' because the purpose is not only to report the listening; since it implies that the listening was in a manner of mockery, by saying 'a madman' or 'a bewitched man,' the listening was expressed with 'bi' and 'ila,' so that it is known that the listening intended is not the understanding of what is heard, apart from this purpose." ﴿When they listen to you, and when they are in private conversation﴾: so the first "idh" is connected to ﴿listen﴾ with "bi," and likewise ﴿and when they are in private conversation﴾, because the meaning is: "We know best what they listen with, to you and to your recitation and your speech; they listen only to find your slip and to track your flaw and to seek what they may use to criticize you," in their supposition. For this reason the transitivity with "bi" and "ila" is mentioned. End of quotation.

Abu al-Baqa' said: "They listen with it." It is said: the "ba'" means "lam," and "idh" is an adverb to the first "yastami'un," and "al-najwa" is a verbal noun; it may be the plural of "najiy," like "qatil" and "qatla"; and "idh" is a substitute for the first "idh." It was said: the estimate is: "Remember when you say." End of quotation.

Ibn Atiyyah said: "The pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ refers to what has the meaning of 'alladhi,' and the intended meaning is disdain and aversion, as if he said: 'We know best of the disdain and mockery with which they listen,' that is, it is constant with them. So God exposed their secret by this verse. The governing element of the first ﴿idh﴾ and of the conjoined ﴿yastami'un﴾ is the first ﴿yastami'un﴾." End of quotation.

They conferred privately. Al-Nadr said: "I do not understand what you are saying." Abu Sufyan said: "I see some of it as true." Abu Jahl said: "He is mad." Abu Lahab said: "He is a soothsayer." Huwaytib said: "He is a poet." Some said: "Fables of the ancients." Others said: "A human is teaching him." It is related that their private conference took place at the house of Utbah, who had invited the chiefs of Quraysh to a meal. The Prophet ﷺ entered upon them, recited the Qur'an to them, and invited them to God. They conferred, saying: "He is a magician, a madman."

The apparent meaning of ﴿mashuran﴾ is from "sihr" (magic), meaning that magic has deprived his intellect. Mujahid said: "Deceived (makhdu'an)," like ﴿How then are you deluded?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 89], meaning "you are deceived." Abu Ubaydah said: ﴿mashuran﴾ means that he has a "sahr," that is, a lung, so he cannot do without food and drink; thus he is like you and is not an angel. The Arabs say of a coward, "his sahr has swollen," and any human or other who eats or drinks is "mashur." He said:

"We see ourselves as having been appointed for some unseen matter, and we are nourished (nusharu) by food and drink."

That is, we are fed, sustained, and "nusharu" (nourished). Labid said:

"If you ask us what we are about, we are, indeed, sparrows of this nourished (musahhar) human kind."

Ibn Qutaybah said: "I do not know what led Abu Ubaydah to this strained interpretation, when the early scholars interpreted it in clear ways." Ibn Atiyyah said: "The verse after this strengthens the view that the word is from 'sihr' with a kasra on the sin; for in their saying 'darb mathal' (striking a comparison)... As for it being from 'sahr' meaning the lung, and from nourishment, and the reference being that he is a human, then no comparison would have been struck for him in that; rather it is a real attribute of him. And ﴿al-amthal﴾ was mentioned in what they said in their private conference, and that was from them by way of diversion and confusion. Then al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah judged that the closest of these to the imagination of those who came upon them was that he is a magician, so they went astray in all of that, the straying of one who seeks in it a path to take and cannot reach it, so he is bewildered in his matter with regard to them, and so they cannot find a way (sabilan) to guidance and to the reflection that leads to faith, or a way to corrupt your affair and extinguish the light of God by their striking comparisons and their following every stratagem against you."

Al-Tabari reported that it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and his companions. ﴿And they said, "When we are..."﴾ This is an interrogative (istifham) expressing wonder, denial and disbelief, as they found it far-fetched. When they had coined these comparisons for him and said of him, "He is bewitched," they mentioned what they had used as evidence for their claim that he had the attributes they ascribed to him. They also deemed it far-fetched that, after a person has become crumbled remains (rufat), God would bring him back to life and restore him. This was answered by saying that it is God who originated them from pure non-existence ('adam al-sirf), as will be explained in the verse that follows. As for the reciters who read *idha* (إذا) and *inna* (إنّا), either both or one of them, in the form of a declarative statement, they do not mean it literally as a statement, because that would amount to affirming the resurrection and the final creation. Rather, they omitted the interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifham) because the meaning makes it clear. The sentence contains an ellipsis, whose supplied form is: "When we are dust and bones, will we be resurrected or restored?" This was omitted because what follows indicates it. According to Sibawayh, this omitted element is the answer of the conditional clause (jawab al-shart), while according to Yunus it is the element to which the interrogation attaches and on which it focuses. *Khalqan* (خلقا) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), and it is originally a verbal noun (masdar) used in the sense of the passive participle, meaning *makhluqan* (مخلوقا), "created."

(p-45)

Al-hadid (iron) is well known. *Naghadat sinnuhu* means its tooth moved, as in: "He said." And *naghadat min harami asnanuha* means her teeth moved from old age. *Yanghidu* and *yanghudu*, *naghdan* and *nughudan*. *Anghada ra's'ahu* means he moved his head up and down. The poet said:

*When she saw me, she moved her head at me*

Another said:

*He moved his head toward me and raised it, as if seeking something to eat*

Al-Farra' said: *anghada ra'sahu* means he moved his head up and down. Abu al-Haytham said: When he is told something and shakes his head in denial, he has *anghada ra'sahu*. Dhu al-Rumma said:

*Women who did not settle on the banks of a village, by the sword, and the bridges did not nod at them*

*Hannaka al-dabbata wa-htanakaha* means he put a rope under its lower jaw to lead it by. *Ihtanaka al-jaradu al-ardha* means the locusts ate its plants. The poet said:

*We complain to you of a year that has crushed us, hardship upon hardship, and weakened us*

*Ihtanakat amwalana* and *hanakta*. From this is what Sibawayh mentioned, such as their saying: *ahnak al-shatayn*, meaning the one who eats both of them.

*Istafazza al-rajula* means he made him light-headed. *Al-fazz* means light. Its original meaning is cutting. From it: *tafazzaza al-thawbu*, meaning the garment was torn. *Istafazzani fulan* means someone deceived me until I fell into a matter he wanted. It is said of a calf: *fazz*, because of its lightness. The poet said:

*As a wild donkey's foal cries out for help, it fears the eyes, and the dark spot is not seen on it*

*Al-jalaba* means shouting. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' said this. Abu 'Ubayda said: *jalaba* and *ajlaba*. Al-Zajjaj said: *ajlaba 'ala al-'aduwwi*, meaning he gathered horses against the enemy. Ibn al-Sikkit said: *jalaba 'alayhi* means he helped him. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *ajlaba 'ala al-rajul*, when he threatened him with evil, and gathered a crowd against him. *Al-sawt* is well known.

*Al-hasib* is the wind that throws pebbles. Al-Farra' said this. *Al-hasab* is throwing pebbles, which are small stones. Al-Farazdaq said:

*Facing the north of Syria, we strike them with pebbles like scattered cotton*

*Al-hasib* is the cloud that throws hail and stones. *Tara* means once. It is plural *tir* and *taratin*. The poet said:

*The pupil of my eye drains the water once, then it appears, and at other times it floods and drowns*

*Al-qasif* is what breaks everything it meets. It is said: *qasafa al-shajara yaqsifuhu qasfan*, meaning he broke the tree. Abu Tammam said:

*When the winds blow strongly, they break the reeds of Najd, and they do not care about the tamarisk*

It is also said: *al-qasif* is the wind that has a *qasif*, which is a strong sound, as if it breaks with a crackling, meaning it shatters.

(p-46) ﴿Say: Be stones or iron﴾ ﴿or a creation of what is great in your breasts. They will say: "Who will restore us?" Say: "He who created you the first time." Then they will shake their heads at you and say: "When is it?" Say: "Perhaps it is near."﴾ ﴿On the day He calls you, you will answer with His praise, and you will think you stayed only a little.﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: When they said ﴿Are we truly to be raised as new creation?﴾ [Al-Isra: 49], it was said to them: ﴿Be stones or iron﴾. He returned their saying "we are" to His saying "be," as if it were said: "Be stones or iron, and do not be bones, for He is able to revive you." The meaning is that you consider it unlikely that God renews your creation and returns you to the state of life, with the moisture and freshness of a living thing, after you were dry bones. Yet bones are part of the living body. They are the pillar of its creation on which the rest is built. So it is not strange that God restores them by His power to their first state. But even if you were the farthest thing from life and the moisture of a living body, and of the same kind as humans, namely dry ﴿stones﴾ or ﴿iron﴾, whose nature is hardness and firmness, He would still be able to return you to the state of life. ﴿Or a creation of what is great﴾ in your view as too far from accepting life, and what in your opinion is too great for the Creator to revive, for He will revive it.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Be, if you can, these difficult things that are impossible to achieve. It is necessary that you be raised." His saying "be" is what the speakers call *al-ta'jiz* (expression of inability as a challenge), which is one of the forms of *af'al* (imperative). Some have given this verse as an example. In my view, this needs consideration. *Al-ta'jiz* is when the command requires doing what the addressee cannot do, such as His saying: ﴿Ward off death from yourselves﴾ [Al Imran: 168] and similar. As for this verse, its meaning is: "Be in imagination and estimation, such and such." ﴿He who created you﴾ in the same way is the one who will restore you. End of quote. Mujahid said: The meaning of ﴿be﴾ is whatever you wish, for you will be restored. Al-Nahhas said: This is a good saying, because they cannot become stones. The meaning is that they had acknowledged their Creator but denied resurrection. So it was said to them: "Imagine that you are whatever you wish. If you were ﴿stones or iron﴾ you would be raised as you were created the first time." End of quote.

﴿Or a creation of what is great in your breasts﴾: its hardness and its increase over the strength and hardness of iron. He did not specify it. He left that to their thoughts and their wandering over what is harder than iron. He began first with the hard, then mentioned, in a gradual way, what is harder than it, then what is harder than iron. That is: suppose yourselves to be one of these, for you will certainly be raised whatever state you are in.

Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: "What is great" is death, meaning: if you were death, He would make you die and then revive you. This explanation is only valid if exaggeration is intended, not the literal reality, because the body is a substance and death is an accident, and a substance does not turn into an accident. Even if its turning into an accident were supposed, it could not accept life because of the opposition between them. Mujahid said: "What is great" means the heavens, the earth and the mountains.

When He mentioned that if they were the hardest thing and the farthest from life inhabiting it, the creation of life in it would still be possible, they said: "Who is able to bring life into us and restore us?" So He alerted them to what requires restoration, which is that He who began and originated you the first time is the one who will restore you. ﴿Who created you﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is omitted. The estimate is: ﴿He who created you the first time﴾ will restore you. Thus the answer matches the question. It is also possible for it to be the agent: "He who created you will restore you." It is also possible for it to be the predicate of a subject: "Your restorer is He who created you." And ﴿the first time﴾ is an adverbial of time (*zarf*), whose governing verb is ﴿created you﴾, as al-Hawfi said.

﴿Then they will shake﴾: that is, they will move their heads as a sign of denial and disbelief, saying: "When is it?" That is, when is the return? They did not say this in acceptance of the return, but as evasion and a move away from what is not asked about, because what is established as possible by rational proof is not asked about regarding the specific time of its occurrence. He answered their question about its nearness, not by specifying its time, because that is among what God has kept to His knowledge. It is possible that in ﴿perhaps﴾ there is an implied subject, meaning "perhaps it (the return) is." It is also possible that its subject is ﴿that it be﴾, so that it is complete. ﴿Near﴾ may be the predicate of *kana* (*kana* as a linking verb), meaning the return is described as near. It may also be an adverbial of time, meaning a near time. On this estimate, ﴿on the day He calls you﴾ replaces ﴿near﴾.

Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿On the day He calls you﴾ is an adverbial of time governed by *yakun* (be). It is not permissible for it to be an adverbial of the *kana* noun, even if it is a pronoun of the verbal noun, because a pronoun does not govern. End of quote. As for it being an adverbial to *yakun*, this is based on the permissibility of the incomplete *kana* governing an adverbial, and there is disagreement about this. As for his saying "because a pronoun does not govern," this is the view of the Basrans. The Kufans permit it to govern, as in: "My passing by Zayd is good, and by 'Amr it is bad," where they attach "by 'Amr" to the word *huwa* (it), meaning: "and my passing by 'Amr is bad."

The apparent meaning is that the calling is literal, meaning He calls you with a call that makes you hear, which is the final blast, as He said: ﴿On the day the caller calls from a near place﴾ [Qaf: 41] and so on. It is said that Israfil, peace be upon him, calls: "O decayed bodies, rotten bones, and scattered parts, return as you were." It is narrated in a hadith that he (ﷺ) said: "You will be called on the Day of Resurrection by your names and the names of your fathers, so make your names good." The meaning of ﴿then you will respond﴾ is that you will agree with the caller in what he calls you to.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Calling and responding are both figurative. The meaning is: on the day He raises you, you will rise, compliant and submissive, not refusing. End of quote. The apparent meaning is that the address is to the disbelievers, since the discourse before this was with them. So the pronoun refers to them, and ﴿with His praise﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) from them. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is an exaggeration of their submission to the resurrection, like your saying to someone you command to ride something difficult for him, and he refuses and resists: "You will ride it while you are praising and thankful." He means: you will be forced onto it and compelled until you yield with the gentleness of one who is tolerant, eager for it, and grateful for it. It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: They will shake the dust off their heads and say: "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You." End of quote. This is because of what became clear to them of His power.

It was said: the meaning of "bi-hamdihi" (with His praise) is that the Messenger is the one saying that, not that they are "bi-hamdihi" as a circumstantial phrase (hal) from them. So it is as if he said: "It may be that the Hour is near, on the day He calls you, and you rise, contrary to what you believe now, and that is by the praise of God for the truthfulness of my report." Just as you say to a man whom you have defeated in argument or debated on some knowledge: "You have erred, by God's praise" - so "bi-hamdillah" is not a circumstantial phrase from the subject of "akhta'ta," rather the meaning is: "You have erred, and praise is to God." This is a strained meaning which al-Tabari inclined towards, and "bi-hamdihi" would be a parenthetical insertion, since its meaning is "and praise is to God." A similar example is the verse of the poet:

"Indeed I, by God's praise, have not worn the garment of the wicked, nor do I cloak myself in treachery."

That is: "Indeed I, and praise is to God," so this is a parenthetical insertion between the noun of "inna" and its predicate, just as "bi-hamdihi" is a parenthetical insertion between the two conjoined elements. What occurred in the wording of Ibn 'Atiyya when he established this meaning was his saying: "It may be that the Hour is near," and this is a construction that is not permissible; you do not say "'asa anna Zaydan qa'imun" (it may be that Zayd is standing), unlike "'asa an yaquma Zaydun" (it may be that Zayd stands). And it is also possible that "bi-hamdihi" is a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun in "fa-tastajibuna."

The exegetes said: they will praise Him at a time when praise will not benefit them. Qatada said: its meaning is "with knowledge of Him and obedience to Him." "And you will think that you remained only a little." Ibn 'Abbas said: between the two blasts, the first and the second, for at that time the punishment is removed from them; and this is supported by "Who has raised us from our resting place?" [Ya-Sin: 52], so this refers to their staying between the two blasts. Al-Hasan said: it is the approximation of the time of resurrection, "as if you were in this world and it had not been, and in the Hereafter you were always there," so this returns to the belittling of the duration of stay in the world. Al-Zamakhshari said: "And you will think" means "and you will see the terror," and at it you will regard the duration of your stay in the world as short, and you will reckon it as a day or part of a day. From Qatada: the world became contemptible in their souls when they witnessed the Hereafter. End quote. It was also said: they considered their stay in the plain of resurrection to be short, because when the end of their affair was entry into the Fire, they regarded the duration of their stay in the intermediate state of the resurrection as short. It was also said: the speech is complete at His saying: "Say: It may be that it is near."

"On the day He calls you" is addressed to the believers and not to the disbelievers, because they respond to God "bi-hamdihi," praising Him for His kindness to them, and this befits only them. It was also said: the believer praises Him by choice and the disbeliever by compulsion. This indicates that the address is to both the disbeliever and the believer, and this is what is indicated by what was narrated from Ibn Jubayr. If the address is to the disbelievers, which is the apparent meaning, then "thinking" may be taken in its literal sense, so that when they return to the state of life, it occurs to them that they had not been separated from the world except for a short time, since in their supposition they had been sleeping. It may also mean certainty, since they knew that this had ended and passed away. The apparent view is that "wa-tazunnuna" is coordinated with "tastajibuna," as al-Hawfi said. Abu al-Baqa' said: that is, "and you (are thinking)," and the clause is a circumstantial phrase. Here "in" is a negating particle; "wa-tazunnu" is suspended from operating, so the clause after it is in a position of accusative. Grammarians rarely mention "in" as a negating particle among the particles of suspension. It appears that "qalilan" is in the accusative as an attribute of an omitted time noun, meaning "except for a short time," like His saying: "They said: We remained a day or part of a day" [Al-Kahf: 19]. It is also possible that it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a short stay," and the indication of the verb on its verbal noun is a strong indication.

Al-Zamakhshari said: When they said ﴿Are we truly to be raised as new creation?﴾ [Al-Isra: 49], it was said to them: ﴿Be stones or iron﴾. He returned their saying "we are" to His saying "be," as if it were said: "Be stones or iron, and do not be bones, for He is able to revive you." The meaning is that you consider it unlikely that God renews your creation and returns you to the state of life, with the moisture and freshness of a living thing, after you were dry bones. Yet bones are part of the living body. They are the pillar of its creation on which the rest is built. So it is not strange that God restores them by His power to their first state. But even if you were the farthest thing from life and the moisture of a living body, and of the same kind as humans, namely dry ﴿stones﴾ or ﴿iron﴾, whose nature is hardness and firmness, He would still be able to return you to the state of life. ﴿Or a creation of what is great﴾ in your view as too far from accepting life, and what in your opinion is too great for the Creator to revive, for He will revive it.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Be, if you can, these difficult things that are impossible to achieve. It is necessary that you be raised." His saying "be" is what the speakers call *al-ta'jiz* (expression of inability as a challenge), which is one of the forms of *af'al* (imperative). Some have given this verse as an example. In my view, this needs consideration. *Al-ta'jiz* is when the command requires doing what the addressee cannot do, such as His saying: ﴿Ward off death from yourselves﴾ [Al Imran: 168] and similar. As for this verse, its meaning is: "Be in imagination and estimation, such and such." ﴿He who created you﴾ in the same way is the one who will restore you. End of quote. Mujahid said: The meaning of ﴿be﴾ is whatever you wish, for you will be restored. Al-Nahhas said: This is a good saying, because they cannot become stones. The meaning is that they had acknowledged their Creator but denied resurrection. So it was said to them: "Imagine that you are whatever you wish. If you were ﴿stones or iron﴾ you would be raised as you were created the first time." End of quote.

﴿Or a creation of what is great in your breasts﴾: its hardness and its increase over the strength and hardness of iron. He did not specify it. He left that to their thoughts and their wandering over what is harder than iron. He began first with the hard, then mentioned, in a gradual way, what is harder than it, then what is harder than iron. That is: suppose yourselves to be one of these, for you will certainly be raised whatever state you are in.

Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: "What is great" is death, meaning: if you were death, He would make you die and then revive you. This explanation is only valid if exaggeration is intended, not the literal reality, because the body is a substance and death is an accident, and a substance does not turn into an accident. Even if its turning into an accident were supposed, it could not accept life because of the opposition between them. Mujahid said: "What is great" means the heavens, the earth and the mountains.

When He mentioned that if they were the hardest thing and the farthest from life inhabiting it, the creation of life in it would still be possible, they said: "Who is able to bring life into us and restore us?" So He alerted them to what requires restoration, which is that He who began and originated you the first time is the one who will restore you. ﴿Who created you﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is omitted. The estimate is: ﴿He who created you the first time﴾ will restore you. Thus the answer matches the question. It is also possible for it to be the agent: "He who created you will restore you." It is also possible for it to be the predicate of a subject: "Your restorer is He who created you." And ﴿the first time﴾ is an adverbial of time (*zarf*), whose governing verb is ﴿created you﴾, as al-Hawfi said.

﴿Then they will shake﴾: that is, they will move their heads as a sign of denial and disbelief, saying: "When is it?" That is, when is the return? They did not say this in acceptance of the return, but as evasion and a move away from what is not asked about, because what is established as possible by rational proof is not asked about regarding the specific time of its occurrence. He answered their question about its nearness, not by specifying its time, because that is among what God has kept to His knowledge. It is possible that in ﴿perhaps﴾ there is an implied subject, meaning "perhaps it (the return) is." It is also possible that its subject is ﴿that it be﴾, so that it is complete. ﴿Near﴾ may be the predicate of *kana* (*kana* as a linking verb), meaning the return is described as near. It may also be an adverbial of time, meaning a near time. On this estimate, ﴿on the day He calls you﴾ replaces ﴿near﴾.

Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿On the day He calls you﴾ is an adverbial of time governed by *yakun* (be). It is not permissible for it to be an adverbial of the *kana* noun, even if it is a pronoun of the verbal noun, because a pronoun does not govern. End of quote. As for it being an adverbial to *yakun*, this is based on the permissibility of the incomplete *kana* governing an adverbial, and there is disagreement about this. As for his saying "because a pronoun does not govern," this is the view of the Basrans. The Kufans permit it to govern, as in: "My passing by Zayd is good, and by 'Amr it is bad," where they attach "by 'Amr" to the word *huwa* (it), meaning: "and my passing by 'Amr is bad."

The apparent meaning is that the calling is literal, meaning He calls you with a call that makes you hear, which is the final blast, as He said: ﴿On the day the caller calls from a near place﴾ [Qaf: 41] and so on. It is said that Israfil, peace be upon him, calls: "O decayed bodies, rotten bones, and scattered parts, return as you were." It is narrated in a hadith that he (ﷺ) said: "You will be called on the Day of Resurrection by your names and the names of your fathers, so make your names good." The meaning of ﴿then you will respond﴾ is that you will agree with the caller in what he calls you to.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Calling and responding are both figurative. The meaning is: on the day He raises you, you will rise, compliant and submissive, not refusing. End of quote. The apparent meaning is that the address is to the disbelievers, since the discourse before this was with them. So the pronoun refers to them, and ﴿with His praise﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) from them. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is an exaggeration of their submission to the resurrection, like your saying to someone you command to ride something difficult for him, and he refuses and resists: "You will ride it while you are praising and thankful." He means: you will be forced onto it and compelled until you yield with the gentleness of one who is tolerant, eager for it, and grateful for it. It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: They will shake the dust off their heads and say: "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You." End of quote. This is because of what became clear to them of His power.

It was said: the meaning of "bi-hamdihi" (with His praise) is that the Messenger is the one saying that, not that they are "bi-hamdihi" as a circumstantial phrase (hal) from them. So it is as if he said: "It may be that the Hour is near, on the day He calls you, and you rise, contrary to what you believe now, and that is by the praise of God for the truthfulness of my report." Just as you say to a man whom you have defeated in argument or debated on some knowledge: "You have erred, by God's praise" - so "bi-hamdillah" is not a circumstantial phrase from the subject of "akhta'ta," rather the meaning is: "You have erred, and praise is to God." This is a strained meaning which al-Tabari inclined towards, and "bi-hamdihi" would be a parenthetical insertion, since its meaning is "and praise is to God." A similar example is the verse of the poet:

"Indeed I, by God's praise, have not worn the garment of the wicked, nor do I cloak myself in treachery."

That is: "Indeed I, and praise is to God," so this is a parenthetical insertion between the noun of "inna" and its predicate, just as "bi-hamdihi" is a parenthetical insertion between the two conjoined elements. What occurred in the wording of Ibn 'Atiyya when he established this meaning was his saying: "It may be that the Hour is near," and this is a construction that is not permissible; you do not say "'asa anna Zaydan qa'imun" (it may be that Zayd is standing), unlike "'asa an yaquma Zaydun" (it may be that Zayd stands). And it is also possible that "bi-hamdihi" is a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun in "fa-tastajibuna."

The exegetes said: they will praise Him at a time when praise will not benefit them. Qatada said: its meaning is "with knowledge of Him and obedience to Him." "And you will think that you remained only a little." Ibn 'Abbas said: between the two blasts, the first and the second, for at that time the punishment is removed from them; and this is supported by "Who has raised us from our resting place?" [Ya-Sin: 52], so this refers to their staying between the two blasts. Al-Hasan said: it is the approximation of the time of resurrection, "as if you were in this world and it had not been, and in the Hereafter you were always there," so this returns to the belittling of the duration of stay in the world. Al-Zamakhshari said: "And you will think" means "and you will see the terror," and at it you will regard the duration of your stay in the world as short, and you will reckon it as a day or part of a day. From Qatada: the world became contemptible in their souls when they witnessed the Hereafter. End quote. It was also said: they considered their stay in the plain of resurrection to be short, because when the end of their affair was entry into the Fire, they regarded the duration of their stay in the intermediate state of the resurrection as short. It was also said: the speech is complete at His saying: "Say: It may be that it is near."

"On the day He calls you" is addressed to the believers and not to the disbelievers, because they respond to God "bi-hamdihi," praising Him for His kindness to them, and this befits only them. It was also said: the believer praises Him by choice and the disbeliever by compulsion. This indicates that the address is to both the disbeliever and the believer, and this is what is indicated by what was narrated from Ibn Jubayr. If the address is to the disbelievers, which is the apparent meaning, then "thinking" may be taken in its literal sense, so that when they return to the state of life, it occurs to them that they had not been separated from the world except for a short time, since in their supposition they had been sleeping. It may also mean certainty, since they knew that this had ended and passed away. The apparent view is that "wa-tazunnuna" is coordinated with "tastajibuna," as al-Hawfi said. Abu al-Baqa' said: that is, "and you (are thinking)," and the clause is a circumstantial phrase. Here "in" is a negating particle; "wa-tazunnu" is suspended from operating, so the clause after it is in a position of accusative. Grammarians rarely mention "in" as a negating particle among the particles of suspension. It appears that "qalilan" is in the accusative as an attribute of an omitted time noun, meaning "except for a short time," like His saying: "They said: We remained a day or part of a day" [Al-Kahf: 19]. Al-hadid (iron) is well known. *Naghadat sinnuhu* means its tooth moved, as in: "He said." And *naghadat min harami asnanuha* means her teeth moved from old age. *Yanghidu* and *yanghudu*, *naghdan* and *nughudan*. *Anghada ra's'ahu* means he moved his head up and down. The poet said:

*When she saw me, she moved her head at me*

Another said:

*He moved his head toward me and raised it, as if seeking something to eat*

Al-Farra' said: *anghada ra'sahu* means he moved his head up and down. Abu al-Haytham said: When he is told something and shakes his head in denial, he has *anghada ra'sahu*. Dhu al-Rumma said:

*Women who did not settle on the banks of a village, by the sword, and the bridges did not nod at them*

*Hannaka al-dabbata wa-htanakaha* means he put a rope under its lower jaw to lead it by. *Ihtanaka al-jaradu al-ardha* means the locusts ate its plants. The poet said:

*We complain to you of a year that has crushed us, hardship upon hardship, and weakened us*

*Ihtanakat amwalana* and *hanakta*. From this is what Sibawayh mentioned, such as their saying: *ahnak al-shatayn*, meaning the one who eats both of them.

*Istafazza al-rajula* means he made him light-headed. *Al-fazz* means light. Its original meaning is cutting. From it: *tafazzaza al-thawbu*, meaning the garment was torn. *Istafazzani fulan* means someone deceived me until I fell into a matter he wanted. It is said of a calf: *fazz*, because of its lightness. The poet said:

*As a wild donkey's foal cries out for help, it fears the eyes, and the dark spot is not seen on it*

*Al-jalaba* means shouting. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' said this. Abu 'Ubayda said: *jalaba* and *ajlaba*. Al-Zajjaj said: *ajlaba 'ala al-'aduwwi*, meaning he gathered horses against the enemy. Ibn al-Sikkit said: *jalaba 'alayhi* means he helped him. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *ajlaba 'ala al-rajul*, when he threatened him with evil, and gathered a crowd against him. *Al-sawt* is well known.

*Al-hasib* is the wind that throws pebbles. Al-Farra' said this. *Al-hasab* is throwing pebbles, which are small stones. Al-Farazdaq said:

*Facing the north of Syria, we strike them with pebbles like scattered cotton*

*Al-hasib* is the cloud that throws hail and stones. *Tara* means once. It is plural *tir* and *taratin*. The poet said:

*The pupil of my eye drains the water once, then it appears, and at other times it floods and drowns*

*Al-qasif* is what breaks everything it meets. It is said: *qasafa al-shajara yaqsifuhu qasfan*, meaning he broke the tree. Abu Tammam said:

*When the winds blow strongly, they break the reeds of Najd, and they do not care about the tamarisk*

It is also said: *al-qasif* is the wind that has a *qasif*, which is a strong sound, as if it breaks with a crackling, meaning it shatters.

*Facing the north of Syria, we strike them with pebbles like scattered cotton*

*The pupil of my eye drains the water once, then it appears, and at other times it floods and drowns*

He left that to their thoughts and their wandering over what is harder than iron. He began first with the hard, then mentioned, in a gradual way, what is harder than it, then what is harder than iron. That is: suppose yourselves to be one of these, for you will certainly be raised whatever state you are in.

Even if its turning into an accident were supposed, it could not accept life because of the opposition between them. Mujahid said: "What is great" means the heavens, the earth and the mountains.

When He mentioned that if they were the hardest thing and the farthest from life inhabiting it, the creation of life in it would still be possible, they said: "Who is able to bring life into us and restore us?" So He alerted them to what requires restoration, which is that He who began and originated you the first time is the one who will restore you. ﴿Who created you﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is omitted. The estimate is: ﴿He who created you the first time﴾ will restore you. Thus the answer matches the question. It is also possible for it to be the agent: "He who created you will restore you." It is also possible for it to be the predicate of a subject: "Your restorer is He who created you." ﴿Then they will shake﴾: that is, they will move their heads as a sign of denial and disbelief, saying: "When is it?" That is, when is the return? They did not say this in acceptance of the return, but as evasion and a move away from what is not asked about, because what is established as possible by rational proof is not asked about regarding the specific time of its occurrence. He answered their question about its nearness, not by specifying its time, because that is among what God has kept to His knowledge. It is possible that in ﴿perhaps﴾ there is an implied subject, meaning "perhaps it (the return) is." It is also possible that its subject is ﴿that it be﴾, so that it is complete. ﴿Near﴾ may be the predicate of *kana* (*kana* as a linking verb), meaning the return is described as near. It may also be an adverbial of time, meaning a near time. On this estimate, ﴿on the day He calls you﴾ replaces ﴿near﴾.

Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿On the day He calls you﴾ is an adverbial of time governed by *yakun* (be). It is not permissible for it to be an adverbial of the *kana* noun, even if it is a pronoun of the verbal noun, because a pronoun does not govern. End of quote. As for it being an adverbial to *yakun*, this is based on the permissibility of the incomplete *kana* governing an adverbial, and there is disagreement about this. As for his saying "because a pronoun does not govern," this is the view of the Basrans. The apparent meaning is that the calling is literal, meaning He calls you with a call that makes you hear, which is the final blast, as He said: ﴿On the day the caller calls from a near place﴾ [Qaf: 41] and so on. It is narrated in a hadith that he (ﷺ) said: "You will be called on the Day of Resurrection by your names and the names of your fathers, so make your names good." The apparent meaning is that the address is to the disbelievers, since the discourse before this was with them. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is an exaggeration of their submission to the resurrection, like your saying to someone you command to ride something difficult for him, and he refuses and resists: "You will ride it while you are praising and thankful." He means: you will be forced onto it and compelled until you yield with the gentleness of one who is tolerant, eager for it, and grateful for it. It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: They will shake the dust off their heads and say: "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You." End of quote. "Indeed I, by God's praise, have not worn the garment of the wicked, nor do I cloak myself in treachery."

That is: "Indeed I, and praise is to God," so this is a parenthetical insertion between the noun of "inna" and its predicate, just as "bi-hamdihi" is a parenthetical insertion between the two conjoined elements. The exegetes said: they will praise Him at a time when praise will not benefit them. Qatada said: its meaning is "with knowledge of Him and obedience to Him." "And you will think that you remained only a little." Ibn 'Abbas said: between the two blasts, the first and the second, for at that time the punishment is removed from them; and this is supported by "Who has raised us from our resting place?" Al-Zamakhshari said: "And you will think" means "and you will see the terror," and at it you will regard the duration of your stay in the world as short, and you will reckon it as a day or part of a day. It was also said: they considered their stay in the plain of resurrection to be short, because when the end of their affair was entry into the Fire, they regarded the duration of their stay in the intermediate state of the resurrection as short.
