**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verses 53-55:**

﴿And say to My servants that they should speak what is best. Indeed, Satan incites discord among them. Indeed, Satan is ever to mankind a clear enemy.﴾ (17:53) ﴿Your Lord knows you best. If He wills, He will have mercy upon you, or if He wills, He will punish you. And We have not sent you as a guardian over them.﴾ (17:54) ﴿And your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth. We have certainly favoured some of the prophets over others, and We gave David the Zabur.﴾ (17:55)

It is said: The occasion of its revelation was that some of the disbelievers insulted 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him). 'Umar cursed him in return and resolved to kill him, and nearly provoked a strife. Then this verse was revealed. It is abrogated (mansukha) by the verse of the sword.

Its connection with what precedes it is that when there was mention of what the disbelievers attributed to Allah, the Exalted, of offspring, their aversion from the Book of Allah when they heard it, their harming of the Messenger (ﷺ), their claim that he was bewitched, and their denial of resurrection, this became an occasion for harming the believers and a cause of the believers' hatred towards them and their treating them as they had treated them. So Allah, the Exalted, commanded His Prophet to instruct the believers to be gentle with the disbelievers, to be kind to them in speech, and not to treat them with the same deeds and words as theirs. According to this, the meaning of ﴿قُلْ لِعِبادِي﴾ [said to My servants] refers to the believers, and ﴿يَقُولُوا﴾ [that they should speak] is directed to the polytheists, the words ﴿الَّتِي هي أحْسَنُ﴾ [that which is best].

It is also said: The meaning of ﴿يَقُولُوا﴾ [that they should speak] is: some believers should say to other believers the words that are best, that is, that they should honour and esteem one another, and that nothing should come from them except good speech and beautiful words. Thus they should not be like the polytheists in dealing with one another through mutual satire, abuse, wars, plunder of wealth, and the taking of women and offspring as captives.

It is also said: "My servants" here refers to the polytheists, since the purpose here is the call to Islam. So they were addressed with good speech (p-49) so that this would be a means to accepting the religion. It is as if it were said: Say to those who acknowledge that they are My servants: ﴿that which is best﴾, which is the affirmation of Allah's oneness and His exemption from having offspring and from taking the angels as daughters, for that is from the incitement and whispering of Satan and his making it appear fair. It is also said: "My servants" includes both groups, the believers and the disbelievers, according to the explanation of ﴿الَّتِي هي أحْسَنُ﴾ [that which is best] that will come. What appears to be the case is that the expression "My servants," being attributed to Him, the Exalted, has been frequently used in the Qur'an for believers, as in His saying: ﴿So give good news to My servants who listen to the word﴾ (39:17), ﴿Enter among My servants﴾ (89:29), ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾ (76:6).

The word "say" (قُلْ) is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ) and is an imperative. The object of the saying is omitted, its estimated form being: "Speak that which is best." The word ﴿يَقُولُوا﴾ [they should speak] is in the jussive mood (the form reading as جَزَمَ, jazama, i.e., in the jussive) because it is an answer to the imperative "say." This was stated by al-Akhfash, and its meaning is sound on the assumption that "My servants" refers to the believers, because on account of their haste in carrying out Allah's command, by the very fact of being told this, they said ﴿that which is best﴾. It is reported from Sibawayh that it was jussive as an answer to an omitted conditional, meaning: if he were to say to them, ﴿that they should speak﴾; so in his view the object of the saying is omitted, and the conditional whose answer is ﴿يَقُولُوا﴾ [that they should speak] is omitted. Al-Mubarrad said: it is jussive as an answer to the imperative which is the object of "say" (قُلْ), i.e., "Speak ﴿that which is best﴾," and then ﴿يَقُولُوا﴾ [they should speak]. It is also said: the object of "say" is mentioned, not omitted, and it is ﴿يَقُولُوا﴾ [they should speak], with an implied imperative particle (لام الأمر, lam al-amr), and it is jussive by it; this was stated by al-Zajjaj. It is also said: ﴿يَقُولُوا﴾ [they should speak] is indeclinable, being a present-tense verb that has taken the place of the indeclinable imperative verb, so it was made indeclinable; the meaning being: "Say to My servants," "speak." This was stated by al-Mazini. These opinions have been given regarding His saying: ﴿Say to My servants who believe that they should establish prayer﴾ (14:31), and the weighing of which view should be preferred is discussed in the science of grammar.

As for ﴿الَّتِي هي أحْسَنُ﴾ [that which is best], a group, including Ibn 'Abbas, said it is the statement "There is no god but Allah." Ibn 'Atiyya said: It follows from this that His saying ﴿لِعِبادِي﴾ [to My servants] means all creation, because all of them are called to "There is no god but Allah." Then His saying after that, ﴿Indeed, Satan incites discord among them﴾, would not fit the meaning except by a stretch, by taking ﴿بَيْنَهم﴾ [among them] to mean "within them and amid them," and taking ﴿النَّزْغُ﴾ [incitement] to mean whispering and inciting. Al-Hasan said: "May Allah have mercy on you," "May Allah forgive you." He also said: it is the command to comply with the commands and to avoid the prohibitions. It is also said: the speech to the believer is "May Allah have mercy on you," and to the disbeliever "May Allah guide you." Al-Jumhur said: it is the most beautiful dialogue according to each meaning in its place. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿الَّتِي هي أحْسَنُ﴾ [that which is best] is explained by His saying: ﴿Your Lord knows you best. If He wills, He will have mercy upon you, or if He wills, He will punish you﴾, meaning: he says to them this word and the like, and does not say to them that you are of the people of the Fire and that you will be punished, and other things like that which anger them and provoke them to evil. And His saying ﴿Indeed, Satan incites discord among them﴾ is a parenthetical clause meaning that he casts corruption among them and stirs some against others, so that enmity and hostility arise among them.

Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said, in summary: When you want to present proof against an opponent, present it in the best manner, which is that it is not mixed with abuse, as in His saying: ﴿Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in the best manner﴾ (16:125), and ﴿Do not argue with the People of the Book except in the best manner﴾ (29:46). Mixing proof with abuse is a cause of being met with the same, and a deterrent from achieving the purpose of presenting proof and its effect. Then He drew attention to this way with His saying ﴿Indeed, Satan incites discord among them﴾, encompassing both groups; that is, whenever proof is mixed with harm, strife occurs. End of quotation.

Talha read ﴿يَنْزِغُ﴾ with the letter zay (ز) vowelled with a kasra (يَنْزِغُ). Abu Hatim said: it is perhaps a dialect form, and the recitation is with the fatha. Sahib al-Lawamih said: it is a dialect. Al-Zamakhshari said: both are dialects, like يَعْرِشُونَ and يَعْرُشُونَ. End of quotation. Had he given the example of يَنْطَحُ and يَنْطِحُ it would have been more apt.

Allah, the Exalted, explained the cause of the incitement, which is the enmity that exists with their father Adam before them, and His saying: ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them﴾ (7:17), etc., and other verses indicating his domination over mankind and his pursuit of destructive calamities for them.

As for the address in His saying ﴿Your Lord﴾ (17:54): if it is directed to the believers, then mercy means deliverance from the disbelievers of Makkah and their harm, and punishment means giving them power over them (p-50).

﴿And We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾ (17:54), meaning over the disbelievers, as a protector and guarantor. So you occupy yourself with the call, and their guidance is up to Allah. It is said: ﴿He will have mercy upon you﴾ (17:54) means by guidance to success and righteous deeds, and if He wills, He will punish you by abandonment. If the address is to the disbelievers, then He said: "Allah will have mercy upon you" corresponds to guidance to faith, and ﴿He will punish you﴾ (17:54) means He will cause you to die in disbelief. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi mentioned: When famine struck the polytheists, they said: ﴿Our Lord, remove from us the punishment; indeed, we are believers﴾ (44:12). Then Allah said: ﴿Your Lord knows you best﴾ (17:54), regarding who believes and who does not believe; ﴿if He wills, He will have mercy upon you﴾ (17:54), so He will lift the famine from you; ﴿or if He wills, He will punish you﴾ (17:54), so He will leave it upon you.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: This verse strengthens the view that the preceding verse concerns the relations between the believing servants and the disbelievers of Makkah, because His saying ﴿Your Lord knows you best﴾ (17:54) is addressed to the disbelievers of Makkah, as evidenced by His saying ﴿And We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾ (17:54). So it is as if He commanded the believers not to be harsh with the disbelievers regarding religion; then He said: He knows them best, and gave them hope and warned them. The meaning of ﴿He will have mercy upon you﴾ (17:54) is by turning to you in repentance; this was said by Ibn Jurayj and others. End of quotation. It has been mentioned earlier, from al-Zamakhshari's words, that His saying ﴿Your Lord knows you best﴾ (17:54) is a statement of the believers to the disbelievers, and that it is an explanation of His saying ﴿that which is best﴾ (17:53).

Ibn al-Anbari said: ("or," أوْ) occurs here to indicate that both matters are equal in the sight of Allah, and not that one of them is intended. So it is like the permissive "or" in their saying: "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin," meaning: "We have granted you latitude in the matter." Al-Karmani said: ("or," أوْ) is for transition (al-idrab), and for this reason ("if," إنْ) is repeated. When He, the Exalted, mentioned that He knows best those whom He addressed by His saying ﴿Your Lord knows you best﴾ (17:54), He moved from the particular to the general, saying, addressing His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿And your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth﴾ (17:55), to show that His knowledge is not restricted to you; rather His knowledge is related to all who are in the heavens and the earth, with their conditions, their measures, and what each of them deserves. ("Who," بِمَن) is related to ("knows best," أعْلَمُ) just as ("you," بِكم) before it was related to ("knows best," أعْلَمُ). Its relation to it does not indicate that the knowledge of the Exalted is exclusive to what it relates to, just as your saying: "Zayd is most knowledgeable in grammar" does not indicate that he is not most knowledgeable in other sciences. Abu 'Ali said: the preposition (بـ, bi) is related to a verb whose implied form is "knows (عَلِمَ) who." He said: because if it were related to ("knows best," أعْلَمُ), it would imply that He is not the most knowledgeable of other than that, and this does not necessarily follow. Also, ("knows," عَلِمَ) does not take the preposition (بـ) directly; it takes one object without a preposition, or a preposition does not appear, as established in the science of grammar.

Since the disbelievers had found it strange that a human being should be sent as a prophet, because that entails the preference of prophets over others, He, the Exalted, informed them of the preference of some prophets over others, as an indication that the preference of prophets over other people is not to be deemed strange, since preference occurs within this class of humans preferred over people. Allah, the Exalted, knows best what distinction He has given each of them, so He prefers whom He wills over whom He wills, for He is the All-Wise, and nothing proceeds except from His wisdom. In this there is also an indication that the preference of Muhammad (ﷺ) over all other prophets is not to be considered strange. David is singled out for mention here because Allah, the Exalted, mentioned in the Zabur that Muhammad is the seal of the prophets and that his community is the best of communities. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We have already written in the Zabur, after the reminder, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ (21:105); they are Muhammad and his community. The Quraysh often referred to the Jews regarding what they reported from their books, so He drew attention to the fact that the Zabur of David contained good news of Muhammad (ﷺ). In this is also a refutation of the obstinate Jews, who said: there is no prophet after Moses, and no book after the Torah. Allah, the Exalted, explicitly mentioned here the giving of the Zabur to David, even though He had given him kingship along with it, as an indication that the pure preference is by the knowledge He gave him and the Book He sent down to him, just as Muhammad (ﷺ) was preferred by the knowledge and the Qur'an with which He specially favoured him.

The explanation of ﴿And We gave David the Zabur﴾ has been given earlier at the end of surah al-Nisa, and the dispute over the vowelling of the letter zay (ز) and its fatha has been mentioned there.

Al-Zamakhshari said here: If you ask, why was the Zabur not defined (with the article) as it was in ﴿We have certainly written in the Zabur﴾ (21:105)? I say: the Zabur may be like al-'Abbas and 'Abbas, and al-Fadl and Fadl, and it may be that ﴿We gave David﴾ means some of the Zabur, namely the scriptures; or it may mean what is mentioned in it about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the Zabur, and that is called a Zabur because it is part of the Zabur, just as part of the Qur'an is called Qur'an.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verse 56–59:

﴿Say: Call upon those whom you claim besides Him; they do not possess the removal of the harm from you, nor its transfer.﴾ ﴿Those whom they call upon themselves seek the means of access to their Lord, [seeking] which of them is nearer, and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is ever to be feared.﴾ ﴿And there is no city but that We will destroy it before the Day of Resurrection or punish it with a severe punishment. That was written in the Book.﴾ ﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them. And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign, but they wronged her. And We do not send the signs except as a warning.﴾

Ibn Mas'ud said: It was revealed concerning the worshippers of the jinn, namely the tribe of Khuza'a, who embraced Islam while the jinn remained, and they continued to worship them. Ibn 'Abbas said: It refers to 'Uzayr, the Messiah and his mother. And from him also, and from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Zayd and al-Hasan: It refers to the worshippers of the angels. And from Ibn 'Abbas: It refers to the worshippers of the sun, the moon and the stars, and 'Uzayr, the Messiah and his mother. End quote. The phrase ﴿those whom you claim besides Him﴾ may be general, with those who have reason given precedence over those who do not, and the meaning is: call upon them, and they are not able to remove from you the harm, whether of sickness, poverty or punishment, nor to transfer it from one person to another or change it.

The majority read ﴿yad'ūna﴾ with the third-person masculine plural prefix (yā’ al-ghayba), while Ibn Mas'ud and Qatadah read it with the second-person prefix (tā’ al-khiṭāb), and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with the third-person prefix in the passive voice. The meaning: they call upon them as gods, or they call upon them to remove the harm that has befallen you, just as something is omitted in His words ﴿Say: Call upon﴾, i.e., call upon them to remove the harm.

In His words ﴿zaʿamtum﴾ there is an omitted pronoun referring to ﴿alladhīna﴾, which is the first object, and the second is omitted, its estimate being: you claimed them to be gods besides Allah. ﴿Ulā'ika﴾ is the subject, ﴿alladhīna﴾ is its attribute, and the predicate is ﴿yabtaghūna﴾. ﴿Al-wasīlah﴾ is nearness to Allah, the Exalted. The apparent reading is that ﴿ulā'ika﴾ refers to the deities worshipped, and the waw in ﴿yad'ūna﴾ refers to the worshippers, and the returning pronoun to ﴿alladhīna﴾ is an omitted object in the accusative, i.e., they call upon them.

Ibn Fawrak said: The indication in His words ﴿ulā'ika﴾ (p-52) refers to the prophets who were previously mentioned, and the pronoun of the nominative in ﴿yad'ūna﴾ and ﴿yabtaghūna﴾ returns to them, and the meaning: they call people to the religion of Allah. The meaning according to this is that those whose status is great, namely the prophets, worship none but Allah and seek the means of access only to Him, so they are most worthy of being followed, and so they should not worship other than Allah.

The majority read ﴿ilā rabbihim﴾ with the third-person masculine plural pronoun. Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿ilā rabbika﴾ with the second-person pronoun, addressing the Messenger. They differed concerning the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ and its estimate. Al-Hawfi said: ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ is an inceptive and predicate, and the meaning: they look at ﴿which of them is nearer﴾, so they seek means of access through it. It is also permissible that ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ be a substitute for the waw in ﴿yabtaghūna﴾. End quote. In the first case he assumed a verb of suspension (fi'l al-ta'līq), and ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ is in a position of accusative by dropping the preposition, since "nazara" if it means thinking takes "fi", and if it is visual it takes "ila", so the clause the verb is suspended from, on both estimates, is in a position of accusative by dropping the preposition, like His words: ﴿then let him look which of them is purer in food﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. Assuming the suspended verb is disputed. The second case was stated by al-Zamakhshari, who said: ﴿ayyu﴾ is a relative (mawsula), i.e., he who is nearer to them and closer seeks the means to Allah, so how about one who is not nearer. End quote. According to this view, ﴿aqrabu﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and ﴿ayyuhum﴾ may be declined, which is the more likely, or be indeclinable due to the presence of a reason for indeclinability. Al-Zamakhshari said: Or ﴿yabtaghūna﴾ with ﴿al-wasīlah﴾ is taken to include the meaning of "yaḥrişūna" (they strive eagerly), as if it were said: they strive eagerly which of them will be nearer to Allah, by obedience and increase in goodness and righteousness, so ﴿yabtaghūna﴾ includes the meaning of a verb of the heart, namely "yaḥrişūna", so that the suspension is valid, and the inceptive clause is in a position of accusative by dropping the preposition, since "ḥaraṣa" takes "ʿalā", like His words: ﴿if you are eager for their guidance﴾ [al-Nahl: 37]. End quote.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿ayyuhum﴾ is an inceptive and ﴿aqrabu﴾ its predicate, and the estimate: their gaze and their longing ﴿which of them is nearer﴾. This is like what 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "So the people spent the night vying with one another as to which of them would be given it," i.e., competing in seeking nearness. So he made the omitted element "their gaze and their longing," and this is an inceptive; if you make ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ in the accusative position by the omitted "their gaze," the inceptive which is "their gaze" remains without a predicate and needs an omitted predicate; and if you make ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ the predicate, it is not valid, since "their gaze" is not ﴿which of them is nearer﴾; and if you make the estimate "their gaze in ﴿which of them is nearer﴾," i.e., existing or obtained, this is not valid, since existing and obtained are not among the things suspended.

Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿ayyuhum﴾ is an inceptive and ﴿aqrabu﴾ its predicate, and it is an interrogative in a position of accusative by ﴿yad'ūna﴾. It is also permissible that ﴿ayyuhum﴾ be in the sense of "alladhī" and be a substitute for the pronoun in ﴿yad'ūna﴾, and the estimate: "the one who is nearer." End quote. In the first case ﴿yad'ūna﴾ was suspended, though it is not a verb of the heart; in the second, the relative clause was separated from its complement by the circumstantial clause, and this does no harm, since it is governed by the relative clause: ﴿and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment﴾, like the other servants of Allah, so how do they claim to be gods? ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is ever to be feared﴾, which every person fears.

﴿And there is no city﴾: ﴿in﴾ is negating, and ﴿min﴾ is additional in the subject, indicating the comprehensiveness of the genus, and the clause after ﴿illā﴾ is the predicate of the subject. It was said: the intended meaning is particularity, and the estimate: "And there is no unjust city." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿min﴾ is to clarify the genus. End quote. The "min" that clarifies the genus, according to those who affirm this meaning for it, requires that before it there be something that conveys some ambiguity, so that "min" comes to clarify what is meant by that ambiguous thing, as in His words: ﴿what Allah opens to people of mercy﴾ [Fatir: 2]. Here nothing ambiguous precedes, for "min" to clarify; and perhaps his words "to clarify the genus" are a copyist's error, and he meant "for the comprehensiveness of the genus," as you see he said after that: "It was said: the intended meaning is particularity." End quote.

The apparent meaning is that all cities will be destroyed before the Day of Resurrection, and their destruction is their ruin and annihilation; and their ruin includes the destruction of their people by extermination, or gradually, or they are punished. The meaning: the destruction of their people by killing and various kinds of punishment. It was said: destruction is for the righteous and punishment for the wicked. Muqatil said: I found in the books of al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim in its interpretation: As for Makkah, Abyssinia will ruin it; Madinah will perish from hunger, Basra by drowning, Kufa by the Turks, the mountains by thunderbolts and quakes; and as for (p-53) Khurasan, its punishments are of various kinds. Then he mentioned them city by city, and similar was narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who mentioned that the destruction and ruin of al-Andalus would come by the hooves of horses and the clashing of armies.

﴿That was written in the Book﴾: that is, in the pre-ordained decree, or in the Preserved Tablet, meaning written as lines. ﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending﴾ the signs. From Ibn 'Abbas: the people of Makkah asked that Safa be made gold for them, and that the mountains be removed from them so that they might cultivate. They proposed this to the Messenger ﷺ, so Allah revealed to him: "If you wish, I shall do that for them; but if they refuse, I shall hasten punishment upon them; and if you wish, I shall grant them respite, perhaps I will choose from among them believers." He said: "Rather, grant them respite, O Lord." Then it was revealed. Prevention is borrowed for abandonment, i.e., We did not abandon sending the proposed signs except that the former peoples denied them, and the denial of the former peoples is not the cause of sending the signs to the Quraysh; so the meaning is: except that they follow the way of the former peoples' denial of them. So "the denial of the former peoples" is the agent with an omitted genitive; when they deny them as the former peoples denied, I would hasten upon them the punishment of annihilation, and wisdom required that I not annihilate them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: We did not turn away from sending what you propose of signs except that those who are like them, of those sealed upon their hearts, such as 'Ad and Thamud, denied them; and were they sent, they would deny them as those denied, and say: "This is manifest magic," as they say about other signs, and they would deserve the total punishment; and We have resolved to delay the matter of those to whom you were sent until the Day of Resurrection. Then he mentioned among those signs that the former peoples proposed, then denied when they were sent to them, and so they were destroyed: one of them, which is the she-camel of Salih; for the traces of their destruction in the land of the Arabs are near their borders, visible to those who depart and arrive. End quote.

The majority read ﴿Thamūd﴾ without tanwin (diptote). Harun said: the people of Kufa read ﴿Thamūd﴾ with tanwin in every case. Abu Hatim said: The common people and the Qur'an scholars do not add tanwin to ﴿Thamūd﴾ in any case, and in four places there is a written alif, but we read it without an alif. End quote. ﴿Mubṣiratan﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and this is the reading of the majority. Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿mubṣiratun﴾ in the nominative, by omitting an inceptive, i.e., it is "visible," and he attributed the seeing to it metaphorically, since people see it, and the estimate: a visible sign. Some read with a fatha on the ṣād as a passive participle, i.e., people see it and witness it. Qatadah read with a fatha on the mīm and ṣād as a place noun (maf'ala) from sight, i.e., a place of seeing, like His words: "The disbelief is a place of corruption for the soul of the benefactor," treating it as the attributes of places, like: "a land abounding in lions" and "a place abounding in mud"; and they said: the child is "a source of stinginess, a source of cowardice." ﴿So they wronged themselves by it﴾, i.e., by slaughtering her, after His words: ﴿Leave her to eat in Allah's earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 73], etc. It was said: the meaning is that they denied that she was from Allah; it was said: they made denial of her in place of acceptance, and this is the sense of the statement before it. The apparent meaning is that the last signs are other than the first signs: in the first the aspect of proposing is considered, and in these the aspect of not being proposed, being signs accompanied by respite and not immediate punishment, such as eclipses, thunder and earthquakes. Al-Hasan said: and the plague. In the hadith of the eclipse: "Hasten to prayer." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The signs of Allah by which one takes warning are of three kinds: a general kind in everything, for wherever you place your gaze you find a sign, and here is the reflection of scholars; a customary kind such as thunder, eclipses and the like, and here is the reflection of the ignorant only; and a kind that breaks custom, which ended with the ending of prophethood, and it is only considered by way of supposing what preceded it. End quote. Regarding this last kind he said: "it ended with the ending of prophethood," though many people affirm this kind for non-prophets and call it a karamah (miraculous favour).

Al-Zamakhshari said: If by the proposed signs is meant, the meaning is: We do not send them except as a warning (takhwif) of the descent of immediate punishment, as a vanguard and forerunner to it; if they do not fear, it befalls them. If other signs are meant, the meaning of "We do not send" is: We do not send signs such as the signs of the Qur'an and others except as a warning and alarm of the punishment of the Hereafter. It was said: the signs that Allah made as a warning to His servants are celestial: eclipses of the sun, eclipses of the moon, thunder, lightning, thunderbolts, meteors and what is similar to these. And terrestrial: earthquakes, landslides, blight (p-54) and fires appearing in some lands, the flooding of springs and their rising beyond the limit until they drown some lands. And neither celestial nor terrestrial: the violent winds, and what results from them of uprooting trees and destroying dwellings, and what they drive of torrents and scorching winds.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verse 56–59:

﴿Say: Call upon those whom you claim besides Him; they do not possess the removal of the harm from you, nor its transfer.﴾ ﴿Those whom they call upon themselves seek the means of access to their Lord, [seeking] which of them is nearer, and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is ever to be feared.﴾ ﴿And there is no city but that We will destroy it before the Day of Resurrection or punish it with a severe punishment. That was written in the Book.﴾ ﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them. And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign, but they wronged her. And We do not send the signs except as a warning.﴾

Ibn Mas'ud said: It was revealed concerning the worshippers of the jinn, namely the tribe of Khuza'a, who embraced Islam while the jinn remained, and they continued to worship them. Ibn 'Abbas said: It refers to 'Uzayr, the Messiah and his mother. And from him also, and from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Zayd and al-Hasan: It refers to the worshippers of the angels. And from Ibn 'Abbas: It refers to the worshippers of the sun, the moon and the stars, and 'Uzayr, the Messiah and his mother. End quote. The phrase ﴿those whom you claim besides Him﴾ may be general, with those who have reason given precedence over those who do not, and the meaning is: call upon them, and they are not able to remove from you the harm, whether of sickness, poverty or punishment, nor to transfer it from one person to another or change it.

The majority read ﴿yad'ūna﴾ with the third-person masculine plural prefix (yā’ al-ghayba), while Ibn Mas'ud and Qatadah read it with the second-person prefix (tā’ al-khiṭāb), and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with the third-person prefix in the passive voice. The meaning: they call upon them as gods, or they call upon them to remove the harm that has befallen you, just as something is omitted in His words ﴿Say: Call upon﴾, i.e., call upon them to remove the harm.

In His words ﴿zaʿamtum﴾ there is an omitted pronoun referring to ﴿alladhīna﴾, which is the first object, and the second is omitted, its estimate being: you claimed them to be gods besides Allah. ﴿Ulā'ika﴾ is the subject, ﴿alladhīna﴾ is its attribute, and the predicate is ﴿yabtaghūna﴾. ﴿Al-wasīlah﴾ is nearness to Allah, the Exalted. The apparent reading is that ﴿ulā'ika﴾ refers to the deities worshipped, and the waw in ﴿yad'ūna﴾ refers to the worshippers, and the returning pronoun to ﴿alladhīna﴾ is an omitted object in the accusative, i.e., they call upon them.

Ibn Fawrak said: The indication in His words ﴿ulā'ika﴾ (p-52) refers to the prophets who were previously mentioned, and the pronoun of the nominative in ﴿yad'ūna﴾ and ﴿yabtaghūna﴾ returns to them, and the meaning: they call people to the religion of Allah. The meaning according to this is that those whose status is great, namely the prophets, worship none but Allah and seek the means of access only to Him, so they are most worthy of being followed, and so they should not worship other than Allah.

The majority read ﴿ilā rabbihim﴾ with the third-person masculine plural pronoun. Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿ilā rabbika﴾ with the second-person pronoun, addressing the Messenger. They differed concerning the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ and its estimate. Al-Hawfi said: ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ is an inceptive and predicate, and the meaning: they look at ﴿which of them is nearer﴾, so they seek means of access through it. It is also permissible that ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ be a substitute for the waw in ﴿yabtaghūna﴾. End quote. In the first case he assumed a verb of suspension (fi'l al-ta'līq), and ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ is in a position of accusative by dropping the preposition, since "nazara" if it means thinking takes "fi", and if it is visual it takes "ila", so the clause the verb is suspended from, on both estimates, is in a position of accusative by dropping the preposition, like His words: ﴿then let him look which of them is purer in food﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. Assuming the suspended verb is disputed. The second case was stated by al-Zamakhshari, who said: ﴿ayyu﴾ is a relative (mawsula), i.e., he who is nearer to them and closer seeks the means to Allah, so how about one who is not nearer. End quote. According to this view, ﴿aqrabu﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and ﴿ayyuhum﴾ may be declined, which is the more likely, or be indeclinable due to the presence of a reason for indeclinability. Al-Zamakhshari said: Or ﴿yabtaghūna﴾ with ﴿al-wasīlah﴾ is taken to include the meaning of "yaḥrişūna" (they strive eagerly), as if it were said: they strive eagerly which of them will be nearer to Allah, by obedience and increase in goodness and righteousness, so ﴿yabtaghūna﴾ includes the meaning of a verb of the heart, namely "yaḥrişūna", so that the suspension is valid, and the inceptive clause is in a position of accusative by dropping the preposition, since "ḥaraṣa" takes "ʿalā", like His words: ﴿if you are eager for their guidance﴾ [al-Nahl: 37]. End quote.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿ayyuhum﴾ is an inceptive and ﴿aqrabu﴾ its predicate, and the estimate: their gaze and their longing ﴿which of them is nearer﴾. This is like what 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "So the people spent the night vying with one another as to which of them would be given it," i.e., competing in seeking nearness. So he made the omitted element "their gaze and their longing," and this is an inceptive; if you make ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ in the accusative position by the omitted "their gaze," the inceptive which is "their gaze" remains without a predicate and needs an omitted predicate; and if you make ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ the predicate, it is not valid, since "their gaze" is not ﴿which of them is nearer﴾; and if you make the estimate "their gaze in ﴿which of them is nearer﴾," i.e., existing or obtained, this is not valid, since existing and obtained are not among the things suspended.

Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿ayyuhum﴾ is an inceptive and ﴿aqrabu﴾ its predicate, and it is an interrogative in a position of accusative by ﴿yad'ūna﴾. It is also permissible that ﴿ayyuhum﴾ be in the sense of "alladhī" and be a substitute for the pronoun in ﴿yad'ūna﴾, and the estimate: "the one who is nearer." End quote. In the first case ﴿yad'ūna﴾ was suspended, though it is not a verb of the heart; in the second, the relative clause was separated from its complement by the circumstantial clause, and this does no harm, since it is governed by the relative clause: ﴿and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment﴾, like the other servants of Allah, so how do they claim to be gods? ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is ever to be feared﴾, which every person fears.

﴿And there is no city﴾: ﴿in﴾ is negating, and ﴿min﴾ is additional in the subject, indicating the comprehensiveness of the genus, and the clause after ﴿illā﴾ is the predicate of the subject. It was said: the intended meaning is particularity, and the estimate: "And there is no unjust city." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿min﴾ is to clarify the genus. End quote. The "min" that clarifies the genus, according to those who affirm this meaning for it, requires that before it there be something that conveys some ambiguity, so that "min" comes to clarify what is meant by that ambiguous thing, as in His words: ﴿what Allah opens to people of mercy﴾ [Fatir: 2]. Here nothing ambiguous precedes, for "min" to clarify; and perhaps his words "to clarify the genus" are a copyist's error, and he meant "for the comprehensiveness of the genus," as you see he said after that: "It was said: the intended meaning is particularity." End quote.

The apparent meaning is that all cities will be destroyed before the Day of Resurrection, and their destruction is their ruin and annihilation; and their ruin includes the destruction of their people by extermination, or gradually, or they are punished. The meaning: the destruction of their people by killing and various kinds of punishment. It was said: destruction is for the righteous and punishment for the wicked. Muqatil said: I found in the books of al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim in its interpretation: As for Makkah, Abyssinia will ruin it; Madinah will perish from hunger, Basra by drowning, Kufa by the Turks, the mountains by thunderbolts and quakes; and as for (p-53) Khurasan, its punishments are of various kinds. Then he mentioned them city by city, and similar was narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who mentioned that the destruction and ruin of al-Andalus would come by the hooves of horses and the clashing of armies.

﴿That was written in the Book﴾: that is, in the pre-ordained decree, or in the Preserved Tablet, meaning written as lines. ﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending﴾ the signs. From Ibn 'Abbas: the people of Makkah asked that Safa be made gold for them, and that the mountains be removed from them so that they might cultivate. They proposed this to the Messenger ﷺ, so Allah revealed to him: "If you wish, I shall do that for them; but if they refuse, I shall hasten punishment upon them; and if you wish, I shall grant them respite, perhaps I will choose from among them believers." He said: "Rather, grant them respite, O Lord." Then it was revealed. Prevention is borrowed for abandonment, i.e., We did not abandon sending the proposed signs except that the former peoples denied them, and the denial of the former peoples is not the cause of sending the signs to the Quraysh; so the meaning is: except that they follow the way of the former peoples' denial of them. So "the denial of the former peoples" is the agent with an omitted genitive; when they deny them as the former peoples denied, I would hasten upon them the punishment of annihilation, and wisdom required that I not annihilate them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: We did not turn away from sending what you propose of signs except that those who are like them, of those sealed upon their hearts, such as 'Ad and Thamud, denied them; and were they sent, they would deny them as those denied, and say: "This is manifest magic," as they say about other signs, and they would deserve the total punishment; and We have resolved to delay the matter of those to whom you were sent until the Day of Resurrection. Then he mentioned among those signs that the former peoples proposed, then denied when they were sent to them, and so they were destroyed: one of them, which is the she-camel of Salih; for the traces of their destruction in the land of the Arabs are near their borders, visible to those who depart and arrive. End quote.

The majority read ﴿Thamūd﴾ without tanwin (diptote). Harun said: the people of Kufa read ﴿Thamūd﴾ with tanwin in every case. Abu Hatim said: The common people and the Qur'an scholars do not add tanwin to ﴿Thamūd﴾ in any case, and in four places there is a written alif, but we read it without an alif. End quote. ﴿Mubṣiratan﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and this is the reading of the majority. Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿mubṣiratun﴾ in the nominative, by omitting an inceptive, i.e., it is "visible," and he attributed the seeing to it metaphorically, since people see it, and the estimate: a visible sign. Some read with a fatha on the ṣād as a passive participle, i.e., people see it and witness it. Qatadah read with a fatha on the mīm and ṣād as a place noun (maf'ala) from sight, i.e., a place of seeing, like His words: "The disbelief is a place of corruption for the soul of the benefactor," treating it as the attributes of places, like: "a land abounding in lions" and "a place abounding in mud"; and they said: the child is "a source of stinginess, a source of cowardice." ﴿So they wronged themselves by it﴾, i.e., by slaughtering her, after His words: ﴿Leave her to eat in Allah's earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 73], etc. It was said: the meaning is that they denied that she was from Allah; it was said: they made denial of her in place of acceptance, and this is the sense of the statement before it. The apparent meaning is that the last signs are other than the first signs: in the first the aspect of proposing is considered, and in these the aspect of not being proposed, being signs accompanied by respite and not immediate punishment, such as eclipses, thunder and earthquakes. Al-Hasan said: and the plague. In the hadith of the eclipse: "Hasten to prayer." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The signs of Allah by which one takes warning are of three kinds: a general kind in everything, for wherever you place your gaze you find a sign, and here is the reflection of scholars; a customary kind such as thunder, eclipses and the like, and here is the reflection of the ignorant only; and a kind that breaks custom, which ended with the ending of prophethood, and it is only considered by way of supposing what preceded it. End quote. Regarding this last kind he said: "it ended with the ending of prophethood," though many people affirm this kind for non-prophets and call it a karamah (miraculous favour).

Al-Zamakhshari said: If by the proposed signs is meant, the meaning is: We do not send them except as a warning (takhwif) of the descent of immediate punishment, as a vanguard and forerunner to it; if they do not fear, it befalls them. If other signs are meant, the meaning of "We do not send" is: We do not send signs such as the signs of the Qur'an and others except as a warning and alarm of the punishment of the Hereafter. It was said: the signs that Allah made as a warning to His servants are celestial: eclipses of the sun, eclipses of the moon, thunder, lightning, thunderbolts, meteors and what is similar to these. And terrestrial: earthquakes, landslides, blight (p-54) and fires appearing in some lands, the flooding of springs and their rising beyond the limit until they drown some lands. And neither celestial nor terrestrial: the violent winds, and what results from them of uprooting trees and destroying dwellings, and what they drive of torrents and scorching winds.

﴿Say: Call upon those whom you claim besides Him; they do not possess the removal of the harm from you, nor its transfer.﴾ ﴿Those whom they call upon themselves seek the means of access to their Lord, [seeking] which of them is nearer, and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is ever to be feared.﴾ ﴿And there is no city but that We will destroy it before the Day of Resurrection or punish it with a severe punishment. That was written in the Book.﴾ ﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them. And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign, but they wronged her. And We do not send the signs except as a warning.﴾

Ibn Mas'ud said: It was revealed concerning the worshippers of the jinn, namely the tribe of Khuza'a, who embraced Islam while the jinn remained, and they continued to worship them. Ibn 'Abbas said: It refers to 'Uzayr, the Messiah and his mother. And from him also, and from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Zayd and al-Hasan: It refers to the worshippers of the angels. And from Ibn 'Abbas: It refers to the worshippers of the sun, the moon and the stars, and 'Uzayr, the Messiah and his mother. End quote. The phrase ﴿those whom you claim besides Him﴾ may be general, with those who have reason given precedence over those who do not, and the meaning is: call upon them, and they are not able to remove from you the harm, whether of sickness, poverty or punishment, nor to transfer it from one person to another or change it.

The majority read ﴿yad'ūna﴾ with the third-person masculine plural prefix (yā’ al-ghayba), while Ibn Mas'ud and Qatadah read it with the second-person prefix (tā’ al-khiṭāb), and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with the third-person prefix in the passive voice. The meaning: they call upon them as gods, or they call upon them to remove the harm that has befallen you, just as something is omitted in His words ﴿Say: Call upon﴾, i.e., call upon them to remove the harm.

In His words ﴿zaʿamtum﴾ there is an omitted pronoun referring to ﴿alladhīna﴾, which is the first object, and the second is omitted, its estimate being: you claimed them to be gods besides Allah. ﴿Ulā'ika﴾ is the subject, ﴿alladhīna﴾ is its attribute, and the predicate is ﴿yabtaghūna﴾. ﴿Al-wasīlah﴾ is nearness to Allah, the Exalted. The apparent reading is that ﴿ulā'ika﴾ refers to the deities worshipped, and the waw in ﴿yad'ūna﴾ refers to the worshippers, and the returning pronoun to ﴿alladhīna﴾ is an omitted object in the accusative, i.e., they call upon them.

Ibn Fawrak said: The indication in His words ﴿ulā'ika﴾ (p-52) refers to the prophets who were previously mentioned, and the pronoun of the nominative in ﴿yad'ūna﴾ and ﴿yabtaghūna﴾ returns to them, and the meaning: they call people to the religion of Allah. The meaning according to this is that those whose status is great, namely the prophets, worship none but Allah and seek the means of access only to Him, so they are most worthy of being followed, and so they should not worship other than Allah.

The majority read ﴿ilā rabbihim﴾ with the third-person masculine plural pronoun. Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿ilā rabbika﴾ with the second-person pronoun, addressing the Messenger. They differed concerning the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ and its estimate. Al-Hawfi said: ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ is an inceptive and predicate, and the meaning: they look at ﴿which of them is nearer﴾, so they seek means of access through it. It is also permissible that ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ be a substitute for the waw in ﴿yabtaghūna﴾. End quote. In the first case he assumed a verb of suspension (fi'l al-ta'līq), and ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ is in a position of accusative by dropping the preposition, since "nazara" if it means thinking takes "fi", and if it is visual it takes "ila", so the clause the verb is suspended from, on both estimates, is in a position of accusative by dropping the preposition, like His words: ﴿then let him look which of them is purer in food﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. Assuming the suspended verb is disputed. The second case was stated by al-Zamakhshari, who said: ﴿ayyu﴾ is a relative (mawsula), i.e., he who is nearer to them and closer seeks the means to Allah, so how about one who is not nearer. End quote. According to this view, ﴿aqrabu﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and ﴿ayyuhum﴾ may be declined, which is the more likely, or be indeclinable due to the presence of a reason for indeclinability. Al-Zamakhshari said: Or ﴿yabtaghūna﴾ with ﴿al-wasīlah﴾ is taken to include the meaning of "yaḥrişūna" (they strive eagerly), as if it were said: they strive eagerly which of them will be nearer to Allah, by obedience and increase in goodness and righteousness, so ﴿yabtaghūna﴾ includes the meaning of a verb of the heart, namely "yaḥrişūna", so that the suspension is valid, and the inceptive clause is in a position of accusative by dropping the preposition, since "ḥaraṣa" takes "ʿalā", like His words: ﴿if you are eager for their guidance﴾ [al-Nahl: 37]. End quote.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿ayyuhum﴾ is an inceptive and ﴿aqrabu﴾ its predicate, and the estimate: their gaze and their longing ﴿which of them is nearer﴾. This is like what 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "So the people spent the night vying with one another as to which of them would be given it," i.e., competing in seeking nearness. So he made the omitted element "their gaze and their longing," and this is an inceptive; if you make ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ in the accusative position by the omitted "their gaze," the inceptive which is "their gaze" remains without a predicate and needs an omitted predicate; and if you make ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ the predicate, it is not valid, since "their gaze" is not ﴿which of them is nearer﴾; and if you make the estimate "their gaze in ﴿which of them is nearer﴾," i.e., existing or obtained, this is not valid, since existing and obtained are not among the things suspended.

Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿ayyuhum﴾ is an inceptive and ﴿aqrabu﴾ its predicate, and it is an interrogative in a position of accusative by ﴿yad'ūna﴾. It is also permissible that ﴿ayyuhum﴾ be in the sense of "alladhī" and be a substitute for the pronoun in ﴿yad'ūna﴾, and the estimate: "the one who is nearer." End quote. In the first case ﴿yad'ūna﴾ was suspended, though it is not a verb of the heart; in the second, the relative clause was separated from its complement by the circumstantial clause, and this does no harm, since it is governed by the relative clause: ﴿and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment﴾, like the other servants of Allah, so how do they claim to be gods? ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is ever to be feared﴾, which every person fears.

﴿And there is no city﴾: ﴿in﴾ is negating, and ﴿min﴾ is additional in the subject, indicating the comprehensiveness of the genus, and the clause after ﴿illā﴾ is the predicate of the subject. It was said: the intended meaning is particularity, and the estimate: "And there is no unjust city." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿min﴾ is to clarify the genus. End quote. The "min" that clarifies the genus, according to those who affirm this meaning for it, requires that before it there be something that conveys some ambiguity, so that "min" comes to clarify what is meant by that ambiguous thing, as in His words: ﴿what Allah opens to people of mercy﴾ [Fatir: 2]. Here nothing ambiguous precedes, for "min" to clarify; and perhaps his words "to clarify the genus" are a copyist's error, and he meant "for the comprehensiveness of the genus," as you see he said after that: "It was said: the intended meaning is particularity." End quote.

The apparent meaning is that all cities will be destroyed before the Day of Resurrection, and their destruction is their ruin and annihilation; and their ruin includes the destruction of their people by extermination, or gradually, or they are punished. The meaning: the destruction of their people by killing and various kinds of punishment. It was said: destruction is for the righteous and punishment for the wicked. Muqatil said: I found in the books of al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim in its interpretation: As for Makkah, Abyssinia will ruin it; Madinah will perish from hunger, Basra by drowning, Kufa by the Turks, the mountains by thunderbolts and quakes; and as for (p-53) Khurasan, its punishments are of various kinds. Then he mentioned them city by city, and similar was narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who mentioned that the destruction and ruin of al-Andalus would come by the hooves of horses and the clashing of armies.

﴿That was written in the Book﴾: that is, in the pre-ordained decree, or in the Preserved Tablet, meaning written as lines. ﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending﴾ the signs. From Ibn 'Abbas: the people of Makkah asked that Safa be made gold for them, and that the mountains be removed from them so that they might cultivate. They proposed this to the Messenger ﷺ, so Allah revealed to him: "If you wish, I shall do that for them; but if they refuse, I shall hasten punishment upon them; and if you wish, I shall grant them respite, perhaps I will choose from among them believers." He said: "Rather, grant them respite, O Lord." Then it was revealed. Prevention is borrowed for abandonment, i.e., We did not abandon sending the proposed signs except that the former peoples denied them, and the denial of the former peoples is not the cause of sending the signs to the Quraysh; so the meaning is: except that they follow the way of the former peoples' denial of them. So "the denial of the former peoples" is the agent with an omitted genitive; when they deny them as the former peoples denied, I would hasten upon them the punishment of annihilation, and wisdom required that I not annihilate them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: We did not turn away from sending what you propose of signs except that those who are like them, of those sealed upon their hearts, such as 'Ad and Thamud, denied them; and were they sent, they would deny them as those denied, and say: "This is manifest magic," as they say about other signs, and they would deserve the total punishment; and We have resolved to delay the matter of those to whom you were sent until the Day of Resurrection. Then he mentioned among those signs that the former peoples proposed, then denied when they were sent to them, and so they were destroyed: one of them, which is the she-camel of Salih; for the traces of their destruction in the land of the Arabs are near their borders, visible to those who depart and arrive. End quote.

The majority read ﴿Thamūd﴾ without tanwin (diptote). Harun said: the people of Kufa read ﴿Thamūd﴾ with tanwin in every case. Abu Hatim said: The common people and the Qur'an scholars do not add tanwin to ﴿Thamūd﴾ in any case, and in four places there is a written alif, but we read it without an alif. End quote. ﴿Mubṣiratan﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and this is the reading of the majority. Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿mubṣiratun﴾ in the nominative, by omitting an inceptive, i.e., it is "visible," and he attributed the seeing to it metaphorically, since people see it, and the estimate: a visible sign. Some read with a fatha on the ṣād as a passive participle, i.e., people see it and witness it. Qatadah read with a fatha on the mīm and ṣād as a place noun (maf'ala) from sight, i.e., a place of seeing, like His words: "The disbelief is a place of corruption for the soul of the benefactor," treating it as the attributes of places, like: "a land abounding in lions" and "a place abounding in mud"; and they said: the child is "a source of stinginess, a source of cowardice." ﴿So they wronged themselves by it﴾, i.e., by slaughtering her, after His words: ﴿Leave her to eat in Allah's earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 73], etc. It was said: the meaning is that they denied that she was from Allah; it was said: they made denial of her in place of acceptance, and this is the sense of the statement before it. The apparent meaning is that the last signs are other than the first signs: in the first the aspect of proposing is considered, and in these the aspect of not being proposed, being signs accompanied by respite and not immediate punishment, such as eclipses, thunder and earthquakes. Al-Hasan said: and the plague. In the hadith of the eclipse: "Hasten to prayer." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The signs of Allah by which one takes warning are of three kinds: a general kind in everything, for wherever you place your gaze you find a sign, and here is the reflection of scholars; a customary kind such as thunder, eclipses and the like, and here is the reflection of the ignorant only; and a kind that breaks custom, which ended with the ending of prophethood, and it is only considered by way of supposing what preceded it. End quote. Regarding this last kind he said: "it ended with the ending of prophethood," though many people affirm this kind for non-prophets and call it a karamah (miraculous favour).

Al-Zamakhshari said: If by the proposed signs is meant, the meaning is: We do not send them except as a warning (takhwif) of the descent of immediate punishment, as a vanguard and forerunner to it; if they do not fear, it befalls them. If other signs are meant, the meaning of "We do not send" is: We do not send signs such as the signs of the Qur'an and others except as a warning and alarm of the punishment of the Hereafter. It was said: the signs that Allah made as a warning to His servants are celestial: eclipses of the sun, eclipses of the moon, thunder, lightning, thunderbolts, meteors and what is similar to these. And terrestrial: earthquakes, landslides, blight (p-54) and fires appearing in some lands, the flooding of springs and their rising beyond the limit until they drown some lands. And neither celestial nor terrestrial: the violent winds, and what results from them of uprooting trees and destroying dwellings, and what they drive of torrents and scorching winds.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verse 60:

﴿And when We told you, "Indeed, your Lord encompasses the people. And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people, and the cursed tree in the Qur'an. And We warn them, but it only increases them in great transgression."﴾

When the disbelievers asked the Messenger for the miraculous signs they proposed, and Allah informed him of the wisdom in not bringing them, the disbelievers criticized him and said: "If he were truly a messenger, he would have brought the signs we proposed." Allah then made clear that He would support and strengthen him, and that He ﴿encompasses the people﴾. It was said: [He encompasses them] with His knowledge, so nothing escapes His knowledge. It was said: [He encompasses them] with His power, for His power overcomes everything. It was also said: the encompassing here means destruction, as in His saying: ﴿and its fruit was encompassed﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. The apparent meaning is that "the people" is general. It was also said: it refers to the people of Makkah, and Allah gave him the good news that He would defeat them and make him victorious over them. Here ﴿encompassed﴾ is in the sense of "encompasses," and the past tense is used for the future because it is certain to occur. As for the time in which the encompassing of them took place, it was said: the Day of Badr. Al-Askari said: this is a report of the unseen that he gave before its time, and it is possible that this refers to the matter of the Trench and the coming of the confederates seeking revenge for Badr, so Allah turned them back in their rage, and they gained no good. It was also said: [it refers to] the Day of Badr and the Day of the Conquest. It was also said: the most likely is that it is the Day of the Conquest, for it is the day in which the command of Allah encompassed the destruction of the people of Makkah and He gave him power over them. Al-Tabari said: ﴿encompassed the people﴾ means [Allah's] protection of you, O Muhammad, His guarding and His preserving of you. So the verse is an informing to him that he is protected from the disbelievers, safe from being killed or suffering a great harm; that is, "So convey the message of your Lord and do not fear any of the creatures." Ibn Atiyyah said: this is a clear interpretation that fits the wording. Something similar has been narrated from al-Hasan and al-Suddi, except that it does not fit what follows with a strong connection, though it is possible to make the speech fit what follows as a preparation for it.

Then I say: the people have differed concerning the vision (al-ru'ya). The majority said: it is a vision of the eye and of wakefulness, and it is what he saw on the night of the Isra' (the night journey) of marvels. The disbelievers said: "Indeed this is a wonder! We travel to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) for two months going and returning, while Muhammad claims he went and returned in one night." Some of the weak Muslims were tempted by this deception and apostatized, and this grieved the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so this verse was revealed. According to this, the meaning of His saying ﴿And when We told you, "Indeed your Lord encompasses the people"﴾ may well be: in their misguidance and their guidance, and that each one is made easy for what he was created for. That is: do not be concerned about the disbelief of those who disbelieve, and do not grieve over them, for it has been said to you that Allah encompasses them and owns their affairs. He made this vision of yours a trial, so that whoever Allah has already decreed disbelief for would disbelieve. In this interpretation the seeing is called a vision (ru'ya), since both ru'ya and ru'yah are verbal nouns of "ra'a" (to see). Al-Naqqash said: this came from the belief of one who believed it was a dream, even though the reality is otherwise. End. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and others: it is the story of the Isra' and the Mi'raj (the ascent) seen with the eye; those who were granted success believed in it, and those who were forsaken disbelieved in it. It was called a vision because it took place during the night and because it passed so quickly, as if it were a dream. It is also narrated from Ibn Abbas that it is his vision that he would enter Makkah; he hastened in that year to al-Hudaybiyyah, but was turned back, and the people were tempted. This fits the beginning of the verse, for the encompassing of Makkah was most frequent. It is narrated from Sahl ibn Sa'd: it is his vision of the Banu Umayyah leaping upon his pulpit (ﷺ) like monkeys leap, so he was greatly distressed by this and was never seen laughing from that day until he died. Then this verse was revealed informing that this was from their kingship, and that their ascending the pulpits is something Allah makes a trial for the people. The phrase ﴿encompasses the people﴾ then means: by His decrees; and even if what Allah has decreed happens, do not be concerned with what will happen after you of that.

Al-Hasan ibn Ali said in his sermon concerning his pledge of allegiance to Mu'awiyah: "I do not know, perhaps it is a trial for you and a enjoyment for a time." 'A'ishah said: "al-ru'ya" is the vision of a dream. Ibn Atiyyah said: this verse refutes this view, because a dream has no trial in it, and no one would deny it. End. But it is not as Ibn Atiyyah said, for the visions of the prophets are true, and the Prophet reports that this will certainly occur, so his reporting of it becomes a trial for whoever Allah wills to be tried by it. The author of al-Tahrir said: I asked Abu al-Abbas al-Qurtubi about this verse, and he said: the commentators went in it to a matter that does not suit the context of the beginning of the verse; the correct view is that it is a vision of the eye while awake. When he came to Badr, Jibril (peace be upon him) showed him the places where the people would fall, and he showed them to the people, and this was a trial for Quraysh, for when they heard it they began to mock and ridicule the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿And the cursed tree﴾ here is Abu Jahl. End.

Al-Zamakhshari said: perhaps Allah showed him their fallen places in his dream, for he used to say when he arrived at the water of Badr: "By Allah, it is as if I am looking at the places where the people will fall," while pointing to the ground and saying: "This is the place of the fall of so-and-so, this is the place of the fall of so-and-so." Then Quraysh heard of what had been revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning Badr and what he was shown in his dream of their falling places, so they used to laugh and mock him in ridicule. It was said: he saw in the dream that the sons of al-Hakam were passing his pulpit among themselves as children pass a ball. End. The apparent meaning is that "the tree" is meant in its literal sense. Ibn Abbas said: it is the dodder (al-kashuth) mentioned in His saying: ﴿like an evil tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability﴾ [Ibrahim: 26]. Also from him: it is the tree that twists around another tree and corrupts it. He said: and the trial is their saying, "What is the matter with the herbs that are mentioned in the Qur'an?" The majority said: it is the zaqqum tree. When its matter was revealed in al-Saffat and elsewhere, Abu Jahl and others said: "This Muhammad threatens you with a fire that burns stones, then claims that it grows trees, and fire eats trees! We do not know the zaqqum except as dates with butter." Then Abu Jahl ordered a slave girl of his, and she brought dates and butter, and he said to his companions: "Eat zaqqum!" So some of the weak were also tempted by this saying.

Al-Zamakhshari said: They did not deny that Allah could make the tree of a kind that fire does not consume. This is the wool of the salamander (al-samandal), a creature in the lands of the Turks, from which handkerchiefs are made; when they become dirty they are thrown into fire, the dirt goes away, and the handkerchief remains intact, untouched by the fire. You also see the ostrich swallow embers and pieces of red-hot iron like embers from the heat of the fire, yet it is not harmed. Then, closer than that, He created in every tree a fire, yet it does not burn it. So they did not deny that He could create a tree in fire that the fire does not burn. The meaning is: We only send signs as a warning to the servants, and these people have been warned of worldly punishment, which is killing on the Day of Badr. So what We showed you in your dream after the revelation to you was only a trial for them, as they took it as a mockery; and they were warned of the punishment of the Hereafter and of the tree of zaqqum, but it did not affect them. Then He said: ﴿And We warn them﴾, that is, with the warnings of this world and the Hereafter, ﴿but it only increases them in great transgression﴾, so how could a people whose condition is this be frightened by sending the signs they propose? End. His saying after "the revelation to you" refers to His saying: ﴿The multitude will be routed and they will turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45], and His saying: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: you will be overcome﴾ [Al 'Imran: 12]. The apparent meaning is that the curse is attributed to "the tree." Cursing (al-la'n) is distance from mercy, and it is in the root of Hellfire, in the farthest place from mercy. It was also said: the Arabs say of every harmful, disgusting food: "cursed" (mal'un).

Al-Zamakhshari said: I asked some of them, and he said: "What a cursed food: foul, bad and harmful!" Ibn Abbas said: ﴿the cursed﴾ means its eater. Al-Zamakhshari embellished this, saying: it is cursed because those among the disbelievers and wrongdoers who eat it are cursed; for the tree has no sin of its own to be cursed in the literal sense, and it is only described as cursed by the curse upon its people, in a figurative sense. End.

It was also said: since its fruit was likened to the heads of devils, and the devil is cursed, the curse was attributed to it. Some said: "the tree" here is a figure for one person, who is Abu Jahl. It was said: it is the devil. It was said: it is a figure for a group, namely the Jews, who banded together against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and whom Allah cursed. Their trial was that they used to await the mission of the Messenger (peace be upon him); when Allah sent him, they disbelieved in him and said: "He is not the one we were awaiting," and so they discouraged many people from Islam by their saying. It was said: [it refers to] the Banu Umayyah, to the extent that some commentators refer to them only as "the cursed tree," because of what they did in permitting the shedding of sacred blood, taking wealth unlawfully, changing the foundations of the religion and altering its rulings. And its curse in the Qur'an is: ﴿Surely the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud: 18], and: ﴿Indeed those who harm Allah and His Messenger, Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾.

The majority read ﴿the cursed tree﴾ in the accusative, as a conjunction with ﴿the vision﴾; so it is included in the restriction, meaning: "And We did not make the vision which We showed you, nor the cursed tree in the Qur'an, except as a trial for the people." Zayd ibn Ali read ﴿and the cursed tree﴾ in the nominative, as a beginning (mubtada'), with the predicate omitted, its estimated form being "likewise," meaning: "a trial." The pronoun in ﴿and We warn them﴾ refers to the disbelievers of Makkah. It was said: it refers to the kings of the Banu Umayyah after the caliphate, concerning which the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The caliphate after me will be thirty years, then it will become a biting kingship," but the first view is more correct. Al-A'mash read ﴿and it warns them﴾ with the third-person yā' (ya-prefix), and the majority read it with the nūn of majesty (nā-prefix).

[p. 57] The connection of this verse to what precedes it is twofold. First, when they disputed with the Messenger, peace be upon him, concerning prophethood and demanded signs from him, this was due to their arrogance and envy toward the Messenger (ﷺ) for what God had given him of prophethood and the lofty rank. So it fits to mention the story of Adam, peace be upon him, and Iblis, whom arrogance and envy led to refuse prostration. Second, when He said, ﴿But it only increases them in great rebellion﴾ [al-Isra: 60], He explained the cause of this rebellion, which is the statement of Iblis, ﴿I will surely seize control of his descendants, except for a few﴾.

[The word] ﴿tinan﴾ (clay) is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), as said by al-Zajjaj, and al-Hawfi followed him. He said: it is from the pronoun in the deleted ﴿khalaqtahu﴾ (I created him), and the operating element is ﴿khalaqta﴾ (You created). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿tinan﴾ is either from the relative pronoun, and the operating element in it is ﴿a-asjudu﴾ (shall I prostrate), with the sense "I prostrate to him who is clay," meaning his origin is clay; or from the pronoun referring back to it from the relative clause, with the sense "shall I prostrate to him who, at the time of his creation, was ﴿tinan﴾ (clay)." End of quote. This is an explanation of meaning. Abu al-Baqa said: the operating element in it is ﴿khalaqta﴾, meaning when it is a ḥāl from the deleted returning pronoun. Al-Hawfi allowed that it be in the accusative by deleting "min" (from), the estimate being "min ṭīn" (from clay), as it is expressly stated in His words: ﴿and created him from clay﴾ [al-A'raf: 12]. Al-Zajjaj also allowed that it be a tamyiz (specification), and Ibn Atiyya followed him; but it does not appear that it is a tamyiz.

His words ﴿a-asjudu﴾ are an interrogative of denial and astonishment. Between His words ﴿a-asjudu﴾ and what precedes it there is a deleted statement, and it seems its estimate is: He said, "Why did you not prostrate to Adam?" He said, ﴿Shall I prostrate...﴾. Between His words ﴿Have you considered﴾ and "he said, shall I prostrate" are sentences that have been mentioned, since the story was lengthened. The kaf in ﴿arayta-ka﴾ is for address, and its discussion has passed in Surat al-An'am. This address kaf does not attach except when it has the meaning of "inform me," and with this meaning al-Hawfi estimated it, and al-Zamakhshari followed him, and it is the view of Sibawayh regarding it and of al-Zajjaj.

Al-Hawfi said: ﴿arayta-ka﴾ means "let me know" and "inform me." This is in the accusative by ﴿arayta-ka﴾, and the meaning is "inform me about this one whom You honored over me, why did You honor him over me, when You created me from fire and created him from clay?" This [last part] is deleted because of the evidence in the speech for it. Al-Zamakhshari said: the kaf is for address, and ﴿hadha﴾ (this) is the direct object; the meaning is "inform me about this one whom You honored over me, that is, preferred, why did You honor him over me, while I am better than him?" So he abbreviated the speech by deleting that and then began, saying: ﴿If You delay me...﴾. It has also been said the sound here is whispering.

The ba' in ﴿bi-khaylika﴾ is said to be superfluous. It is also said [the horses and foot soldiers are] from humans, and they are attributed to him because they are joined in his obedience and are his helpers against others, as Mujahid said.

End of quote. The majority read ﴿wa-rajlika﴾ (and your foot) with a fatha on the ra' and a sukun on the jim; it is a collective noun whose singular is "rajil," like "rakb" and "rakib." "On foot, except with companions."

Al-Zamakhshari said: it was also read ﴿wa-rajilika﴾ with fa'il in the sense of fa'il, like "ta'ib" and "ta'ib" (weary), and its meaning is "and your gathering of the man"; its jim may also be dammed, so it is like "haddutha" and "hadutha," "nadisa" and "nadusa," and their like. [p. 57] The connection of this verse to what precedes it is twofold. So it fits to mention the story of Adam, peace be upon him, and Iblis, whom arrogance and envy led to refuse prostration. Second, when He said, ﴿But it only increases them in great rebellion﴾ [al-Isra: 60], He explained the cause of this rebellion, which is the statement of Iblis, ﴿I will surely seize control of his descendants, except for a few﴾.

Mujahid said: non-invocation of the name [of God] at intercourse, for the jinn then wraps itself in its member and copulates with it. It has been said: inciting them to fighting and killing, and memorizing poetry containing obscenity. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿and promise them﴾ means false promises: intercession by the gods, honour with God through noble lineages, postponing repentance, forgiveness of sins without it, reliance on mercy and the intercession of the Messenger (ﷺ) for major sins and exit from the Fire after they become charcoal, and preferring the immediate over the deferred.
