End of quote. Qatada and Ikrima read ﴿wa-rijalika﴾ (and your men). It was also read ﴿wa-rujjila lak﴾ with a damma on the ra' and a shadda on the jim.

As for sharing in wealth, al-Dahhak said: what they slaughter for their gods; Qatada said: the baḥīra and the sā'iba (types of animals dedicated to idols). It has also been said: what is obtained from wealth through what is unlawful; it has been said: what they dedicated from their wealth to other than God; it has been said: what is spent on fornication. The preferable view is: what is taken from other than its right and what is placed in other than its right. Sharing in children: Ibn Abbas said: their naming them ʿAbd al-ʿUzza, ʿAbd al-Lat, ʿAbd al-Shams, and ʿAbd al-Harth (servant of al-Uzza, of al-Lat, of the sun, of the tiller). From him also: their inclining them toward false religions such as Judaism and Christianity. From him also: their proceeding to kill children. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: and what they made them Magians, Jews, and Christians, and dyed them with other than the dye of Islam. Mujahid said: non-invocation of the name [of God] at intercourse, for the jinn then wraps itself in its member and copulates with it. It has been said: inciting them to fighting and killing, and memorizing poetry containing obscenity. The preferable view is that it is every action regarding children that leads to committing something abominable and ugly. As for his promise, it is the false promise, like their promise that there is no resurrection; and this is sharing in souls.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿and promise them﴾ means false promises: intercession by the gods, honour with God through noble lineages, postponing repentance, forgiveness of sins without it, reliance on mercy and the intercession of the Messenger (ﷺ) for major sins and exit from the Fire after they become charcoal, and preferring the immediate over the deferred. End of quote. This is in accordance with the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) that sins are not forgiven without repentance, that there is no intercession for major sins, and that whoever enters the Fire, a sinful believer, never comes out of it. The word ﴿ghurur﴾ (deception) is in the accusative as a verbal noun, being a descriptive of a deleted verbal noun, that is, "a promise of deception" in the manner of a man who is ... Or it may be an accusative of purpose, meaning "and what Satan promises you and makes you hope for is nothing but deception, which will never be fulfilled and will not occur except so that it may deceive you." The attribution to Him, exalted is He, in ﴿Indeed My servants﴾ is an attribution of honour, meaning those specifically characterized by being ﴿My servants﴾, who are not attributed to other than Me, just as He said regarding their opposites: ﴿Their allies are the Taghut﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257] and ﴿allies of Satan﴾ [al-Nisa: 76].

It is also said: there is an omitted qualifier, meaning "Indeed My servants who are righteous." He negated authority, which is proof and capability, over their being led astray from faith. The qualifier's implied presence is supported by His saying: ﴿Indeed, his authority is only over those who take him as an ally﴾ [al-Nahl: 100]. Al-Jubba'i said: ﴿My servants﴾ is general, covering those who are legally responsible (mukallafun), and for this reason He made an exception from it, in another verse, for those who followed him, in His saying: ﴿except those among the deviators who follow you﴾ [al-Hijr: 42]. He used this as evidence that Satan has no path and no power to confuse the intellect; his power is only in whispering (waswasah). Had he had power over that, he would have confused the scholars so that his harm would be more complete. The meaning of ﴿a guardian (wakilan)﴾ is a protector of His servants, those over whom he has no authority of misguidance by Satan's seduction. Or it means ﴿a guardian﴾ to whom they entrust their affairs, so He is their protector because of their reliance (tawakkul) upon Him.

[p. 57] The connection of this verse to what precedes it is twofold. First, when they disputed with the Messenger, peace be upon him, concerning prophethood and demanded signs from him, this was due to their arrogance and envy toward the Messenger (ﷺ) for what God had given him of prophethood and the lofty rank. So it fits to mention the story of Adam, peace be upon him, and Iblis, whom arrogance and envy led to refuse prostration. Second, when He said, ﴿But it only increases them in great rebellion﴾ [al-Isra: 60], He explained the cause of this rebellion, which is the statement of Iblis, ﴿I will surely seize control of his descendants, except for a few﴾.

[The word] ﴿tinan﴾ (clay) is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), as said by al-Zajjaj, and al-Hawfi followed him. He said: it is from the pronoun in the deleted ﴿khalaqtahu﴾ (I created him), and the operating element is ﴿khalaqta﴾ (You created). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿tinan﴾ is either from the relative pronoun, and the operating element in it is ﴿a-asjudu﴾ (shall I prostrate), with the sense "I prostrate to him who is clay," meaning his origin is clay; or from the pronoun referring back to it from the relative clause, with the sense "shall I prostrate to him who, at the time of his creation, was ﴿tinan﴾ (clay)." End of quote. This is an explanation of meaning. Abu al-Baqa said: the operating element in it is ﴿khalaqta﴾, meaning when it is a ḥāl from the deleted returning pronoun. Al-Hawfi allowed that it be in the accusative by deleting "min" (from), the estimate being "min ṭīn" (from clay), as it is expressly stated in His words: ﴿and created him from clay﴾ [al-A'raf: 12]. Al-Zajjaj also allowed that it be a tamyiz (specification), and Ibn Atiyya followed him; but it does not appear that it is a tamyiz.

His words ﴿a-asjudu﴾ are an interrogative of denial and astonishment. Between His words ﴿a-asjudu﴾ and what precedes it there is a deleted statement, and it seems its estimate is: He said, "Why did you not prostrate to Adam?" He said, ﴿Shall I prostrate...﴾. Between His words ﴿Have you considered﴾ and "he said, shall I prostrate" are sentences that have been mentioned, since the story was lengthened. The kaf in ﴿arayta-ka﴾ is for address, and its discussion has passed in Surat al-An'am. This address kaf does not attach except when it has the meaning of "inform me," and with this meaning al-Hawfi estimated it, and al-Zamakhshari followed him, and it is the view of Sibawayh regarding it and of al-Zajjaj.

Al-Hawfi said: ﴿arayta-ka﴾ means "let me know" and "inform me." This is in the accusative by ﴿arayta-ka﴾, and the meaning is "inform me about this one whom You honored over me, why did You honor him over me, when You created me from fire and created him from clay?" This [last part] is deleted because of the evidence in the speech for it. Al-Zamakhshari said: the kaf is for address, and ﴿hadha﴾ (this) is the direct object; the meaning is "inform me about this one whom You honored over me, that is, preferred, why did You honor him over me, while I am better than him?" So he abbreviated the speech by deleting that and then began, saying: ﴿If You delay me...﴾. Ibn Atiyya said: the kaf in ﴿arayta-ka﴾ is a particle of address and emphasis in alerting, with no place in grammatical case, so it is superfluous; and the meaning of "arayta" is "did you reflect" and the like; the one who addresses with it is alerting the addressee so that he gathers himself for what he is about to specify afterward. Sibawayh said: it means "inform me," and he gave the example: "arayta-ka Zaydan a-yu'minu huwa" (Do you see yourself: Zayd, does he believe?). Al-Zajjaj said the same without giving an example. Sibawayh's statement is correct where an interrogative follows it, as in his example; but in this verse it is as I have said, and it is not the one Sibawayh mentioned, may God have mercy on him. End of quote. What al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari went to regarding ﴿arayta-ka﴾ here is the correct view, and for this reason the interrogative was estimated, namely "why did You honor him over me?" For from His words "this one whom You honored over me" there is formed a nominal sentence of subject and predicate, "why did You honor him over me," and it becomes like "Zayd, a-yu'minu huwa" (Zayd, does he believe?), which ﴿arayta-ka﴾ entered and governed the first part, while the interrogative sentence is in the place of the second. The fixed element in "arayta" with the meaning of "inform me" is that it enters upon a nominal sentence whose predicate is an interrogative. If it is stated explicitly, that is clear; otherwise it is estimated. We have fully discussed this in al-An'am and in the commentary on al-Tashil.

Al-Farra' said: here the kaf has a grammatical position, which is the accusative, meaning "have you seen yourself?" He said: this is like your saying, "Have you reflected on the end of your affair? For I am doing such-and-such in it." Then he began, ﴿this one whom You honored over me﴾. End of quote. The refutation of it is mentioned in the science of grammar. Had someone gone to the view that ﴿hadha﴾ is the first object of ﴿arayta-ka﴾ with the meaning of "inform me," and the second is the oath clause after it, since the two form a subject and predicate before ﴿arayta-ka﴾ entered upon them, that would be a fine view, since there would be no deletion in the speech. From all this it is concluded that the kaf is either in the place of the accusative and "hadha" is the subject; or it is a particle of address and "hadha" is the object of "arayta" with a deleted meaning, namely the interrogative sentence (p. 58), or an expressed meaning, namely the oath clause. The meaning of ﴿If You delay me﴾ is: if You delay my death and keep me alive.

Ibn Abbas said: ﴿la-ahtanikanna﴾ (I will surely seize control) means "I will surely gain mastery over them," and al-Farra' said the same. Ibn Zayd said: "I will surely lead them astray." Al-Tabari said: "I will surely uproot them." Iblis, through his ignorance, disbelieved in the attribute of justice from God when pride and arrogance seized him, and this appeared in his words: ﴿Have you considered this one whom You honored over me?﴾, for he expressly stated that it was not fitting that one whom he considered better than himself be honored by prostration from him. Iblis swore that he would seize control of the descendants of Adam, and he knew this either by hearing it from the angels, to whom God had told it, or he inferred it from their words: ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]; or he looked at him and discerned in his features that he possessed desire and accidental traits such as anger and the like, and he saw his creation as hollow and composed of differing parts. Al-Hasan said: he assumed this because he had whispered to Adam and found in him no resolve, so he assumed the same about his descendants. This is not evident, because this statement was made before his whispering to Adam about eating from the tree. He made an exception of the few, because he knew that among the descendants of Adam there would be those over whom he has no power, as He said: ﴿I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [Sad: 82]. The command to "go" is not literally the opposite of "come," but the meaning is "go about your affair which you have chosen." He followed this with mention of what the evil of his act brought upon him as punishment, and the punishment of his followers: Hell. Since a third-person noun and a second-person pronoun preceded, the address prevailed, and He said ﴿Your recompense﴾. It is possible that the pronoun ﴿min﴾ (of them) is by way of iltifat (shift of person). The mawfur means the complete, and wafara is transitive, as in his words:

"And whoever makes kindness at the expense of his honour, it diminishes him; and whoever does not guard against insult, will be insulted."

It is also intransitive: one says "wafara al-mal yafiru wufuran" (the wealth became complete). ﴿Jaza'an﴾ (as a recompense) is in the accusative as a verbal noun, and its operating element is ﴿jaza'ukum﴾ (your recompense), or it exceeds its implied element, or it is an accusative of circumstance preparing the way (ḥāl al-muwaṭṭi'a). It has also been said it is a tamyiz, but it is not conceivable. ﴿Wa-istafziz﴾ (and incite) is coordinated with ﴿fa-idhhab﴾ (go), and what follows it of commands is coordinated with it, and all of them carry the meaning of threat, as in His words: ﴿Do what you will﴾ [Fussilat: 40]. The "man" in ﴿man istata'ta﴾ (whomever you can) is a relative pronoun, the object of ﴿istafziz﴾. Abu al-Baqa said: ﴿man istata'ta﴾, "man" is an interrogative in the place of the accusative by ﴿istata'ta﴾; but this is not evident, because ﴿istafziz﴾ and the object of ﴿istata'ta﴾ are deleted, its estimate being ﴿man istata'ta﴾ "whomever you are able to incite." The sound here is the call to disobedience of God. Mujahid said: singing, flutes, and play. Al-Dahhak said: the sound of the flute. Al-Ghaznawi mentioned that Adam settled the offspring of Habil on the top of the mountain and the offspring of Qabil at its base, and among them were beautiful daughters, so Satan played the flute, and they could not restrain themselves from descending and coupling. It has also been said the sound here is whispering.

Al-Hasan read ﴿wa-ajlib﴾ with a connected alif and a damma on the lam, from "jalaba" in its triliteral form. The apparent meaning is that Iblis has horsemen and foot soldiers from the jinn, his kind, as Qatada said. ﴿Khayl﴾ (horses) applies to the mares literally and to their riders metaphorically, who are the horsemen; and from this the saying "O cavalry of God, ride!" The ba' in ﴿bi-khaylika﴾ is said to be superfluous. It is also said [the horses and foot soldiers are] from humans, and they are attributed to him because they are joined in his obedience and are his helpers against others, as Mujahid said.

Ibn Atiyya said: His words ﴿with your horses and your foot soldiers﴾ are said to be a metaphor and figure of speech meaning "strive your striving and exert your utmost effort." End of quote. Abu Ali said: Satan has no horses or foot soldiers, and he is not commanded; rather, this is a rebuke and belittling of him, just as you say to one you threaten: "Go and do what you wish, and seek help in whatever you wish." Al-Zamakhshari said: if you ask, what is the meaning of inciting Iblis with his voice and rallying against them with his horse and foot? I say: it is a speech coming in the manner of a figure, in which his situation of dominance over whomever he misleads is depicted as a ravager who attacks a people, shouts at them in a way that incites them from their places and disturbs them from their positions, and rallies against them with his army of cavalry and infantry until he uproots them. End of quote. The majority read ﴿wa-rajlika﴾ (and your foot) with a fatha on the ra' and a sukun on the jim; it is a collective noun whose singular is "rajil," like "rakb" and "rakib." Al-Hasan and Abu Amr in one narration, and Hafs, read it with a kasra on the jim. The author of al-Lawami said it means "men." Ibn Atiyya said: it is a descriptive adjective; one says "Fulan yamshi rajilan," meaning "not riding," and from it the poet's words:

"On foot, except with companions."

Al-Zamakhshari said: it was also read ﴿wa-rajilika﴾ with fa'il in the sense of fa'il, like "ta'ib" and "ta'ib" (weary), and its meaning is "and your gathering of the man"; its jim may also be dammed, so it is like "haddutha" and "hadutha," "nadisa" and "nadusa," and their like. End of quote. Qatada and Ikrima read ﴿wa-rijalika﴾ (and your men). It was also read ﴿wa-rujjila lak﴾ with a damma on the ra' and a shadda on the jim.

As for sharing in wealth, al-Dahhak said: what they slaughter for their gods; Qatada said: the baḥīra and the sā'iba (types of animals dedicated to idols). It has also been said: what is obtained from wealth through what is unlawful; it has been said: what they dedicated from their wealth to other than God; it has been said: what is spent on fornication. The preferable view is: what is taken from other than its right and what is placed in other than its right. Sharing in children: Ibn Abbas said: their naming them ʿAbd al-ʿUzza, ʿAbd al-Lat, ʿAbd al-Shams, and ʿAbd al-Harth (servant of al-Uzza, of al-Lat, of the sun, of the tiller). From him also: their inclining them toward false religions such as Judaism and Christianity. From him also: their proceeding to kill children. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: and what they made them Magians, Jews, and Christians, and dyed them with other than the dye of Islam. Mujahid said: non-invocation of the name [of God] at intercourse, for the jinn then wraps itself in its member and copulates with it. It has been said: inciting them to fighting and killing, and memorizing poetry containing obscenity. The preferable view is that it is every action regarding children that leads to committing something abominable and ugly. As for his promise, it is the false promise, like their promise that there is no resurrection; and this is sharing in souls.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿and promise them﴾ means false promises: intercession by the gods, honour with God through noble lineages, postponing repentance, forgiveness of sins without it, reliance on mercy and the intercession of the Messenger (ﷺ) for major sins and exit from the Fire after they become charcoal, and preferring the immediate over the deferred. End of quote. This is in accordance with the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) that sins are not forgiven without repentance, that there is no intercession for major sins, and that whoever enters the Fire, a sinful believer, never comes out of it. The word ﴿ghurur﴾ (deception) is in the accusative as a verbal noun, being a descriptive of a deleted verbal noun, that is, "a promise of deception" in the manner of a man who is ... Or it may be an accusative of purpose, meaning "and what Satan promises you and makes you hope for is nothing but deception, which will never be fulfilled and will not occur except so that it may deceive you." The attribution to Him, exalted is He, in ﴿Indeed My servants﴾ is an attribution of honour, meaning those specifically characterized by being ﴿My servants﴾, who are not attributed to other than Me, just as He said regarding their opposites: ﴿Their allies are the Taghut﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257] and ﴿allies of Satan﴾ [al-Nisa: 76].

It is also said: there is an omitted qualifier, meaning "Indeed My servants who are righteous." He negated authority, which is proof and capability, over their being led astray from faith. The qualifier's implied presence is supported by His saying: ﴿Indeed, his authority is only over those who take him as an ally﴾ [al-Nahl: 100]. Al-Jubba'i said: ﴿My servants﴾ is general, covering those who are legally responsible (mukallafun), and for this reason He made an exception from it, in another verse, for those who followed him, in His saying: ﴿except those among the deviators who follow you﴾ [al-Hijr: 42]. He used this as evidence that Satan has no path and no power to confuse the intellect; his power is only in whispering (waswasah). Or it means ﴿a guardian﴾ to whom they entrust their affairs, so He is their protector because of their reliance (tawakkul) upon Him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verses 66–70:

﴿Your Lord is the One who drives the ships for you upon the sea, that you may seek of His bounty. Indeed He is ever Merciful to you.﴾ ﴿And when harm touches you at sea, those you call upon vanish, except Him. But when He delivers you to the land, you turn away. And man is ever ungrateful.﴾ ﴿Do you then feel secure that He will not cause the side of the land to swallow you, or send against you a violent wind, and then you will not find for yourselves any protector?﴾ ﴿Or do you feel secure that He will not return you to it another time and send against you a furious wind and drown you for your disbelief, and then you will not find for yourselves against Us any avenger?﴾

When the Exalted mentioned the attribute of the polytheists in their belief about their gods, that they harm and benefit, and followed this with the story of Iblis with Adam, and his being granted power to whisper to his offspring and to beautify (evil) for them, He mentioned what points, through His acts, to His oneness, and that He is the one who benefits and harms, who disposes of His creation as He wills. So He mentioned His kindness to them by sea and by land, and that the Exalted is empowered by His might to do what He wills. "Izja' al-fulk" (izjaʾ, "driving") means moving ships from one place to another by a gentle wind and by oars, and that is of His mercy toward His servants. "Ibtigha' al-fadl" (seeking His bounty) means seeking trade, or the pilgrimage (hajj) by it, or raiding (ghazw). "Ḍurr" at sea means the fear of drowning, due to its turbulence and the force of the wind. The meaning of "ḍalla" (vanished) is: the one you call upon as a god, so that he intercedes or benefits, has gone away from your imaginations; or "ḍalla" means: the one you worship has vanished, except Allah alone, so that you single Him out at that time by seeking refuge in Him and believing that none removes harm but Him, and you do not hope for anyone other than Him to remove harm. Then He mentioned their condition when the harm was lifted from them: their turning away from Him and their denial of the blessing of their deliverance from drowning. The attribute "kafūr" (ungrateful) came to express intensity. Then He did not address them with this directly, but attributed it to "man" out of gentleness toward them and as a reference to the category, since every person hardly fulfills the thanks due for Allah's blessings.

Al-Zajjaj said: What is meant by "al-insan" (man) is the disbelievers. Apparently, "illa iyyahu" (except Him) is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), since it is not included in His words "those you call upon", for the meaning is: their gods vanished, i.e., their worshipped ones, while they themselves do not worship Allah. It was also said that it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), and on this reading the meaning is: those they seek refuge in vanish; in some of their affairs they sought refuge in their deities, but in this state they seek refuge only in Allah. The hamza in "afa-amintum" (do you then feel secure) is interrogative of denial. Al-Zamakhshari said: the fa' is for conjunction with an omitted element, its estimate being "anjawtum fa-amintum" (were you delivered, then you felt secure). End. We have previously discussed with him his claim that the fa' and the waw in this type of construction conjoin with an omitted element between the hamza and the conjunctive particle, whereas the position of the majority is that there is no omitted element there, and that the fa' and the waw conjoin with what precedes them, and that he gave importance to the interrogative hamza because it has the front position of the speech, so it was placed first, while the intention is posterior; and that the estimate is "fa-amintum." Al-Zamakhshari has returned to the position of the majority. The address is to those previously mentioned, i.e., "Do you then feel secure, O you who were delivered and turned away from Allah's handiwork, who delivered you?" "Janiba" (the side) is put as the object of "nakhsifa" (We cause to swallow), like His words: "So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home" (al-Qasas: 81). The meaning is that We cause it to turn over with you, so that you perish by that. Al-Zamakhshari said: "an naqliba-hu wa-antum 'alayhi" (that We overturn it while you are upon it). Al-Hawfi said: "janiba al-barr" is in the accusative as an adverb of place, and since swallowing is concealment in the earth, he said "janiba al-barr", and "bikum" is a circumstantial clause, i.e., We cause the side of the land to swallow while you are with it. It was also said: the "ba'" is causal, i.e., because of you, and the meaning is "the side of the land in which you are", so that by its swallowing their destruction occurs; otherwise it does not follow that the swallowing of the side of the land because of them entails their destruction.

Qatadah said: "al-hasib" is stones. Al-Suddi said: a shooter who shoots you with stones of sijjil. The meaning is that His power is complete; if He has delivered you from drowning and you have denied His blessing, then do not feel secure against His destroying you while you are on land, either by a command from beneath you, which is the sinking of the earth with you, or from above you by sending a stone-storm upon you. This is the extreme of the manifestation of power. Then "la tajidu" (you will not find) at the arrival of either of these upon you, any one to whom you entrust your affairs, who would then act as a guardian in averting that from you. The "am" in "am amintum" is disjunctive, estimated as "bal" (rather), and the hamza: i.e., "rather, do you feel secure?" The pronoun in "fihi" refers to the sea, and "tara" (another time) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, i.e., a time other than the first time. The "ba'" in "bima kafartum" is causal and "ma" is verbal (masdariyyah), i.e., because of your previous disbelief, meaning the time when He delivered you, or because of your disbelief which is your constant habit.

The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the verbal noun implied by "fa-nughriqakum", since it is the nearest mentioned thing, and it is the result of the sending. It was also said that it refers to the sending; it was said that it refers to both, so it is like the demonstrative, and the meaning is "by what occurred of the sending and the drowning." "Al-tabi'" (avenger): Ibn 'Abbas said: the helper. Al-Farra' said: one who seeks vengeance. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the pursuer. Al-Zajjaj said: one who follows up with denunciation what has befallen you. Its parallel is His words: "So He levelled it, and He does not fear its consequence" (al-Shams: 14). In a hadith: "If one of you is referred to a wealthy person, let him follow." Al-Shammakh said:

"As the debtor seeks refuge from the avenger."

It is said: "Fulan 'ala fulan tabi'" (so-and-so is an avenger against so-and-so), i.e., he is in control of him by his right, pursuing him for it. Ibn 'Atiyyah recited:

"They went, and their gazelles went, as if they were guarantors of a debt for a pledge that is pursued."

i.e., one who pursues his right.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read: "nakhsifu," "aw nursilu," "an nu'idakum," "fa-nursilu," and "fa-nughriqakum" — all five with the nun. The rest of the readers read with the yā' of the third person. Mujahid and Abu Ja'far read "fa-tughriqakum" with the tā' of address, attributing it to the wind. Al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read "fa-yughriqakum" with the yā' of the third person, with a fatha on the ghayn and a shadda on the rā', making it transitive by doubling. The reader transmitted from Abu Ja'far is the same, except that it has the tā' of address. Humayd read it with the nun, with sukun on the ghayn, and idgham of the qaf into the kaf; it is also narrated from Abu 'Amr and Ibn Muhaysin. The majority read "min al-rih" (from the wind) in the singular, and Abu Ja'far read "min al-riyah" (from the winds) in the plural.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verses 66–70:

Indeed He is ever Merciful to you.﴾ ﴿And when harm touches you at sea, those you call upon vanish, except Him. But when He delivers you to the land, you turn away. This is the extreme of the manifestation of power. Then "la tajidu" (you will not find) at the arrival of either of these upon you, any one to whom you entrust your affairs, who would then act as a guardian in averting that from you. The "am" in "am amintum" is disjunctive, estimated as "bal" (rather), and the hamza: i.e., "rather, do you feel secure?" The pronoun in "fihi" refers to the sea, and "tara" (another time) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, i.e., a time other than the first time. The "ba'" in "bima kafartum" is causal and "ma" is verbal (masdariyyah), i.e., because of your previous disbelief, meaning the time when He delivered you, or because of your disbelief which is your constant habit.

The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the verbal noun implied by "fa-nughriqakum", since it is the nearest mentioned thing, and it is the result of the sending. It was also said that it refers to the sending; it was said that it refers to both, so it is like the demonstrative, and the meaning is "by what occurred of the sending and the drowning." "Al-tabi'" (avenger): Ibn 'Abbas said: the helper. Al-Farra' said: one who seeks vengeance. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the pursuer. Al-Zajjaj said: one who follows up with denunciation what has befallen you. Its parallel is His words: "So He levelled it, and He does not fear its consequence" (al-Shams: 14). In a hadith: "If one of you is referred to a wealthy person, let him follow." Al-Shammakh said:

"As the debtor seeks refuge from the avenger."

It is said: "Fulan 'ala fulan tabi'" (so-and-so is an avenger against so-and-so), i.e., he is in control of him by his right, pursuing him for it. Ibn 'Atiyyah recited:

"They went, and their gazelles went, as if they were guarantors of a debt for a pledge that is pursued."

i.e., one who pursues his right.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read: "nakhsifu," "aw nursilu," "an nu'idakum," "fa-nursilu," and "fa-nughriqakum" — all five with the nun. The rest of the readers read with the yā' of the third person. Mujahid and Abu Ja'far read "fa-tughriqakum" with the tā' of address, attributing it to the wind. Al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read "fa-yughriqakum" with the yā' of the third person, with a fatha on the ghayn and a shadda on the rā', making it transitive by doubling. The reader transmitted from Abu Ja'far is the same, except that it has the tā' of address. Humayd read it with the nun, with sukun on the ghayn, and idgham of the qaf into the kaf; it is also narrated from Abu 'Amr and Ibn Muhaysin. The majority read "min al-rih" (from the wind) in the singular, and Abu Ja'far read "min al-riyah" (from the winds) in the plural.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verse 71–72 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam and carried them on land and sea and provided for them of the good things and preferred them over much of what We have created, with [definite] preference.﴾ [al-Isra: 70] ﴿The Day We will call every people with their leader. So whoever is given his record in his right hand - those will read their records, and they will not be wronged even [as much as] a thread.﴾ ﴿And whoever was blind in this [world] will be blind in the Hereafter and even more astray in way.﴾.

When Allah mentioned what He had bestowed upon them of making the ship run in the sea and saving them from drowning, He completed the mention of the favor by mentioning their honor, their provision, and their preference. Or, when He threatened them with what He threatened of being swallowed up and drowned, and that they were ungrateful for His blessing, He mentioned what He had bestowed upon them so that they would remember and be thankful for His blessings, and cease from the disbelief they were in, and obey Him, the Exalted. In mentioning the blessings and enumerating them there is a stirring toward gratitude for them. "Karrama" is intensified from "karuma," meaning: We made them possessors of nobility (karam), in the sense of honor and many virtues, as you say: "a noble garment" (thawb karim) and "a noble horse" (faras karim), meaning one that combines excellent qualities, and it is not from the generosity of wealth. What has come from the people of tafsir about their honoring and preferring with things they mentioned is by way of example, not by way of restriction to these alone. As related from Ibn 'Abbas, the preference is by reason ('aql); from al-Dahhak, by speech (nutq); from 'Ata', by the proportion and uprightness of stature; from Zayd ibn Aslam, by foods and pleasures; from Yaman, by beauty of form; from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, by making Muhammad - peace and blessings be upon him - from among them; from Ibn Jarir, by their being given dominion over other creation and having it subjected to them. It was said: by writing (al-khatt), and it was said: by the beard for men and the braid for women. From Ibn 'Abbas: by eating with his hand while others eat with their mouths. It was said: by managing the affairs of this life and the Hereafter; and it was said: by Allah creating Adam with His hand.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It has been mentioned that among animals there are some that surpass the son of Adam in one respect, such as the speed of the horse, its hearing and sight, the strength of the elephant, the courage of the lion, and the generosity of the rooster. He said: Honor and preference are only by reason, by which all animals are ruled, and by which Allah is known, His speech is understood, and one reaches His bliss. End.

﴿And We carried them on land and sea﴾ [al-Isra: 70] — this too is from their honoring. Ibn 'Abbas said: on land, upon horses, mules, donkeys and camels; and at sea, upon ships. Others said: upon moist livers and dry planks. ("And the good things") — as previously mentioned, the lawful or the pleasant. No other animal has such a broad provision as man's, because he earns wealth, wears garments, and eats compound foods, unlike animals, which generally do not earn, do not wear clothing, and do not eat except raw flesh and non-compound food. The apparent meaning is that "much" remains on its literal sense. A group said: they were preferred over all creatures except Gabriel, Michael, Israfil, Azrael and their likes; this is from Ibn 'Abbas. And from him: man is not better than the angel; this is the view chosen by al-Zajjaj. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The animals and jinn are the "much" that is surpassed, while the angels are those excluded from the "much" that is surpassed. Another group said: the verse requires the angels' superiority over humankind from the standpoint that they are the exceptions (p-62), and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿nor do the angels brought near﴾ [al-Nisa: 172]. This does not necessarily follow from the verse; rather, the preference between humankind and jinn is not what the verse intends, and it is possible that the angels are superior, and it is possible that they are equal, and the preference of angels can only be validly established from other places in the Shari'a. End.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿over much of what We have created﴾ [al-Isra: 70] refers to all besides the angels, peace be upon them. It suffices for the children of Adam in "preference" that angels be made to rise above them, while they are what they are and their station with Allah is their station. It is strange how the Mujbira reversed everything and were so stubborn that their obstinacy led them to the great claim of man's preference over the angel; then he mentioned a vile and foul censure which is found in his book. It was said: ﴿And We preferred them over much﴾ [al-Isra: 70] by dominance and power. It was said: by reward and recompense on the Day of Resurrection. On these two views, the verse does not address the disputed preference between humans and angels. It was said: the intended meaning of "much" is metaphorical, namely applying it to all, as the Arabs do; but this is a view that should not be said here, because if you took "all," you would say "over all of what We have created," which would be remote from eloquence, and the speech of Allah, which is the most eloquent of speech, should not be interpreted that way. Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi has a discourse on the honoring and preferring of the son of Adam drawn from the words of those they call philosophers, which can be consulted in his tafsir, for it proceeds on a course other than the way of the Arabs in their speech.

When Allah mentioned kinds of human honor in this world, He mentioned some of the conditions of the Hereafter, saying: ﴿The Day We will call every people with their leader﴾. They differed over the governing element of "the Day" (yawm). It was said: its governing element is what is indicated by His saying "when is it?" It was said: "then you will respond." It was said: it is a substitute for "the Day He calls you." These are opinions of extreme weakness, and if they had not mentioned them I would have turned away from mentioning them. In these views it is an adverbial phrase (zarf). Al-Hawfi and Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is in the accusative as an adverb, and its governing element is "udhkur" (remember); but on the assumption of "udhkur," it would not be an adverb but an object. Ibn 'Atiyya also said, after saying it is an adverb: its governing element is "udhkur," or a verb indicated by His saying: ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾, and Abu al-Baqa' related it and estimated it as: ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ on the Day We call. Ibn 'Atiyya also said: it is valid that the governing element be ﴿and We preferred them﴾ [al-Isra: 70], because the preference of humankind on the Day of Resurrection over the rest of the animals is clear, since they are the ones blessed, the accountable, the ones called to account, who have worth; except that this is refuted by the fact that the disbelievers that day are more losers than any animal, since the disbeliever says: "Would that I were dust." Ibn 'Atiyya also said: it is valid that "the Day" be in the accusative by being built, since it is attached to a non-declinable element, and its position would be nominative as subject, and the predicate is in the division that comes afterward in His saying: ﴿whoever is given his record﴾ to His saying: ﴿and whoever was﴾. End. His saying "in the accusative by being built" should have said "built on fatha," and his saying "since it is attached to a non-declinable element" is not good, because what is divided into declinable and non-declinable is the noun, not the verb, and this is attached to a present-tense verb, and the view of the Basrans is that when it is attached to a declinable present-tense verb it cannot be built; this aspect he mentioned is according to the view of the Kufans. As for his saying "the predicate in the division is devoid of a connecting pronoun to this divisional sentence with the subject," it is possible only if one estimates an omitted element, i.e., "of those who ﴿are given his record﴾ in which (with his right hand)"; and this, after that derivation, is a strained derivation.

Some grammarians said: its governing element is ﴿and We preferred them﴾ [al-Isra: 70], estimated as ﴿and We preferred them﴾ with reward; this view is close to Ibn 'Atiyya's view we mentioned before. Al-Zajjaj said: it is an adverb governed by "then you will not find." Al-Farra' said: it is an object of "We will return you," with an implied "We will return you on the Day We call." The closest of these views is that it is in the accusative as an object of "udhkur" implied.

The majority read "nad'u" with the first-person plural "we" (nun of majesty). Mujahid read "yad'u" with the third-person singular, i.e., "He calls Allah." Al-Hasan, as Abu 'Amr al-Dani reported, read "yud'a" in the passive, with "kull" as its subject; and as others reported, "yad'u" with a waw, derived according to the dialect of one who says "af'u" in pause for "af'a" (viper), making the connected form like pause, with "kull" as its subject; and the waw could be a pronoun as the unnamed subject, its original being "yad'una," the nun being deleted as in his saying:

"I spend the night traveling, and you spend the night rubbing your face with ambergris and pure musk,"

meaning: "you spend the night rubbing," and "kull" is a substitute for the waw of the pronoun. "Unas" (people) is a collective noun with no singular from its own form. The preposition in "bi-imamihim" apparently attaches to "nad'u," meaning: by the name of their leader. It was said: it is the preposition of circumstance, meaning: accompanied by their leader. "Al-imam" here: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Rabi' said: their book in which their deeds are recorded. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: their book which was sent down to them. Mujahid and Qatada said: their prophet. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "al-imam" encompasses all of this, since it is what one is led by. Al-Zamakhshari said: their leader is whoever they followed, a prophet, or one put forward in religion, or a book, or a religion, so it is said: "O people of such-and-such a religion, or such-and-such a book." It was said: with the book of their deeds: "O companions of the book of good, and O companions of the book of evil." In the reading of al-Hasan: "bi-kitabihim." Among the strange interpretations is that "imam" is the plural of "umm" (mother), and that people are called on the Day of Resurrection by their mothers, and that the wisdom in calling by mothers rather than fathers is to honor the right of 'Isa and the nobility of al-Hasan and al-Husayn, and so that the children of fornication are not disgraced; and I wonder which is more wondrous, the soundness of his wording or the splendor of his wisdom. End.

The giving of the book is evidence for the pages established in the Shari'a which both believer and disbeliever are given. Its being given in the right hand is evidence of the salvation of the obedient and the deliverance of the sinner from the Fire, if he enters it, and of the good news that he will not be dwelt in it forever. ("Then those") came in plural according to the meaning of "man," since it was first treated according to its wording and was made singular in ﴿is given his record in his right hand﴾. Their reading of their books is for the sake of delight in becoming acquainted with the good news contained in them; otherwise, from the fact that they are given them in the right hand, they already know that they are among the people of happiness, and from their joy at that, the Creator says to the people of the gathering: ﴿Here, read my record!﴾ [al-Haqqa: 19]. The opposite of "whoever is given his record in his right hand" — who is given his record in his left hand — does not appear here, though it appears in another verse, and its counterpart is His saying:

﴿And whoever was blind in this [world]﴾. This is its opposite in meaning, since "whoever is given his record in his right hand" are the people of happiness, and "whoever was blind in this [world]" are the people of wretchedness. ﴿They will not be wronged even [as much as] a thread﴾, i.e., they will not be diminished in the least; the explanation of "fatil" (thread) was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Nisa'. The apparent meaning of the reference in "in this" is to the world, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, meaning: whoever was blind in this abode to looking at the signs and lessons of Allah and to believing in His prophets, then he is blind in the Hereafter. Either this is an elision of a modifier, meaning: concerning the matter of the Hereafter, or it means: he is blind on the Day of Resurrection; the meaning being that they are two statements with no correct direction for him and no success shining for him. Mujahid said: he is blind in the Hereafter to his proofs. Ibn 'Abbas also said: "whoever was in this" refers to the blessings, pointing to the blessings of honor and preference, so he is blind in the Hereafter, which he has not seen or witnessed. It was said: whoever was in the world astray and a disbeliever, then he is blind in the Hereafter ﴿and even more astray in way﴾, because in this world his repentance is accepted and in the Hereafter it is not; in this world he can find his way to escape calamities, and in the Hereafter he cannot find his way to that at all. It was said: he is blind in the Hereafter regarding the way to Paradise. It was said: blind of sight, as He said: ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind﴾ [al-Isra: 97], and His saying: ﴿And We will bring him on the Day of Resurrection blind. He will say: My Lord, why have You brought me blind, when I was seeing?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 124]. It was said: whoever was blind in the world to seeing the truth and taking lessons, then he is blind in the Hereafter to making excuses.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The more apparent view to me is that the reference of "this" (hādhihi) is to the present world (al-dunyā). That is, whoever was blind in this world of his, at the time of his perception and understanding, to looking into the signs of Allah, then on the Day of Resurrection he will be even more bewildered and blind, because he has come face to face with loss and has seen the signs of punishment. With this interpretation, the phrase is balanced against what precedes it, concerning the one who is given his book in his right hand. And if we take His saying, ﴿in the Hereafter﴾, to mean 'concerning the matter of the Hereafter,' the balance between the two verses does not hold consistently."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: (p-64) "The word 'blind' (aʿmā) is used metaphorically for one whose faculty of perception of visible things is corrupted, and so for one who is not guided to the path of salvation. In this world, it is due to the lack of sight; and in the Hereafter, it is because guidance to it will no longer benefit him. Some have also permitted that the second [aʿmā] be understood in the sense of the comparative (tafḍīl). For this reason, Abū ʿAmr read the first with imāla and the second without imāla (tafkhīm), because the comparative form (afʿal al-tafḍīl) is completed by min, so its alif is treated as if it stood in the middle of the utterance, like His saying: (aʿmālukum). As for the first, nothing is attached to it, so its alif stands at the end and is open to imāla." End of quotation.

Abū Ḥayyān's reasoning for leaving out imāla in the second aʿmā was taken by al-Zamakhsharī from Abū ʿAlī. Abū ʿAlī said: "Imāla is only good at the ends of words, and (aʿmā) is not of that kind, because its full form (aʿmā) min kadhā is not complete except with the phrase 'min kadhā'; so it is therefore not at the end." This interpretation is strengthened by the conjunction ﴿and more astray in way﴾, because a person in this world can believe and be saved, whereas in the Hereafter this is not possible for him, so he is ﴿more astray in way﴾ [al-Furqān: 42], more bewildered, and nearer to punishment. Here, (aʿmā) means blindness of the heart, not blindness of the eye, because comparison applies to the former and not to the latter.

It was said: with the book of their deeds: "O companions of the book of good, and O companions of the book of evil." In the reading of al-Hasan: "bi-kitabihim." Among the strange interpretations is that "imam" is the plural of "umm" (mother), and that people are called on the Day of Resurrection by their mothers, and that the wisdom in calling by mothers rather than fathers is to honor the right of 'Isa and the nobility of al-Hasan and al-Husayn, and so that the children of fornication are not disgraced; and I wonder which is more wondrous, the soundness of his wording or the splendor of his wisdom. End.

The giving of the book is evidence for the pages established in the Shari'a which both believer and disbeliever are given. Its being given in the right hand is evidence of the salvation of the obedient and the deliverance of the sinner from the Fire, if he enters it, and of the good news that he will not be dwelt in it forever. ("Then those") came in plural according to the meaning of "man," since it was first treated according to its wording and was made singular in ﴿is given his record in his right hand﴾. Their reading of their books is for the sake of delight in becoming acquainted with the good news contained in them; otherwise, from the fact that they are given them in the right hand, they already know that they are among the people of happiness, and from their joy at that, the Creator says to the people of the gathering: ﴿Here, read my record!﴾ [al-Haqqa: 19]. The opposite of "whoever is given his record in his right hand" — who is given his record in his left hand — does not appear here, though it appears in another verse, and its counterpart is His saying:

﴿And whoever was blind in this [world]﴾. This is its opposite in meaning, since "whoever is given his record in his right hand" are the people of happiness, and "whoever was blind in this [world]" are the people of wretchedness. ﴿They will not be wronged even [as much as] a thread﴾, i.e., they will not be diminished in the least; the explanation of "fatil" (thread) was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Nisa'. The apparent meaning of the reference in "in this" is to the world, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, meaning: whoever was blind in this abode to looking at the signs and lessons of Allah and to believing in His prophets, then he is blind in the Hereafter. Either this is an elision of a modifier, meaning: concerning the matter of the Hereafter, or it means: he is blind on the Day of Resurrection; the meaning being that they are two statements with no correct direction for him and no success shining for him. Mujahid said: he is blind in the Hereafter to his proofs. Ibn 'Abbas also said: "whoever was in this" refers to the blessings, pointing to the blessings of honor and preference, so he is blind in the Hereafter, which he has not seen or witnessed. It was said: whoever was in the world astray and a disbeliever, then he is blind in the Hereafter ﴿and even more astray in way﴾, because in this world his repentance is accepted and in the Hereafter it is not; in this world he can find his way to escape calamities, and in the Hereafter he cannot find his way to that at all. It was said: he is blind in the Hereafter regarding the way to Paradise. It was said: blind of sight, as He said: ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind﴾ [al-Isra: 97], and His saying: ﴿And We will bring him on the Day of Resurrection blind. He will say: My Lord, why have You brought me blind, when I was seeing?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 124]. It was said: whoever was blind in the world to seeing the truth and taking lessons, then he is blind in the Hereafter to making excuses.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The more apparent view to me is that the reference of "this" (hādhihi) is to the present world (al-dunyā). That is, whoever was blind in this world of his, at the time of his perception and understanding, to looking into the signs of Allah, then on the Day of Resurrection he will be even more bewildered and blind, because he has come face to face with loss and has seen the signs of punishment. With this interpretation, the phrase is balanced against what precedes it, concerning the one who is given his book in his right hand. And if we take His saying, ﴿in the Hereafter﴾, to mean 'concerning the matter of the Hereafter,' the balance between the two verses does not hold consistently."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: (p-64) "The word 'blind' (aʿmā) is used metaphorically for one whose faculty of perception of visible things is corrupted, and so for one who is not guided to the path of salvation. In this world, it is due to the lack of sight; and in the Hereafter, it is because guidance to it will no longer benefit him. Some have also permitted that the second [aʿmā] be understood in the sense of the comparative (tafḍīl). For this reason, Abū ʿAmr read the first with imāla and the second without imāla (tafkhīm), because the comparative form (afʿal al-tafḍīl) is completed by min, so its alif is treated as if it stood in the middle of the utterance, like His saying: (aʿmālukum). As for the first, nothing is attached to it, so its alif stands at the end and is open to imāla." End of quotation.

Abū Ḥayyān's reasoning for leaving out imāla in the second aʿmā was taken by al-Zamakhsharī from Abū ʿAlī. Abū ʿAlī said: "Imāla is only good at the ends of words, and (aʿmā) is not of that kind, because its full form (aʿmā) min kadhā is not complete except with the phrase 'min kadhā'; so it is therefore not at the end." This interpretation is strengthened by the conjunction ﴿and more astray in way﴾, because a person in this world can believe and be saved, whereas in the Hereafter this is not possible for him, so he is ﴿more astray in way﴾ [al-Furqān: 42], more bewildered, and nearer to punishment. Here, (aʿmā) means blindness of the heart, not blindness of the eye, because comparison applies to the former and not to the latter.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 17, verses 73–77:**

﴿And indeed they almost tempted you away from that which We have revealed to you, so that you would fabricate against Us other than it; then they would have taken you as a close friend.﴾ ﴿And had We not made you firm, you would have almost inclined toward them a little.﴾ ﴿Then We would have made you taste a double portion of life and a double portion of death; then you would not find for yourself any helper against Us.﴾ ﴿And indeed they almost tried to drive you out of the land to expel you from it; then they would not have remained after you except a little.﴾ ﴿[This is] the way of those We sent before you of Our messengers, and you will not find any alteration in Our way.﴾

Regarding the pronoun in ﴿وإنْ كادُوا﴾ (wa-in kadu, "and indeed they almost"), it has been said that it refers to Quraysh, and it has been said that it refers to Thaqif. They mentioned various occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul), and some of them contain what cannot be correctly attributed to the Messenger ﷺ. This can be consulted in the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyyah, al-Zamakhshari, al-Tahrir, and others.

The connection (munasabah) of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah the Exalted enumerated His blessings upon the children of Adam, and then mentioned their condition in the Hereafter, including the giving of the record in the right hand to the people of happiness and the blindness of the people of misery, He followed this with what the wretched in this world intend, namely deceit, trickery and confusion against the master of the people of happiness, who is definitively guaranteed protection (al-ma'sum). The meaning of ﴿لَيَفْتِنُونَكَ﴾ (la-yaftinunaka) is "they would deceive you." This refers to their assumption, not that they had come close to it, since he, peace be upon him, is protected from having them come close to tempting him away from what Allah revealed to him. Their approach to this, in their view, was caused by their hope that he would fabricate against Allah something other than what Allah revealed to him, such as changing a promise into a threat or a threat into a promise, and by what Thaqif proposed, namely that he attribute to Allah what had not been sent down to him. [p. 65]

The (إنْ) in this verse is the lightened form (al-mukhaffafah) of the heavy (al-thaqilah) إنَّ. Its governed element is the verbal clause (al-jumlah al-fi'liyyah), which is ﴿كادُوا﴾ (kadu), because it is among the verbs of approximation (af'al al-muqarabah). It enters on the verbs that govern the affirmative particles (al-nawasikh), according to the school of the Basrans, as is established in the science of grammar. The lam in ﴿لَيَفْتِنُونَكَ﴾ (la-yaftinunaka) is the lam that distinguishes this إنْ from the negating إنِ. The word ﴿وإذًا﴾ (wa-idhan, "then") is a particle of response and consequence. An oath is presumed here, and ﴿لاتَّخَذُوكَ﴾ (la-ittakhadhukum, "they would have taken you") is its answer. The estimation is: "by Allah, then [they would have taken you as a friend]", i.e., if you were tempted and fabricated, they would have taken you [as a close friend]. The phrase ﴿لاتَّخَذُوكَ﴾ has the meaning of ﴿لَيَتَّخِذُونَكَ﴾ (la-yattakhidhunaka, "they will take you"), like His saying ﴿وَلَئِنْ أَرْسَلْنَا رِيحًا فَرَأَوْهُ مُصْفَرًّا لَظَلُّوا﴾ (Al-Rum: 51), meaning "they will surely remain" (la-yazallunna), because إذًا implies the future, since in meaning it is a conditional, so its place is estimated with a conditional particle.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿وإذًا لاتَّخَذُوكَ﴾ means: "And if you followed their desire, they would have taken you as a close friend, and you would have become their ally, and you would have left My guardianship." End of quotation. This is an explanation of the meaning, and it is not that ﴿لاتَّخَذُوكَ﴾ is the answer of an omitted لو (law). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ولَوْلا أنْ ثَبَّتْناكَ﴾ (wa-law la an thabbatnaka) means: "Had it not been for Our making you firm and Our protection, you would have almost inclined toward them," meaning you would have come close to leaning toward their deceit and their trickery. This is an incitement from Allah to him and an act of grace in making him firm, and in it is gentleness toward the believers. ﴿إذَنْ لَوْ قارَبْتَ تَرْكَنُ إلَيْهِمْ أدْنى رَكْنَةٍ﴾ means: if you had come close to inclining toward them even by the least inclination, ﴿لَأذَقْناكَ ضِعْفَ الحَياةِ وضِعْفَ المَماتِ﴾ means: We would have made you taste the punishment of the Hereafter and the punishment of the grave, doubled. If you ask: what is the real structure of this speech? I say: its origin is ﴿لَأذَقْناكَ﴾ punishment of life and punishment of death, because punishment is of two kinds: punishment at death, which is the punishment of the grave, and punishment in the life of the Hereafter, which is the punishment of the Fire. The word "double" (ḍi'f) can be described by it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فَآتِهِمْ عَذابًا ضِعْفًا مِنَ النّارِ﴾ (Al-A'raf: 38), meaning "doubled." So the original speech was ﴿لَأذَقْناكَ﴾ a double punishment in life and a double punishment at death. Then the described noun was omitted and the attribute was put in its place, which is "double", and then the attribute was made an annexed noun in the manner of the described noun, so it was said ﴿ضِعْفَ الحَياةِ وضِعْفَ المَماتِ﴾, just as it is said ﴿لَأذَقْناكَ﴾ "painful life and painful death." It is also permissible that "double of life" means the punishment of the worldly life, and "double of death" means what follows death of the punishment of the grave and the punishment of the Fire. The meaning is: We would have doubled for you the punishment hastened for the disobedient in worldly life, and what We delay for after death. End of quotation.

The answer to (لَوْلا) (law la), when it is affirmative, requires its negation because of the existence of what precedes it. So the approach to inclining did not occur from him, let alone the inclining itself, and what prevented that is the existence of Allah's making him firm. Qatadah, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ibn Musarrif read ﴿تَرْكُنُ﴾ (tarkunu) with a damma on the kaf, as the present tense of ركَنَ (raka-na) with a fatha on it. The word ﴿شَيْئًا﴾ (shay'an) is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar) [of degree]. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: he means the doubled punishment of life and the doubled punishment of death, in the sense that what the one who sins deserves of Our punishment in this world and the Hereafter, We would have doubled. Ibn al-Anbari held that the meaning is: they almost reported about you that you had inclined to their speech because of their action toward it, figuratively and by extension, as you say to a man: "You almost killed yourself", meaning: "the people almost killed you because of what you did."

Ibn 'Abbas said: The Messenger ﷺ was protected, but this is an instruction for the community, lest anyone among them incline toward the polytheists in any matter of Allah's rulings and laws. End of quotation. The lam in ﴿لَأذَقْناكَ﴾ (la-adhaqnaka) is the answer of an omitted oath before (إذًا) (idhan), meaning: "by Allah, if inclining occurs, then it would certainly be such." The discussion of ﴿لَأذَقْناكَ﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿لاتَّخَذُوكَ﴾ regarding the past tense being placed in the position of the present tense that is preceded by the lam and the nun. Among those who explicitly stated that the lam in ﴿لاتَّخَذُوكَ﴾ and ﴿لَأذَقْناكَ﴾ is the lam of the oath is al-Hawfi. Al-Zamakhshari said: In the mention of the great wrong and its causation, together with following it with a severe threat of doubled punishment in both abodes, is clear evidence that a wrong's ugliness is magnified in proportion to the greatness of the status of its doer and the elevation of his rank. End of quotation. Among this is His saying: ﴿يا نِساءَ النَّبِيِّ مَن يَأْتِ مِنكُنَّ بِفاحِشَةٍ مُبَيِّنَةٍ﴾ (Al-Ahzab: 30), "O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear immorality..." etc. Al-Zamakhshari said: In it there is a slight flattery toward the deluded, opposition to Allah, and departure from His guardianship, and a cause that requires His anger and His punishment. End of quotation.

It has been narrated that when this was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Allah, do not leave me to myself even for the blink of an eye." (p. 66) Al-Hadrami said: The pronoun in ﴿وإنْ كادُوا﴾ refers to the Jews of Medina and its surroundings, such as Huyayy ibn Akhtab and others, because they went to plot against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, saying: "This land is not the land of the prophets; the land of the prophets is al-Sham. But you fear the Romans. So if you are a prophet, go out to it, for Allah will protect you as He protected other prophets." So this verse was revealed, and Allah the Exalted informed that if he had gone out, He would not have left them after that ﴿إلّا قَلِيلًا﴾ (illa qalilan, "except a little").

Al-Naqqash related that he went out because of their words, and encamped at Dhu al-Hulayfah, and remained waiting for his companions, and then this verse was revealed and he returned. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is weak; it did not occur in any biography or any book that is relied upon, and Dhu al-Hulayfah is not on the route from Medina to al-Sham. End of quotation.

A group said: The pronoun refers to Quraysh, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. Their attempt to expel him (istifzazuhum) is what they undertook of expelling him from Mecca, as they undertook to confine him in the valley (al-Shi'b). Their attempt at expulsion occurred after the revelation of the verse, and they constrained him until he went out, and they followed him to the cave, and the threat was carried out against them in that they did not remain ﴿إلّا قَلِيلًا﴾ on the day of Badr. Al-Zajjaj, reporting that their attempt to expel him was what they agreed upon in the Dar al-Nadwah (the assembly house of Quraysh) of killing him, and the "land" in this view is the world. Mujahid said: Quraysh went in that direction, but it did not happen from them, because when Allah the Exalted wanted to preserve Quraysh and not to uproot them, He permitted His Messenger to emigrate, so he went out by His permission, not by the compulsion of Quraysh, and Quraysh was preserved so that from them and their descendants those who would accept Islam might become Muslims. He said: Had Quraysh expelled him, they would have been punished. Mujahid held that the pronoun in ﴿يَلْبَثُونَ﴾ (yalbathuna) refers to all of them.

Al-Hasan said: ﴿لَيَسْتَفِزُّونَكَ﴾ (la-yastafizzunaka) means "they would tempt you away from your opinion." Ibn 'Isa said: "they would unsettle you and make you light." And he recited:

*He obeys the fool of the people when he provokes him, and disobeys the forbearing one whom the calamities have whitened.*

The apparent meaning is that the verse indicates the approach of their attempt to drive him out, so the attempt did not occur, nor did their actual expulsion of him, which was the cause of the attempt. Then the Qur'an says: ﴿وكَأيِّنْ مِن قَرْيَةٍ هي أشَدُّ قُوَّةً مِن قَرْيَتِكَ الَّتِي أخْرَجَتْكَ﴾ (Muhammad: 13), "And how many a town, stronger than your town which expelled you..." meaning: its people expelled you. In the hadith: "Would that I were a young man when your people expel you." He said: "Will they expel me?" etc. This indicates that they did expel him, but the expulsion that is the cause of the attempt did not occur, so there is no contradiction between the two verses and the hadith. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: He did not go out because of their expulsion, but went out by Allah's command, and thus the contradiction disappears. End of quotation.

﴿ولا يَلْبَثُونَ﴾ (wa-la yalbathuna, "and they would not remain") is the answer of an omitted oath, meaning: "by Allah, if they had driven you out and you went out, they would not remain." For this reason (idhan) did not govern, because it was placed between the estimated oath and the verb, and ﴿فَلا يَلْبَثُونَ﴾ is not directed at it from the standpoint of grammatical case (i'rab). It is possible that ﴿لا يَلْبَثُونَ﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, indicated by the meaning, whose estimation is: "and they, [then] they would not remain," so ﴿وإذًا﴾ fell between the subject and its predicate and was thus disregarded.

Ubayy read ﴿وإذًا لا يَلْبَثُوا﴾ (wa-idhan la yalbathu) with the nun deleted, making idhan operative and putting the verb in the subjunctive, according to the view of the majority; and with an implied "an" (an) after it, according to the view of some. Likewise it is so in the codex of 'Abd Allah, with the nun deleted.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: what is the basis of the two readings? I say: As for the widely known reading, in it the verb is conjoined to the verb while it is in the nominative, because it occurs as the predicate of kada, and the verb in the predicate of kada occupies the position of a noun. As for the reading of Ubayy, in it the whole clause, which is "wa-idhan la yalbathu", is conjoined to the clause of His saying: ﴿وإنْ كادُوا لَيَسْتَفِزُّونَكَ﴾. End of quotation. 'Ata' read ﴿لا يُلَبَّثُونَ﴾ (la yulabbathuna) with a damma on the ya and a fatha on the lam and the ba' doubled. Ya'qub read likewise, except that he kasra'd the ba'. The Two Brothers (al-Akhawan), Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read ﴿خِلافَكَ﴾ (khilafaka, "after you / in opposition to you"), and the rest of the seven read ﴿خَلْفَكَ﴾ (khalfaka, "behind you"), and the meaning is one. The poet said:

*The dwellings have been effaced after them, as if the palm-branch-weavers had spread a mat between them.*

This is like His saying: ﴿فَرِحَ المُخَلَّفُونَ بِمَقْعَدِهِمْ خِلافَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ﴾ (Al-Tawbah: 81), meaning: "behind the Messenger of Allah," according to one of the interpretations. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah read: ﴿بَعْدَكَ﴾ (ba'daka, "after you") in place of ﴿خَلْفَكَ﴾. The better view is that it be taken as an explanation of khalfaka rather than as a reading, because it does not contradict the written text of the codex. He intended to make clear that khalfaka here is not a place-adverb; rather, it is used as a time-adverb with the meaning of ba'daka ("after you"). These adverbs, such as qabl and ba'd and the like, are regularly annexed to concrete nouns, with an omitted modifier indicated by what precedes it, as in khalfaka, meaning "behind your expulsion" (khalfa ikhrajika); and "Zayd came before 'Amr," meaning "before the coming of 'Amr"; and "Bakr laughed after Khalid," meaning "after the laughter of Khalid."

﴿سُنَّةَ﴾ (sunnata) is in the accusative as an emphatic infinitive, meaning: Allah established a sunnah (established way). The meaning is that every people who expelled their messenger from among them, Allah's sunnah is that He destroys them after his expulsion and uproots them, and they do not remain after him except a little. Al-Farra' said: ﴿سُنَّةَ﴾ is in the accusative by dropping the preposition, because the meaning is "like the sunnah," so it is put in the accusative after the omission of the kaf; and according to this, one does not stop at His saying: ﴿إلّا قَلِيلًا﴾ (Al-Isra': 85). Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿سُنَّةَ﴾ is in the accusative as an infinitive, meaning: "We have established with you a sunnah like that of those prophets who came before," and it is permissible that it be an object, meaning: "follow the sunnah of those whom We sent," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿فَبِهُداهُمُ اقْتَدِهْ﴾ (Al-An'am: 90). End of quotation. This is a meaning other than the first, and the exegetes follow the first, which is the one that fits the meaning of the verse before it. ﴿ولَنْ تَجِدَ﴾ (and you will not find) for what We have made habitual a ﴿تَحْوِيلًا﴾ (taḥwil, "alteration") from it to something else, since every event has a specific time and a specific attribute. The negation of finding here, and in what is similar to it, means the negation of existence.

An oath is presumed here, and ﴿لاتَّخَذُوكَ﴾ (la-ittakhadhukum, "they would have taken you") is its answer. The phrase ﴿لاتَّخَذُوكَ﴾ has the meaning of ﴿لَيَتَّخِذُونَكَ﴾ (la-yattakhidhunaka, "they will take you"), like His saying ﴿وَلَئِنْ أَرْسَلْنَا رِيحًا فَرَأَوْهُ مُصْفَرًّا لَظَلُّوا﴾ (Al-Rum: 51), meaning "they will surely remain" (la-yazallunna), because إذًا implies the future, since in meaning it is a conditional, so its place is estimated with a conditional particle.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿وإذًا لاتَّخَذُوكَ﴾ means: "And if you followed their desire, they would have taken you as a close friend, and you would have become their ally, and you would have left My guardianship." End of quotation. This is an explanation of the meaning, and it is not that ﴿لاتَّخَذُوكَ﴾ is the answer of an omitted لو (law). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ولَوْلا أنْ ثَبَّتْناكَ﴾ (wa-law la an thabbatnaka) means: "Had it not been for Our making you firm and Our protection, you would have almost inclined toward them," meaning you would have come close to leaning toward their deceit and their trickery. This is an incitement from Allah to him and an act of grace in making him firm, and in it is gentleness toward the believers. ﴿إذَنْ لَوْ قارَبْتَ تَرْكَنُ إلَيْهِمْ أدْنى رَكْنَةٍ﴾ means: if you had come close to inclining toward them even by the least inclination, ﴿لَأذَقْناكَ ضِعْفَ الحَياةِ وضِعْفَ المَماتِ﴾ means: We would have made you taste the punishment of the Hereafter and the punishment of the grave, doubled. If you ask: what is the real structure of this speech? I say: its origin is ﴿لَأذَقْناكَ﴾ punishment of life and punishment of death, because punishment is of two kinds: punishment at death, which is the punishment of the grave, and punishment in the life of the Hereafter, which is the punishment of the Fire. The word "double" (ḍi'f) can be described by it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فَآتِهِمْ عَذابًا ضِعْفًا مِنَ النّارِ﴾ (Al-A'raf: 38), meaning "doubled." So the original speech was ﴿لَأذَقْناكَ﴾ a double punishment in life and a double punishment at death. Then the described noun was omitted and the attribute was put in its place, which is "double", and then the attribute was made an annexed noun in the manner of the described noun, so it was said ﴿ضِعْفَ الحَياةِ وضِعْفَ المَماتِ﴾, just as it is said ﴿لَأذَقْناكَ﴾ "painful life and painful death." It is also permissible that "double of life" means the punishment of the worldly life, and "double of death" means what follows death of the punishment of the grave and the punishment of the Fire. The meaning is: We would have doubled for you the punishment hastened for the disobedient in worldly life, and what We delay for after death. End of quotation.

The answer to (لَوْلا) (law la), when it is affirmative, requires its negation because of the existence of what precedes it. So the approach to inclining did not occur from him, let alone the inclining itself, and what prevented that is the existence of Allah's making him firm. Qatadah, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ibn Musarrif read ﴿تَرْكُنُ﴾ (tarkunu) with a damma on the kaf, as the present tense of ركَنَ (raka-na) with a fatha on it. The word ﴿شَيْئًا﴾ (shay'an) is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar) [of degree]. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: he means the doubled punishment of life and the doubled punishment of death, in the sense that what the one who sins deserves of Our punishment in this world and the Hereafter, We would have doubled. Ibn al-Anbari held that the meaning is: they almost reported about you that you had inclined to their speech because of their action toward it, figuratively and by extension, as you say to a man: "You almost killed yourself", meaning: "the people almost killed you because of what you did."

Ibn 'Abbas said: The Messenger ﷺ was protected, but this is an instruction for the community, lest anyone among them incline toward the polytheists in any matter of Allah's rulings and laws. End of quotation. The lam in ﴿لَأذَقْناكَ﴾ (la-adhaqnaka) is the answer of an omitted oath before (إذًا) (idhan), meaning: "by Allah, if inclining occurs, then it would certainly be such." The discussion of ﴿لَأذَقْناكَ﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿لاتَّخَذُوكَ﴾ regarding the past tense being placed in the position of the present tense that is preceded by the lam and the nun. Among those who explicitly stated that the lam in ﴿لاتَّخَذُوكَ﴾ and ﴿لَأذَقْناكَ﴾ is the lam of the oath is al-Hawfi. Al-Zamakhshari said: In the mention of the great wrong and its causation, together with following it with a severe threat of doubled punishment in both abodes, is clear evidence that a wrong's ugliness is magnified in proportion to the greatness of the status of its doer and the elevation of his rank. End of quotation. Among this is His saying: ﴿يا نِساءَ النَّبِيِّ مَن يَأْتِ مِنكُنَّ بِفاحِشَةٍ مُبَيِّنَةٍ﴾ (Al-Ahzab: 30), "O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear immorality..." etc. Al-Zamakhshari said: In it there is a slight flattery toward the deluded, opposition to Allah, and departure from His guardianship, and a cause that requires His anger and His punishment. End of quotation.

It has been narrated that when this was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Allah, do not leave me to myself even for the blink of an eye." (p. 66) Al-Hadrami said: The pronoun in ﴿وإنْ كادُوا﴾ refers to the Jews of Medina and its surroundings, such as Huyayy ibn Akhtab and others, because they went to plot against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, saying: "This land is not the land of the prophets; the land of the prophets is al-Sham. But you fear the Romans. So if you are a prophet, go out to it, for Allah will protect you as He protected other prophets." So this verse was revealed, and Allah the Exalted informed that if he had gone out, He would not have left them after that ﴿إلّا قَلِيلًا﴾ (illa qalilan, "except a little").

Al-Naqqash related that he went out because of their words, and encamped at Dhu al-Hulayfah, and remained waiting for his companions, and then this verse was revealed and he returned. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is weak; it did not occur in any biography or any book that is relied upon, and Dhu al-Hulayfah is not on the route from Medina to al-Sham. End of quotation.

Their attempt to expel him (istifzazuhum) is what they undertook of expelling him from Mecca, as they undertook to confine him in the valley (al-Shi'b). Their attempt at expulsion occurred after the revelation of the verse, and they constrained him until he went out, and they followed him to the cave, and the threat was carried out against them in that they did not remain ﴿إلّا قَلِيلًا﴾ on the day of Badr. Al-Zajjaj, reporting that their attempt to expel him was what they agreed upon in the Dar al-Nadwah (the assembly house of Quraysh) of killing him, and the "land" in this view is the world. Mujahid said: Quraysh went in that direction, but it did not happen from them, because when Allah the Exalted wanted to preserve Quraysh and not to uproot them, He permitted His Messenger to emigrate, so he went out by His permission, not by the compulsion of Quraysh, and Quraysh was preserved so that from them and their descendants those who would accept Islam might become Muslims. He said: Had Quraysh expelled him, they would have been punished. Mujahid held that the pronoun in ﴿يَلْبَثُونَ﴾ (yalbathuna) refers to all of them.

*He obeys the fool of the people when he provokes him, and disobeys the forbearing one whom the calamities have whitened.*

The apparent meaning is that the verse indicates the approach of their attempt to drive him out, so the attempt did not occur, nor did their actual expulsion of him, which was the cause of the attempt. Then the Qur'an says: ﴿وكَأيِّنْ مِن قَرْيَةٍ هي أشَدُّ قُوَّةً مِن قَرْيَتِكَ الَّتِي أخْرَجَتْكَ﴾ (Muhammad: 13), "And how many a town, stronger than your town which expelled you..." meaning: its people expelled you. In the hadith: "Would that I were a young man when your people expel you." He said: "Will they expel me?" etc. This indicates that they did expel him, but the expulsion that is the cause of the attempt did not occur, so there is no contradiction between the two verses and the hadith. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: He did not go out because of their expulsion, but went out by Allah's command, and thus the contradiction disappears. End of quotation.

For this reason (idhan) did not govern, because it was placed between the estimated oath and the verb, and ﴿فَلا يَلْبَثُونَ﴾ is not directed at it from the standpoint of grammatical case (i'rab). It is possible that ﴿لا يَلْبَثُونَ﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, indicated by the meaning, whose estimation is: "and they, [then] they would not remain," so ﴿وإذًا﴾ fell between the subject and its predicate and was thus disregarded.

Ubayy read ﴿وإذًا لا يَلْبَثُوا﴾ (wa-idhan la yalbathu) with the nun deleted, making idhan operative and putting the verb in the subjunctive, according to the view of the majority; and with an implied "an" (an) after it, according to the view of some. Likewise it is so in the codex of 'Abd Allah, with the nun deleted.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: what is the basis of the two readings? I say: As for the widely known reading, in it the verb is conjoined to the verb while it is in the nominative, because it occurs as the predicate of kada, and the verb in the predicate of kada occupies the position of a noun. As for the reading of Ubayy, in it the whole clause, which is "wa-idhan la yalbathu", is conjoined to the clause of His saying: ﴿وإنْ كادُوا لَيَسْتَفِزُّونَكَ﴾. End of quotation. The poet said:

*The dwellings have been effaced after them, as if the palm-branch-weavers had spread a mat between them.*

This is like His saying: ﴿فَرِحَ المُخَلَّفُونَ بِمَقْعَدِهِمْ خِلافَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ﴾ (Al-Tawbah: 81), meaning: "behind the Messenger of Allah," according to one of the interpretations. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah read: ﴿بَعْدَكَ﴾ (ba'daka, "after you") in place of ﴿خَلْفَكَ﴾. The better view is that it be taken as an explanation of khalfaka rather than as a reading, because it does not contradict the written text of the codex. He intended to make clear that khalfaka here is not a place-adverb; rather, it is used as a time-adverb with the meaning of ba'daka ("after you"). These adverbs, such as qabl and ba'd and the like, are regularly annexed to concrete nouns, with an omitted modifier indicated by what precedes it, as in khalfaka, meaning "behind your expulsion" (khalfa ikhrajika); and "Zayd came before 'Amr," meaning "before the coming of 'Amr"; and "Bakr laughed after Khalid," meaning "after the laughter of Khalid."
