First: that "ba'th" is the opposite of "ijlas" (seating): "ba'athtu al-tarik" (I sent off the one who abandons) and "ba'atha Allah al-mayyit" (Allah raised the dead), meaning He caused him to rise from his grave. So interpreting "ba'th" as "ijlas" is interpreting an opposite by its opposite.

Second: if He were seated, Exalted, upon the Throne, He would be bounded and finite, and would thus be created.

Third: He said "maqaman," and did not say "maq'adan," and "maqam" is the place of standing, not the place of sitting.

Fourth: that the foolish and ignorant say that all the people of Paradise sit with Him, Exalted, and He asks them about their worldly circumstances, so there is no distinction for him through his being seated with Him.

Fifth: that if it is said "the sultan sent so-and-so," it is not understood from it that he seated him with himself. End. There is some abridgement in it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verse 78–86 (part 3 of 3):

When the Exalted One commanded him to establish the prayer and the tahajjud (night prayer), and promised him that He would raise him to "a praiseworthy station" (maqaman mahmudan), which is in the Hereafter, He commanded him to supplicate with words that encompass his worldly and otherworldly affairs, saying: ﴿And say: "My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and cause me to exit a sound exit."﴾ The apparent meaning is that it is general in all its occasions of entering and exiting, worldly and otherworldly. Here, "sidq" (sound, truthful) is a term that requires the removal of blame and the comprehensiveness of praise, just as you say "rajul sidq" (a man of truth), as it is the opposite of "rajul su'" (a man of evil).

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it is a specific entrance, which is into Madinah, and a specific exit, which is from Makkah. Thus what is mentioned first is what occurs last, and the place of the conjunction "wa" (and) is the more important, so it was begun with. Mujahid and Abu Salih said: its meaning is his entering into what he was burdened with of the responsibilities of prophethood and the conveying of the Shari'ah, and his exiting from it having fulfilled what he was charged with, without negligence. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Cause me to enter the grave" (adkhilni al-qabra) ﴿a sound entrance﴾, an entrance that is pleasing, in a state of purity and goodness from misdeeds; and "cause me to exit from it at the resurrection" an exit that is pleasing, met with honour, safe from wrath; this is indicated by his mention of it alongside the mention of resurrection. It was also said: his entering Makkah victorious over it by conquest, and his exiting from it safe from the polytheists. Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir said: his entering the cave and his exiting from it safe. It was also said: the exit from Madinah and the entrance to Makkah by conquest. It was said: the entrance into the prayer and the exit from it. It was said: the entrance into Paradise and the exit from Makkah. It was said: the entrance into what he was commanded and the exit from what he was forbidden. It was said: ﴿cause me to enter﴾ into the seas of the proofs of Divine unity and transcendence, ﴿and cause me to exit﴾ from occupation with the proof to knowledge of what is proven, and contemplation of the traces of His created things, to total absorption in knowledge of the One, the Unique. Abu Sahl said: when he returned from Tabuk, after the hypocrites had said: ﴿The mightier will surely expel the meaner from it﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8], he meant the entrance of might and the exit of victory into Makkah. The best of these sayings is that they be taken as examples rather than specifications, and the wording, as we have mentioned, encompasses all occasions of entering and exiting.

The reading of the majority is ﴿mudkhala﴾ and (mukhraja) with a dammah on their mim, and this is a regular verbal noun (masdar) on the pattern of af'ala, as in "akramtuhu makraman," meaning "ikraman" (I honoured him with honour). Qatadah, Abu Haywah, Humayd and Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ablah read them with a fathah on both. The author of al-Lawami' said: they are both verbal nouns from "dakhala" and "kharaja," but they come from the meaning of the preceding ﴿adkhilni﴾ and ﴿akhrijni﴾ rather than their wording, and like them is ﴿and He made you grow from the earth a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17]. It is also permissible that both be nouns of place, and their accusative is as adverbs of place. Others said: they are both in the accusative as verbal nouns, under an implied verb, i.e., "cause me to enter, so I enter a sound entrance, and cause me to exit, so I exit a sound exit."

As for "sultan" (authority) here: al-Hasan said: the empowerment over the disbelievers by the sword, and over the hypocrites by establishing the hudud (prescribed punishments). Qatadah said: a mighty kingdom by which You help me against everyone who opposes me. Mujahid said: a clear proof. It was said: a Book containing the hudud and rulings. It was said: the conquest of Makkah. It was said: in every age, a sultan that supports your religion; and "nasir" (helper) is an intensive form of "nasir" (one who helps). It was said: "fa'il" here is in the sense of "maf'ul," i.e., "mansur" (one who is helped). All these sayings are possible for His words: ﴿a sultan, a helper﴾. (p-74) It is narrated that the Exalted One promised him this, fulfilled it for him during his life, and completed it after his death.

Qatadah said: "al-haqq" (the truth) is the Qur'an and "al-batil" (falsehood) is Satan. Ibn Jurayj said: "al-haqq" is jihad and "al-batil" is shirk. It was said: faith and disbelief. Muqatil said: the worship of Allah has come, and the worship of Satan has departed. This verse was revealed in Makkah. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to cite it on the day of the conquest of Makkah, when he struck the idols and they fell, by his striking them with a staff, as is mentioned in the biographies. "Zahuqan" (vanishing) is an intensive adjective describing its perishing and its not being established at any time.

The "min" in ﴿min al-Qur'an﴾ is for the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah). It was said: it is for partitive (tab'id), said by al-Hawfi, but he denied this, since it entails that some of it has no healing in it; this denial was rejected, because its sending down is only in parts. It was said: it is for explaining the kind (bayan al-jins), said by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyyah and Abu al-Baqa'; and we have mentioned that "min" which is for explaining the kind does not precede the ambiguous term it clarifies, but is always placed after it. The majority read ﴿nunazzilu﴾ with a nun, and Mujahid with a ya' and lightened, which al-Marwazi narrated from Hafs. Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿shifa'an wa rahmatan﴾ with accusative on both; the accusative can be explained as a circumstantial accusative (hal), and the predicate of "huwa" is his saying "lil-mu'minin" (for the believers), and the governing element in it is the verb contained in the prepositional phrase, similar to the reading of one who read ﴿and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾ [al-Zumar: 67] with the accusative of "matwiyyat." And the poet's verse:

"The kinsmen of Ibn Kuz, wearing their armour, among them and the kinsmen of Rabi'ah ibn Hidhar."

Placing the circumstantial accusative before its governing element when it is an adverb or prepositional phrase is not permitted except according to al-Akhfash; whoever prohibits it makes it an accusative by an implied "a'ni" (I mean). Its healing is its being a remover of doubt and a uncoverer of the veil of the heart by grasping the miracles and the matters indicating Allah that establish His religion; thus it becomes for the ailments of hearts what healing is for the ailments of bodies. It was also said: it is healing by ruqyah and 'awdh (incantation), as in the hadith of the one who performed ruqyah with al-Fatihah for a scorpion's sting. They differed regarding al-nushrah, which is to write something of the names of Allah the Exalted or of the Qur'an, then wash it with water, then wipe the sick person with it or have him drink it; Ibn al-Musayyib permitted this, while Mujahid did not consider it. From 'A'ishah: she used to recite the two mu'awwidhatayn over a vessel, then instruct that it be poured over the sick person. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Mazini said: al-nushrah is a matter well known among the people of ta'widh (spells), named so because it "unties" (tanshuru) from its owner, i.e., it releases; al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i prohibited it. Abu Dawud narrated from the hadith of Jabir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when asked about al-nushrah, said: "It is from the work of Satan." This is to be understood as applying when it is outside what is in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger. Al-nushrah is of the kind of medicine in washing something that has merit.

Malik said: there is no harm in hanging books containing the names of Allah the Exalted on the necks of the sick, seeking blessing through them, provided the one who hangs them does not intend thereby to ward off the evil eye. This applies before any affliction of the evil eye has befallen; but after the affliction has come, it is permitted, hoping for relief and cure. Sickness is like the permitted ruqyah for which the Sunnah has come, from the evil eye and other things. Ibn al-Musayyib said: it is permitted to hang an 'awdhah (amulet) in a reed or a piece of paper from the Book of Allah, and one may place it when having intercourse and when relieving oneself. Al-Baqir permitted an 'awdhah hung on children. Ibn Sirin saw no harm in a person hanging something from the Qur'an.

And the loss of the wrongdoers, who are those who place a thing in other than its place, is through their turning away from it and not reflecting upon it, unlike the believer, for he increases in faith by looking into it and reflecting upon its meanings.

(p-75) When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the various kinds of the Qur'an that He had sent down as healing and mercy for the believer, and as an increase in loss for the wrongdoer, He alluded to the blessings He had bestowed on mankind and the subtle legal rulings it contained. Yet despite this, man (turned away) from it, distanced himself, out of aversion to it and arrogance toward hearing it near, and in place of thanking for the blessing he returned disbelief. Al-Jumhur read (wa-na'a) from al-nay', which means distance. Ibn 'Amir read wa-na'a. It was said that it is an inverted form of na'a, meaning he withdrew. It was also said that it means he rose up on his side. The poet said:

*Until, when its joints were knit together, and its shoulder rose up on the left side.*

That is, he rose, leaning on his left side. The meaning of *yā'ūsan* [al-Isra': 83] is despairing that Allah would bestow blessing upon him. The apparent meaning of "man" here is not one specific individual but the species, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, man is ungrateful to his Lord﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 6] and ﴿Indeed, man was created anxious﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 19], and so on. This returns to the meaning of the disbeliever. Turning away is with the face, and withdrawing the side is by turning the shoulder, or it may be intended that withdrawing the side is arrogance, since that is the habit of the arrogant. As for *al-shakilah*, Ibn 'Abbas said: its direction. Mujahid said: its nature. al-Dahhak said: its sharpness. Qatada and al-Hasan said: its intention. Ibn Zayd said: its religion. Muqatil said: its creation. These statements are close in meaning. al-Zamakhshari said: according to the way that corresponds to his condition in guidance and error, from their saying: "a path with many branches (dhu shawakil)," which are the roads that diverge from it. The evidence for this is His words: ﴿Your Lord knows best who is best guided in the way﴾ [al-Isra': 84], that is, more correct in course and path.

It is related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have not seen in the Qur'an a verse more hopeful than this: nothing corresponds to the servant except disobedience, and nothing corresponds to the Lord except forgiveness." It is related from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have not seen a verse more hopeful than the one that says ﴿Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance﴾ [Ghafir: 3], where forgiveness is mentioned before acceptance of repentance." It is related from 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have not seen a verse more hopeful than ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [al-Hijr: 49]." It is related from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face and be pleased with him: "I have not seen a verse more hopeful than ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾ [al-Zumar: 53]," and the verse. They said: this was when they discussed the Qur'an. It is related from al-Qurtubi: "I have not seen a verse more hopeful than ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing﴾ [al-An'am: 82]," and the verse.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: souls and selves differ in their essence. Some are luminous and pure, in which the Qur'an manifests as light upon light, and some are turbid and dark, in which the Qur'an manifests as misguidance and punishment. End of his words. It is established in the Sahih from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I was with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a field in Medina, and he was leaning on a palm stalk. Some Jews passed by us, and he said: 'Ask him about the spirit.' Some of them said: 'Do not ask him, for he will answer you with what you dislike.' Then a group of them came to him and said: 'O Abu al-Qasim, what do you say about the spirit?' He remained silent, then he shook, and I held my hand to his forehead, and I knew that revelation was descending upon him. Then there was revealed: ﴿And they ask you about the spirit﴾ [al-Isra': 85], and the verse." It is also narrated that the Jews said to the Quraysh: "Ask him about the spirit, about the youths who vanished in the earliest times, and about a man who reached the east and west of the earth. If he answers all of that, or does not answer any of it, then he is a liar; but if he answers some of it and is silent about some, then he is a prophet." In some versions of this: "If he explains the three, he is a liar; and if he is silent about the spirit, he is a prophet." Then there was revealed concerning the youths: ﴿Do you think that the companions of the cave...﴾ [al-Kahf: 9], and there was revealed concerning the one who reached the east and the west: ﴿And they ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn﴾ [al-Kahf: 83], and there was revealed concerning the spirit: ﴿And they ask you about the spirit﴾ [al-Isra': 85]. The apparent indication of the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud is that the verse is Medinan, and from the question of the Quraysh it is Meccan.

According to the view of the majority, the spirit here is the spirit that is in living beings, and it is a generic noun, which is the apparent meaning. Qatada said: it is Jibril, peace be upon him. He said: Ibn 'Abbas used to conceal this. It was said: it is 'Isa son of Maryam, peace be upon him. It is related from 'Ali that it is an angel, and he mentioned a description of it that only Allah knows; but this is not authentically reported from 'Ali.

It was said: the spirit is the Qur'an, and the verse before it and the verse after it indicate this. It was said: it is a great spiritual creation, greater than an angel. It was said: the spirit is an army among the armies of Allah, who have hands and feet and eat food, as mentioned by al-'Aziz. Abu Salih said: it is a creation like the creation of Adam, but they are not the children of Adam; they have hands and feet, and no angel descends from the heaven except with one of them. The most correct of these statements is the first. The apparent meaning is that they asked about its quiddity and reality. It was also said: they asked about the manner in which it enters the animal body and is set in motion there, and the form of its attachment to it; both of these are difficult, and no one knows them except Allah. I have seen a book translated as *The Book of the Breathing and the Shaping*, by one of the Sufi jurists, in which it is mentioned that the answer in His words: ﴿Say: the spirit is of the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra': 85] is only for the common people, while the elite, according to him, know the spirit. The scholars of Islam agree that the spirit is created, while the impious philosophers and many who attribute themselves to Islam held that it is eternal. People's disagreement about the spirit reached seventy opinions. Likewise they differed on whether the spirit is the soul (nafs) or something other than it. The meaning of ﴿of the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra': 85] is: its existence is by the act of my Lord, by His command, and in this there is an indication of its being originated. "Command" in the sense of "act" occurs, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ [Hud: 97], that is, his act. It may also be that "command" is the singular of "affairs" and is a generic noun for them, that is, among the affairs of Allah which He has kept exclusively known to Himself. It was said: it is from the revelation of my Lord, and His speech is not the speech of humans; this is derived on the view of those who said that the spirit here is the Qur'an. It was said: it is from the knowledge of my Lord.

The apparent address in ﴿And you have been given﴾ [al-Isra': 85] is to those who asked about the spirit, who were a group of the Jews. It was said: the Jews as a whole. It was said: all people.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is the correct view, because His words ﴿Say: the spirit...﴾ [al-Isra': 85] are a command to say it to the entire world, since all their knowledge is limited, whereas His knowledge, exalted is He, has no end. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read *wa-ma utu* with the pronoun of the third person, referring back to the questioners.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the blessing He had bestowed through the sending down of the Qur'an upon His Messenger (ﷺ) as healing and mercy, and His power to do so, He mentioned His power to take it away: that if He willed, He would take away what He had revealed. But He, exalted is He, did not will that. The meaning is that just as We are able to send it down, We are able to remove it. Abu Sahl said: this is a threat to someone other than the Messenger (ﷺ) of removing what they were given, so as to prevent them from asking about what they were not given, such as the knowledge of the spirit and the knowledge of the Hour. It is narrated: "The Hour will not come until the Qur'an and the hadith are lifted." In the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud: "He will be taken by night, and what is in the copies and what is in the hearts will be removed." Then 'Abd Allah recited: ﴿And if We willed, We would surely take away that which We have revealed to you﴾ [al-Isra': 86].

The author of *al-Tahrir* said: in my view there may be another possibility in interpreting the verse, which is that when revelation was delayed for the Prophet (ﷺ) when he was asked about the spirit, this grieved him greatly and reached its limit. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse to console him and instruct him in courtesy. The meaning would be: "Does the delay of revelation weigh heavily upon you? For if We willed, We could take away all that We have revealed to you." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) fell silent, his heart was at ease, and he kept to good manners. End of his words. The *ba'* in ﴿surely take away that which﴾ [al-Isra': 86] is for transitivity, like the hamzah, and the discussion of this was already covered in His words: ﴿Allah would have taken away their hearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20], at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

Regarding *al-kafil* here, it was said: one who protects what We have revealed to you. It was said: a guarantor for its return to the breasts. It was said: a guarantor who ensures for you that He will give you back what was taken from you. al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is that if We willed, We would take away the Qur'an and erase it from the breasts and the copies, and leave no trace of it, and you would remain as you were, not knowing the Book. Then you would not find for yourself, after this removal, anyone who would take responsibility before Us for its restoration and its return preserved and written down. ﴿Except as a mercy from your Lord﴾ [al-Isra': 87]: except that your Lord has mercy on you and returns it to you. His mercy would be taking responsibility for its return. Or it is an exception of disconnection (*istithna' munqati'*), meaning: but rather it is a mercy from your Lord, that We leave it not taken away. This is a favour from Allah, exalted is He, that the Qur'an remains preserved after the favour of its sending down and its protection. End of his words. Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn 'Atiyya also derived it as an exception of disconnection.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "But rather a mercy from your Lord" prevents you from being stripped of the Qur'an. In *Zad al-Masir* he said: the meaning is that Allah has mercy on you, so establish that in your heart. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "but rather ﴿a mercy from your Lord﴾" keeps that upon you. As for al-Zamakhshari's first explanation, he made it a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*), placing His mercy, exalted is He, under His words: ﴿a guarantor﴾ [al-Isra': 86].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verses 88–93 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn were to gather together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if they were helpers of one another.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly varied for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, yet most of the people refuse except disbelief.﴾ ﴿And they said: "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush for us from the earth,﴾ ﴿or until you have a garden of palm trees and grapes, and you cause rivers to gush forth within it abundantly,﴾ ﴿or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed, or you bring God and the angels before us as a guarantee,﴾ ﴿or you have a house of gold, or you ascend into the sky. And we will not believe in your ascent until you bring down to us a book that we can read." Say: "Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?"﴾

[p. 78] When the Exalted (ta'ala) mentioned His favour upon His Prophet ﷺ through prophethood and the sending down of His revelation to him, and His wondrous power, in that if He willed He could take away the Qur'an, He then mentioned what He had granted him as proof of his prophethood, which remains for the duration of time: the Qur'an, which the whole world has been unable to match. It is among the greatest blessings and bounties, one which has preserved his remembrance until the end of time and raised his station in this world and the Hereafter. If the eloquent speakers of the tongue in which it was revealed, and its masters of rhetoric, were unable to produce a single surah like it, then they are all the more unable to produce the like of all of it. And even if the two weighty groups (humans and jinn) were to cooperate upon it, ﴿they would not produce its like, even if﴾ the jinn ... They perform wondrous acts, as God related about them in the story of Solomon, peace be upon him. They were included with mankind in the challenge so that the incapacity would be more emphatic. It is also possible that the angels are included under the term "jinn," since this name is sometimes applied to them, as in His saying: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158], although the more common usage of it is for other than the angels, namely the jinn forms hidden from human eyes. It is also possible that the jinn are mentioned here because he, peace be upon him, was sent to both mankind and the jinn, so the challenge was addressed to both groups together for this reason.

It is related that a group of [p. 78] Quraysh said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Bring us a remarkable sign other than this Qur'an, for we are able to bring the like of this." So it was revealed: ﴿and they will not produce﴾ as the answer to the omitted oath preceding the emphatic lam in ﴿la-in﴾ ("if indeed"), which is the one that enters upon the conditional. Like His saying: ﴿If they are expelled, they will not go forth with them; and if they are fought against, they will not help them﴾ [al-Hashr: 12]. So the answer in such a case belongs to the omitted oath, not to the condition, and that is why it is in the nominative. As for the verse of al-A'sha:

"If you were to be taken from us after the aftermath of a battle, we would destroy the blood of the people in retaliation."

Here the lam in ﴿la-in﴾ is superfluous and is not an emphatic introduction to an oath preceding it, which is why it is in the jussive in his words "la-atlafna." Al-Farra' used such examples to support his claim that when an oath and a conditional are combined, and the oath comes first without anything with a predicate preceding both of them, the answer may belong to the oath, which is the more common, or to the condition. The school of the Basrans, however, makes the answer belong to the oath exclusively. Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned here a good section on the matter of inimitability, which we have quoted in full. He said: "The Arabs, by the purity of their understanding, their discernment in the distinction of speech and their familiarity with it, understood what we and everyone affected by civilisation do not understand. So they understood the incapacity to match it by necessity. Later people witnessed and knew it through reasoning and reflection. Each group attained a definite knowledge, but not at the same level. This is like the way the Companions knew the Law of the Prophet ﷺ, his actions and his attestations by necessary knowledge, and we know what is mass-transmitted of that through mass transmission. So all attained certainty, but at two levels. And the masters of eloquence, who have rare insights into the distinction of speech, understood the inimitability of the Qur'an. Do you not see how al-Farazdaq understood the poetry of Jarir and Dhu al-Rumma in the words of al-Farazdaq:

'Why do you look around while you are beneath me?'

and in the words of Jarir:

'She looks around, for she is beneath the son of a smith.'

Do you not see the saying of the Bedouin: 'He was mighty, so he judged and cut off.' And do you not see the other argument for the resurrection through His saying: ﴿until you visit the graves﴾ [al-Takathur: 2], where he said: 'Visiting entails departing.' And from this Bashshar knew through the words of Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' concerning the poetry of al-A'sha:

'She disowned me, yet what she disowned was not what was disowned.'

And from this came the saying of the Bedouin to al-Asma'i:

'Who has made the noble man need to swear?'

With these understandings they acknowledged the incapacity. The swordsmen among them had recourse to the sword, and accepted killing, captivity and violation of sacred things, although they had the alternative of opposition." End of quotation. We have restricted ourselves to what we quoted from his words. He had previously stated before that: "The incapacity to oppose the Qur'an occurred only in its arrangement, and the reason for this is the comprehensiveness which no one possesses except God, the Mighty and Majestic. Man is necessarily deficient by ignorance, forgetfulness, heedlessness and various kinds of deficiency. So when he arranges a word, the causes we mentioned remain hidden from him."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿They will not produce﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath. Were it not for the emphatic lam, it would be permissible for it to be the answer to the condition, as in his words:

'He says: neither my property is absent nor is my family unprotected,'

because the condition occurred in the past tense." End of quotation. He means by the condition his words, which is the first half of the verse:

"And if a friend comes to him on the day of asking,"

Here ﴿atahu﴾ ("came to him") is a past verb, to which the particle of condition was attached, thereby making it refer to the future. Al-Zamakhshari's statement implies that he says: even if it is in the nominative, it is the answer to the condition ("and if he comes to him"). This view he holds differs from the position of Sibawayh, of the Kufans and of al-Mubarrad. For Sibawayh's position in such a construction, where the verb of the condition is in the past and is followed by a present verb in the nominative, is that this present verb is intended to be placed first, and the answer to the condition is omitted. The Kufans and al-Mubarrad hold that it is the answer, but with the fa' omitted. A third position is that it is the answer to the condition, and this is what al-Zamakhshari maintained. The discussion of these positions is recorded in the science of grammar.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: "It is strange that they hold the Qur'an to be eternal while admitting that it is inimitable. Inimitability only occurs where there is power. One says: God is capable of creating bodies, and His servants are incapable of it. But an impossibility, in which there is no room for power and no entry for it, like a second eternal being, cannot be described as something the agent is unable to do, nor as inimitable. If that were said, it would be permissible to describe God as incapable, because He is not described as capable of the impossible, unless they contend and say: 'He is capable of the impossible.' For the principle of their wealth is obstinacy and reversal of realities." End of quotation.

The phrase ﴿like﴾ is repeated in His saying ﴿they will not produce its like﴾ for emphasis and clarification, and to indicate that what is required of them is that they produce "its like," since the phrase "like of a thing" can sometimes mean the thing itself. So the repetition of "its like" clarifies this, and the construction ﴿they will not produce it﴾ would not remove this possibility. And what is demanded of them is that they produce a like, not that they produce the Qur'an itself.

When the Exalted mentioned the incapacity of mankind and the jinn to produce the like of this Qur'an, He drew attention to His favour by what He repeated in it, and by the various examples and lessons that point to His oneness. Despite the abundance of examples He repeated and the blessings He lavished, they were nothing but disbelievers in Him and in His blessings.

The majority read ﴿ṣarraf-nā﴾ with a doubled rāʾ, while al-Ḥasan read it with a single rāʾ. Apparently the object of ﴿ṣarraf-nā﴾ is omitted, its supposed reading being "the clear signs and lessons." The ﴿min﴾ here denotes the starting point. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is also possible that it is emphatic and superfluous for the sake of the estimate, so that it reads: 'And We have varied for the people every example.'" End of quotation. He means that the object of ﴿ṣarraf-nā﴾ is then ﴿kulli mathal﴾ ("every example"). This analysis follows the position of the Kufans and al-Akhfash, not that of the majority of the Basrans. Apparently the word "example" here means the strange saying that travels through the regions, and the Qur'an is full of the examples that God the Exalted has coined.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿min kulli mathal﴾ means: from every meaning which is like an example in its strangeness and beauty." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "﴿min kulli mathal﴾ is an indication of the challenge in its various aspects: the challenge with the whole Qur'an as in this passage, with a surah like it, and with a discourse of a surah, as in His saying: ﴿Then let them produce a discourse like it﴾ [al-Tur: 34]. Despite the evident incapacity of these people, they refused except disbelief." End of summary. It has also been said: ﴿min kulli mathal﴾ refers to encouragement and warning, the histories of the former and later peoples, and the mention of Paradise and Hell. ﴿Most of the people﴾ — it was said: those among the polytheists and the People of the Book who lived at the time of the Messenger. It was also said: the people of Mecca, and this is the apparent meaning, as shown by what follows: ﴿And they said: We will not believe you﴾. The discussion of the exception ﴿illa﴾ after ﴿abā﴾ ("refused") has already been mentioned in Surah Bara'a.

Lengthy reports have been related about this speech of theirs, which are in the books of hadith and biography. Their summary is that the chieftains of Quraysh gathered and sent to the Prophet ﷺ. When he came to them, exchanges took place between them concerning abandoning their religion and their request that he affirm the oneness of God and worship Him. They tempted him with wealth, leadership and kingship, but he refused and said: "I am not seeking that." So they proposed to him the six signs that God mentioned here. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He challenged them to produce the like of this Qur'an, and it became clear that they were incapable of it and of its inimitability, and other miracles and clear proofs were added to it, the argument became binding upon them. When they were overcome, they began to make excuses by proposing signs, like the bewildered, perplexed one who is refuted. So they said what God related about them.

The Kufans read ﴿tafjura﴾ from fajara (without doubling, as an intransitive form). The rest of the seven read it from fajjara with doubling, and the doubling is for intensification, not for transitivity. Al-A'mash and 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar read it from afjara in the quadriliteral form, which is a dialect of fajjara. "The earth" here means the land of Mecca, which is the land where the inhabitants of the world carry out their affairs and livelihoods. It is related about them that they said to him: "Remove the mountains of Mecca and cause a spring (yanbu') to gush forth for us, so that tilling and planting become easy for us, and revive Qusayy for us, for he was truthful and would tell us about your truthfulness." They first proposed this sign, and then they proposed another to him, peace be upon him: that there should be for him ﴿a garden of palm trees and grapes﴾. These two were the predominant produce of their lands and among the most valuable things they owned. The meaning of ﴿khilālahā﴾ is: in the middle of that garden and within it, so that it waters those palm trees and vines. ﴿Khilālahā﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of place.

The majority read ﴿tusqiṭa﴾ with the second person ta' of address, the present of asqaṭa, with ﴿al-samā'﴾ ("the sky") in the accusative. Mujahid read it with the third person ya' of absence, the present of saqaṭa, with ﴿al-samā'﴾ in the nominative. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿kisfan﴾ with a sukun on the sin, while the rest of the seven read it with a fatha. Their saying ﴿as you claimed﴾ refers to His saying: ﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them, or We shall cause pieces of the sky to fall upon them﴾ [Saba': 9]. It was also said: ﴿as you claimed﴾ refers to the claim that your Lord, if He wills, does it. It was also said it refers to what is in this surah: ﴿Do you feel secure that He will not cause the earth to swallow you on the side of the land, or send upon you a violent wind?﴾ Abu 'Ali said: ﴿qabīlan﴾ means "face to face," like His saying: ﴿Why are the angels not sent down upon us, or do we see our Lord?﴾ [al-Furqan: 21].

Others said: ﴿qabīlan﴾ means "guarantor," from taqabbalahu bi-kadhā, meaning he made himself responsible for such and such. Al-Qabil, al-Za'im and al-Kafil have the same meaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: "A guarantor for what you say, a witness to its truth. The meaning is: or you bring God as a guarantor and the angels as guarantors," like his saying:

"I was disowned by him and my father, and I and Qayyar are strangers here."

I need to translate this passage faithfully, but I should flag one point before producing it: the text is a classical Arabic commentary with Qur'anic quotations, poetry, and technical terms, and I'll render all of them as the instructions require.

**Translation:**

That is: facing us, like "al-'Ashir," in the sense of "al-mu'ashir" (the companion), and similar. ﴿Why were not the angels sent down to us, or [why] do we not see our Lord?﴾ [al-Furqan: 21], or [they are] a group, as a circumstantial state (hal) from "the angels." Al-A'raj read *qubulan* (ﷺ), from "al-muqabalah" (facing). The majority read ﴿min zukhrufin﴾ (of adornment), and 'Abd Allah [ibn Mas'ud] read *min dhahabin* (of gold). It should not be taken as a variant reading to oppose the consensus text; rather it is an explanation (tafsir). Mujahid said: "We did not know what *al-zukhruf* was until I saw it in the reading of 'Abd Allah: *min dhahabin*." Al-Zajjaj said: *al-zukhruf* is adornment, and the explanation of *al-zukhruf* has already been given.

﴿And in the sky﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 22], with an elided modifier, meaning: in the ascending ways of the sky. The apparent meaning is that "the sky" here is the canopy above. It has been said that the intended meaning is a high place, and everything that rises high is called "sky." A poet said:

"Every elevated thing may be called a sky,
but the excellence lies where the sun and moon are."

It is said that the one who says this is Ibn Abi Umayyah, who said: "We will not believe until you place a ladder against the sky and climb up in it while I watch, until you reach it and then come back to us with a written scroll, accompanied by four angels who testify for you that the matter is as you say." It is possible that these were the collective notables, who said this and made their belief conditional on the fulfilment of one of these demands. It is also possible that each one proposed one of them and it was attributed to all of them because they were content with it. Or *aw* here may indicate choice: each of them made a specific demand from among them.

They did not stop at the condition of ascending into the sky, but further made it conditional that He send down to them a book they could read. Since their demands included something impossible for God Most High, namely that He come ﴿with God and the angels as a guarantee﴾, He commanded him to glorify and exalt Him above what is unfitting for Him, and above having demands made upon Him such as those you mention. So He said: ﴿Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?﴾, meaning: I was only a human messenger, sent from God to you, not one who proposes upon Him what you have mentioned of signs.

Al-Zamakhshari said: They intended by these demands nothing but obstinacy and contentiousness; and had every sign come to them they would have said, "This is sorcery," as He, Mighty and Exalted, said: ﴿Even if We had sent down to you a book on paper﴾ [al-An'am: 7], and ﴿Even if We opened for them a gate from the sky, and they continued to ascend through it﴾ [al-Hijr: 14]. And when they denied the enduring sign, which is the Qur'an and the rest of the signs, which are not less than what they proposed but greater, [it shows they were not sincere]. End of quote. The splitting of the moon is greater than the splitting of the earth, and water gushing from between his fingers is greater than water gushing from a stone.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read *qala subhana rabbi* (he said, "Glory be to my Lord") as a report, the Prayer and Peace of God be upon him expressing wonder at their demands on him, and glorifying his Lord above what they attributed to Him of coming and moving, which is impossible with respect to God. ﴿Am I anything but a human﴾ like them, a messenger. Messengers do not bring except what God makes manifest through them of signs, and the matter of those signs is not theirs to decide; it belongs to God.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verses 88–93 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn were to gather together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if they were helpers of one another.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly varied for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, yet most of the people refuse except disbelief.﴾ ﴿And they said: "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush for us from the earth,﴾ ﴿or until you have a garden of palm trees and grapes, and you cause rivers to gush forth within it abundantly,﴾ ﴿or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed, or you bring God and the angels before us as a guarantee,﴾ ﴿or you have a house of gold, or you ascend into the sky. And we will not believe in your ascent until you bring down to us a book that we can read." Say: "Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?"﴾

[p. 78] When the Exalted (ta'ala) mentioned His favour upon His Prophet ﷺ through prophethood and the sending down of His revelation to him, and His wondrous power, in that if He willed He could take away the Qur'an, He then mentioned what He had granted him as proof of his prophethood, which remains for the duration of time: the Qur'an, which the whole world has been unable to match. It is among the greatest blessings and bounties, one which has preserved his remembrance until the end of time and raised his station in this world and the Hereafter. If the eloquent speakers of the tongue in which it was revealed, and its masters of rhetoric, were unable to produce a single surah like it, then they are all the more unable to produce the like of all of it. And even if the two weighty groups (humans and jinn) were to cooperate upon it, ﴿they would not produce its like, even if﴾ the jinn ... They perform wondrous acts, as God related about them in the story of Solomon, peace be upon him. They were included with mankind in the challenge so that the incapacity would be more emphatic. It is also possible that the angels are included under the term "jinn," since this name is sometimes applied to them, as in His saying: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158], although the more common usage of it is for other than the angels, namely the jinn forms hidden from human eyes. It is also possible that the jinn are mentioned here because he, peace be upon him, was sent to both mankind and the jinn, so the challenge was addressed to both groups together for this reason.

It is related that a group of [p. 78] Quraysh said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Bring us a remarkable sign other than this Qur'an, for we are able to bring the like of this." So it was revealed: ﴿and they will not produce﴾ as the answer to the omitted oath preceding the emphatic lam in ﴿la-in﴾ ("if indeed"), which is the one that enters upon the conditional. Like His saying: ﴿If they are expelled, they will not go forth with them; and if they are fought against, they will not help them﴾ [al-Hashr: 12]. So the answer in such a case belongs to the omitted oath, not to the condition, and that is why it is in the nominative. As for the verse of al-A'sha:

"If you were to be taken from us after the aftermath of a battle, we would destroy the blood of the people in retaliation."

Here the lam in ﴿la-in﴾ is superfluous and is not an emphatic introduction to an oath preceding it, which is why it is in the jussive in his words "la-atlafna." Al-Farra' used such examples to support his claim that when an oath and a conditional are combined, and the oath comes first without anything with a predicate preceding both of them, the answer may belong to the oath, which is the more common, or to the condition. The school of the Basrans, however, makes the answer belong to the oath exclusively. Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned here a good section on the matter of inimitability, which we have quoted in full. He said: "The Arabs, by the purity of their understanding, their discernment in the distinction of speech and their familiarity with it, understood what we and everyone affected by civilisation do not understand. So they understood the incapacity to match it by necessity. Later people witnessed and knew it through reasoning and reflection. Each group attained a definite knowledge, but not at the same level. This is like the way the Companions knew the Law of the Prophet ﷺ, his actions and his attestations by necessary knowledge, and we know what is mass-transmitted of that through mass transmission. So all attained certainty, but at two levels. And the masters of eloquence, who have rare insights into the distinction of speech, understood the inimitability of the Qur'an. Do you not see how al-Farazdaq understood the poetry of Jarir and Dhu al-Rumma in the words of al-Farazdaq:

'Why do you look around while you are beneath me?'

and in the words of Jarir:

'She looks around, for she is beneath the son of a smith.'

Do you not see the saying of the Bedouin: 'He was mighty, so he judged and cut off.' And do you not see the other argument for the resurrection through His saying: ﴿until you visit the graves﴾ [al-Takathur: 2], where he said: 'Visiting entails departing.' And from this Bashshar knew through the words of Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' concerning the poetry of al-A'sha:

'She disowned me, yet what she disowned was not what was disowned.'

And from this came the saying of the Bedouin to al-Asma'i:

'Who has made the noble man need to swear?'

With these understandings they acknowledged the incapacity. The swordsmen among them had recourse to the sword, and accepted killing, captivity and violation of sacred things, although they had the alternative of opposition." End of quotation. We have restricted ourselves to what we quoted from his words. He had previously stated before that: "The incapacity to oppose the Qur'an occurred only in its arrangement, and the reason for this is the comprehensiveness which no one possesses except God, the Mighty and Majestic. Man is necessarily deficient by ignorance, forgetfulness, heedlessness and various kinds of deficiency. So when he arranges a word, the causes we mentioned remain hidden from him."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿They will not produce﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath. Were it not for the emphatic lam, it would be permissible for it to be the answer to the condition, as in his words:

'He says: neither my property is absent nor is my family unprotected,'

because the condition occurred in the past tense." End of quotation. He means by the condition his words, which is the first half of the verse:

"And if a friend comes to him on the day of asking,"

Here ﴿atahu﴾ ("came to him") is a past verb, to which the particle of condition was attached, thereby making it refer to the future. Al-Zamakhshari's statement implies that he says: even if it is in the nominative, it is the answer to the condition ("and if he comes to him"). This view he holds differs from the position of Sibawayh, of the Kufans and of al-Mubarrad. For Sibawayh's position in such a construction, where the verb of the condition is in the past and is followed by a present verb in the nominative, is that this present verb is intended to be placed first, and the answer to the condition is omitted. The Kufans and al-Mubarrad hold that it is the answer, but with the fa' omitted. A third position is that it is the answer to the condition, and this is what al-Zamakhshari maintained. The discussion of these positions is recorded in the science of grammar.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: "It is strange that they hold the Qur'an to be eternal while admitting that it is inimitable. Inimitability only occurs where there is power. One says: God is capable of creating bodies, and His servants are incapable of it. But an impossibility, in which there is no room for power and no entry for it, like a second eternal being, cannot be described as something the agent is unable to do, nor as inimitable. If that were said, it would be permissible to describe God as incapable, because He is not described as capable of the impossible, unless they contend and say: 'He is capable of the impossible.' For the principle of their wealth is obstinacy and reversal of realities." End of quotation.

The phrase ﴿like﴾ is repeated in His saying ﴿they will not produce its like﴾ for emphasis and clarification, and to indicate that what is required of them is that they produce "its like," since the phrase "like of a thing" can sometimes mean the thing itself. So the repetition of "its like" clarifies this, and the construction ﴿they will not produce it﴾ would not remove this possibility. And what is demanded of them is that they produce a like, not that they produce the Qur'an itself.

When the Exalted mentioned the incapacity of mankind and the jinn to produce the like of this Qur'an, He drew attention to His favour by what He repeated in it, and by the various examples and lessons that point to His oneness. Despite the abundance of examples He repeated and the blessings He lavished, they were nothing but disbelievers in Him and in His blessings.

The majority read ﴿ṣarraf-nā﴾ with a doubled rāʾ, while al-Ḥasan read it with a single rāʾ. Apparently the object of ﴿ṣarraf-nā﴾ is omitted, its supposed reading being "the clear signs and lessons." The ﴿min﴾ here denotes the starting point. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is also possible that it is emphatic and superfluous for the sake of the estimate, so that it reads: 'And We have varied for the people every example.'" End of quotation. He means that the object of ﴿ṣarraf-nā﴾ is then ﴿kulli mathal﴾ ("every example"). This analysis follows the position of the Kufans and al-Akhfash, not that of the majority of the Basrans. Apparently the word "example" here means the strange saying that travels through the regions, and the Qur'an is full of the examples that God the Exalted has coined.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿min kulli mathal﴾ means: from every meaning which is like an example in its strangeness and beauty." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "﴿min kulli mathal﴾ is an indication of the challenge in its various aspects: the challenge with the whole Qur'an as in this passage, with a surah like it, and with a discourse of a surah, as in His saying: ﴿Then let them produce a discourse like it﴾ [al-Tur: 34]. Despite the evident incapacity of these people, they refused except disbelief." End of summary. It has also been said: ﴿min kulli mathal﴾ refers to encouragement and warning, the histories of the former and later peoples, and the mention of Paradise and Hell. ﴿Most of the people﴾ — it was said: those among the polytheists and the People of the Book who lived at the time of the Messenger. It was also said: the people of Mecca, and this is the apparent meaning, as shown by what follows: ﴿And they said: We will not believe you﴾. The discussion of the exception ﴿illa﴾ after ﴿abā﴾ ("refused") has already been mentioned in Surah Bara'a.

Lengthy reports have been related about this speech of theirs, which are in the books of hadith and biography. Their summary is that the chieftains of Quraysh gathered and sent to the Prophet ﷺ. When he came to them, exchanges took place between them concerning abandoning their religion and their request that he affirm the oneness of God and worship Him. They tempted him with wealth, leadership and kingship, but he refused and said: "I am not seeking that." So they proposed to him the six signs that God mentioned here. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He challenged them to produce the like of this Qur'an, and it became clear that they were incapable of it and of its inimitability, and other miracles and clear proofs were added to it, the argument became binding upon them. When they were overcome, they began to make excuses by proposing signs, like the bewildered, perplexed one who is refuted. So they said what God related about them.

The Kufans read ﴿tafjura﴾ from fajara (without doubling, as an intransitive form). The rest of the seven read it from fajjara with doubling, and the doubling is for intensification, not for transitivity. Al-A'mash and 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar read it from afjara in the quadriliteral form, which is a dialect of fajjara. "The earth" here means the land of Mecca, which is the land where the inhabitants of the world carry out their affairs and livelihoods. It is related about them that they said to him: "Remove the mountains of Mecca and cause a spring (yanbu') to gush forth for us, so that tilling and planting become easy for us, and revive Qusayy for us, for he was truthful and would tell us about your truthfulness." They first proposed this sign, and then they proposed another to him, peace be upon him: that there should be for him ﴿a garden of palm trees and grapes﴾. These two were the predominant produce of their lands and among the most valuable things they owned. The meaning of ﴿khilālahā﴾ is: in the middle of that garden and within it, so that it waters those palm trees and vines. ﴿Khilālahā﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of place.

The majority read ﴿tusqiṭa﴾ with the second person ta' of address, the present of asqaṭa, with ﴿al-samā'﴾ ("the sky") in the accusative. Mujahid read it with the third person ya' of absence, the present of saqaṭa, with ﴿al-samā'﴾ in the nominative. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿kisfan﴾ with a sukun on the sin, while the rest of the seven read it with a fatha. Their saying ﴿as you claimed﴾ refers to His saying: ﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them, or We shall cause pieces of the sky to fall upon them﴾ [Saba': 9]. It was also said: ﴿as you claimed﴾ refers to the claim that your Lord, if He wills, does it. It was also said it refers to what is in this surah: ﴿Do you feel secure that He will not cause the earth to swallow you on the side of the land, or send upon you a violent wind?﴾ Abu 'Ali said: ﴿qabīlan﴾ means "face to face," like His saying: ﴿Why are the angels not sent down upon us, or do we see our Lord?﴾ [al-Furqan: 21].

Others said: ﴿qabīlan﴾ means "guarantor," from taqabbalahu bi-kadhā, meaning he made himself responsible for such and such. Al-Qabil, al-Za'im and al-Kafil have the same meaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: "A guarantor for what you say, a witness to its truth. The meaning is: or you bring God as a guarantor and the angels as guarantors," like his saying:

"I was disowned by him and my father, and I and Qayyar are strangers here."

I need to translate this passage faithfully, but I should flag one point before producing it: the text is a classical Arabic commentary with Qur'anic quotations, poetry, and technical terms, and I'll render all of them as the instructions require.

**Translation:**

That is: facing us, like "al-'Ashir," in the sense of "al-mu'ashir" (the companion), and similar. ﴿Why were not the angels sent down to us, or [why] do we not see our Lord?﴾ [al-Furqan: 21], or [they are] a group, as a circumstantial state (hal) from "the angels." Al-A'raj read *qubulan* (ﷺ), from "al-muqabalah" (facing). The majority read ﴿min zukhrufin﴾ (of adornment), and 'Abd Allah [ibn Mas'ud] read *min dhahabin* (of gold). It should not be taken as a variant reading to oppose the consensus text; rather it is an explanation (tafsir). Mujahid said: "We did not know what *al-zukhruf* was until I saw it in the reading of 'Abd Allah: *min dhahabin*." Al-Zajjaj said: *al-zukhruf* is adornment, and the explanation of *al-zukhruf* has already been given.

﴿And in the sky﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 22], with an elided modifier, meaning: in the ascending ways of the sky. The apparent meaning is that "the sky" here is the canopy above. It has been said that the intended meaning is a high place, and everything that rises high is called "sky." A poet said:

"Every elevated thing may be called a sky,
but the excellence lies where the sun and moon are."

It is said that the one who says this is Ibn Abi Umayyah, who said: "We will not believe until you place a ladder against the sky and climb up in it while I watch, until you reach it and then come back to us with a written scroll, accompanied by four angels who testify for you that the matter is as you say." It is possible that these were the collective notables, who said this and made their belief conditional on the fulfilment of one of these demands. It is also possible that each one proposed one of them and it was attributed to all of them because they were content with it. Or *aw* here may indicate choice: each of them made a specific demand from among them.

They did not stop at the condition of ascending into the sky, but further made it conditional that He send down to them a book they could read. Since their demands included something impossible for God Most High, namely that He come ﴿with God and the angels as a guarantee﴾, He commanded him to glorify and exalt Him above what is unfitting for Him, and above having demands made upon Him such as those you mention. So He said: ﴿Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?﴾, meaning: I was only a human messenger, sent from God to you, not one who proposes upon Him what you have mentioned of signs.

Al-Zamakhshari said: They intended by these demands nothing but obstinacy and contentiousness; and had every sign come to them they would have said, "This is sorcery," as He, Mighty and Exalted, said: ﴿Even if We had sent down to you a book on paper﴾ [al-An'am: 7], and ﴿Even if We opened for them a gate from the sky, and they continued to ascend through it﴾ [al-Hijr: 14]. And when they denied the enduring sign, which is the Qur'an and the rest of the signs, which are not less than what they proposed but greater, [it shows they were not sincere]. End of quote. The splitting of the moon is greater than the splitting of the earth, and water gushing from between his fingers is greater than water gushing from a stone.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read *qala subhana rabbi* (he said, "Glory be to my Lord") as a report, the Prayer and Peace of God be upon him expressing wonder at their demands on him, and glorifying his Lord above what they attributed to Him of coming and moving, which is impossible with respect to God. ﴿Am I anything but a human﴾ like them, a messenger. Messengers do not bring except what God makes manifest through them of signs, and the matter of those signs is not theirs to decide; it belongs to God.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He challenged them to produce the like of this Qur'an, and it became clear that they were incapable of it and of its inimitability, and other miracles and clear proofs were added to it, the argument became binding upon them. **Translation:**

That is: facing us, like "al-'Ashir," in the sense of "al-mu'ashir" (the companion), and similar. ﴿Why were not the angels sent down to us, or [why] do we not see our Lord?﴾ [al-Furqan: 21], or [they are] a group, as a circumstantial state (hal) from "the angels." Al-A'raj read *qubulan* (ﷺ), from "al-muqabalah" (facing). The majority read ﴿min zukhrufin﴾ (of adornment), and 'Abd Allah [ibn Mas'ud] read *min dhahabin* (of gold). It should not be taken as a variant reading to oppose the consensus text; rather it is an explanation (tafsir). Mujahid said: "We did not know what *al-zukhruf* was until I saw it in the reading of 'Abd Allah: *min dhahabin*." Al-Zajjaj said: *al-zukhruf* is adornment, and the explanation of *al-zukhruf* has already been given.

﴿And in the sky﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 22], with an elided modifier, meaning: in the ascending ways of the sky. The apparent meaning is that "the sky" here is the canopy above. It has been said that the intended meaning is a high place, and everything that rises high is called "sky." A poet said:

"Every elevated thing may be called a sky,
but the excellence lies where the sun and moon are."

It is said that the one who says this is Ibn Abi Umayyah, who said: "We will not believe until you place a ladder against the sky and climb up in it while I watch, until you reach it and then come back to us with a written scroll, accompanied by four angels who testify for you that the matter is as you say." It is possible that these were the collective notables, who said this and made their belief conditional on the fulfilment of one of these demands. It is also possible that each one proposed one of them and it was attributed to all of them because they were content with it. Or *aw* here may indicate choice: each of them made a specific demand from among them.

They did not stop at the condition of ascending into the sky, but further made it conditional that He send down to them a book they could read. Since their demands included something impossible for God Most High, namely that He come ﴿with God and the angels as a guarantee﴾, He commanded him to glorify and exalt Him above what is unfitting for Him, and above having demands made upon Him such as those you mention. So He said: ﴿Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?﴾, meaning: I was only a human messenger, sent from God to you, not one who proposes upon Him what you have mentioned of signs.

Al-Zamakhshari said: They intended by these demands nothing but obstinacy and contentiousness; and had every sign come to them they would have said, "This is sorcery," as He, Mighty and Exalted, said: ﴿Even if We had sent down to you a book on paper﴾ [al-An'am: 7], and ﴿Even if We opened for them a gate from the sky, and they continued to ascend through it﴾ [al-Hijr: 14]. The splitting of the moon is greater than the splitting of the earth, and water gushing from between his fingers is greater than water gushing from a stone.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read *qala subhana rabbi* (he said, "Glory be to my Lord") as a report, the Prayer and Peace of God be upon him expressing wonder at their demands on him, and glorifying his Lord above what they attributed to Him of coming and moving, which is impossible with respect to God. ﴿Am I anything but a human﴾ like them, a messenger. And we will not believe in your ascent until you bring down to us a book that we can read." Say: "Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?"﴾

If the eloquent speakers of the tongue in which it was revealed, and its masters of rhetoric, were unable to produce a single surah like it, then they are all the more unable to produce the like of all of it. And even if the two weighty groups (humans and jinn) were to cooperate upon it, ﴿they would not produce its like, even if﴾ the jinn ... Here the lam in ﴿la-in﴾ is superfluous and is not an emphatic introduction to an oath preceding it, which is why it is in the jussive in his words "la-atlafna." Al-Farra' used such examples to support his claim that when an oath and a conditional are combined, and the oath comes first without anything with a predicate preceding both of them, the answer may belong to the oath, which is the more common, or to the condition. The school of the Basrans, however, makes the answer belong to the oath exclusively. Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned here a good section on the matter of inimitability, which we have quoted in full. He said: "The Arabs, by the purity of their understanding, their discernment in the distinction of speech and their familiarity with it, understood what we and everyone affected by civilisation do not understand. So they understood the incapacity to match it by necessity. Later people witnessed and knew it through reasoning and reflection. Each group attained a definite knowledge, but not at the same level. This is like the way the Companions knew the Law of the Prophet ﷺ, his actions and his attestations by necessary knowledge, and we know what is mass-transmitted of that through mass transmission. So all attained certainty, but at two levels. And the masters of eloquence, who have rare insights into the distinction of speech, understood the inimitability of the Qur'an. Do you not see how al-Farazdaq understood the poetry of Jarir and Dhu al-Rumma in the words of al-Farazdaq:

'Why do you look around while you are beneath me?'

and in the words of Jarir:

'She looks around, for she is beneath the son of a smith.'

Do you not see the saying of the Bedouin: 'He was mighty, so he judged and cut off.' And do you not see the other argument for the resurrection through His saying: ﴿until you visit the graves﴾ [al-Takathur: 2], where he said: 'Visiting entails departing.' And from this Bashshar knew through the words of Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' concerning the poetry of al-A'sha:

'She disowned me, yet what she disowned was not what was disowned.'

And from this came the saying of the Bedouin to al-Asma'i:

'Who has made the noble man need to swear?'

With these understandings they acknowledged the incapacity. The swordsmen among them had recourse to the sword, and accepted killing, captivity and violation of sacred things, although they had the alternative of opposition." End of quotation. We have restricted ourselves to what we quoted from his words. He had previously stated before that: "The incapacity to oppose the Qur'an occurred only in its arrangement, and the reason for this is the comprehensiveness which no one possesses except God, the Mighty and Majestic. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿They will not produce﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath. Were it not for the emphatic lam, it would be permissible for it to be the answer to the condition, as in his words:

'He says: neither my property is absent nor is my family unprotected,'

"And if a friend comes to him on the day of asking,"

Here ﴿atahu﴾ ("came to him") is a past verb, to which the particle of condition was attached, thereby making it refer to the future. This view he holds differs from the position of Sibawayh, of the Kufans and of al-Mubarrad. It is related that a group of [p. 78] Quraysh said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Bring us a remarkable sign other than this Qur'an, for we are able to bring the like of this." So it was revealed: ﴿and they will not produce﴾ as the answer to the omitted oath preceding the emphatic lam in ﴿la-in﴾ ("if indeed"), which is the one that enters upon the conditional. Like His saying: ﴿If they are expelled, they will not go forth with them; and if they are fought against, they will not help them﴾ [al-Hashr: 12]. So the answer in such a case belongs to the omitted oath, not to the condition, and that is why it is in the nominative. As for the verse of al-A'sha:

"If you were to be taken from us after the aftermath of a battle, we would destroy the blood of the people in retaliation."

Here the lam in ﴿la-in﴾ is superfluous and is not an emphatic introduction to an oath preceding it, which is why it is in the jussive in his words "la-atlafna." Al-Farra' used such examples to support his claim that when an oath and a conditional are combined, and the oath comes first without anything with a predicate preceding both of them, the answer may belong to the oath, which is the more common, or to the condition. The school of the Basrans, however, makes the answer belong to the oath exclusively. Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned here a good section on the matter of inimitability, which we have quoted in full. He said: "The Arabs, by the purity of their understanding, their discernment in the distinction of speech and their familiarity with it, understood what we and everyone affected by civilisation do not understand. So they understood the incapacity to match it by necessity. Later people witnessed and knew it through reasoning and reflection. Each group attained a definite knowledge, but not at the same level. This is like the way the Companions knew the Law of the Prophet ﷺ, his actions and his attestations by necessary knowledge, and we know what is mass-transmitted of that through mass transmission. 'Why do you look around while you are beneath me?'

and in the words of Jarir:

'She looks around, for she is beneath the son of a smith.'

Do you not see the saying of the Bedouin: 'He was mighty, so he judged and cut off.' And do you not see the other argument for the resurrection through His saying: ﴿until you visit the graves﴾ [al-Takathur: 2], where he said: 'Visiting entails departing.' And from this came the saying of the Bedouin to al-Asma'i:

When they were overcome, they began to make excuses by proposing signs, like the bewildered, perplexed one who is refuted. So they said what God related about them.

They first proposed this sign, and then they proposed another to him, peace be upon him: that there should be for him ﴿a garden of palm trees and grapes﴾. These two were the predominant produce of their lands and among the most valuable things they owned. I need to translate this passage faithfully, but I should flag one point before producing it: the text is a classical Arabic commentary with Qur'anic quotations, poetry, and technical terms, and I'll render all of them as the instructions require.

**Translation:**

That is: facing us, like "al-'Ashir," in the sense of "al-mu'ashir" (the companion), and similar. ﴿Why were not the angels sent down to us, or [why] do we not see our Lord?﴾ [al-Furqan: 21], or [they are] a group, as a circumstantial state (hal) from "the angels." Al-A'raj read *qubulan* (ﷺ), from "al-muqabalah" (facing). The majority read ﴿min zukhrufin﴾ (of adornment), and 'Abd Allah [ibn Mas'ud] read *min dhahabin* (of gold). It should not be taken as a variant reading to oppose the consensus text; rather it is an explanation (tafsir). Mujahid said: "We did not know what *al-zukhruf* was until I saw it in the reading of 'Abd Allah: *min dhahabin*." Al-Zajjaj said: *al-zukhruf* is adornment, and the explanation of *al-zukhruf* has already been given.

﴿And in the sky﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 22], with an elided modifier, meaning: in the ascending ways of the sky. The apparent meaning is that "the sky" here is the canopy above. It has been said that the intended meaning is a high place, and everything that rises high is called "sky." A poet said:

"Every elevated thing may be called a sky,
but the excellence lies where the sun and moon are."

It is said that the one who says this is Ibn Abi Umayyah, who said: "We will not believe until you place a ladder against the sky and climb up in it while I watch, until you reach it and then come back to us with a written scroll, accompanied by four angels who testify for you that the matter is as you say." It is possible that these were the collective notables, who said this and made their belief conditional on the fulfilment of one of these demands. It is also possible that each one proposed one of them and it was attributed to all of them because they were content with it. Or *aw* here may indicate choice: each of them made a specific demand from among them.

They did not stop at the condition of ascending into the sky, but further made it conditional that He send down to them a book they could read. Since their demands included something impossible for God Most High, namely that He come ﴿with God and the angels as a guarantee﴾, He commanded him to glorify and exalt Him above what is unfitting for Him, and above having demands made upon Him such as those you mention. So He said: ﴿Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?﴾, meaning: I was only a human messenger, sent from God to you, not one who proposes upon Him what you have mentioned of signs.

Al-Zamakhshari said: They intended by these demands nothing but obstinacy and contentiousness; and had every sign come to them they would have said, "This is sorcery," as He, Mighty and Exalted, said: ﴿Even if We had sent down to you a book on paper﴾ [al-An'am: 7], and ﴿Even if We opened for them a gate from the sky, and they continued to ascend through it﴾ [al-Hijr: 14]. And when they denied the enduring sign, which is the Qur'an and the rest of the signs, which are not less than what they proposed but greater, [it shows they were not sincere]. End of quote. The splitting of the moon is greater than the splitting of the earth, and water gushing from between his fingers is greater than water gushing from a stone.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read *qala subhana rabbi* (he said, "Glory be to my Lord") as a report, the Prayer and Peace of God be upon him expressing wonder at their demands on him, and glorifying his Lord above what they attributed to Him of coming and moving, which is impossible with respect to God. ﴿Am I anything but a human﴾ like them, a messenger. Messengers do not bring except what God makes manifest through them of signs, and the matter of those signs is not theirs to decide; it belongs to God.

﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn were to gather together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if they were helpers of one another.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly varied for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, yet most of the people refuse except disbelief.﴾ ﴿And they said: "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush for us from the earth,﴾ ﴿or until you have a garden of palm trees and grapes, and you cause rivers to gush forth within it abundantly,﴾ ﴿or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed, or you bring God and the angels before us as a guarantee,﴾ ﴿or you have a house of gold, or you ascend into the sky.
