It was also said it refers to what is in this surah: ﴿Do you feel secure that He will not cause the earth to swallow you on the side of the land, or send upon you a violent wind?﴾ Abu 'Ali said: ﴿qabīlan﴾ means "face to face," like His saying: ﴿Why are the angels not sent down upon us, or do we see our Lord?﴾ [al-Furqan: 21].

Others said: ﴿qabīlan﴾ means "guarantor," from taqabbalahu bi-kadhā, meaning he made himself responsible for such and such. Al-Qabil, al-Za'im and al-Kafil have the same meaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: "A guarantor for what you say, a witness to its truth. The meaning is: or you bring God as a guarantor and the angels as guarantors," like his saying:

"I was disowned by him and my father, and I and Qayyar are strangers here."

I need to translate this passage faithfully, but I should flag one point before producing it: the text is a classical Arabic commentary with Qur'anic quotations, poetry, and technical terms, and I'll render all of them as the instructions require.

**Translation:**

That is: facing us, like "al-'Ashir," in the sense of "al-mu'ashir" (the companion), and similar. ﴿Why were not the angels sent down to us, or [why] do we not see our Lord?﴾ [al-Furqan: 21], or [they are] a group, as a circumstantial state (hal) from "the angels." Al-A'raj read *qubulan* (ﷺ), from "al-muqabalah" (facing). The majority read ﴿min zukhrufin﴾ (of adornment), and 'Abd Allah [ibn Mas'ud] read *min dhahabin* (of gold). It should not be taken as a variant reading to oppose the consensus text; rather it is an explanation (tafsir). Mujahid said: "We did not know what *al-zukhruf* was until I saw it in the reading of 'Abd Allah: *min dhahabin*." Al-Zajjaj said: *al-zukhruf* is adornment, and the explanation of *al-zukhruf* has already been given.

﴿And in the sky﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 22], with an elided modifier, meaning: in the ascending ways of the sky. The apparent meaning is that "the sky" here is the canopy above. It has been said that the intended meaning is a high place, and everything that rises high is called "sky." A poet said:

"Every elevated thing may be called a sky,
but the excellence lies where the sun and moon are."

It is said that the one who says this is Ibn Abi Umayyah, who said: "We will not believe until you place a ladder against the sky and climb up in it while I watch, until you reach it and then come back to us with a written scroll, accompanied by four angels who testify for you that the matter is as you say." It is possible that these were the collective notables, who said this and made their belief conditional on the fulfilment of one of these demands. It is also possible that each one proposed one of them and it was attributed to all of them because they were content with it. Or *aw* here may indicate choice: each of them made a specific demand from among them.

They did not stop at the condition of ascending into the sky, but further made it conditional that He send down to them a book they could read. Since their demands included something impossible for God Most High, namely that He come ﴿with God and the angels as a guarantee﴾, He commanded him to glorify and exalt Him above what is unfitting for Him, and above having demands made upon Him such as those you mention. So He said: ﴿Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?﴾, meaning: I was only a human messenger, sent from God to you, not one who proposes upon Him what you have mentioned of signs.

Al-Zamakhshari said: They intended by these demands nothing but obstinacy and contentiousness; and had every sign come to them they would have said, "This is sorcery," as He, Mighty and Exalted, said: ﴿Even if We had sent down to you a book on paper﴾ [al-An'am: 7], and ﴿Even if We opened for them a gate from the sky, and they continued to ascend through it﴾ [al-Hijr: 14]. And when they denied the enduring sign, which is the Qur'an and the rest of the signs, which are not less than what they proposed but greater, [it shows they were not sincere]. End of quote. The splitting of the moon is greater than the splitting of the earth, and water gushing from between his fingers is greater than water gushing from a stone.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read *qala subhana rabbi* (he said, "Glory be to my Lord") as a report, the Prayer and Peace of God be upon him expressing wonder at their demands on him, and glorifying his Lord above what they attributed to Him of coming and moving, which is impossible with respect to God. ﴿Am I anything but a human﴾ like them, a messenger. Messengers do not bring except what God makes manifest through them of signs, and the matter of those signs is not theirs to decide; it belongs to God.

[p. 81]

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿Nothing prevented the people from believing when the guidance came to them, except that they said: "Has God sent a human as a messenger?"﴾ is that God, exalted is He, is informing us of the weak reason that kept them from faith. The sign (mu'jiz) had appeared to them, yet they found it improbable that God would send as a messenger to creation one of their own, a human and not an angel. Once the miracle had appeared, it was obligatory to acknowledge and confess his prophethood. Their claim that the messenger must necessarily be one of the angels is therefore a corrupt arbitrary demand. From the words of Ibn 'Atiyya (a Qur'an commentator), it appears that the phrase ﴿Nothing prevented the people﴾ is part of the speech of the Messenger (ﷺ). He said this verse in the sense of rebuke and grief on the part of the Prophet, peace be upon him, as if he were saying in wonder at them: "Whatever God wills comes to pass." ﴿Nothing prevented the people from believing when the guidance came to them, except﴾ this trivial cause and this improbable claim, which has no supporting proof. Sending humans as messengers is not a novelty, nor is there anything strange in it, by which understanding and the ability to reflect would be achieved. If there were angels living on the earth, peacefully settled in it, the messenger to them would have to be an angel, so that understanding could take place. As for humans, if an angel were sent to them, their natures would recoil from seeing him, their eyes would not bear him, and their hearts would not endure him. God has ordered their circumstances according to what is customary for them. End of quotation.

The word ﴿أن يؤمنوا﴾ (an yu'minu, "that they should believe") is in the accusative position, and ﴿أن قالوا﴾ (an qalu, "that they said") is in the nominative position. The adverb ﴿إذ﴾ (idh, "when") is a time expression whose governing verb is ﴿منع﴾ (mana'a, "prevented"). The disbelievers of Quraysh are the ones who uttered those earlier statements. ﴿الهدى﴾ (al-huda, "the guidance") is the Qur'an and the one who brought it. The intended meaning is not mere speech, but their speech arising from belief. The interrogative hamza in ﴿أبعث﴾ (a-ba'atha, "has He sent") is for denial. The word ﴿رسولا﴾ (rasulan, "a messenger") apparently functions as an adjective. It may also be the object of ﴿بعث﴾ (ba'atha, "sent"), with ﴿بشرا﴾ (basharan, "a human") as an anticipated circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: "Has God sent a messenger while being a human?" Likewise, in His words ﴿مَلَكًا رَسُولًا﴾ (malakan rasulan, "an angel as a messenger"), it is permissible to read it as: "We would have sent down to them from heaven a messenger while being an angel." As for His words ﴿يمشون﴾ (yamshuna, "walking"), it means they move about in it on foot. They have no ascent to heaven by which they could hear from its inhabitants and know what must be known. Rather, they dwell on the earth, bound by the specific acts of worship and rulings that the obligated are bound by, whose details are not grasped by reason. ﴿لنزلنا عليهم﴾ (lanazzalna 'alayhim, "We would have sent down to them") means: from their own kind, one who would teach them that and convey it to them.

When he (ﷺ) called them to faith and challenged them concerning the truth of his prophethood through a miracle matching his claim, God commanded him to inform them that He, exalted is He, is the witness between him and them, regarding his delivery of the message, his bearing of the burdens of prophethood, their non-acceptance and their disbelief, and the signs they proposed to him out of obstinacy. He followed this with something containing a threat, namely His words ﴿Indeed He is ever, of His servants, Well-Acquainted, All-Seeing﴾. He is ever aware (khabir) of the hidden secrets of His servants, and all-seeing (basir) of what appears of their actions and words. The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿Whomever God guides﴾ are a statement from God, exalted is He, and are not included under "Say" (qul). They are not included under His words ﴿And We will gather them﴾. It is possible that they are included, since the conjunction ﴿ومن﴾ (wa-man, "and whoever") comes with a waw. In that case, ﴿ونحشرهم﴾ (wa-nahshuruhum, "and We will gather them") would be a statement from God, exalted is He. According to the first view, it is an iltifat (a shift of grammatical person) since it moves from the third-person absent to the first-person speaker. Since the call of the Messenger to faith had preceded, and he had challenged them with the miracle God gave him, they persisted in their disbelief and obstinacy and found in them no acceptance of what he had brought of guidance. He informed them that all of this returns to God's will, exalted is He, that He is the one who guides and the one who grants favor. Thus God consoled him with this, and God, exalted is He, informed them in the manner of a threat and a true warning about their state at the time of their gathering on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Zamakhshari (a Mu'tazili exegete; Mu'tazila is a theological school that emphasized human free will and divine justice) said: "Whomever God guides" means whomever He grants success and treats with kindness (yalutfu bihi), "then he is the guided one" because He shows kindness only to one who knows that kindness benefits him. "Whomever He leaves astray" means whomever He forsakes, "you will not find for them protectors," meaning helpers. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila. The word ﴿من﴾ (man, "whomever") is the object of ﴿يهد﴾ (yahdi, "guides") and of ﴿يضلل﴾ (yudlil, "leaves astray"). It was treated according to the form of the word in ﴿فهو المهتدي﴾ (fahuwa al-muhtadi, "then he is the guided one"), so the singular was used, observing that the path of guidance is one, and the singular suited the singular. It was treated according to the meaning in ﴿فلن تجد لهم أولياء﴾ (falan tajida lahum awliya'a, "then you will not find for them protectors"), not according to the form, observing that the paths of misguidance are many and diverse, so the plural and multiplicity suited the plural. This is one of the places where the treatment according to meaning occurs from the outset, without first treating it according to form. Such places are few in the Qur'an. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿على وجوههم﴾ ('ala wujuhihim, "on their faces") is literal, as God, exalted is He, says: ﴿On the Day they are dragged into the Fire on their faces﴾ (Qamar 54:48). Those who are gathered on their faces are gathered to Hell. There is a hadith on this: "It was said: O Messenger of God, how does the disbeliever walk on his face? He said: 'Is not the One who made him walk on two legs able to make him walk on his face in the Hereafter?'" Qatada (a Successor and Qur'an commentator) said: "Yes, by the might of our Lord." It has also been said that ﴿على وجوههم﴾ is metaphorical, as it is said of one who leaves a matter disappointed and distressed: "He left on his face," and of a camel: "It is as if it walks on its face." It has also been said that it is a metaphor for dragging them on their faces with speed, from the Arab expression "the people came upon their faces" when they hastened.

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿عميًا وبكمًا وصمًّا﴾ ('umyan wa-bukman wa-summan, "blind, mute and deaf") is literal, occurring when they rise from their graves. Then God returns to them their sight, hearing and speech, so they see the Fire, hear its roar, and speak with what God recounts of them. It has also been said that these are metaphors: either because from bewilderment and stupefaction they resemble people with these attributes, or because they see nothing that would delight them, hear nothing that would please them, and utter no proof. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Just as they did not perceive insightfully in the world, did not speak the truth, and turned deaf to hearing it, so in the Hereafter they do not see what would gladden their eyes, do not hear what would delight their ears, and do not speak what would be accepted from them. Whoever was blind in this world is blind in the Hereafter." End of quotation. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, who said: the meaning of ﴿عميًا﴾ is blind to what would please them, ﴿بكمًا﴾ mute from speaking with proof, and ﴿صمًّا﴾ (Furqan 25:73) deaf to what would benefit them. It has also been said: ﴿عميًا﴾ means blind to looking at what God prepared for His friends, ﴿بكمًا﴾ mute in addressing God, and ﴿صمًّا﴾ deaf to what God praised His friends for. The words ﴿عميًا﴾ and what follows it are in the accusative of circumstance (hal), and the governing verb is ﴿نحشرهم﴾ (nahshuruhum, "We will gather them"). It has also been said that this state occurs for them literally at His words: ﴿He will say: "Be gone into it, and do not speak to Me."﴾ (Mu'minun 23:108). According to this view, it is a hal muqaddara (an anticipated circumstance), since that did not coincide with them at the time of gathering.

﴿كلما خبت﴾ (kullama khabat, "whenever it dies down"). Ibn 'Abbas said: "Whenever it finishes burning them, the flame standing over them subsides for the time needed for them to be restored, then it flares up again. That is the increase of the blaze." So the increase is within their space. As for Hell itself, it remains in its intensity and its heat does not abate. According to this, ﴿خبت﴾ is a metaphor for the subsiding of its flame for the amount of time needed for their restoration. It is as if, since they denied the restoration after annihilation, God made their recompense that He set the Fire upon their parts, consuming them and annihilating them, then restores them. They continue in cycles of annihilation and restoration, so that this increases their regret over their denial. It is also because it is more intense in punishing the one who denies. This is indicated by His words ﴿That is their recompense﴾. The demonstrative ﴿ذلك﴾ (dhalika, "that") refers to what was mentioned before: their gathering in that state, their arrival at Hell, and the punishment in it. The word ﴿آيات﴾ (ayat, "signs") encompasses the Qur'an and the proofs that the Messenger (ﷺ) brought. He specifically mentioned denial of resurrection, since it is an attack on divine power. This is despite their acknowledgment that He, exalted is He, is the originator and creator of the world. Then they deny the restoration, and so this becomes a challenge to His power.

The discussion of His words ﴿And they say: "When we are bones and crumbled dust, shall we truly be raised in a new creation?"﴾ has already been given in this surah, so there is no need to repeat it. Since they denied resurrection, God alerted them to His great power and His dazzling wisdom, and said: ﴿Have they not seen...﴾ (awa lam yaraw). This is an interrogative of denial and rebuke for them regarding what they used to deem improbable concerning restoration, and an argument against them: they have seen God's power in creating these great bodies, of which the human is a small part. How then do they acknowledge the creation of this great creation, yet deny the restoration of some of what He created? That is something reason does not deem impossible; rather, reason permits it. Then the Truthful One (al-Sadiq, i.e., the Messenger) informed of its occurrence, so acceptance of it became obligatory. The seeing here is the seeing of the heart, which is knowledge. The meaning of ﴿مثلهم﴾ (mithlahum, "their like") is of humankind, since they are not stronger in creation than them, as He said: ﴿Are you stronger in creation, or the heaven?﴾ (Nazi'at 79:27). Since He is able to bring into existence the like of them from humankind out of pure nothingness, He is able to restore them, as He said: ﴿It is He who begins creation, then repeats it﴾ (Rum 30:27), and that is easier for Him. The phrase ﴿وجعل لهم﴾ (wa-ja'ala lahum, "and He has appointed for them") is conjoined to ﴿أولم يروا﴾ because the interrogative contains the sense of affirmation. The meaning is: they have known by the proof of reason such-and-such, and such-and-such. ﴿وجعل لهم﴾ means: He appointed for the worlds that term. ﴿أجلا لا ريب فيه﴾ (ajalan la rayba fihi, "a term about which there is no doubt") is death or the Resurrection. This appointment is not a single one within the interrogative containing affirmation. Or, if the term is the Resurrection, since they deny it, and if the term is death, then it is a generic noun standing in place of plural terms. ﴿فأبى الظالمون﴾ (fa-aba al-zalimun, "yet the wrongdoers refused") refers to those who put a thing in other than its proper place by way of transgression. ﴿إلا كفورًا﴾ (illa kufuran, "except disbelief") means denial of what the Truthful One brought concerning God's oneness, His singling out for worship, and their resurrection on the Day of Resurrection for recompense.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verses 100–104 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Say: "Even if you possessed the treasuries of the mercy of my Lord, you would withhold them for fear of spending. And man is ever tight-fisted."﴾ ﴿And We certainly gave Moses nine clear signs. So ask the Children of Israel, when he came to them, and Pharaoh said to him, "Indeed, I think you, O Moses, are bewitched."﴾ ﴿He said, "You know well that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence. And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed."﴾ ﴿So he intended to drive them out of the land, but We drowned him and those with him, all together. And We said after him to the Children of Israel, "Dwell in the land; and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you together as a mixed multitude."﴾

The occasion of His saying: ﴿Say: "Even if you possessed the treasuries…"﴾ (the verse), is that the polytheists said: "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush for us from the earth." So they asked for rivers and springs to be made to flow in their land, so that their provisions would increase and be abundant for them. Then God, exalted is He, explained that if they possessed the treasuries of God's mercy, they would remain upon their miserliness and stinginess, and would not hasten to bring benefit to anyone. Accordingly, there is no benefit in fulfilling what they requested. This is what has been said regarding the connection of this verse, and al-'Askari said it. What appears to me, however, is that the appropriate connection is that he, peace be upon him, had been granted by God what He had not granted anyone else of prophethood and messengerhood to humankind and jinn. He is therefore the most eager of people to bring good and to rescue them from misguidance. He persists in this, and risks himself in calling them to God, and presents this to the tribes and the clans of the Arabs, generously, without seeking any wage from them. Yet these were his relatives, from whom hardly anyone answered except one after another, and they had persisted in their obstinacy and enmity towards him, so nothing reached him from them except harm. (p-84) So God, through this verse, drew attention to his generosity, peace be upon him, and to his giving away what God had bestowed upon him, and to the refusal of these people to let any good come from them to him. He said: even if they possessed the power to dispose of the (treasuries of the mercy of) God, which encompass everything, they would be more miserly than anyone with what they had been given of that, such that nothing of benefit would reach anyone from them, since their nature is niggardliness, which is withholding from expanding in expenditure. This is in addition to what they had been given of treasuries. Thus this verse came clarifying what lies between them and him, peace be upon him, of his eagerness for their benefit and the non-arrival of any good from them to him.

What is established regarding ﴿lau﴾ (if), which is a particle for what would have occurred on account of the occurrence of something else, is that the verb follows it, either in the past or the present, as in His saying: ﴿If We willed, We would have made it into debris﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 65], or negated by ﴿lam﴾ or ﴿in﴾. Here, in His saying: ﴿Say: "Even if you (antum) possess…"﴾, a noun follows it, so they differed about its analysis. Al-Hawfi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu al-Baqa' and others went to the view that it is in the nominative by an elided verb that is explained by the verb after it. When that verb, which is "tamliku" (you possess), was elided, the pronoun, which is the subject of "tamliku", became detached, as in His saying:

"And if he does not bear its injustice upon himself…"

The estimation is: "And if he does not bear", so "lam yahmil" was elided and the pronoun concealed in "yahmilu" became detached, so it became "huwa" (he). Here, the attached manifest pronoun, which is the waw, became detached, so it became "antum" (you). This analysis is based on the premise that "lau" is followed by the verb, whether manifest or implied, in eloquent speech. This, however, is not the doctrine of the Basrans.

The Shaykh Abu al-Hasan ibn 'Usfur said: "Lau" is followed only by a manifest verb, and is followed by an implied one only in cases of necessity or in rare speech, such as what has come in the proverb of their saying:

"Had a woman wearing bracelets slapped me…"

Our shaykh, the Ustadh Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Sa'igh, said: The Basrans explicitly affirm the impermissibility of "lau Zayd qama la-akramtuhu" (had Zayd stood, I would have honoured him) in the eloquent usage, and they permit it as an anomaly, as in their saying:

"Had a woman wearing bracelets slapped me…"

According to them, it is on an implied verb, as in His exalted saying: ﴿And if anyone among the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection﴾ [al-Tawba: 6]. This is from the category of ishtighal (the verb being occupied with a pronoun referring to the noun). End of quotation. Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Fadal al-Mujashi'i analysed it as the implied "kana" (was), the estimation being: "Say: 'Had you (antum) been the ones who possess…'" The apparent sense of this analysis is that "kuntum" was elided in its entirety, and "antum" remained as an emphasis for that elided pronoun together with the verb. Our shaykh, Abu al-Hasan al-Sa'igh, went to the view of eliding "kana", so its subject, which was attached to it, became detached, and the estimation is: "Say: 'Had you (kuntum) been…" So when the verb was elided, the nominative became detached. This analysis is the better one, since the elision of "kana" after "lau" is well-attested in the language of the Arabs. The mercy here means provision and all of His blessings upon His creation.

As for the discussion of ﴿idhan la-amsaktum﴾ (then you would have withheld), its parallel has been mentioned in His saying: ﴿then We would have made you taste a double [punishment]﴾ [al-Isra': 75]. The word ﴿khashyata﴾ (for fear of) is a mafʿul li-ajlih (object of purpose, an accusative of cause). The apparent meaning of ﴿al-infaq﴾ (spending) is its well-known signification, so it would be an elision of an annexed noun, meaning: "for fear of the consequence of spending", which is depletion. Abu 'Ubayda said: anfaqa, amlaqa, a'dama and asrama have one meaning, so the meaning would be: "for fear of poverty." Al-qatur is the one who withholds, the miser. ﴿al-insan﴾ (man) here is generic.

When God, exalted is He, related what He related of the Quraysh regarding their insolence in their demands and their obstinacy towards the Messenger ﷺ, He consoled him with what had happened to Moses with Pharaoh and with his people, from their saying: ﴿Show us God openly﴾ [al-Nisa': 153], and when the Quraysh said: (p-85) ﴿or you bring God and the angels before us﴾ [al-Isra': 92], and said: ﴿or we see our Lord﴾ [al-Furqan: 21]. He calmed his heart and drew attention to the fact that their end is destruction and perdition, as happened to Pharaoh, when God destroyed him and those with him.

As for ﴿nine clear signs﴾: Ibn 'Abbas and a group of the Companions said: they are the white hand, the staff, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood. These seven are agreed upon. As for the other two, it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that his tongue had a knot in it which God untied, and the sea that was split for him. And it is also reported from him: the sea and the mountain that was lifted over them. And also from him: the years of famine and the decrease of the fruits. This was said by Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, 'Ikrimah and Qatadah. Al-Hasan said: the years of famine and the decrease of the fruits are one sign. It is reported from al-Hasan and Wahb: the sea and death, which were sent upon them. It is reported from Ibn Jubayr: the stone and the sea. And from Muhammad ibn Ka'b: the sea and the years of famine. It was also said: ﴿nine clear signs﴾ are from the Book. The reason is that a Jew said to his companion: "Come, let us ask this Prophet." The other said: "Do not say he is a prophet; for if he hears your words, he will have four eyes." So they came to him and asked him about ﴿nine clear signs﴾, and he said: "Do not associate anything with God, do not consume usury, do not walk with an innocent person to a ruler so that he may kill him, do not mock, do not slander chaste women, do not flee from the battlefield, and upon you, O Jews, in particular: do not transgress on the Sabbath." He said: They then kissed his hand and said: "We testify that you are a prophet." He said: "What has prevented you from becoming Muslims?" They said: "David supplicated God that there would never cease to be a prophet among his descendants, and we fear that if we became Muslims the Jews would kill us." Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: this is a hasan sahih hadith.

The majority recited: ﴿fas-al Bani Isra'il﴾ (so ask the Children of Israel), and "Bani Isra'il" are his contemporaries. ﴿fas-al﴾ is governed by an implied utterance, i.e., "So We said: ask." The apparent meaning is that it is an address to the Messenger Muhammad ﷺ, commanding him to ask them about what God had informed him of the unseen details of the story. Then He said: ﴿when he came to them﴾, meaning their forefathers, and He included them in the pronoun, since they are of them. Al-Zamakhshari said: Ask them about their faith and the condition of their religion, or ask them to support you, so that their hearts and hands are with you. This is supported by the reading of the Messenger of God ﷺ: ﴿fa-sa'ala Bani Isra'il﴾ (he asked), in the past tense without hamza, and this is the dialect of the Quraysh. It was said: ﴿fas-al﴾, O Messenger of God, the believers among the Children of Israel, namely 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions, about the signs, in order that they may increase in certainty and tranquillity of heart; since when proofs converge, that is stronger and more firmly established, like the saying of Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿but that my heart may be at rest﴾ [al-Baqara: 260]. Since the object of the question is elided, it allows these estimations. The apparent meaning of the command to ask the Children of Israel is literal.

The searching and seeking was expressed by asking. For this reason al-Hasan said: "Your asking them is your looking into the Qur'an." The apparent meaning is that ﴿idh﴾ (when) is governed by ﴿ataynā﴾ (We gave), meaning: We gave when he came to them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: with what is ﴿idh jā'ahum﴾ (when he came to them) connected? I say: According to the first mode, it is connected to the implied utterance, i.e., "So We said to him: ask them when he came to them." According to the other, it is connected to ﴿ataynā﴾ or to an implied ﴿udhkur﴾ (mention) or ﴿yukhbirūnaka﴾ (they will inform you). End of quotation. It cannot be connected to ﴿udhkur﴾ nor to ﴿yukhbirūnaka﴾, because it is an adverbial of past time. The reading ﴿fa-sa'ala﴾ is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn 'Abbas said: there is an elided utterance, and its estimation is: "So Moses asked Pharaoh for the Children of Israel," meaning: he sought them, so that he might deliver them from the punishment. End of quotation. On the reading ﴿fas-al﴾, the estimation is: "So We said to him: ask Pharaoh to release the Children of Israel."

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: ﴿fas-al Bani Isra'il﴾ is an interjection in the speech, and the estimation is: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses nine clear signs﴾ when the Children of Israel came, so ask them. The aim of asking the Children of Israel is not that he would obtain this knowledge from them; rather the intent is that the truth of what the Messenger, peace be upon him, had mentioned should become manifest to the common Jews, so this asking is an asking for testimony. End of quotation. On the reading ﴿fa-sa'ala﴾ as a past verb, and estimating it as "So Pharaoh asked the Children of Israel," the first object of "sa'ala" would be elided and the second would be "Bani Isra'il." It may be from the category of the governing of two verbs (tanazu'), since both "sa'ala" and "fa-qala" were applied to Pharaoh, and the second was made to govern, as it is the more preferred (p-86).

The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿masḥūran﴾ (bewitched) is that it is a passive participle, meaning: "You have been bewitched by this speech of yours," which is an accusation of being deranged; what he brings is not upright, and this is an address by way of contrariety. Al-Farra' and al-Tabari said: it is a passive form with the meaning of an active one, i.e., "a sorcerer," so these marvels that he brings are from the matter of sorcery. They also said: a passive form with the meaning of an active one, as in ﴿mash'um﴾ (ill-omened) and ﴿maymun﴾ (blessed), whereas the proper forms are ﴿shā'im﴾ and ﴿yāmin﴾.

That is: "You certainly know that what I have brought is not of the category of sorcery, nor that I have been deceived in my intellect; rather you know that none sent it down except God." How excellent is what He brought of attributing its sending down to the expression ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾, since when Pharaoh asked him at the beginning of their dialogue, saying to him: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾, he said: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾, drawing his attention to his deficiency and that he has no control over existence, so his claim of lordship is a claim of impossibility. Thus he rebuked him and informed him that he knows the signs of God and who sent them down, but he is arrogant and obstinate, as in His saying: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and haughtiness﴾ [al-Naml: 14]. He addressed him thus by way of reproach, meaning: "You are in the state of one who knows this, and they are so clear that you know them." His address was not on the basis of informing him of his knowledge.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿'alimtu﴾ (I certainly know) with a ḍamma on the ta', informing that Moses, about himself, that he is not bewitched as Pharaoh described him, but rather he knows that ﴿none sent these down﴾, the signs, except God.

It is reported from 'Ali that he said: "The enemy of God never knew at all; it was only Moses who knew." This statement from 'Ali is not sound, since it was transmitted by Kulthum al-Muradi, who is unknown. And how could this statement be sound when the reading of the community is with the fatha, as an address to Pharaoh?

The passage is a classical tafsir text, so I translate it faithfully below.

"And (what He sent down) is a clause in a position of accusative, governed by (you know) [ʿalimta, i.e., the verb 'ʿalima' whose object is the clause]. The meaning of (clear proofs) (baṣāʾir) is evidences of the Oneness of God and the truthfulness of His Messenger, and the reference of (these) is to the nine signs. (Baṣāʾir) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) according to the opinion of Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ḥawfī and Abu al-Baqāʾ, and they said: it is a circumstantial state of (these). But this is not valid except according to the school of al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash, since they permit [the construction] 'What struck Hind except Zayd laughing?' The school of the majority is that it is not permitted. If something that outwardly appears to be like that occurs, it is interpreted as implying a verb indicated by what precedes it; the estimate is 'he struck her laughing,' and similarly they estimate here: 'He sent it down as clear proofs.' According to these [grammarians], what precedes does not govern anything except what follows it, unless it is an exception from it or a follower of it.

Moses matched his supposition with the supposition of Pharaoh, so he said: ﴿And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed﴾. The difference between the two suppositions is vast: Pharaoh's supposition was a false supposition, while Moses' supposition was a supposition of truth; and for this reason the affair of Pharaoh ended in destruction. Moses, peace be upon him, had first been anticipating harm from Pharaoh, as he said: (Indeed, we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress), so he was commanded to speak to him gently. When God said to him, 'Do not fear,' and he trusted in God's protection, he rose against Pharaoh with the assault of one who is protected, and he responded to him with words he would not have used before that.

(Mathbūr) means destroyed, according to al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid; cursed, according to Ibn ʿAbbās; of deficient intellect, as transmitted by Maymūn ibn Mihrān; and bewitched, according to al-Ḍaḥḥāk, who said: he returned to him the same as what Pharaoh had said to him, with a difference in wording. From al-Farrāʾ: (mathbūr) means turned away from good, sealed upon your heart, from their saying: 'What turned you away from this?' i.e., what prevented you and diverted you.

Ubayy recited: ﴿Indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are surely doomed﴾, where it is the light (khafīfa) form of inna with the distinguishing lām. His "inciting them" (istifzāzuhu iyyāhum) means his belittling of Moses and his people, by intending to uproot them from the land of Egypt through killing or expulsion. So the scheme recoiled upon him, and God drowned him and his Coptic people. He intended that the land of Egypt be emptied of them, so God emptied it of him. ﴿And after him﴾: the pronoun in (min baʿdihi) refers to Pharaoh, i.e., after his drowning. (The land) whose inhabitation they were commanded is the land of Syria, and the apparent meaning is that the command to this was literally conveyed through the tongue of Moses, peace be upon him. The promise of the Hereafter is the establishment of the Hour."

The aim of asking the Children of Israel is not that he would obtain this knowledge from them; rather the intent is that the truth of what the Messenger, peace be upon him, had mentioned should become manifest to the common Jews, so this asking is an asking for testimony. End of quotation. On the reading ﴿fa-sa'ala﴾ as a past verb, and estimating it as "So Pharaoh asked the Children of Israel," the first object of "sa'ala" would be elided and the second would be "Bani Isra'il." It may be from the category of the governing of two verbs (tanazu'), since both "sa'ala" and "fa-qala" were applied to Pharaoh, and the second was made to govern, as it is the more preferred (p-86).

The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿masḥūran﴾ (bewitched) is that it is a passive participle, meaning: "You have been bewitched by this speech of yours," which is an accusation of being deranged; what he brings is not upright, and this is an address by way of contrariety. Al-Farra' and al-Tabari said: it is a passive form with the meaning of an active one, i.e., "a sorcerer," so these marvels that he brings are from the matter of sorcery. They also said: a passive form with the meaning of an active one, as in ﴿mash'um﴾ (ill-omened) and ﴿maymun﴾ (blessed), whereas the proper forms are ﴿shā'im﴾ and ﴿yāmin﴾.

The majority recited: ﴿la-qad 'alimta﴾ (You certainly know) with a fatha on the ta', as an address from Moses to Pharaoh, and a rebuke in His saying, concerning him, that he is bewitched. That is: "You certainly know that what I have brought is not of the category of sorcery, nor that I have been deceived in my intellect; rather you know that none sent it down except God." How excellent is what He brought of attributing its sending down to the expression ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾, since when Pharaoh asked him at the beginning of their dialogue, saying to him: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾, he said: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾, drawing his attention to his deficiency and that he has no control over existence, so his claim of lordship is a claim of impossibility. Thus he rebuked him and informed him that he knows the signs of God and who sent them down, but he is arrogant and obstinate, as in His saying: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and haughtiness﴾ [al-Naml: 14]. He addressed him thus by way of reproach, meaning: "You are in the state of one who knows this, and they are so clear that you know them." His address was not on the basis of informing him of his knowledge.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿'alimtu﴾ (I certainly know) with a ḍamma on the ta', informing that Moses, about himself, that he is not bewitched as Pharaoh described him, but rather he knows that ﴿none sent these down﴾, the signs, except God.

It is reported from 'Ali that he said: "The enemy of God never knew at all; it was only Moses who knew." This statement from 'Ali is not sound, since it was transmitted by Kulthum al-Muradi, who is unknown. And how could this statement be sound when the reading of the community is with the fatha, as an address to Pharaoh?

The passage is a classical tafsir text, so I translate it faithfully below.

"And (what He sent down) is a clause in a position of accusative, governed by (you know) [ʿalimta, i.e., the verb 'ʿalima' whose object is the clause]. The meaning of (clear proofs) (baṣāʾir) is evidences of the Oneness of God and the truthfulness of His Messenger, and the reference of (these) is to the nine signs. (Baṣāʾir) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) according to the opinion of Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ḥawfī and Abu al-Baqāʾ, and they said: it is a circumstantial state of (these). But this is not valid except according to the school of al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash, since they permit [the construction] 'What struck Hind except Zayd laughing?' The school of the majority is that it is not permitted. If something that outwardly appears to be like that occurs, it is interpreted as implying a verb indicated by what precedes it; the estimate is 'he struck her laughing,' and similarly they estimate here: 'He sent it down as clear proofs.' According to these [grammarians], what precedes does not govern anything except what follows it, unless it is an exception from it or a follower of it.

Moses matched his supposition with the supposition of Pharaoh, so he said: ﴿And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed﴾. The difference between the two suppositions is vast: Pharaoh's supposition was a false supposition, while Moses' supposition was a supposition of truth; and for this reason the affair of Pharaoh ended in destruction. Moses, peace be upon him, had first been anticipating harm from Pharaoh, as he said: (Indeed, we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress), so he was commanded to speak to him gently. When God said to him, 'Do not fear,' and he trusted in God's protection, he rose against Pharaoh with the assault of one who is protected, and he responded to him with words he would not have used before that.

(Mathbūr) means destroyed, according to al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid; cursed, according to Ibn ʿAbbās; of deficient intellect, as transmitted by Maymūn ibn Mihrān; and bewitched, according to al-Ḍaḥḥāk, who said: he returned to him the same as what Pharaoh had said to him, with a difference in wording. From al-Farrāʾ: (mathbūr) means turned away from good, sealed upon your heart, from their saying: 'What turned you away from this?' i.e., what prevented you and diverted you.

Ubayy recited: ﴿Indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are surely doomed﴾, where it is the light (khafīfa) form of inna with the distinguishing lām. His "inciting them" (istifzāzuhu iyyāhum) means his belittling of Moses and his people, by intending to uproot them from the land of Egypt through killing or expulsion. So the scheme recoiled upon him, and God drowned him and his Coptic people. He intended that the land of Egypt be emptied of them, so God emptied it of him. ﴿And after him﴾: the pronoun in (min baʿdihi) refers to Pharaoh, i.e., after his drowning. (The land) whose inhabitation they were commanded is the land of Syria, and the apparent meaning is that the command to this was literally conveyed through the tongue of Moses, peace be upon him. The promise of the Hereafter is the establishment of the Hour."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verses 100–104 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Say: "Even if you possessed the treasuries of the mercy of my Lord, you would withhold them for fear of spending. And man is ever tight-fisted."﴾ ﴿And We certainly gave Moses nine clear signs. So ask the Children of Israel, when he came to them, and Pharaoh said to him, "Indeed, I think you, O Moses, are bewitched."﴾ ﴿He said, "You know well that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence. And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed."﴾ ﴿So he intended to drive them out of the land, but We drowned him and those with him, all together. And We said after him to the Children of Israel, "Dwell in the land; and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you together as a mixed multitude."﴾

The occasion of His saying: ﴿Say: "Even if you possessed the treasuries…"﴾ (the verse), is that the polytheists said: "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush for us from the earth." So they asked for rivers and springs to be made to flow in their land, so that their provisions would increase and be abundant for them. Then God, exalted is He, explained that if they possessed the treasuries of God's mercy, they would remain upon their miserliness and stinginess, and would not hasten to bring benefit to anyone. Accordingly, there is no benefit in fulfilling what they requested. This is what has been said regarding the connection of this verse, and al-'Askari said it. What appears to me, however, is that the appropriate connection is that he, peace be upon him, had been granted by God what He had not granted anyone else of prophethood and messengerhood to humankind and jinn. He is therefore the most eager of people to bring good and to rescue them from misguidance. He persists in this, and risks himself in calling them to God, and presents this to the tribes and the clans of the Arabs, generously, without seeking any wage from them. Yet these were his relatives, from whom hardly anyone answered except one after another, and they had persisted in their obstinacy and enmity towards him, so nothing reached him from them except harm. (p-84) So God, through this verse, drew attention to his generosity, peace be upon him, and to his giving away what God had bestowed upon him, and to the refusal of these people to let any good come from them to him. He said: even if they possessed the power to dispose of the (treasuries of the mercy of) God, which encompass everything, they would be more miserly than anyone with what they had been given of that, such that nothing of benefit would reach anyone from them, since their nature is niggardliness, which is withholding from expanding in expenditure. This is in addition to what they had been given of treasuries. Thus this verse came clarifying what lies between them and him, peace be upon him, of his eagerness for their benefit and the non-arrival of any good from them to him.

What is established regarding ﴿lau﴾ (if), which is a particle for what would have occurred on account of the occurrence of something else, is that the verb follows it, either in the past or the present, as in His saying: ﴿If We willed, We would have made it into debris﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 65], or negated by ﴿lam﴾ or ﴿in﴾. Here, in His saying: ﴿Say: "Even if you (antum) possess…"﴾, a noun follows it, so they differed about its analysis. Al-Hawfi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu al-Baqa' and others went to the view that it is in the nominative by an elided verb that is explained by the verb after it. When that verb, which is "tamliku" (you possess), was elided, the pronoun, which is the subject of "tamliku", became detached, as in His saying:

"And if he does not bear its injustice upon himself…"

The estimation is: "And if he does not bear", so "lam yahmil" was elided and the pronoun concealed in "yahmilu" became detached, so it became "huwa" (he). Here, the attached manifest pronoun, which is the waw, became detached, so it became "antum" (you). This analysis is based on the premise that "lau" is followed by the verb, whether manifest or implied, in eloquent speech. This, however, is not the doctrine of the Basrans.

The Shaykh Abu al-Hasan ibn 'Usfur said: "Lau" is followed only by a manifest verb, and is followed by an implied one only in cases of necessity or in rare speech, such as what has come in the proverb of their saying:

"Had a woman wearing bracelets slapped me…"

Our shaykh, the Ustadh Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Sa'igh, said: The Basrans explicitly affirm the impermissibility of "lau Zayd qama la-akramtuhu" (had Zayd stood, I would have honoured him) in the eloquent usage, and they permit it as an anomaly, as in their saying:

"Had a woman wearing bracelets slapped me…"

According to them, it is on an implied verb, as in His exalted saying: ﴿And if anyone among the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection﴾ [al-Tawba: 6]. This is from the category of ishtighal (the verb being occupied with a pronoun referring to the noun). End of quotation. Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Fadal al-Mujashi'i analysed it as the implied "kana" (was), the estimation being: "Say: 'Had you (antum) been the ones who possess…'" The apparent sense of this analysis is that "kuntum" was elided in its entirety, and "antum" remained as an emphasis for that elided pronoun together with the verb. Our shaykh, Abu al-Hasan al-Sa'igh, went to the view of eliding "kana", so its subject, which was attached to it, became detached, and the estimation is: "Say: 'Had you (kuntum) been…" So when the verb was elided, the nominative became detached. This analysis is the better one, since the elision of "kana" after "lau" is well-attested in the language of the Arabs. The mercy here means provision and all of His blessings upon His creation.

As for the discussion of ﴿idhan la-amsaktum﴾ (then you would have withheld), its parallel has been mentioned in His saying: ﴿then We would have made you taste a double [punishment]﴾ [al-Isra': 75]. The word ﴿khashyata﴾ (for fear of) is a mafʿul li-ajlih (object of purpose, an accusative of cause). The apparent meaning of ﴿al-infaq﴾ (spending) is its well-known signification, so it would be an elision of an annexed noun, meaning: "for fear of the consequence of spending", which is depletion. Abu 'Ubayda said: anfaqa, amlaqa, a'dama and asrama have one meaning, so the meaning would be: "for fear of poverty." Al-qatur is the one who withholds, the miser. ﴿al-insan﴾ (man) here is generic.

When God, exalted is He, related what He related of the Quraysh regarding their insolence in their demands and their obstinacy towards the Messenger ﷺ, He consoled him with what had happened to Moses with Pharaoh and with his people, from their saying: ﴿Show us God openly﴾ [al-Nisa': 153], and when the Quraysh said: (p-85) ﴿or you bring God and the angels before us﴾ [al-Isra': 92], and said: ﴿or we see our Lord﴾ [al-Furqan: 21]. He calmed his heart and drew attention to the fact that their end is destruction and perdition, as happened to Pharaoh, when God destroyed him and those with him.

As for ﴿nine clear signs﴾: Ibn 'Abbas and a group of the Companions said: they are the white hand, the staff, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood. These seven are agreed upon. As for the other two, it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that his tongue had a knot in it which God untied, and the sea that was split for him. And it is also reported from him: the sea and the mountain that was lifted over them. And also from him: the years of famine and the decrease of the fruits. This was said by Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, 'Ikrimah and Qatadah. Al-Hasan said: the years of famine and the decrease of the fruits are one sign. It is reported from al-Hasan and Wahb: the sea and death, which were sent upon them. It is reported from Ibn Jubayr: the stone and the sea. And from Muhammad ibn Ka'b: the sea and the years of famine. It was also said: ﴿nine clear signs﴾ are from the Book. The reason is that a Jew said to his companion: "Come, let us ask this Prophet." The other said: "Do not say he is a prophet; for if he hears your words, he will have four eyes." So they came to him and asked him about ﴿nine clear signs﴾, and he said: "Do not associate anything with God, do not consume usury, do not walk with an innocent person to a ruler so that he may kill him, do not mock, do not slander chaste women, do not flee from the battlefield, and upon you, O Jews, in particular: do not transgress on the Sabbath." He said: They then kissed his hand and said: "We testify that you are a prophet." He said: "What has prevented you from becoming Muslims?" They said: "David supplicated God that there would never cease to be a prophet among his descendants, and we fear that if we became Muslims the Jews would kill us." Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: this is a hasan sahih hadith.

The majority recited: ﴿fas-al Bani Isra'il﴾ (so ask the Children of Israel), and "Bani Isra'il" are his contemporaries. ﴿fas-al﴾ is governed by an implied utterance, i.e., "So We said: ask." The apparent meaning is that it is an address to the Messenger Muhammad ﷺ, commanding him to ask them about what God had informed him of the unseen details of the story. Ibn 'Atiyya said, in substance: It is possible that the asking is an expression for seeking their reports and examining their conditions and what is in their books, like His saying: ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾. The apparent meaning is that ﴿idh﴾ (when) is governed by ﴿ataynā﴾ (We gave), meaning: We gave when he came to them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: with what is ﴿idh jā'ahum﴾ (when he came to them) connected? I say: According to the first mode, it is connected to the implied utterance, i.e., "So We said to him: ask them when he came to them." According to the other, it is connected to ﴿ataynā﴾ or to an implied ﴿udhkur﴾ (mention) or ﴿yukhbirūnaka﴾ (they will inform you). End of quotation. The estimation is: "And if he does not bear", so "lam yahmil" was elided and the pronoun concealed in "yahmilu" became detached, so it became "huwa" (he). Here, the attached manifest pronoun, which is the waw, became detached, so it became "antum" (you). The Shaykh Abu al-Hasan ibn 'Usfur said: "Lau" is followed only by a manifest verb, and is followed by an implied one only in cases of necessity or in rare speech, such as what has come in the proverb of their saying:

"Had a woman wearing bracelets slapped me…"

"Had a woman wearing bracelets slapped me…"

According to them, it is on an implied verb, as in His exalted saying: ﴿And if anyone among the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection﴾ [al-Tawba: 6]. This is from the category of ishtighal (the verb being occupied with a pronoun referring to the noun). End of quotation. Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Fadal al-Mujashi'i analysed it as the implied "kana" (was), the estimation being: "Say: 'Had you (antum) been the ones who possess…'" The apparent sense of this analysis is that "kuntum" was elided in its entirety, and "antum" remained as an emphasis for that elided pronoun together with the verb. Our shaykh, Abu al-Hasan al-Sa'igh, went to the view of eliding "kana", so its subject, which was attached to it, became detached, and the estimation is: "Say: 'Had you (kuntum) been…" So when the verb was elided, the nominative became detached. This analysis is the better one, since the elision of "kana" after "lau" is well-attested in the language of the Arabs. The mercy here means provision and all of His blessings upon His creation.

As for the discussion of ﴿idhan la-amsaktum﴾ (then you would have withheld), its parallel has been mentioned in His saying: ﴿then We would have made you taste a double [punishment]﴾ [al-Isra': 75]. The word ﴿khashyata﴾ (for fear of) is a mafʿul li-ajlih (object of purpose, an accusative of cause). The apparent meaning of ﴿al-infaq﴾ (spending) is its well-known signification, so it would be an elision of an annexed noun, meaning: "for fear of the consequence of spending", which is depletion. Abu 'Ubayda said: anfaqa, amlaqa, a'dama and asrama have one meaning, so the meaning would be: "for fear of poverty." Al-qatur is the one who withholds, the miser. ﴿al-insan﴾ (man) here is generic.

When God, exalted is He, related what He related of the Quraysh regarding their insolence in their demands and their obstinacy towards the Messenger ﷺ, He consoled him with what had happened to Moses with Pharaoh and with his people, from their saying: ﴿Show us God openly﴾ [al-Nisa': 153], and when the Quraysh said: (p-85) ﴿or you bring God and the angels before us﴾ [al-Isra': 92], and said: ﴿or we see our Lord﴾ [al-Furqan: 21]. He calmed his heart and drew attention to the fact that their end is destruction and perdition, as happened to Pharaoh, when God destroyed him and those with him.

As for ﴿nine clear signs﴾: Ibn 'Abbas and a group of the Companions said: they are the white hand, the staff, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood. These seven are agreed upon. As for the other two, it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that his tongue had a knot in it which God untied, and the sea that was split for him. And it is also reported from him: the sea and the mountain that was lifted over them. And also from him: the years of famine and the decrease of the fruits. This was said by Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, 'Ikrimah and Qatadah. Al-Hasan said: the years of famine and the decrease of the fruits are one sign. It is reported from al-Hasan and Wahb: the sea and death, which were sent upon them. It is reported from Ibn Jubayr: the stone and the sea. And from Muhammad ibn Ka'b: the sea and the years of famine. It was also said: ﴿nine clear signs﴾ are from the Book. The reason is that a Jew said to his companion: "Come, let us ask this Prophet." The other said: "Do not say he is a prophet; for if he hears your words, he will have four eyes." So they came to him and asked him about ﴿nine clear signs﴾, and he said: "Do not associate anything with God, do not consume usury, do not walk with an innocent person to a ruler so that he may kill him, do not mock, do not slander chaste women, do not flee from the battlefield, and upon you, O Jews, in particular: do not transgress on the Sabbath." He said: They then kissed his hand and said: "We testify that you are a prophet." He said: "What has prevented you from becoming Muslims?" They said: "David supplicated God that there would never cease to be a prophet among his descendants, and we fear that if we became Muslims the Jews would kill us." Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: this is a hasan sahih hadith.

The majority recited: ﴿fas-al Bani Isra'il﴾ (so ask the Children of Israel), and "Bani Isra'il" are his contemporaries. ﴿fas-al﴾ is governed by an implied utterance, i.e., "So We said: ask." The apparent meaning is that it is an address to the Messenger Muhammad ﷺ, commanding him to ask them about what God had informed him of the unseen details of the story. Then He said: ﴿when he came to them﴾, meaning their forefathers, and He included them in the pronoun, since they are of them. Al-Zamakhshari said: Ask them about their faith and the condition of their religion, or ask them to support you, so that their hearts and hands are with you. This is supported by the reading of the Messenger of God ﷺ: ﴿fa-sa'ala Bani Isra'il﴾ (he asked), in the past tense without hamza, and this is the dialect of the Quraysh. The apparent meaning is that ﴿idh﴾ (when) is governed by ﴿ataynā﴾ (We gave), meaning: We gave when he came to them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: with what is ﴿idh jā'ahum﴾ (when he came to them) connected? I say: According to the first mode, it is connected to the implied utterance, i.e., "So We said to him: ask them when he came to them." According to the other, it is connected to ﴿ataynā﴾ or to an implied ﴿udhkur﴾ (mention) or ﴿yukhbirūnaka﴾ (they will inform you). End of quotation. End of quotation. On the reading ﴿fas-al﴾, the estimation is: "So We said to him: ask Pharaoh to release the Children of Israel."

It is reported from 'Ali that he said: "The enemy of God never knew at all; it was only Moses who knew." This statement from 'Ali is not sound, since it was transmitted by Kulthum al-Muradi, who is unknown. And how could this statement be sound when the reading of the community is with the fatha, as an address to Pharaoh?

The passage is a classical tafsir text, so I translate it faithfully below.

"And (what He sent down) is a clause in a position of accusative, governed by (you know) [ʿalimta, i.e., the verb 'ʿalima' whose object is the clause]. The meaning of (clear proofs) (baṣāʾir) is evidences of the Oneness of God and the truthfulness of His Messenger, and the reference of (these) is to the nine signs. (Baṣāʾir) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) according to the opinion of Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ḥawfī and Abu al-Baqāʾ, and they said: it is a circumstantial state of (these). But this is not valid except according to the school of al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash, since they permit [the construction] 'What struck Hind except Zayd laughing?' The school of the majority is that it is not permitted. If something that outwardly appears to be like that occurs, it is interpreted as implying a verb indicated by what precedes it; the estimate is 'he struck her laughing,' and similarly they estimate here: 'He sent it down as clear proofs.' According to these [grammarians], what precedes does not govern anything except what follows it, unless it is an exception from it or a follower of it.

Moses matched his supposition with the supposition of Pharaoh, so he said: ﴿And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed﴾. The difference between the two suppositions is vast: Pharaoh's supposition was a false supposition, while Moses' supposition was a supposition of truth; and for this reason the affair of Pharaoh ended in destruction. Moses, peace be upon him, had first been anticipating harm from Pharaoh, as he said: (Indeed, we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress), so he was commanded to speak to him gently. When God said to him, 'Do not fear,' and he trusted in God's protection, he rose against Pharaoh with the assault of one who is protected, and he responded to him with words he would not have used before that.

(Mathbūr) means destroyed, according to al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid; cursed, according to Ibn ʿAbbās; of deficient intellect, as transmitted by Maymūn ibn Mihrān; and bewitched, according to al-Ḍaḥḥāk, who said: he returned to him the same as what Pharaoh had said to him, with a difference in wording. From al-Farrāʾ: (mathbūr) means turned away from good, sealed upon your heart, from their saying: 'What turned you away from this?' i.e., what prevented you and diverted you.

Ubayy recited: ﴿Indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are surely doomed﴾, where it is the light (khafīfa) form of inna with the distinguishing lām. His "inciting them" (istifzāzuhu iyyāhum) means his belittling of Moses and his people, by intending to uproot them from the land of Egypt through killing or expulsion. So the scheme recoiled upon him, and God drowned him and his Coptic people. He intended that the land of Egypt be emptied of them, so God emptied it of him. ﴿And after him﴾: the pronoun in (min baʿdihi) refers to Pharaoh, i.e., after his drowning. (The land) whose inhabitation they were commanded is the land of Syria, and the apparent meaning is that the command to this was literally conveyed through the tongue of Moses, peace be upon him. The promise of the Hereafter is the establishment of the Hour."

Then God, exalted is He, explained that if they possessed the treasuries of God's mercy, they would remain upon their miserliness and stinginess, and would not hasten to bring benefit to anyone. That is: "You certainly know that what I have brought is not of the category of sorcery, nor that I have been deceived in my intellect; rather you know that none sent it down except God." How excellent is what He brought of attributing its sending down to the expression ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾, since when Pharaoh asked him at the beginning of their dialogue, saying to him: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾, he said: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾, drawing his attention to his deficiency and that he has no control over existence, so his claim of lordship is a claim of impossibility. Thus he rebuked him and informed him that he knows the signs of God and who sent them down, but he is arrogant and obstinate, as in His saying: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and haughtiness﴾ [al-Naml: 14]. He addressed him thus by way of reproach, meaning: "You are in the state of one who knows this, and they are so clear that you know them." His address was not on the basis of informing him of his knowledge.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿'alimtu﴾ (I certainly know) with a ḍamma on the ta', informing that Moses, about himself, that he is not bewitched as Pharaoh described him, but rather he knows that ﴿none sent these down﴾, the signs, except God.

It is reported from 'Ali that he said: "The enemy of God never knew at all; it was only Moses who knew." This statement from 'Ali is not sound, since it was transmitted by Kulthum al-Muradi, who is unknown. And how could this statement be sound when the reading of the community is with the fatha, as an address to Pharaoh?

The passage is a classical tafsir text, so I translate it faithfully below.

"And (what He sent down) is a clause in a position of accusative, governed by (you know) [ʿalimta, i.e., the verb 'ʿalima' whose object is the clause]. The meaning of (clear proofs) (baṣāʾir) is evidences of the Oneness of God and the truthfulness of His Messenger, and the reference of (these) is to the nine signs. (Baṣāʾir) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) according to the opinion of Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ḥawfī and Abu al-Baqāʾ, and they said: it is a circumstantial state of (these). But this is not valid except according to the school of al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash, since they permit [the construction] 'What struck Hind except Zayd laughing?' The school of the majority is that it is not permitted. If something that outwardly appears to be like that occurs, it is interpreted as implying a verb indicated by what precedes it; the estimate is 'he struck her laughing,' and similarly they estimate here: 'He sent it down as clear proofs.' According to these [grammarians], what precedes does not govern anything except what follows it, unless it is an exception from it or a follower of it.

Moses matched his supposition with the supposition of Pharaoh, so he said: ﴿And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed﴾. The difference between the two suppositions is vast: Pharaoh's supposition was a false supposition, while Moses' supposition was a supposition of truth; and for this reason the affair of Pharaoh ended in destruction. Moses, peace be upon him, had first been anticipating harm from Pharaoh, as he said: (Indeed, we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress), so he was commanded to speak to him gently. When God said to him, 'Do not fear,' and he trusted in God's protection, he rose against Pharaoh with the assault of one who is protected, and he responded to him with words he would not have used before that.

(Mathbūr) means destroyed, according to al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid; cursed, according to Ibn ʿAbbās; of deficient intellect, as transmitted by Maymūn ibn Mihrān; and bewitched, according to al-Ḍaḥḥāk, who said: he returned to him the same as what Pharaoh had said to him, with a difference in wording. From al-Farrāʾ: (mathbūr) means turned away from good, sealed upon your heart, from their saying: 'What turned you away from this?' i.e., what prevented you and diverted you.

Ubayy recited: ﴿Indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are surely doomed﴾, where it is the light (khafīfa) form of inna with the distinguishing lām. His "inciting them" (istifzāzuhu iyyāhum) means his belittling of Moses and his people, by intending to uproot them from the land of Egypt through killing or expulsion. So the scheme recoiled upon him, and God drowned him and his Coptic people. He intended that the land of Egypt be emptied of them, so God emptied it of him. ﴿And after him﴾: the pronoun in (min baʿdihi) refers to Pharaoh, i.e., after his drowning. (The land) whose inhabitation they were commanded is the land of Syria, and the apparent meaning is that the command to this was literally conveyed through the tongue of Moses, peace be upon him. The promise of the Hereafter is the establishment of the Hour."

[p. 87] **"And with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it descended"** (﴿وبِالحَقِّ أنْزَلْناهُ﴾) refers back to His saying: **"If mankind and the jinn were to gather to produce the like of this Qur'an..."** (﴿لَئِنِ اجْتَمَعَتِ الإنْسُ والجِنُّ﴾) [al-Isra: 88], and so on. This is the manner and style of Arabic speech: it takes up one matter, digresses from it to another, then to yet another, and then returns to what it mentioned first. Far-fetched is the view of one who held that the pronoun in (أنْزَلْناهُ, "We sent it down") refers to Musa, peace be upon him, making the verb mean "We caused it to be sent down," as in His saying: **"And We sent down iron"** (﴿وأنْزَلْنا الحَدِيدَ﴾) [al-Hadid: 25]. Or that it refers to the nine signs, mentioned in meaning. Or that it refers to the promise mentioned before it.

Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: **"And with the truth We sent it down"** means with monotheism (al-tawhid). **"And with the truth it descended"** means with the promise and the threat, and with the command and the prohibition. Al-Zahrawi said: with what is obligatory, which is the welfare and the rectitude of mankind. **"And with the truth it descended"** means with the truth in its commands, its prohibitions and its reports. Al-Zamakhshari said: We did not send down the Qur'an except with the wisdom that necessitates its being sent down, and it did not descend except conjoined with truth and wisdom, since it includes guidance to every good. And We did not send it down from the heaven except with truth, guarded by watchers from among the angels, and it did not descend upon the Messenger except guarded by them from the confusion of the devils. End of quotation.

It is possible that **"And with the truth it descended"** is an emphasis in meaning, since it was said: "We sent it down, so it descended," and "We sent it down, but it did not descend," when some obstacle prevented its descent. So **"And with the truth it descended"** came to remove this possibility and to emphasize the reality of **"And with the truth We sent it down."** Al-Tabari inclined toward this sense of emphasis.

**(مُبَشِّرًا ونَذِيرًا, "a bearer of good tidings and a warner")** is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: bearing good tidings to them of Paradise, and warning them of the Fire. "You have no part in compelling them to the religion."

The majority read **(فَرَقْناهُ, "We divided it")** with a light *rā'* (فَرَقْناهُ), meaning: We made clear its lawful and its unlawful, said Ibn Abbas. And from al-Hasan: We distinguished in it between truth and falsehood. Al-Farra' said: We made it firm and detailed, like His saying: **"Therein is decreed every wise matter"** (﴿فِيها يُفْرَقُ كُلُّ أمْرٍ حَكِيمٍ﴾) [al-Dukhan: 4].

Ubayy, Abdullah, Ali, Ibn Abbas, Abu Raja', Qatada, al-Sha'bi, Humayd, Amr ibn Qa'id, Zayd ibn Ali, Amr ibn Dharr, Ikrima and al-Hasan (according to one report from him) read it with a doubled *rā'* (فَرَّقْناهُ), meaning: We sent it down by stages, one stage after another, and We detailed it across the stages. Some who chose this reading said: It was not sent down in one day or two, nor in one month or two, nor in one year or two. Ibn Abbas said: between its beginning and its end there were twenty years. This is what al-Zamakhshari related from Ibn Abbas. It is also reported from Ibn Abbas: twenty-three years. It was said: twenty-five years. This difference is based on the difference concerning his age, peace be upon him. And from al-Hasan: it descended over eighteen years. Ibn Atiyya said: this is an unsound view that is not authentically from al-Hasan.

It was said that the meaning of **(فَرَّقْناهُ, "We divided it," with doubling)** is: We divided its verses among command and prohibition, wisdoms and rulings, admonitions and parables, stories and reports of unseen matters that have come and that are yet to come.

The apparent connection of **(عَلى مُكْثٍ, "at leisure")** is to His saying **(لِتَقْرَأهُ)**. Al-Hawfi said: **(عَلى مُكْثٍ)** is a substitute for **(عَلى النّاسِ, "to the people")**, but this is not correct, because His saying **(عَلى مُكْثٍ)** is a description of the Messenger, peace be upon him, who is the reciter, or a description of what is recited in meaning, and it is not a description of people, so it cannot be a substitute for them. It was said that **(عَلى مُكْثٍ)** is connected to **(فَرَقْناهُ)**. It is said: *mukth* with a *ḍamma*, *fatḥa* and *kasra* on the *mīm*. Ibn Atiyya said: the readers agreed on the *ḍamma* on the *mīm* of **(مُكْثٍ)**. Al-Hawfi said: *al-mukth* with *ḍamma* and with *fatḥa* are two dialects, and it has been read with both; there is another dialect with a *kasra* on the *mīm*.

**(قُلْ آمِنُوا بِهِ أوْ لا تُؤْمِنُوا, "Say: Believe in it or do not believe")** includes turning away from them, belittling them, disdaining them, disregarding them and their faith, and their refusal of it, and that they had not entered into faith nor affirmed the Qur'an, and they are people of ignorance and polytheism. For there are better and more excellent than them: the scholars who read the Book and knew what revelation is and what the sacred laws are. They believed in it and affirmed it, and it was established for them that he is the Arab Prophet promised in their books. So when it is recited to them they fall **(سُجَّدًا, "prostrate")** and glorify God, exalting His promise and its fulfillment of what He promised in the revealed books and gave good tidings of, namely the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the sending down of the Qur'an upon him. This is what is meant by the promise in His saying: **"Indeed, the promise of our Lord is ever fulfilled"** (﴿إنْ كانَ وعْدُ رَبِّنا لَمَفْعُولًا﴾).

**(إنَّ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا العِلْمَ مِن قَبْلِهِ, "Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it")** may be a justification for His saying **"Believe in it or do not believe,"** meaning: if you do not believe in it, then one better than you has believed in it. Or it may be a justification for **"Say"** by way of consolation, as if it were said: "Say, [concerning] the faith of the Jahiliyyah, by the faith of the scholars." End of al-Zamakhshari's words, with some abridgment. Others said: **"Say: Believe in it..."** and what follows is a belittling of the disbelievers, and within it is a kind of threat. The meaning is: you are not a proof, so whether we believe or you disbelieve is all the same to us; the harm of that falls only upon yourselves, and the proof is the people of knowledge. End of quotation. The apparent sense is that the pronoun in **"Believe in it"** refers to the Qur'an, and **(الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا العِلْمَ, "those given knowledge")** are the believers among the People of the Book. It was said: they are Waraqa ibn Nawfal, Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl and those who went their way, for they were among those given knowledge, and they looked into the Torah and the Gospel and found in them his description, peace be upon him. It was said: they are a group of People of the Book who sat, still upon their religion, and they remembered the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ) and what was revealed to him. Something of it was recited to them, so they humbled themselves and prostrated to God, and said: "This is the time of the prophethood mentioned in the Torah, and this is its description, and God's promise concerning it is certain to come about." And they inclined toward Islam with this inclination, so this verse was revealed concerning them.

It was said: what is meant by **"those given knowledge before it"** is Muhammad (ﷺ). The apparent sense is that the pronouns in **(بِهِ, "in it")** and **(مِن قَبْلِهِ, "before it")** both refer to the Messenger, peace be upon him.

He resumed the mention of the Qur'an in His saying **(إذا يُتْلى عَلَيْهِمْ, "when it is recited to them")**. The apparent sense of **(يُتْلى, "is recited")** is that its pronoun refers to the Qur'an. It was said that it refers to the Torah and what is in it of confirmation of the Qur'an and knowledge of the Prophet, peace be upon him. **(الخُرُورُ, "falling down")** is falling quickly, and from it is His saying **"The roof fell down upon them"** (﴿فَخَرَّ عَلَيْهِمُ السَّقْفُ﴾) [al-Nahl: 26]. **(سُجَّدًا, "prostrate")** is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. Prostration, which is placing the forehead on the ground, is the utmost of falling down and the extreme of submission, and the first part to touch the ground in prostration is the chin (al-dhaqan). Or the faces are expressed by the chins, as every thing is expressed by some part of what touches it. The poet said:

*They fell upon the chins of their faces, while the ravening birds of prey tore at them and plucked.*

It was said: the literal chins are meant, because that is the utmost of humility, and their prostration was so. Ibn Abbas said: the meaning is the faces.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, the preposition of elevation (على) is clear in meaning when you say "he fell on his face" and "on his chin," so what is the meaning of the *lām* in "fell for his chin"? He said: *"So he fell prostrate for the two hands and for the mouth."* I say: its meaning is that he made his chin and his face ready for falling, and singled it out for that, since the *lām* denotes specification. End of quotation. It was also said: the *lām* has the meaning of *ʿalā* (on). **(سُبْحانَ رَبِّنا, "Glory be to our Lord")**: they exalted God above what the disbelieving Quraysh and others attributed to Him, that He does not send mortals as messengers, and that He does not restore them for recompense. **(إنْ, "indeed")** here is the lightened form of the heavy one (إنَّ), meaning: that what He promised of sending Muhammad, peace be upon him, and sending down the Qur'an upon him, has indeed been done and fulfilled. **(الخُرُورُ, "falling")** is left indefinite because the two states, of prostration and of weeping, differ. The first state is expressed by a noun, and the second state by a verb, because the verb indicates renewal, since weeping arises from reflection, and they are constantly in thought and remembrance, so mention of the verb fits, as it indicates renewal. And since the state of prostration does not renew itself at every moment, it is expressed by a noun.

**(ويَزِيدُهم, "and it increases them")**, that is, what is recited to them, **(خُشُوعًا, "in humility")**, that is, humbleness. Abd al-A'la al-Taymi said: whoever has been given of knowledge that which does not make him weep, it is fitting that he has not been given knowledge that benefits him, for He, exalted is He, described the scholars, saying: **"Indeed, those who were given knowledge"** and the verse. Ibn Atiyya said: another meaning may be conveyed by this verse, namely that His saying **"Say: Believe in it or do not believe"** is a warning and not a belittling. The meaning: "You will soon see what you are repaid with." Then He set forth for them an example by way of rebuke, through those of the People of the Book who came before them, meaning: people were not as you are in disbelief; rather, those who had been given the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the revealed books in general, when what was revealed to them was recited to them, they humbled themselves and believed. End of quotation. The indication of part of this has already been given above.

Al-Hawfi said: **(عَلى مُكْثٍ)** is a substitute for **(عَلى النّاسِ, "to the people")**, but this is not correct, because His saying **(عَلى مُكْثٍ)** is a description of the Messenger, peace be upon him, who is the reciter, or a description of what is recited in meaning, and it is not a description of people, so it cannot be a substitute for them. It was said that **(عَلى مُكْثٍ)** is connected to **(فَرَقْناهُ)**. It is said: *mukth* with a *ḍamma*, *fatḥa* and *kasra* on the *mīm*. Ibn Atiyya said: the readers agreed on the *ḍamma* on the *mīm* of **(مُكْثٍ)**. Al-Hawfi said: *al-mukth* with *ḍamma* and with *fatḥa* are two dialects, and it has been read with both; there is another dialect with a *kasra* on the *mīm*.

For there are better and more excellent than them: the scholars who read the Book and knew what revelation is and what the sacred laws are. They believed in it and affirmed it, and it was established for them that he is the Arab Prophet promised in their books. So when it is recited to them they fall **(سُجَّدًا, "prostrate")** and glorify God, exalting His promise and its fulfillment of what He promised in the revealed books and gave good tidings of, namely the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the sending down of the Qur'an upon him. This is what is meant by the promise in His saying: **"Indeed, the promise of our Lord is ever fulfilled"** (﴿إنْ كانَ وعْدُ رَبِّنا لَمَفْعُولًا﴾).

End of quotation. It was said: they are a group of People of the Book who sat, still upon their religion, and they remembered the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ) and what was revealed to him. Something of it was recited to them, so they humbled themselves and prostrated to God, and said: "This is the time of the prophethood mentioned in the Torah, and this is its description, and God's promise concerning it is certain to come about." And they inclined toward Islam with this inclination, so this verse was revealed concerning them.
