It was said that it refers to the Torah and what is in it of confirmation of the Qur'an and knowledge of the Prophet, peace be upon him. **(الخُرُورُ, "falling down")** is falling quickly, and from it is His saying **"The roof fell down upon them"** (﴿فَخَرَّ عَلَيْهِمُ السَّقْفُ﴾) [al-Nahl: 26]. **(سُجَّدًا, "prostrate")** is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. Or the faces are expressed by the chins, as every thing is expressed by some part of what touches it. The poet said:

*They fell upon the chins of their faces, while the ravening birds of prey tore at them and plucked.*

It was said: the literal chins are meant, because that is the utmost of humility, and their prostration was so. Ibn Abbas said: the meaning is the faces.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, the preposition of elevation (على) is clear in meaning when you say "he fell on his face" and "on his chin," so what is the meaning of the *lām* in "fell for his chin"? End of quotation. It was also said: the *lām* has the meaning of *ʿalā* (on). **(سُبْحانَ رَبِّنا, "Glory be to our Lord")**: they exalted God above what the disbelieving Quraysh and others attributed to Him, that He does not send mortals as messengers, and that He does not restore them for recompense. **(إنْ, "indeed")** here is the lightened form of the heavy one (إنَّ), meaning: that what He promised of sending Muhammad, peace be upon him, and sending down the Qur'an upon him, has indeed been done and fulfilled. **(الخُرُورُ, "falling")** is left indefinite because the two states, of prostration and of weeping, differ. The first state is expressed by a noun, and the second state by a verb, because the verb indicates renewal, since weeping arises from reflection, and they are constantly in thought and remembrance, so mention of the verb fits, as it indicates renewal. And since the state of prostration does not renew itself at every moment, it is expressed by a noun.

**(ويَزِيدُهم, "and it increases them")**, that is, what is recited to them, **(خُشُوعًا, "in humility")**, that is, humbleness. Ibn Atiyya said: another meaning may be conveyed by this verse, namely that His saying **"Say: Believe in it or do not believe"** is a warning and not a belittling. The meaning: "You will soon see what you are repaid with." Then He set forth for them an example by way of rebuke, through those of the People of the Book who came before them, meaning: people were not as you are in disbelief; rather, those who had been given the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the revealed books in general, when what was revealed to them was recited to them, they humbled themselves and believed. End of quotation. The indication of part of this has already been given above.

[p. 87] **"And with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it descended"** (﴿وبِالحَقِّ أنْزَلْناهُ﴾) refers back to His saying: **"If mankind and the jinn were to gather to produce the like of this Qur'an..."** (﴿لَئِنِ اجْتَمَعَتِ الإنْسُ والجِنُّ﴾) [al-Isra: 88], and so on. This is the manner and style of Arabic speech: it takes up one matter, digresses from it to another, then to yet another, and then returns to what it mentioned first. Far-fetched is the view of one who held that the pronoun in (أنْزَلْناهُ, "We sent it down") refers to Musa, peace be upon him, making the verb mean "We caused it to be sent down," as in His saying: **"And We sent down iron"** (﴿وأنْزَلْنا الحَدِيدَ﴾) [al-Hadid: 25]. Or that it refers to the nine signs, mentioned in meaning. Or that it refers to the promise mentioned before it.

Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: **"And with the truth We sent it down"** means with monotheism (al-tawhid). **"And with the truth it descended"** means with the promise and the threat, and with the command and the prohibition. Al-Zahrawi said: with what is obligatory, which is the welfare and the rectitude of mankind. **"And with the truth it descended"** means with the truth in its commands, its prohibitions and its reports. Al-Zamakhshari said: We did not send down the Qur'an except with the wisdom that necessitates its being sent down, and it did not descend except conjoined with truth and wisdom, since it includes guidance to every good. And We did not send it down from the heaven except with truth, guarded by watchers from among the angels, and it did not descend upon the Messenger except guarded by them from the confusion of the devils. End of quotation.

It is possible that **"And with the truth it descended"** is an emphasis in meaning, since it was said: "We sent it down, so it descended," and "We sent it down, but it did not descend," when some obstacle prevented its descent. So **"And with the truth it descended"** came to remove this possibility and to emphasize the reality of **"And with the truth We sent it down."** Al-Tabari inclined toward this sense of emphasis.

**(مُبَشِّرًا ونَذِيرًا, "a bearer of good tidings and a warner")** is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: bearing good tidings to them of Paradise, and warning them of the Fire. "You have no part in compelling them to the religion."

The majority read **(فَرَقْناهُ, "We divided it")** with a light *rā'* (فَرَقْناهُ), meaning: We made clear its lawful and its unlawful, said Ibn Abbas. And from al-Hasan: We distinguished in it between truth and falsehood. Al-Farra' said: We made it firm and detailed, like His saying: **"Therein is decreed every wise matter"** (﴿فِيها يُفْرَقُ كُلُّ أمْرٍ حَكِيمٍ﴾) [al-Dukhan: 4].

Ubayy, Abdullah, Ali, Ibn Abbas, Abu Raja', Qatada, al-Sha'bi, Humayd, Amr ibn Qa'id, Zayd ibn Ali, Amr ibn Dharr, Ikrima and al-Hasan (according to one report from him) read it with a doubled *rā'* (فَرَّقْناهُ), meaning: We sent it down by stages, one stage after another, and We detailed it across the stages. Some who chose this reading said: It was not sent down in one day or two, nor in one month or two, nor in one year or two. Ibn Abbas said: between its beginning and its end there were twenty years. This is what al-Zamakhshari related from Ibn Abbas. It is also reported from Ibn Abbas: twenty-three years. It was said: twenty-five years. This difference is based on the difference concerning his age, peace be upon him. And from al-Hasan: it descended over eighteen years. Ibn Atiyya said: this is an unsound view that is not authentically from al-Hasan.

It was said that the meaning of **(فَرَّقْناهُ, "We divided it," with doubling)** is: We divided its verses among command and prohibition, wisdoms and rulings, admonitions and parables, stories and reports of unseen matters that have come and that are yet to come.

**(قُرْآنًا, "a Qur'an")** is in the accusative by an implied verb which the following **(فَرَقْناهُ)** explains, meaning: "And We divided a Qur'an which We divided." So it is of the category of *ishtighal* (the verb governing a pronoun attached to the noun, which is therefore construed with it), and the accusative is preferred to the nominative because it is conjoined to a verbal clause, namely His saying **(وما أرْسَلْناكَ, "and We did not send you")**. It is necessary to posit a qualifier for **(وقُرْآنًا)** so that it may be correct for it to be in the nominative as an indefinite subject, since it is indefinite and there is no apparent justification for beginning with it. The estimate is: "And a Qur'an, what a Qur'an," that is, a great and magnificent one. The Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari took it as accusative by an implied verb explained by what follows. Ibn Atiyya said this is the view of Sibawayh. Al-Farra' said: it is accusative by **(أرْسَلْناكَ, "We sent you")**, meaning: "And We did not send you except as a bearer of good tidings and a warner and a Qur'an, as you say 'a mercy,' because the Qur'an is a mercy." This grammatical analysis (i'rab, the analysis of case and syntax) is contrived, and more contrived than it is the view of Ibn Atiyya. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verse 110–111:

﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ ﴿And do not recite your prayer aloud, nor be silent therein, but seek a way between that.﴾ ﴿And say: All praise is due to Allah, who has not taken a son, and has no partner in dominion, and has no ally out of weakness; and glorify Him with great glorification.﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The Messenger ﷺ performed the night prayer (tahajjud) one night in Mecca, and in his prostration he began to say: (O Most Merciful, O Compassionate). The polytheists said: Muhammad used to call upon one God, and now he calls upon two gods, Allah and the Most Merciful (al-Rahman). Al-Rahman is nothing but the Rahman of al-Yamama, meaning Musaylima. So this was revealed." He related it in al-Tahrir. Ibn ʿAtiyya transmitted something similar from Makhul. He also said, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas: "The polytheists heard him calling: O Allah, O Rahman. They said: He used to call upon one God, and now he calls upon two gods. So this was revealed." Maymun ibn Mihran said: "He ﷺ used to write: In Your name, O Allah, until the revelation: ﴿Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed it is: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Compassionate﴾ [al-Naml: 30], and he wrote it." The polytheists of the Arabs said: "This Compassionate (al-Rahim) we know; what is al-Rahman?" So this was revealed. Al-Dahhak said: The People of the Book said to the Messenger ﷺ: "You make little mention of al-Rahman, while Allah has greatly mentioned this name in the Torah." So this was revealed, when they persisted in denying that the Qur'an had been sent down by Allah to His Messenger ﷺ, and they were unable to oppose it. The Messenger ﷺ had brought them the Oneness of Allah and the rejection of their deities, so they turned to accusing him, peace and blessings be upon him, that what he forbade them had returned to him. So Allah the Exalted responded to them with His saying: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah﴾, the verse.

The apparent meaning from the occasions of revelation is that the calling here is his saying "O Rahman, O Compassionate" or "O Allah, O Rahman." It is thus calling in the sense of addressing: if you call upon Allah, it is His name, and if you call upon al-Rahman, it is His attribute. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Calling (al-du'a) here means naming, not addressing, and it takes two objects. You say: I called him Zayd, then you omit one of them as being unnecessary, so you say: I called Zayd." End of quote. "Daʿawtu" is among the verbs that take two objects, the second with a preposition: you say "I called my father with Zayd," then you broaden and drop the preposition. The poet said regarding this verb:

Umm ʿAmr called me her brother, though I was not her brother, nor had I suckled from her milk.

These are verbs which take one object directly and the other with a preposition; they are preserved and limited to what is heard, and according to what al-Zamakhshari said, the second object of "ud'u" is the name of Allah and the word "al-Rahman," which had the preposition attached and then was dropped. It is as if the implied sense is: "Call upon your God by Allah, or call upon Him by al-Rahman." For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: "What is meant by both is the name of the named, and 'aw' is for choice, so the meaning of ﴿Call upon Allah or call upon al-Rahman﴾ is: name Him by this name or by that, and mention either this or that." End of quote. Likewise Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "They are two names for one named Being; if you call upon Him by Allah, it is that, and if you call upon Him by al-Rahman, it is that. And ayyu here is conditional." It was said that the tanwin is a substitute for the omitted word, and "ma" is an additional emphasizing particle. It was also said that "ma" is a conditional particle, and a conditional entered upon a conditional. Talha ibn Musarrif read "ayyan" with "tadʿu" (ayyan min tadʿū), and it is possible that "min" is extra according to the view of al-Kisa'i, since he claimed its extra use in the saying:

O ewe, from game, for whomever it is lawful for him.

It is also possible that two conditional particles were combined irregularly, as a poet combined two prepositions in the saying:

So they no longer ask me about what is with him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 17, verse 110–111:

﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ ﴿And do not recite your prayer aloud, nor be silent therein, but seek a way between that.﴾ ﴿And say: All praise is due to Allah, who has not taken a son, and has no partner in dominion, and has no ally out of weakness; and glorify Him with great glorification.﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The Messenger ﷺ performed the night prayer (tahajjud) one night in Mecca, and in his prostration he began to say: (O Most Merciful, O Compassionate). The polytheists said: Muhammad used to call upon one God, and now he calls upon two gods, Allah and the Most Merciful (al-Rahman). Al-Rahman is nothing but the Rahman of al-Yamama, meaning Musaylima. So this was revealed." He related it in al-Tahrir. Ibn ʿAtiyya transmitted something similar from Makhul. He also said, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas: "The polytheists heard him calling: O Allah, O Rahman. They said: He used to call upon one God, and now he calls upon two gods. So this was revealed." Maymun ibn Mihran said: "He ﷺ used to write: In Your name, O Allah, until the revelation: ﴿Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed it is: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Compassionate﴾ [al-Naml: 30], and he wrote it." The polytheists of the Arabs said: "This Compassionate (al-Rahim) we know; what is al-Rahman?" So this was revealed. Al-Dahhak said: The People of the Book said to the Messenger ﷺ: "You make little mention of al-Rahman, while Allah has greatly mentioned this name in the Torah." So this was revealed, when they persisted in denying that the Qur'an had been sent down by Allah to His Messenger ﷺ, and they were unable to oppose it. The Messenger ﷺ had brought them the Oneness of Allah and the rejection of their deities, so they turned to accusing him, peace and blessings be upon him, that what he forbade them had returned to him. So Allah the Exalted responded to them with His saying: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah﴾, the verse.

The apparent meaning from the occasions of revelation is that the calling here is his saying "O Rahman, O Compassionate" or "O Allah, O Rahman." It is thus calling in the sense of addressing: if you call upon Allah, it is His name, and if you call upon al-Rahman, it is His attribute. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Calling (al-du'a) here means naming, not addressing, and it takes two objects. You say: I called him Zayd, then you omit one of them as being unnecessary, so you say: I called Zayd." End of quote. "Daʿawtu" is among the verbs that take two objects, the second with a preposition: you say "I called my father with Zayd," then you broaden and drop the preposition. The poet said regarding this verb:

Umm ʿAmr called me her brother, though I was not her brother, nor had I suckled from her milk.

These are verbs which take one object directly and the other with a preposition; they are preserved and limited to what is heard, and according to what al-Zamakhshari said, the second object of "ud'u" is the name of Allah and the word "al-Rahman," which had the preposition attached and then was dropped. It is as if the implied sense is: "Call upon your God by Allah, or call upon Him by al-Rahman." O ewe, from game, for whomever it is lawful for him.
